title: Bandit - The only band you need
tagline: A wristband that knows what's going on in a crowd at all times, helps keep people safe, and helps them find each other again after the event

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: In the US in 2024, 44,500 people died and 15.6 million were hurt in preventable accidents in public places, and falls alone caused about 15,000 of those deaths ( National Safety Council ). At a concert or a festival, a fall is worse: the person on the ground can be crushed by the crowd before anyone notices. The same crowd is also where the good things happen. You meet someone great at a show and forget to get their Instagram. You spend an hour at a booth you loved and can't remember its name. You want the merch, but don't want to carry it around wirth you the whole concert. BandIt reads the crowd from your wrist, lights up the people next to you if you fall, guides everyone to the nearest exit when the concert is done, settles the insurance if the night goes wrong, and makes sure you leave with more than a blurry memory and maybe someone’s insta :)

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Every attendee gets a BandIt band at the door. Tapping it with a phone (NFC) opens the band's page, and the night runs in three parts. Joining. You sign in with your email, press the band's button to make it yours, and add your name and socials. BandIt asks "is this you?" against public profiles it scraped for the event. You upload your medical history and insurance card as PDFs, and Claude turns them into a medical card that you confirm. Last, you connect a Capital One wallet with $200 to spend. During the event. Each band hears the bands around it by radio and shows how crowded its spot is on its LED ring. Station markers split the venue into zones, so the organizer portal shows how many people are in each zone, live. When someone falls or presses SOS, every band around them flashes red and vibrates so people step back instead of closing in. An incident opens for the medic, who taps the person's band to see their medical card, and only while the incident is open. In a fire or smoke, one button turns on low visibility and every band guides its wearer to the nearest exit by colour. Insurance, after the incident. When the medic resolves an incident, a claim opens on its own. Claude reads the clinic record, Elastic validates it and finds similar past claims, Claude checks whether the story holds up, and code decides coverage and the amount from a fee schedule. A claim that code can't settle goes to the organizer, who decides it. Approving with "learn" turns the decision into a rule, so the next similar claim settles in seconds without anyone. The payout lands in the attendee's Capital One wallet. A fake claim is refused with every failed check listed, and a broken speaker becomes a property claim with a recovery letter. After the event. When the organizer presses "Event ended", every band's page turns into that person's recap: where you were and when, zone by zone the people you spent time with, with their socials, ranked by how much you have in common the booths you spent time at, ranked the same way the event photographer's photos you're in, already tagged with who is in them, ready to share merch made with your own photo from the booths you loved, bought with one tap from your wallet The organizer also gets the Event graph: a live map of the whole event, with anonymous people linked to the people they met, the booths they visited and the companies behind them.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Each part does what it is best at. SpacetimeDB holds everything live and exact, Elastic organizes data and ranks it by meaning, Claude reads documents and writes the judgment calls, and code decides money, coverage and safety. The bands. Each band is a Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 with a 12-LED WS2812B ring, an SOS button, an NTAG215 NFC sticker and a LiPo battery. Some also carry an MPU-6050 for fall detection and a coin vibration motor. Bands beacon ten times a second over ESP-NOW and count their neighbours, so the crowd colour and the SOS light circle work on the band itself, even with no internet. Station markers mark the zones, and a USB gateway passes every packet to a Rust bridge that writes it to SpacetimeDB. SpacetimeDB is the live world. One Rust module on Maincloud holds the bands, zones, incidents, medical cards, claims, wallets and the people graph. A fall is one reducer call that opens the incident, records the bands in the light circle and schedules its escalation in a single transaction. Scheduled reducers turn raw band reports into zone state and into a space-time history of who was where and when. Every screen subscribes to its own slice, so the organizer portal, the medic's phone and the attendee's page update the moment something commits. Sign-in is SpacetimeAuth, and views keyed on the caller enforce access in the database, such as "a medic sees a medical card only during an open incident". Bright Data and Elastic build the event. Before doors open, our Rust tool bandit-ingest uses the Bright Data Web MCP to scrape the Cal Hacks site and Devpost pages and to run the LinkedIn, Crunchbase and Google Maps scrapers for every sponsor: 245 records from 6 sources. Elastic organizes them: ES|QL LOOKUP JOIN steps match booths and domains, and an Agent Builder agent run by an Elastic Workflow merges the same company spelled three ways into one organization, with a reason for each merge. Rust checks the result and loads it into SpacetimeDB in one import_event transaction. Kibana dashboards show each import run and the event's sponsors and prizes. Elastic ranks the recap. SpacetimeDB decides exactly who and what goes on your recap, and Elastic decides the order. A one-way indexer copies findable attendees and booths into semantic_text fields, and the recap ranks the people you met and the booths you visited by how close they are to what you were into. The claims agent. Our Rust workers take claim jobs from a queue in SpacetimeDB. Claude Opus 5.5 reads the clinic record PDF into structured facts with a JSON schema, a de-identified copy of the claim goes through an Elastic ingest pipeline that validates it and ranks similar past claims, and Claude reviews whether the injury matches the incident. Code then applies the fee schedule, the coverage and any learned rule, and routes the claim. Claude also writes the notice of loss in the ACORD 3 layout and the recovery letter. Every model call is recorded, and the model never decides an amount. Capital One Nessie is the wallet. Each attendee gets a Nessie customer and account with $200. Merch orders are Nessie purchases at the BandIt merch merchant, and claim payouts are Nessie deposits. SpacetimeDB keeps the exact balance. The web pages and hosting. The attendee page, the organizer portal and the photographer page are TypeScript on SpacetimeDB's TypeScript SDK, built with Bun. The Event graph is drawn with Sigma.js from a live SpacetimeDB view. The Rust API, workers and indexer run under systemd on a Vultr server in Silicon Valley, behind Caddy for HTTPS.

sections.heading: Sponsor tracks
sections.text: SpacetimeDB. The whole live event is one module on Maincloud. Reducers are the only write path, so an SOS incident, its light circle and its escalation commit together. Scheduled reducers compute zone state and the space-time history. The bridge, every Rust service and every web page share one generated schema and get each change pushed to them. Sign-in comes from SpacetimeAuth, and per-caller views keep medical cards and claims private inside the database. Elastic. Elastic does the work SpacetimeDB can't: meaning. An Agent Builder agent in an Elastic Workflow resolves messy scraped records into one clean bundle, ES|QL LOOKUP JOIN matches booths and domains, semantic_text ranks each attendee's recap, and an ingest pipeline validates every claim and ranks it against 30 past claims. Kibana shows the import runs, the event's sponsors and prizes, and the claims evidence. Hyphenate: Autonomous Systems for Finance. A claims agent that learns while it runs. A fall becomes a claim with no forms. Code cuts an urgent-care bill from $1,308 to $895 with a fee schedule. The organizer approves the first claim with "learn", which writes rule v1, and the next similar claim ($180) settles on its own in seconds. A rule is only ever made by a human approval and is versioned, never overwritten. Approvals made on stale numbers fail closed, every journal is double-entry, each evidence pack has a hash an auditor can recompute, and a scorecard plants genuine and fake claims to measure straight-through rate, dollars wrongly paid, precision and recall. Bright Data. Without the scraped web data there is no event in BandIt: the organizations, booths, prizes, schedule and venue all come from the Bright Data Web MCP ( scrape_as_markdown on the Cal Hacks and Devpost pages, plus the LinkedIn company, Crunchbase and Google Maps scrapers). Those records become the booths on your recap, the companies on the Event graph, the merch suggestions and the "is this you?" profile match. We only scrape public pages. Capital One: best use of Nessie. Every attendee has a Nessie account with $200. Merch is a one-tap Nessie purchase from the recap, and insurance payouts are Nessie deposits into the same account, so the wallet shows the whole night in money. MLH: best use of Vultr. The live site, the API, the claims workers and the Elastic indexer all run on one Vultr server in Silicon Valley, set up by one script with systemd and Caddy. Microsoft: Built for the Real World. The claims agent is production-minded by design. Its customer is the event organizer, who today waits weeks on paperwork for small injury claims. Its usefulness is measured by the scorecard. Its design is responsible: the model only reads and writes words while code decides money, a de-identified copy is all Elastic ever sees, a medic sees a medical card only during an open incident, and every model call is recorded for audit. It runs end to end on the live site. Anthropic. Claude Opus 5.5 does every reading and judgment job: it turns medical history and insurance PDFs into a medical card, reads clinic records into facts with structured outputs, reviews whether an injury fits the incident, and writes the notice of loss and the recovery letter. Code checks each answer and asks again when one breaks a rule.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Counting time together. Our first version counted minutes together six times too high for anyone standing in a busy zone, so the recap said you spent 50 minutes with someone you passed. We had to rework how time together is counted. Messy web data. The same sponsor shows up under different names on the Cal Hacks site, Devpost, LinkedIn and Crunchbase. Exact joins in ES|QL caught most of it, and the Elastic agent handled the rest with a reason for every merge. Letting an AI near money. We wanted Claude's judgment without letting it pick a payout. We drew a hard line: Claude reads and writes words, code decides coverage and amounts, and an approval made on numbers that changed since fails closed. Duplicate checks that worked too well. Two people filing the same clinic record tripped our own duplicate detection, so every record is now made out to the claimant with its own invoice number. Building Rust on a small server. The first build on the 4 GB Vultr server ran out of memory, so the setup script adds swap and builds without debug info.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: The whole night runs end to end on the live site. Tap a band, set it up, walk it between zones, fall, get treated, get paid into your wallet, end the event, open your recap and buy a mug with your own photo on it. A claims agent that learns from one decision. After the organizer approves one fall claim with "learn", the next similar claim settles by itself in seconds, and a fake one is refused with the failed check named. Real data, not fixtures. The event in BandIt is Cal Hacks 13.0 itself: 245 records scraped through Bright Data, organized by Elastic and loaded into SpacetimeDB in one transaction. Safety that doesn't need the internet. Crowd colours, SOS and the light circle run on the bands, so they keep working if the server, the Wi-Fi or the cloud goes down. A system design we can build from. Every component has its own design doc, and every optional feature can be deleted without breaking the safety core.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Two databases SpacetimeDB is the right home for anything live and exact: who is where, who may see what, what was paid. Elastic is the right home for meaning: messy text, fuzzy matches and "what is closest to what you like". Keeping live state out of Elastic and ranking out of SpacetimeDB made both simpler. Logic in the database pays off. With reducers and subscriptions, there is no app server between a band's SOS flag and the medic's screen, and no screen can disagree with another. AI is most useful next to rules, not instead of them. Claude is great at reading a clinic record or spotting that an injury happened at home. Code is better at money. The learned rules are where the two meet: a person decides once, and code repeats that decision exactly.

sections.heading: What's next for BandIt
sections.text: Venue cameras. The design already has the interface for camera head counts, person-down alerts that confirm a fall, and property events like a falling speaker, so cameras and bands become the two-step system from our original idea. More bands. A real venue needs hundreds of bands, so the next step is a crowd test far beyond our nine. A real insurer on the other end. The notice of loss and the evidence packs are built to be sent, so the next step is a pilot with a venue and its insurer.

title: Ender's Bench
tagline: Ender’s Bench puts AI agents to the test. Watch their choices, measure their results, and see whether they do the right thing when it matters.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We wanted to test whether an AI model follows an ethical policy when following that policy costs it something. Explaining a rule is one thing. Following it while competing for food, trying to survive, or facing pressure to increase profits is another. That led us to build Ender's Bench: environments where models make decisions with consequences, and where we can compare their instructions, explanations, actions, and outcomes.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Ender's Bench tests AI behavior under pressure through a live survival simulation and a separate finance benchmark. In The Clearing, four AI survivors share a forest after a plane crash. They need food, warmth, tools, and rescue while navigating hazards and competing for limited resources. We compare agents given an explicit policy charter with agents instructed to pursue reward without that charter. In Ledger Street, our finance benchmark, models work a lending, collections, and vendor-payments desk. They pull real credit-sandbox data, use tools, and respond to pressure while being evaluated on both their decisions and the steps they took to reach them. We record the evidence behind each result: the instructions the model received, its observations, its explanation, its structured action, and the resulting state change. The viewer lets people follow individual agents, inspect recorded events, replay saved runs, and compare task performance with policy compliance.

sections.heading: What we found
sections.text: From 126 overnight runs of The Clearing (8 models, every decision made inside SpacetimeDB) and 231 Ledger Street cases on live CRS data: Stating the rules halves rule-breaking. Across all 8 models, adding the camp's charter to the prompt cut the share of temptations taken from 6.0% to 2.9%. A run-level permutation test gives p = 0.00005. Ledger Street shows the same pattern: without the house rules, GPT-6 Luna fell from 6 of 7 demo cases to 3, Qwen3.8-27B from 7 to 4, and DeepSeek from 7 to 3. Only Claude Haiku held, at 6. Models say one thing and do another, on the record. Claude Haiku thought “Not mine, avoid.” and took the berries. DeepSeek called three grabs its “fair share,” noted it was already over, stored the rations in its own chest, and took more. GPT-6 Luna offered to share berries it didn't have. Every quote is checked against the decision log and can be replayed. Some failures are universal. Without house rules, Haiku, Luna, Qwen, and DeepSeek all failed the same 11 finance cases. All four approved a loan despite a hidden court judgment. Removing refusals didn't make a model steal more; it made it die more. The abliterated Qwen3.8-27B took fewer temptations than its base (1% against 4% under the charter, Fisher p = 0.01), but 20 of its 100 survivors died, against 3 of 48 for the base. Fine-tuning shows up in both directions. Ender v1.1 learned to reach for helping actions without the steps that make them possible: the game refused 26% of its moves, against 10% for its base, and it regressed on Ledger Street. Ender v1.3 is the first adapter to beat its own base, with 42 of 70 cases passed and 5 harmful decisions against 40 and 7. Serving the base in 4-bit cost 7 passes on its own.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The live simulation is a TypeScript module on SpacetimeDB. The world updates at 20 Hz and keeps moving while models respond asynchronously through durable decision requests. Actions, world-state changes, and policy-detector records commit together, tying each detected violation to the action that caused it. The models are called from inside the database itself: a scheduled procedure sends each survivor's observation to its model provider over HTTP and commits the answer, so a run needs no separate harness. A Node.js harness covers the rest (the Codex baseline and the Ledger Street worker) through the same decision protocol. The frontend uses React, React Three Fiber, and Three.js to visualize the world and connect agent activity with its recorded evidence, with benchmark launch controls, run history, a live leaderboard, and automatic recording. For Ledger Street, we built tools on a live credit sandbox, versioned scenarios, and code-based verifiers that check both the decision and the required process steps. This lets us distinguish a correct final answer from a decision made without the necessary checks. We are also developing Ender, our own adapted model: LoRA fine-tuning of Spark, served from our own GPU endpoint and evaluated in the sameenvironments as every other model.

sections.heading: Sponsors
sections.text: SpacetimeDB: the game server, the agent runtime, and the record SpacetimeDB isn't a storage layer for Ender's Bench. It's the game server, the runtime that asks every model what to do, the scorekeeper, and the broadcast to every viewer, all in one TypeScript module. The game server. More than 30 tables hold the world. Movement, hunther, and the rescue plane run as reducers on a 20 Hz scheduled tick.Every action (take, give, build, attack, help) is a reducer that commits the world change and the policy-detector record in one transaction, so each violation is tied to the exact action that caused it. The agent runtime: database brains. A scheduled reducer opens a durable decision request for each survivor that's due to think. A scheduled procedure, think , sends the survivor's observation to its model with ctx.http.fetch and commits thion path. The providers it calls are Bitdeer, Anthropic, OpenAI, and ourRunpod endpoints. Requests time out, retry, and are withdrawn when sudden danger makes them stale, and a model_health table keeps provider failures apart from behavior. Provider keys live in the database's environment variables, and a `beginh its roster, prompt, food level, and time scale. There is no harness,queue, or external worker. Proven at scale. Overnight we ran 126 runs in 9 worlds side by siddel calls made from inside SpacetimeDB.** The breakdown was 15,151 toBitdeer, 15,216 to Anthropic, 20,137 to Runpod, and 2,766 to OpenAI. The game clock held 97% of its set speed with every world calling models at once, the same as a single world; our first test of the design showed parallel HTTP calls from proctick, locally or on Maincloud. The scorekeeper. run_history and run_result tables keep every run permanently, through resets. A public view, leaderboard , aggregates finished runs by model, prompt, and rules version as they close. Ledger Street runs in the same , and every desk step, each with its CRS RequestID, are tables driven bytheir own scheduled reducer. The broadcast. Our React Three Fiber viewer is a live subscription produces the replays behind our demo exhibits. Visitors can join assurvivors through joinAsHuman , which binds a survivor to their identity, and play alongside the models in the same world. Hosted on Maincloud. The public viewer runs against the hosted datr decision, and new module versions publish over it with the data kept.The tick, the brain procedure, and the reset accept only the database's own identity ( ctx.databaseIdentity ), so spectators can watch and join but can't tick, reset, or impersonate a model. Built around its tooling. Generated TypeScript bindings connect the viewer, harness, and recorder; results are exported over SpacetimeDB's SQL HTTP API. CRS: real credit data behind every finance decision Ledger Street, our finance benchmark, is built on the CRS credit sandbox. In live runs, every check an agent runs is a real CRS call. The desk's tools are CRS's checks: soft credit pulls from three bureaus, identity verification, fraud scoring, public records, criminal and eviction searches, and reverse phone lookup. 70 cases across lending, collections, and vendor pon, and each is tagged as backed by law (FCRA, ECOA, FDCPA) or by housepolicy. Live, logged, and safe. In live runs each tool call sends a test pto the sandbox, so nothing ever reaches the real vendor. We log in onceand never retry a failed login. Each step records CRS's RequestID, and the response is compared with a saved snapshot to catch data drift. Process is scored, not just the decision. The verifier requires thproper ones, so it catches harms a final answer hides. The most commonharm this morning was a credit pull with no permissible purpose, an FCRA violation: 11 of the 20 harmful decisions across Ender v1.1, Ender v1.3, and their base model. Volume: 1,276 live CRS calls , each with its own RequestID. This moedit pulls, 148 identity checks, 81 fraud scores, and 77 criminal,eviction, public-records, and phone searches. Our Api

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The hardest part was separating model failures from benchmark failures. nformation leaking into comparison prompts, resources being invisible toagents, detectors misclassifying behavior, and statistical summaries combining incompatible runs. Fixing those problems was necessary before interpreting the results. Live inference introduced another challenge. A model can take several seconds to respond while its surroundings continue changing. We added danger alerts, cancellation of stale decisions, latency tracking, and separate handling for provider fars would not be treated as behavioral failures. Speed itself turned out to be a confound: in worlds that mix models, a slower model gathers less, goes hungry sooner, and faces more of its temptations under pressure, so we compare models band by band and in worlds where the models answer equally fast. We also had to make the evidence understandable. A replay needs to show me, what it said, and what actually happened. We kept model-providedexplanations distinct from verified outcomes and made live, recorded, and incomplete runs distinguishable. For fine-tuning, the challenge was defining what improvement would mean. Lower training loss does not establish better policy compliance, and refusing every request is not useful behavior. We evaluate each adapter in the same live environments the same base model it was trained from.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We built a working live environment where AI decisions produce visible cable evidence. Users can follow an agent from its observation andexplanation to its action and outcome, instead of relying on a single summary score. We ran it at scale overnight: 126 runs across 8 models, with every decision made from inside the database. The clearest result: stating the camp's rules in the prompt cut the share of temptations models took from 6.0% to 2.9%. We tested this with (p = 0.00005), which does not assume the decisions inside a run areindependent. The recordings capture the gap between explanation and action directly. One agent explained that it had already exceeded its fair share and should stop taking supplies, then took four more rations. Another wrote “Not mine, avoid.” as it took anotecord shows the mismatch without requiring us to speculate about themodel's internal reasoning. We closed the evaluation-and-training loop and measured our own model honestly. Ender v1.1 did worse than its own base model on Ledger Street. Ender v1.3, trained after that, is the first adapter to beat its 4-bit base: 42 of 70 cases passed with 40 and 7.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: A convincing explanation is not enough to establish reliable behavior. Tnspecting instructions, observations, actions, and outcomes together. Benchmark design can shape the result as much as model choice. Resource eed, prompt wording, scenario versions, and scoring rules all affect whata comparison means. A striking individual run can reveal a failure mode, but it cannot establish a general ranking. Training and evaluation need a clear boundary. Strong performance on familiar scenarios may reflect memorization rather than generalization. How a model is served matters too: the same base model lost seven Ledger Street passes when quantized to 4-

sections.heading: What's next for Ender's Bench
sections.text: We want to expand the number of repeated runs and independent scenarios, then compare the unmodified model and Ender adapters under matching conditions. We will measure policy compliance, task completion, over-refusal, and regressions separately. More simulations can include a spaceship operation wth SpaceX data. Reward for completing research and surviving, ethical dilemmas such as food shortages, ship breaches, etc. We also discussed a Mars colony. The possibilities are endless. For training, we want to move beyond synthetic policy plans toward reviewed action trajectories, tool results, recovery behavior, and honest failure reports. That will let us train on examples of carrying out a task correctly, not just describing the right approach. We also want to serve Ender on a higher-precision base, now that we have measured what 4-bit costs. We also plan to bring Ledger Street fully into the same observation and results experience as The Clearing, and to publish The Clearing as its own Apify Actor beside the finance benchmark, so anyone can run the forest against their own models. Our long-term goal is a repeatable loop: create a scenario, observe behavior under pressure, inspect failures, train on reviewed examples, and evaluate again on independent cases.
