title: GeonosisAI
tagline: The Agentic Robot Deployment Factory

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Agents that pay people. I saw a YC hackathan where AI agents pay people to do the things the agent can't do itself. That stuck with me, because robotics has the clearest version of that problem: the thing an agent can't do is collect robot data . It can't reset a cube, take over a stuck arm, or record a clean demo. A person with a phone can, and a lot of people will do it for $5. I spent this whole week doing evals. Getting a robot to actually do something is painful. You run the policy, watch it fail, guess why, collect more demos, retrain, run the eval again. Most of my time went to manual steps that could have been automated: setting up runs, resetting the scene, tracking which trial failed and why, converting data, kicking off training, and the small mistakes in between that cost an hour each. Underneath both is cost. Robot data is expensive, and so is the infrastructure to collect, review and train on it. Data companies also aren't set up to collect data for your task on your robot. But someone will give you a few good episodes for five bucks. Scale that out and you have a usable dataset. Robot Deployment is also just hard and tedious, a perfect usecase for agents. So I built GeonosisAI: a factory where agents run the robot deployment loop end to end and buy the exact data the robot needs from people on their phones.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: You register a robot and file a ticket: "Put the cube in the bin, 80% reliable, $50 budget." The ticket moves down a line of agent stations: Baseline. The robot runs the task on its current policy. Every trial is recorded with its outcome. Diagnose. Claude groups the failed trials by why they failed, from trial notes, timings and camera frames. Plan data. The planner reads the failure clusters, the success rate and the budget, and decides what kind of data fixes them: recovery takeovers (the robot pauses mid-failure and a person takes over) or clean demos , and how many. Its reasoning has to quote a failure cluster, and a human approves the spend. Collect. Paid tasks go out as job drops on Discord and as texts ("Reply YES to claim"). A contributor claims a task on their phone, sees the robot's cameras, drives the arm from the browser and hands control back. Review. Deterministic checks (timestamps, jerk, dropped frames, length) plus a Claude vision review. Rejected episodes show why. Accepted ones get paid (Stripe test mode). Train. A π0.5 LoRA fine-tune on an H100 on Modal, from the accepted episodes converted to LeRobot format. Eval and ship. The new checkpoint runs the same eval. If it clears the target it ships with a report. If not, the line loops back and buys more data. Everything is live on the web app: a factory floor where each ticket is a lane of agent stations, the planner's decision, every episode with video, every payout, and an append-only event log you can audit. Success rates always show a Wilson 95% interval, because with ~10 trials the point estimate alone lies: $$\frac{\hat p + \frac{z^2}{2n} \pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n}}$$ At 10/10 the lower bound is only 0.72.

sections.heading: How I built it
sections.text: SpacetimeDB is the bus. Every service, agent, robot and phone reads and writes the same tables on maincloud. Reducers keep the risky actions atomic: one arm-control lease per robot, a budget check on every payout, and an event log that nothing can edit or delete. Factory Droids that sleep on the database. A droid ends its turn with something like WAITING_FOR dataset:accepted_count>=5 and goes idle for free. A resume bridge re-checks that predicate on every row change and wakes the same session with what changed. In testing, an accepted review woke a parked data droid in 597 ms. Orchestrator (Python, FastAPI) runs the line as a state machine: baseline, diagnose, plan, dispatch, review, train, eval, ship. Every Claude call goes through one switch (API, Claude Code, or Factory Droid backends), and each decision records which model made it. Robot client for the real I2RT YAM on an NVIDIA Jetson , plus a MuJoCo sim of the same arm behind the same interface. A safety layer sits in front of every command: joint limits, velocity and acceleration caps, a workspace box, a watchdog and a soft e-stop. It records synced cameras and actions on one clock. Modal for π0.5 LoRA training on H100 and a policy server that hot-swaps checkpoints. Inference is remote, so the robot runs 50-step action chunks asynchronously and crossfades between them to hide the ~157 ms round trip. Next.js + three.js web app on Vercel: the factory floor, a 3D twin of the robot, phone teleop pages, the marketplace, earnings and a printable report. The backend runs on my laptop behind tunnels whose URLs change every start, so it publishes its URL into SpacetimeDB with an HMAC proof and Vercel finds it from there. No backend keys live on Vercel. Claude writes a 3D scene for each new ticket, clusters failures, plans the data buy, reviews episodes, and judges real-arm trials from the live cameras. I built it with a team of coding agents working off one shared task board, which was its own lesson in coordination.

sections.heading: Challenges I ran into
sections.text: No arm overnight. Nobody could be next to the YAM all night, so I built a physics sim of the same arm behind the same adapter and safety layer, and made "sim or real" a fact on every row. Sim and real numbers are never mixed. Droids that have to wait for hours. Agents normally run and finish. I needed them to park on a database condition and resume later with full context, so I built the wait-for protocol and resume bridge myself. Remote inference at control rate. A 157 ms round trip is several control steps. Async action chunks, dropping the stale prefix and crossfading made it smooth. A real arm is not a sim. Gravity pulls joints off their targets, the Jetson's ffmpeg has no H.264 encoder, the arm has to fold back to rest safely after every trial. Each one cost hours. Ten trials is a small sample. A strict confidence-interval rule can never certify 80% from 10 trials, so the factory ships on the point estimate and always shows the interval. Many agents, one repo. Agents with stale git state reverted each other's work more than once. A pre-commit hook now refuses silent deletions.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.text: The hard part of "AI deploys your robot" isn't the model. It's the plumbing that touches the physical world: who resets the cube, who takes over when it drops, how a GPU job wakes an agent, how a payout waits on a review. Agents need to be able to sleep. A session parked on a database condition costs nothing and comes back with full context. That turns a coding agent into a long-running worker. Guardrails belong in code, not prompts. The planner must cite a failure, a payout can't exceed the approved budget, the event log can't be rewritten. A sim is only useful if nobody can mistake it for the real thing. Everything simulated or stubbed is labelled [SIM] or [STUB] wherever it shows up.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: Run more real-arm tickets end to end and publish the before/after numbers. More data types for the planner: phone video, UMI-style handheld demos, autonomous rollouts. Open tickets automatically from failures in production, and rank contributors by accepted episodes.

sections.heading: Sponsor Tracks
sections.text: Anthropic, Factory, SpacetimDB

title: Luyten
tagline: An agentic finance ERP where AI agents do the month-end close but requires approval before postage: a Red Team critiques, an Advisor rules, and the CFO confirms.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: At a growing startup, the month-end close still takes the finance team about ten days. Most of that time goes to matching deposits to invoices, chasing receipts and rebuilding revenue schedules in spreadsheets. Agents could already do most of this work. But ask a CFO whether they'd let a model post straight to the general ledger and the answer is no, because nobody can see what the agent did or stop it before it lands. We wanted agents that do the work and still can't change the books on their own.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Luyten is automated finance for 10x growth startups , built first for SaaS companies. Agents run the month-end close for a group of companies in two currencies, and every change passes through a gate: Worker agents propose. Bookkeeper, Revenue, Credit & Risk and Consolidation create Proposals. None of them can post. The Red Team critiques. It runs on models the workers don't use: Grok goes first, then Gemini adds what Grok missed. The Advisor rules. It approves, amends or rejects each Proposal and writes down why. The CFO confirms anything material. Anything at or above the $10,000 Materiality threshold, and every amendment, waits in the Needs your OK queue until the CFO confirms it with one click or sends it back. Before money moves, Credit & Risk checks the people behind each customer and vendor. It runs identity, fraud, all three credit bureaus and public records through the CRS Credit API, and Bright Data collects their public footprint. The database derives the Risk Tier from those facts, and the tier sets payment terms. Each agent follows a plain-English Charter, which the finance team can tighten but never loosen. Every number in the Board Pack drills down to its journal lines, then to the Proposal, then to the agent debate behind it. Luyten also runs as an agent on Fetch.ai's Agentverse, so you can ask the Advisor how the business is doing from ASI:One.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: SpacetimeDB is the whole backend : the ledger, the approval queue, the audit trail and the message bus between agents. The SvelteKit app subscribes to it and updates as rows change. Each agent role connects with its own identity, and every reducer checks who is calling, so the approval gate lives in the database and not in a prompt. The CFO seat is claimed once with a one-time secret. The bank feed has its own identity, and all it can do is add raw bank lines and invoices. The accounting runs in a pure double-entry engine that stores money as 64-bit integer minor units. The database recomputes what matters before anything posts: consolidation entries are rebuilt from the books, and credit tiers come from the recorded facts, never from the agent. The workers and the Advisor run on the Claude Agent SDK , and a local bridge can send the same calls to OpenAI. The Red Team runs on Grok and Gemini through the Vercel AI SDK , and Credit & Risk runs its cascade against the CRS sandbox over MCP . Every external provider has a recorded stand-in. The full demo runs with no API keys, through the same identities and reducers as a live run.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The hardest product question was what a startup CFO would open this app for between closes. An automated close is useful once a month, but a CFO also watches runway, burn, margin and the next raise, so we had to decide which features earned a place beyond the close. We chose a dashboard for cash, burn, runway, ARR and churn, a cost-of-service view for gross margin, and views for financing and payroll. Agent communication was the other hard part. Getting six agents on three model vendors to propose, critique, rule and escalate in order meant defining one Proposal format that every agent reads and writes, and sending every message through the database.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A rogue agent can't write to the books, and our tests prove it. On every pull request, CI runs the module smoke test, which tries every gate and refusal against a real SpacetimeDB. 156 ledger engine unit tests (1,085 across the workspace), and the CRS cascade reproduces all 20 decisions in the sandbox dataset. One click starts the close for a two-company group. That close produces 52 Proposals, catches a duplicate payment, and blocks two vendors before their first payment: one owner is a synthetic identity and the other is deceased. Real financial analysis beyond the close. The consolidated Board Pack has the P&L, balance sheet, ARR waterfall and NRR. The dashboard tracks cash, burn, runway, DSO, churn and gross margin by cost of service, and every figure drills down to its journal lines. An interface for two kinds of reader: a founder who wants the one-sentence summary on each Proposal, and a controller who wants the journal lines underneath.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: SpacetimeDB turned out to be far more than a database. Its reducers became our permission layer and its identities became our agent roles. Its subscriptions gave us a live UI and an audit trail without writing a separate backend. We also learned that agents work better when they communicate in structure. Agents that hand each other typed Proposals and written rationales are easier to debug, test and trust than agents chatting freely. And putting a second model vendor in the critic's seat caught mistakes the first model had agreed with.

sections.heading: What's next for Luyten
sections.text: First comes an Intake agent that reads the payables inbox, Stripe and bank accounts through read-only connectors. It writes through the same ingest-only role as today's feed. A hijacked Intake agent could add evidence but couldn't propose, rule or post. After that come per-company locks and hosted instances for a handful of SaaS design partners, and we'll widen the rollout as the Charter evals show each agent is reliable. For customers, the payoff is a close that takes days instead of weeks, a smaller finance team, fraud and credit risk caught earlier, and books that are ready for audit at any point. Longer term, those audited books become leverage: Luyten will use them to negotiate working-capital terms for its customers, with the CFO confirming every offer through the same gate.

title: Orkio
tagline: Is your code Orkio?Connecting agents from different devices to work together.Replace github, 0 conflicts, more efficient, keep human in the right loop.

sections.text: Orkio — Making Multi-Agent Coding Work Together

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: AI coding agents have made writing software faster than ever. But when multiple developers use their own AI agents to build the same project, a familiar problem remains: integration. Each agent works on a separate computer, with limited visibility into what other agents are doing. Even when tasks are carefully divided, agents still share dependencies, interfaces, and assumptions. For example, one agent might change an API to return timestamps in milliseconds while another continues writing code that expects seconds. Their Git branches can merge perfectly, yet the application breaks. Git knows whether code can merge. It doesn't necessarily know whether that code works together. As more agents work in parallel, developers become responsible for communicating changes, resolving conflicts, and keeping everyone aligned. Faster code generation doesn't necessarily translate into faster development when humans still have to coordinate everything. That's why we built Orkio , a real-time coordination layer that helps AI coding agents on different computers work together with less human intervention.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Orkio connects AI coding agents across different laptops through a shared coordination system. It gives agents visibility into their teammates' work, detects integration problems, and coordinates their resolution. The system has four main capabilities: 1. Shared Context Across Computers Orkio gives agents access to a common source of information about what their teammates are doing. Through MCP, agents can publish their intentions, including planned changes to files, interfaces, and dependencies. Other agents can access this context while they're still coding, reducing the risk of making incompatible assumptions. 2. Continuous Integration and Conflict Resolution Orkio captures snapshots of agents' unfinished code through Git. Factory Droid, our orchestrator, combines changes from different agents and runs integration checks to identify incompatibilities before they reach the main branch. When a conflict is detected, the system identifies the affected agents and provides the relevant context for resolution. Rather than relying on another agent to rewrite their code, the affected agents can communicate directly and coordinate a fix. 3. Intelligent Task Orchestration Factory Droid manages task delegation, tracks dependencies, and coordinates agents' work. When integration issues arise, the orchestrator determines which agents need to be involved and routes the relevant information to them. This allows agents to continue independent work without requiring developers to manually relay every update between computers. 4. Human in the Right Loop Orkio aims to automate routine coordination while preserving human control over important decisions. Ambiguous or high-risk changes can be escalated to developers, and final publication to main remains a human-controlled step. The goal isn't to remove humans from software development. It's to remove the repetitive coordination work that prevents developers from benefiting fully from parallel AI coding.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built Orkio using Factory Droid SDK, SpacetimeDB, Claude Code hooks, MCP, Git, TypeScript, and Vitest . The architecture connects agents running in their existing local development environments to a shared, real-time coordination layer. Hooks and MCP — Connecting Agents Across Laptops Each developer runs a coding agent on their own computer. Hooks capture changes to the agent's working tree and create temporary Git snapshots on dedicated wip/<agent> branches. This lets Orkio access unfinished code without requiring developers to manually commit their work. Through MCP, agents publish their intentions and retrieve updates from teammates. They can share relevant context without switching to a separate chat application or development environment. Factory Droid — Our Orchestrator We use Factory Droid as the central orchestrator for multi-agent collaboration. Factory coordinates task assignments, tracks development progress, combines agents' code for integration testing, and identifies conflicts between independently developed components. When it encounters an integration failure, it uses the available code changes, test results, and agent context to determine which agents should participate in resolving the issue. The affected agents can communicate directly rather than relying on a separate conflict-resolution agent. One of our biggest technical challenges was determining what information the orchestrator actually needs to make effective decisions. Providing more context isn't always better; we need to identify which task dependencies, intentions, and implementation details are relevant to each decision. SpacetimeDB — The Shared Context SpacetimeDB is the real-time coordination backbone of Orkio. It maintains shared information about: Agent activity and status Code snapshots and development intentions Task assignments and dependencies Integration results and detected conflicts Repair responsibilities and notifications SpacetimeDB's subscriptions synchronize updates across connected agents and our dashboard. We also use transactional reducers to keep related coordination operations consistent, such as recording a conflict and assigning its resolution. Rather than treating SpacetimeDB as a passive message store, we use it as a shared source of coordination state for independently running AI agents. Git — Integrating Unfinished Code Git provides a reproducible record of what each agent is working on. Orkio creates temporary snapshots of unfinished changes and uses them to reconstruct the combined state of the project for testing. These checks occur outside developers' active branches, so incompatible changes can be identified without disrupting their normal workflows. Importantly, Orkio doesn't automatically publish changes to main . Developers retain control over final integration. Dashboard — Visualizing Agent Collaboration We built a dashboard to make the distributed coordination process visible. It shows agent activity, shared context, task progress, integration results, and communication between agents. Since most of Orkio's functionality happens through background processes and tool calls, designing an understandable visualization was an important part of the project.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Rethinking Our Architecture Our original proposal involved centrally hosted agents, strict file ownership, and a controlled Git publishing system. While this architecture provided stronger enforcement, it required much more infrastructure and would have forced developers to change their existing workflows. After evaluating the tradeoffs, we moved toward local coding agents connected through hooks, MCP, Git, and SpacetimeDB. We also originally considered introducing a separate agent to resolve conflicts. After discussions with mentors, we realized that this introduced unnecessary complexity. The agents responsible for the conflicting components already have the most relevant context. Instead, we decided to let these agents communicate directly, with Factory Droid coordinating the process. Effective Task Delegation One of our hardest challenges was making the orchestrator delegate work effectively. Factory needs sufficient information about agent responsibilities, dependencies, implementation progress, and conflicts to make useful decisions. However, providing excessive or irrelevant context can make orchestration less reliable. We're still refining how to structure and filter that information so the orchestrator can coordinate agents more effectively. Supporting Different Coding Environments Orkio works in our tested setup, but not everyone who downloaded it could run it successfully. Different coding agents and environments use different MCP and hook protocols, creating compatibility challenges. Making Orkio reliably installable across multiple development environments is an important engineering problem we want to address. Making Agent Communication Visible Another challenge was designing the frontend. Our backend coordinates multiple agents, Git operations, tasks, and real-time state changes. Representing these processes in a way developers can quickly understand was difficult. We wanted the UI to explain not just what each agent was doing, but how agents were communicating and resolving dependencies.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're most proud of building a new, lightweight coordination layer that connects AI coding agents across different computers in real time . Instead of replacing existing AI coding tools, Orkio makes them work together. We integrated Factory Droid and SpacetimeDB into a system that coordinates development across independent agent environments, while allowing developers to continue using their normal Git workflows. We're also proud that we built a working prototype and tested its value through a real development task. Putting Orkio to the Test We compared two development setups on the same task: building a Flappy Bird game. One setup used Orkio, while the other used ordinary GitHub collaboration across two computers. Metric Orkio GitHub only Prompts required 2 9 Conflicts recorded 0 1 Total completion time 10 minutes 16 minutes Tokens used 380K (including 26K for planning) 430K In this benchmark, Orkio required 78% fewer prompts , finished 37.5% faster , and used approximately 11.6% fewer tokens . While this was one comparison rather than a statistically validated performance study, the results supported our initial hypothesis: better coordination can reduce the human effort required to turn independently generated code into a working application. The most encouraging result was the reduction in human prompting. It suggests that agents can handle more of the coordination themselves instead of relying on developers to constantly relay information.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: The biggest lesson was that making individual AI agents faster doesn't automatically make a team of agents more productive . Parallel execution creates opportunities for faster development, but it also introduces coordination overhead. Even when tasks are divided carefully, components share interfaces and assumptions that can change during implementation. We also learned that more agents aren't always the solution. Our initial conflict-resolution architecture introduced another agent to coordinate changes, but we eventually realized that direct communication between the affected agents could be simpler and more effective. Another important lesson was that shared context needs to be structured. Giving an orchestrator access to everything isn't necessarily useful; the challenge is delivering the right information at the right time. Finally, we learned how important it is to distinguish between automated coordination and human judgment. Agents should handle routine communication and integration work, but developers still need control over consequential decisions and final code publication.

sections.heading: What's next for Orkio
sections.text: We want Orkio to become a general-purpose collaboration layer for AI coding agents, independent of the tools or machines developers use. Our next priorities are: Broader compatibility: Support more AI coding tools and address differences in MCP and hook protocols. Better orchestration: Improve how Factory receives task context and delegates work across agents. Proactive negotiation: Enable agents to agree on shared interfaces and implementation decisions before conflicts arise. Smarter conflict detection: Improve attribution when several agents make overlapping changes, including semantic conflicts that existing tests may not detect. Configurable autonomy: Let development teams define which conflicts agents can resolve independently and which require human approval. Improved visualization: Build a clearer real-time interface for observing agent communication, dependencies, and integration progress. Our long-term vision is simple: developers should be able to run multiple AI coding agents across different computers without becoming the communication bridge between them.

title: Pacioli
tagline: The simplest way to get your accounting done on one collaborative canvas.

sections.text: ​## Inspiration At small companies, accounting always got left for later, which we both personally experienced. That's why we built Pacioli, the simplest way to get your accounting done, all on one collaborative canvas. ​ Pacioli autonomously handles books, chase vendors, writes reports, and learns over time based on your patterns.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Pacioli takes in your bank (Capital One’s Nessie), Stripe and QuickBooks (bills you owe and invoices owed to you) and runs the back office on one live canvas. A Bookkeeper agent sorts every transaction, matches it to a bill, voids duplicates and posts it to the ledger, with a reason for each call. Anything it isn’t sure about goes to “Needs you” with the evidence and a suggested answer, where it can email the vendor and follow up for you. Your answers become patterns it uses next time. A Reports agent turns the ledger into a weekly P&L and charts you ask for in plain English. ​

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: ​ The app is built using SpacetimeDB. This allows for a simple collaborative environment where events need to be synced in real time and shown upon every change. The agents run on Factory's Droid API and runs with a cloud computer. Vendor emails go through AgentMail and the frontend uses React & React Flow for the canvas. We integrated Capital One's Nessie to mock messy bank input data. The project was designed in Figma.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: ​ Getting the factory agents to run in the cloud with its own computer was interesting. We couldn't find any open-facing Factory Cloud Agent SDK, so we built our own. Furthermore, we spent a lot of time to get the user experience write and landed upon the flow design.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we’re proud of
sections.text: ​ Everything works end to end and is very simple to swap with live data. It is a self improving system that learns off of the decisions of items initially flagged for human review.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: ​ Bookkeeping is routine, and what matters is the small set of judgement calls. Once you keep track of the judgement calls, you can use patterns to automate the book keeping.

sections.heading: What’s next for Pacioli
sections.text: Connecting real bank and accounting accounts, adding more agents for payroll, taxes and month-end close, and testing it with a real small business.

title: Rally
tagline: Your phone is the racket, your laptop is the court: low-latency sport video games, powered by SpacetimeDB.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We wanted the fun of Wii Sports badminton without the console, using the phone already in your pocket as the racket. Plus, you can play from anywhere - with friends across cities, countries, and continents!!

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Rally turns your laptop into a badminton court and your phone into a motion-controlled racket, so you can play 1v1 across two laptops or against the CPU.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built it with Three.js for the 3D court, phone motion sensors for swings and SpacetimeDB as the referee, which decides every shot, landing, point and CPU move on the server. SpacetimeDB is our reactive backend: database, game server, and real-time sync in one!

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The hardest part was keeping swing timing fair over a network, so the server checks every swing against its own clock and rejects faked "perfect" hits.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're proudest of fog of war, where the opponent's shot never reaches your laptop until it crosses the net, enforced by the database rather than hidden on screen.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned how to use a database as a real-time game server, with private tables, views and scheduled reducers replacing a traditional game loop.

sections.heading: What's next for Rally
sections.text: We’re scaling Rally into an enterprise. By combining the devices people already own—their laptop and phone—we eliminate the high hardware barrier of a $300 Nintendo Switch or $500 Meta Quest. No store trips, no complex setup, and no physical limits: just seamless, global multiplayer gaming accessible to anyone, anywhere.

title: skyFall
tagline: Live forecasts of which satellites are falling, what survives re-entry, and where it could land, powered by GPU Monte Carlo physics and SpacetimeDB.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: In March 2024, a piece of a discarded ISS battery pallet survived re-entry and crashed through the roof of a house in Naples, Florida. Thousands of objects are decaying out of orbit right now. Low Earth orbit holds thousands of short-lived satellites; Starlink alone de-orbits satellites almost daily, and rocket stages and old debris come down too. The public answer to "what's coming down, and where?" is usually a single date with a window of hours, and no idea what actually survives. Break-up and survivability analyses stay inside agencies. We wanted to build the tool we wished existed: a live globe that shows which objects are re-entering, which pieces survive, how heavy and how dangerous they are, and where they could land , with honest uncertainty.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: SKYFALL runs that analysis openly and continuously, on live public data: Track every decaying satellite and rocket body from live orbit data (CelesTrak) and space weather (NOAA SWPC). Forecast when and where each one re-enters, as a probability distribution from about 20,000 simulated futures per object. Break it up into its components (bus, solar arrays, tanks, reaction wheels, batteries, engine parts) and fly every piece down through the atmosphere with heating and melting, thousands of times. Show it all live on a 3D globe. Each object is colored by its earliest plausible re-entry, so anything that could come down within a day stands out. A ring marks objects with at least a 10% chance that a piece lands with more than 15 J of energy, the usual threshold for a dangerous fragment. Clicking an object shows: its live altitude, drop rate, and a probabilistic re-entry window , with a ground corridor that widens as uncertainty grows, impact zones (50% and 90%) where surviving debris could fall, computed from thousands of simulated descents, a 3D model of its components , each with its chance of reaching the ground, surviving mass and impact energy. Hover a part and the globe shows only that part's debris tracks and zones. Forecasts update live as new orbit and space-weather data arrive. If our GPU goes down, the system fails over to CPU automatically and keeps forecasting. Every debris number is labeled as a modeled estimate .

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: SpacetimeDB is the entire backend. It isn't just storage; it's the orchestrator. There is no other server, no side database and no message queue. One TypeScript module (about 2,400 lines: 32 tables, 29 reducers, 4 procedures, 6 schedules) does all of this: Ingest: scheduled procedures make outbound HTTP calls from inside the database to poll NOAA SWPC space weather (every 15 min), CelesTrak decaying objects (every 2 h) and SATCAT decay dates (every 6 h). Job queue with leases: forecast and debris jobs run in two lanes per worker (one bulk job, one fast job), with lease expiry, retries and oldest-first ordering. A scheduled sweep reducer requeues expired leases and evicts silent workers every 2 seconds. Failover as a database rule: CPU workers get no jobs while a healthy GPU worker exists, so failover happens with no extra coordinator. Measured: after we killed the GPU worker, the CPU worker finished the next job 7 seconds later. Chaining: publishing a forecast versions and archives it, then automatically queues a debris job when the chance of re-entry within 72 h is at least 20%. Orbits in the database: SGP4 runs inside the module to keep every object's live position current. Self-scoring: when an official decay date arrives, the module scores the last forecast made before it (hours of error, inside the window or not, lead time). Streaming: the web client subscribes to the tables directly, so the globe updates the moment a result lands, with no polling and no API layer. The workers are stateless. Kill one mid-job and the database requeues the job and someone else finishes it. Forecast physics (GPU Monte Carlo on an ASUS Ascent GX10). Each object starts from its SGP4 state and is propagated with RK4 under Earth's oblateness (\(J_2\)) and atmospheric drag against a co-rotating atmosphere: $$ \mathbf a_{\text{drag}} = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{C_D A}{m}\rho(h,t)\left|\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}\right|\mathbf v_{\text{rel}} $$ Density \(\rho\) comes from the NRLMSIS 2.1 atmosphere model, driven by live solar (F10.7) and geomagnetic (Ap) indices. We don't trust a single ballistic coefficient. We calibrate drag per object so its simulated decay matches the decay actually observed in its orbital elements. Then we run about 20,000 particles per object, each with its own perturbed drag and position: the drag spread widens when Kp is high, and the position error grows with the age of the elements. All particles are batched in PyTorch on the GPU. The re-entry window is the spread of the particles: $$ P(t_{\text{reentry}} \le t) \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{1}\left[t^{(i)}_{\text{reentry}} \le t\right] $$ Ground sightings can be fused by Bayesian updating with adaptive importance sampling, so corridors narrow as evidence arrives. Debris survival model. Each object is split into a documented archetype's components. There are nine archetypes so far (Starlink-class, 3U/6U CubeSats, microsat, large satellite, cargo vehicle, rocket upper stage, and others), each with its material, shape, mass, size and sources. Starting from each particle's state at 80 km, every (particle × component) flies its own 3-DOF trajectory on the GPU with stagnation-point heating from the Sutton–Graves relation: $$ \dot{q} = k\,\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{r_n}}\;v^{3} $$ A component demises if the absorbed heat exceeds what it needs to reach its melting point and melt: $$ Q_{\text{demise}} = m\left[c_p\,(T_{\text{melt}} - T_0) + L_f\right] $$ The model covers seven materials (aluminium, titanium, stainless steel, CFRP, glass, copper, Inconel) and includes radiative cooling. Survivors are carried to the ground, where we record impact speed, energy and 50%/90% footprint zones. It's a reduced version of the object-oriented approach used by NASA DAS and ESA DRAMA. What the GX10 made possible. From our live database so far: 32.7 million simulated futures and 752 billion particle integration steps about 48 million particle-steps per second , roughly 22× faster than the CPU fallback l

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Re-entry is hard to predict. Atmospheric density can swing a lot with solar activity, and small errors in drag compound over days. Against official re-entry predictions, our early forecasts ran 7 to 11 hours late . We'd rather show that honestly than hide it, and per-object drag calibration was our biggest fix. Ground truth is scarce. Validating against past re-entries means using only the orbital data available before the event. Historical element sets and recovered-debris locations are hard to find, so building fair test cases was a project in itself. Object physical data is incomplete. Mass, shape and materials aren't public for most objects, so we built sourced archetypes, label every number as real, modeled or assumed, and show a confidence rating. Making failover trustworthy. Getting leases, heartbeats and requeues right, so no job is lost or run twice when the GPU drops, took several iterations. Making debris physics fast enough to run continuously. Batching every particle × component × time step into GPU tensors turned a one-off analysis into something we run for every object about to come down. Time. We built a database-driven job system, two GPU physics engines and a live 3D frontend in one weekend.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A complete live pipeline, from public feeds to GPU physics to a 3D globe, with SpacetimeDB as the only stateful component . GPU-to-CPU failover in 7 seconds , coordinated entirely by database rules. Hundreds of billions of physics steps on a desk-side GX10. Forecasts that score themselves against official decay dates. A per-component survivability view of live re-entries, something the public hasn't had before.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: A real-time database can be the whole backend : ingestion, scheduling, job orchestration, failover, archiving and streaming, with no separate queue or worker coordinator. It made failure handling simpler, not harder. How much re-entry prediction depends on the atmosphere, and why showing uncertainty matters more than a single confident answer. How to write physics that runs fast in parallel on a GPU, and how to keep a CPU path that runs the same physics, visibly degraded, when the GPU is gone. How to work with AI agents as teammates: Grok Bot for planning and coordination, and Cursor for writing and reviewing code.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: Hindcast validation at scale: our forecasts are already scored against official decay dates in the database. Next is a public scorecard comparing us to official predictions over many past re-entries. Better object data: Space-Track and DISCOSweb for real object mass, shape and materials, and more archetypes (Long March stages, Falcon 9 second stage, OneWeb, Kuiper, Starlink v2 mini). Better atmosphere: density that varies with latitude and local time, time-varying solar activity, a spread of break-up altitudes, and winds for light debris. Population-weighted casualty risk under each footprint.

title: Vouch
tagline: Vouch is trust infrastructure for agentic commerce: AI agents investigate refund evidence and build "Vouch scores” for individual shoppers so merchants can identify and resolve credible claims faster.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Vouch began with three experiences in the days before Cal Hacks. At the airport before his flight to the hackathon, Shubhay tried to resolve an order issue and found that requesting his refund required him to submit a written request followed by a call. Shivam spoke with a single father living paycheck to paycheck who had several hundred dollars tied up in a refund for weeks and his repeated follow-ups brought only "verification pending." Aadi was exploring an agent to simplify airline-ticket refunds and became familiar with the trend towards development of agents to complete these tasks. Together, these experiences made us ask what personal finance will look like when agents can buy, document problems, and request refunds for us. We decided that merchants need a signal they can trust while consumers needed a faster way to verify. We chose refunds as a focused starting point: simplify the consumer's work while helping merchants detect fraudulent claims, coordinated abuse, and scalping behavior as agent-driven commerce grows. The stakes already exist: Appriss Retail's research with Deloitte estimated $103 billion in U.S. losses from fraudulent returns and claims in 2024 , while NRF's 2025 survey found 71% of consumers were less likely to return to a retailer after a poor returns experience . Appriss Retail / Deloitte · NRF / Happy Returns Refunds are our first workflow and the focus of our scope for this project. Portable trust for an economy of people and agents is the larger picture.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: For customers, the product offers an accessible, phone-ready claim flow across product categories and refund reasons. They record the item while explaining the problem verbally, and complete an in-video verification challenge. The claim page tracks 10 processing stages as FFmpeg and faster-whisper prepare the footage, Factory Droid investigates it, and CREAO supplies review and trust judgments. A recorded test completed the review in 155 seconds , using live Droid sessions and a fixture CREAO reviewer. When evidence is incomplete, Vouch can request one additional clip with a specific explanation of what is missing. For merchants, Vouch prepares an evidence-backed case: what was ordered, what the customer said, what Factory Droid's footage analysis supports or contradicts, the return policy, relevant shopping and return history using the customer's Vouch Score , and a recommendation. Findings link to timestamps and proof clips, making audits and company-specific workflow additions easy. When the investigation supports approval, Vouch immediately submits the refund recommendation into the merchant's decision workflow; recommendations to reject go to the company for human review rather than automatically denying the customer. Eligible approvals can proceed automatically within the configured reviewer and amount checks; payment settlement remains separate, and demo payouts are simulated. For merchants, this means less time spent collecting evidence and reviewing routine claims, and faster resolution for credible customers, reducing churn. It also provides clearer signals for which requests need closer scrutiny, while keeping merchants in control of their policies and decisions. For trust, Vouch maintains a shopping reliability score built on a customer's historical purchases and returns, evaluating their shopping and return integrity with a recorded reason for each change. CREAO's Refund Investigator and Risk Scorecard contribute to the score judgment; SpacetimeDB bounds the applied change and prevents applying it twice. The planned CRS identity and contact-risk integration will add context about who is submitting the claim, separately from whether the refund itself is valid. An unresolved request for an extra clip does not itself change the score. Signed credentials let another merchant verify selected attributes, such as a purchase threshold or trust band, without needing the customer's full transaction history. For testing at scale and across multiple interacting players, we built a deterministic shopping economy in SpacetimeDB , with 10,000 simulated shoppers and 100 simulated merchants. Shoppers purchase, receive items, request refunds, and accumulate histories. The globe, event stream, merchant cashflow view, and agent timelines expose those events and their consequences, demonstrating how each shopper interacts with multiple merchants and vice versa. Behavioral detectors flag coordinated claims, repeated defect patterns, and unusual refund frequency for CREAO's Pattern Analyst to review. For finance teams, the Refund Finance Desk exposes backend simulation analysis of cash, accounting, conditional obligations, reserves, and close. SpacetimeDB stores finance events; deterministic code reconciles decision, processor, bank, warehouse, and ledger records. CREAO provides impact, review, close, forecast, and exposure roles, with outputs validated before use. A synthetic one-million-order book supplies planted errors and legitimate decoys.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built Vouch around three essential systems: Factory Droid SDK for tool-using video investigation, CREAO for specialized review and trust judgments, and SpacetimeDB for the shared economy, operational records, and enforceable transaction rules. A Next.js interface and Node.js worker connect those systems into one customer-to-merchant workflow.

sections.heading: CREAO Agents
sections.text: Vouch's core refund decisions run on CREAO agents. Vouch Refund Investigator (core decision agent) Recommends accept, decline, or more_evidence for a single refund claim, with amount, method, cited reasons, and confidence. Agent ID: 68d1ff37-70a8-4eab-8b7c-3cfaf38f9041 Agent: https://agent.creao.ai/apps/68d1ff37-70a8-4eab-8b7c-3cfaf38f9041 Run share link: https://agent.creao.ai/share/9305bd3bde180c07e376d62bb96d5286 Vouch Risk Scorecard Reads every contextual indicator for a refund claim and returns a JSON scorecard of supports, neutral, and caution readings. It never recommends a decision. Agent ID: 62b56cf6-cb4b-4f15-a320-93c89a261577 Agent: https://agent.creao.ai/apps/62b56cf6-cb4b-4f15-a320-93c89a261577 Install link: https://agent.creao.ai/install/62b56cf6-cb4b-4f15-a320-93c89a261577?version=23e28040-85bf-4780-a9da-a0a2c4643903 SpacetimeDB: shared state and enforceable rules. SpacetimeDB holds shoppers, purchases, claims, analysis steps, artifacts, findings, recommendations, decisions, and score changes. Its scheduled reducers run the simulated economy inside the database, while browser subscriptions keep the customer's progress tracker, merchant case, globe, and trust history synchronized. Authorization, controller escalation, and duplicate-update checks live in SpacetimeDB reducers. Without SpacetimeDB, Vouch loses its shared case state, running economy, and consistent record of trust decisions; it is the operational backbone. Preparing evidence for Factory Droid. The worker uses FFmpeg and ffprobe to inspect and normalize the upload, extract audio, sample frames, and create timestamped contact sheets; faster-whisper supplies word-level transcription. Factory Droid's image checks inspect the randomized finger challenge, while deterministic probes examine reused footage, blank or frozen frames, scene changes, and metadata inconsistencies. Each result becomes evidence the investigator can inspect, with limitations recorded when a tool cannot complete its work. These checks establish internal consistency, not proof of authenticity. Factory Droid SDK: a custom investigation loop. We built a case workflow on top of the SDK, with custom MCP tools including get_case , get_policy , get_customer_summary , list_artifacts , list_findings , and recommend_refund . Factory Droid's Case Analyst retrieves the customer issue, order, policy, history summary, and video evidence in one consistent case format. It works across the timeline, revisits frames, runs measurements or writes probes, inspects its own findings, and records evidence for and against each statement. Every case follows the same report schema while preserving its specific evidence. Tool calls, findings, files, and fence decisions form a run record that merchants can inspect. The permission handler checks consequential operations, including nested script calls, without giving the agent payment authority. Factory Droid Report Auditor and merchant verification. Each finding must cite a registered artifact and a time window. The worker builds proof clips and audits artifact existence, hashes, timing, and coverage. An additional Factory Droid Report Auditor can independently test findings against those artifacts. Rejected findings do not contribute to the evidence score. Merchants receive the same timestamped findings, proof clips, method, and limitations, so they can verify the investigation themselves rather than accept an unexplained model verdict. CREAO: the trust-decision layer. Saved CREAO agents occupy distinct roles for evidence analysis, refund investigation, policy and risk assessment, pattern review, and Vouch Score judgment. The worker calls them through CREAO API Trigger , polls or receives a webhook, validates their outputs, and records each run's provenance. The live Refund Investigator and Risk Scorecard panel judge how a reviewed claim should affect the shopper's Vouch Score; SpacetimeDB applies the bounded change once. The configured Refund Reviewer role is al

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Giving agents useful tools within enforceable limits. Droid's tool behavior differed between autonomy settings, and script batches required inspecting their nested calls. We built explicit permission checks and recovery messages so a refused operation did not silently end an otherwise useful investigation. Handling asynchronous and imperfect agent outputs. CREAO runs can take minutes, and live responses do not always match the expected structure. We separated background execution from HTTP requests, showed progress through database rows, and added defensive parsing, validation, retry limits, and labeled fallbacks. Keeping the shared simulation responsive. The worker needs detailed history, while a browser needs a manageable view. We used indexed worker-side maps, aggregate merchant-flow records, bounded event feeds, throttled rendering, and subscriptions scoped to the selected case or shopper. Following a refund through time. An approved refund, money settled, an item returned, and an obligation accrued can occur in different periods. The finance extension models those as separate events and specifies which source answers each question. Its remaining integration work is explicitly tracked.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: An inspectable refund workflow: video evidence becomes findings, proof clips, a reviewed recommendation, and a recorded outcome. Agents doing product work: Factory investigates cases with tools; CREAO contributes review, pattern analysis, and trust judgments through defined roles. A reproducible environment for testing trust: synthetic shoppers generate histories and adversarial behavior, with hidden ground truth available for evaluation. Controls behind the interface: database rules enforce approval limits, role separation, balanced entries, and one score review per refund. A foundation beyond support tickets: signed credentials and the finance extension connect one customer's claim to merchant trust and operational consequences.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that trust has to be built into the full decision process: what an agent can read, what evidence it cites, which actions it can propose, who can approve them, and how an error can be traced afterward. We also learned that claim validity, customer history, and payment status are different questions . Combining them into one confidence number hides the information a merchant needs. A credible history can justify a faster route, but it cannot replace evidence or store policy. Finally, simulation gave us repeatable histories and difficult cases within a weekend, while showing us what remains unproven. Synthetic detector results do not establish real-world fraud accuracy, and a local simulation benchmark does not establish production capacity. Those require merchant pilots and measurements on actual workflows.

sections.heading: What's next for Vouch
sections.text: 1. Move from a simulated economy to real commerce. We will connect merchant order systems, shipping and warehouse events, and payment processors so Vouch can investigate actual purchases and execute approved refunds with settlement tracking. We will pilot with merchants, measure review time, false flags, customer outcomes, and investigation cost, and use reviewed outcomes to calibrate the prototype's scoring rules. Scaling beyond 10,000 shoppers will require efficient subscriptions, durable job scheduling, and investigation workers that can process many independent cases concurrently. 2. Expand beyond refunds into agent-driven financial workflows. The reusable process is evidence, policy, authority, action, and a verifiable outcome. We want to apply it to shopping-agent purchases, exchanges, warranties, subscription disputes, reimbursements, invoice disputes, and payment reconciliation. The finance extension is our first step toward connecting those actions to cash planning, reserves, accounting, and close. Each workflow will have its own evidence requirements and approval boundaries. 3. Become the "credit score" for the agentic commerce era. Our ambition is a portable, verifiable record of transactional reliability that businesses can use when a person or an authorized agent acts across services. Companies need validity and accountability; consumers need speed and ease. Vouch should let earned trust carry between merchants without making every customer start from zero at every store. 4. Earn trust as the custodian of consumer data. Accurate records and privacy must develop together. Merchants should receive the evidence for their own claims and the verified attributes needed to apply their policies, without access to a consumer's detailed purchases at other stores, where they shopped, or when. We will strengthen selective disclosure, merchant-specific permissions, access logs, retention limits, and ways for consumers to correct disputed records. As the entity collecting valuable shopping data, Vouch must be accountable to consumers as well as merchants. We intend to charge for verification and workflow services, with an explicit commitment against brokering or selling individual purchase histories.

title: Portable Braille
tagline: Educational device that encourages young visually impaired people to learn and practice Braille in order to increase chances for future employment and expand general literacy level of the community.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Literacy level of Blind and Visually impaired community even in United States is lower than 10%. And the reason is simple - Braille (tactile text) is not affordable and not accessible today. I follow Haben Girma - the first deaf-blind person graduated Harvard Law school. She is a brilliant person, wrote books, influencer and advocates for people with disabilities rights. I saw how efficient she is in communications with people. However, she needs a special person who assists her by typing speech of her interlocutors, so it can be converted to Braille format and Haben can read it in tactile format. I believe that she could do even more if there is a device that could do handle it, keeping her communication private and without relying on assistance.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: For visually impaired people the device allows users to read and write text on the phone privately, texting, surfing web, swiping Instagram, and of course learn and practice reading and writing. It is the first device that encourages blind users to improve their reading skills in most delightful ways - communication with loved ones and friends. Also device allows to "read" face expressions while talking to people, by face expression recognition using RayBan|Meta glasses and doing computing on the Jetson Orin Nano. It is the only solution today that doesn't require connection to internet and work even faster than BeMyEyes (powered by OpenAI). For deaf-blind users convert all speeches to text, and then converts it to tactile Braille and render in on the device, so user doesn't need an assistant.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We 3d-printed an enclosure of the device on the 3d printer. Soldered Li-Po battery to battery-management-System module for correct charging/discharging and powered the microcontroller and Step-up boost DC-DC converter to power up braille module, which needs 200V for operating. Braille module gets data from microcontroller. There is a keypad of at least 6 buttons for typing braille combinations. Keypad also connected to the microcontroller. Microcontroller syncs with a phone over Bluetooth Low Energy. We hacked RayBan|Meta glasses in analog way to connect in to Jetson Orin Nano.

title: Ranger
tagline: Audio is a luxury we take for granted, that deaf folks don't get. Ranger is a wearable AR solution aiming to fix that, visualizing audio around them, and bringing them into the world of *sound*.

sections.heading: 💭 Inspiration
sections.text: Sometimes helpful ideas come from the silliest places. One day, as our team was playing Fortnite instead of doing our homework, we realized how helpful it was to have a "sound ring" in game. Noises like enemy footsteps or gunshots are displayed with a visual indicator to show what direction they came from. Luckily, we aren't trapped in Moisty Mire shotgunning ChugJugs, but we did realize people hard of hearing could benefit from this in real life. Both innocuous situations (dropping your wallet in the street and a parent calling you down to dinner) and intense situations (scary noises that would make anyone want to pick up the pace a bit walking home at night, an ambulance screaming by) are much more difficult to navigate for those who can't process auditory input. Visualizing sound helps you enter and understand conversations easily, avoid dangerous situations, and generally be aware of important goings-on in your surroundings. We wanted to build portable, wearable technology that would bring our vision from our colorful video game screen to the real world. We see our product as a proof-of-concept for something that could truly - cheaply, portably, fashionably - transform the lives of deaf people.

sections.heading: 🖥 What it does
sections.text: Ranger is an edge-based AR solution for audio visualization that uses a Meta Quest frontend to indicate to the wearer where sounds are coming from. The user wears a hat, which has a microphone array to capture omnidirectional audio and send it to our processing unit, a Jetson Nano. Ranger classifies all different sorts of real-world sounds using a classifier model and displays them as icons on a circular grid, placing markers according to distance and direction. For speech, we live-transcribe conversations using Whisper which allows those hard of hearing to immediately parse what's happening, even if speech comes from behind them. The sound visualization does not interfere with your real-world view, only enhancing the information already available. It's a real-life HUD, enriching the wearer's experience and using edge computing to bring them into the wonderful world of sound.

sections.heading: 🛠 How we built it
sections.text: Hardware : 1 Meta Quest 3 1 Jetson Orin Nano Mics (ReSpeaker 4-Mic Circular Microphone Array, Boya Bluetooth TX/RX) (Most importantly) A giant cowboy hat Software : Python Unity ML Models (Yamnet, Whisper) Ranger runs completely on the edge! All heavy computation is done on a Jetson Orin Nano; all communication is done with direct wired USB-C connections. For a TL;DR: using the Jetson Orin Nano, we developed an audio processing software that takes in a 4-channel microphone input, triangulates the direction, amplitude, and type of the loudest sound occurring at any time step, transcribes any detected speech, and sends all this information to the Meta Quest 3 using network-over-USB. For those interested in a more in-depth overview: Real-time Voice Transcription We use Whisper Mini running on the Jetson Nano for real-time voice transcription. To accomplish real-time voice transcription, we capture the last 10 seconds of a user’s audio and process it immediately. Although the Jetson Nano has the ability to run larger Whisper versions (up to the recently released turbo one with 800M parameters), our priority was reducing latency. Sound triangulation To determine where sound comes from relative to the user, we use a ReSpeaker microphone array. We set it up to triangulate the audio channels to pinpoint where audio comes from (an example of this technique below). This approach gave us a vector with angle and volume, which allows us to position our classified sounds as relatively positioned icons in our 3D scene. Sound classification Sound classification is done using a convolutional neural network (CNN). The model runs on the Jetson and classifies audio in a probability distribution of up to 500 candidate labels. Using this class along with the latest source of noise from the sound triangulation, we’re able to accurately pinpoint what a noise is and where it comes from relative to the user!

sections.heading: 🛑 Challenges we ran into
sections.text: This was our first time doing a hardware-based project, and our inexperience showed up immediately . We found ourselves sifting through mountains of cables, walking back and forth to the hardware booth every 20 minutes, and flipping between "ITSSOOVER" and "WERESOBACK" faster than the GPU fan on our Jetson Nano. We all loved Operating Systems, Concurrency, and Computer Architecture in school, but building a project completely from scratch, with very little electric or audio engineering knowledge, through largely un-trekked territory was an uphill battle. We had several significant challenges: 1) Parsing raw input data intelligently We planned this out without a pretty cursory understanding of auditory science, so we had to spend a lot of time understanding hardware synchronization concerns, channel mixing, and in-built audio driver configurations. Spending a lot of time thinking and diagramming though, rather than just spurting out poorly written code, was incredibly helpful later during integration. 2) Interfacing between backend and frontend We originally wanted to use bluetooth to communicate between the Jetson Nano and Meta Quest but ran into a ton of issues with trying to get low fidelity bluetooth communication schemes working. After a lot of tinkering, we decided to connect them together with a USB-C cable and used Android Debug Bridge to treat the wire as a network connection through a server socket. 3) Developing a fully on-the-edge system The Jetson Nano relies on a DC power supply, which we tried to get around with a USB-A adapter and a power bank. Our lack of electric engineering know-how showed here, though, as we didn’t realize the USB-A adapter was inherently capping our voltage. We want to give a huge thank you to Mr. Chitoku Yato at Nvidia for saving us on this with a custom USB-C to DC cord.

sections.heading: 🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: The thing we’re all the most proud of is that we actually built what we set out to build! For our first hardware hack, with three different, distinct devices, across different frameworks, operating systems, and modalities of energy, this was an incredible feat. In the trenches of every challenge - Unity running slower than molasses on our rundown Intel Macs, bugs with multithreaded audio device access, bizarre audio sampling configurations provoking questions that not a soul on StackOverflow seemed to ask - we pushed past it and got things working. Each of us had a different moment we started jumping for joy: “I started going crazy when we first saw the visualization of the DOA (direction of audio)“ - Tyler “When I got to see a radar - like white dots on the circle - and the dots started to move when I did, I almost teared up“ - Samuel “After I spent 4 hours straight on our second Jetson Mini getting the Whisper model working with Cuda“ - Charan “I will never again feel happiness like I did when I saw the Android Debug logs on the Meta Quest print the first packet we sent“ - Sarvesh

sections.heading: 🧠 What we learned
sections.text: Hardware is called hardware because it’s hard and you can wear it. Getting through our first hardware hack gave us a lot of confidence both for building on this idea and pursuing new ones. Hardware : Nuances of DC power conversion and portability Mechanics of audio input processing Remote usage and sharing of graphic/audio drivers Software : Supporting machine learning for edge devices Cabled network communication Unity scripting and scene visualization

sections.heading: ✏️ What's next for Ranger
sections.text: The Meta Quest is the best affordable AR wearable right now, but eventually, we'd want the lightest-weight solution so people would be happy to use Ranger for long periods. We fiddled around with some AR glasses, but many smaller companies focus on treating the glasses as an external monitor, and the Meta RayBans do not have a display. This year, though, the new Meta RayBans will have a visual display, so we could easily swap our (lovably) bulky Quest for a sleek, non-invasive pair of shades. Our team has been chewing on this idea for a long time, and we want to develop this beyond our 36-hour sprint here at TreeHacks. During our development, we thought of a million insanely cool stretch goals to upgrade our current version, and each could be a project on its own. Special audio software that can perform Single Source Separation would let us transcribe multiple voices at once. A more advanced beam-forming location and tracking algorithm would let us intelligently classify objects over time. Porting over multilingual Voice Language Models to our brave little Jetson could expand this project globally, unlocking a new world of interaction for deaf people. This idea has a remarkable depth that we only scratched the surface of, and our intention in the future is to dive deep .

title: WiiWork
tagline: Everyone is hyped about AI agents that can interact with the world. Problem: Websites weren't built with LLMs in mind What would it look like if a website was built ground up with Agent usage first?

sections.text: WiiWork: Making AI-Native Websites

sections.heading: Why:
sections.text: Everyone's excited about AI agents interacting with the world. Companies are pouring billions into development. But there's a problem: websites weren't built with AI in mind. Over this weekend, I sought to answer: what would it look like to build a website from the ground up to be AI-native?

sections.heading: How
sections.text: I built WiiWork solo over the weekend, drawing inspiration from web accessibility patterns. Just like screen readers use ARIA labels, I created a context-rich system where AI agents can understand and interact with web elements naturally. The core innovation is a Higher Order Component (HOC) system that wraps around UI elements and communicates their purpose, appearance, and location to the agent. This "Agentic Web Component" system is paired with a comprehensive global state manager (using Zustand) that synchronizes user and agent interactions in real-time and prevents errors from getting out of control.

sections.heading: Agent
sections.text: The agent system is especially interesting. Instead of using a one-size-fits-all approach, I built a multi-model router that classifies user requests into categories: Simple tasks → GPT-4-mini (fast & efficient) Medium → Claude 3.5 Sonnet (more thoughtful) Complex Logic → NVIDIA DeepSeek (specialized reasoning) Conversational → GPT-4 (natural interaction) Malicious messages get flagged and a AI alignment model interferes Each category has its own carefully engineered system prompt, optimizing for both performance and cost. I prompt engineered all the models using Theo, and prompt engineering tool I built over winter break: https://trytheo.dev

sections.heading: Cool Features
sections.text: Real-time voice interaction using ElevenLabs for speech synthesis and Open AI whisper for speech regognition Mobile-desktop pairing system for voice input Virtual cursor system with smooth animations Tool calling framework using regex parsing Reading list demo app Oh yeah, and the whole Wii thing. I was just feeling nostalgic. ## Technical Challenges The biggest challenge was maintaining state synchronicity between user and agent interactions. I solved this by creating a central state management system that handles both input streams consistently. Another tricky part was getting the voice interaction just right - dealing with audio streams and buffers, especially managing faulty recording features on mobile phone browsers, was a learning experience for me. ## What I Learned This project pushed my full-stack skills to the limit. I got deep experience with: Building complex AI orchestration systems Swapping between multiple LLM providers and maintaining chat history Real-time audio processing Low level web component code Accessibility-inspired design patterns

sections.heading: What's Next
sections.text: I believe this pattern of AI-native web development is the future. In a few years, I expect many websites will use similar patterns to make themselves agent-friendly. WiiWork is just the beginning, a proof of concept showing what's possible when we make websites with Agents in mind from the start. Built solo at TreeHacks 2025 using React, TypeScript, Convex, Zustand, and working about 25/36 possible hours. Check it out at https://WiiWork.dev
