title: scalpal.
tagline: The future of surgery.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Surgical training depends on repetition. Residents learn an operation by doing it many times under supervision, and before they reach that point there are few ways to practice the whole sequence. Simulators exist, but the capable ones are expensive and concentrated in teaching hospitals. We wanted to see how much of a real case a Quest 3S could reproduce: taking a history from a patient, reaching a diagnosis, and then performing the operation that diagnosis calls for, with feedback at each step. We were also interested in what that practice produces. Surgical robots are trained on recorded demonstrations of hand and tool motion, and collecting those demonstrations is slow and costly. A learner practicing in VR generates exactly that kind of motion data as a side effect, so Scalpal records each attempt and replays it on a simulated robot hand. FinchNode's synthetic health records made the cases credible. A real chart carries constraints that a generic case doesn't: a penicillin allergy that affects antibiotic choice, a patient on apixaban and aspirin, a latex allergy that changes how the room is prepared, and a nine-year-old with asthma whose mother answers most of the questions.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Scalpal takes a learner through a single surgical case in a Meta Quest 3S, from the first conversation with the patient to the end of the operation. It starts on a board of synthetic patients from FinchNode. Each card shows the patient's chart (medications, allergies, labs, and problems) along with the risk flags Scalpal derives from it, such as bleeding risk from apixaban or reduced kidney function from a low eGFR. The learner picks a patient and enters a doctor's office, where the patient speaks with an ElevenLabs voice. After each thing the patient says, the learner chooses the next move from four options by tapping or saying it, working through history, examination and tests before committing to a diagnosis and a plan. Findings appear on screen, and the patient responds the way the person in the chart would. The diagnosis determines the operation. In the operating room the learner chooses full VR with a virtual patient, or mixed reality, where generic teaching anatomy is fitted to a real person lying on a table. Scalpal, the voice coach, runs the Time-Out using the risks the learner found or missed in the office, then coaches through the procedure. The open appendectomy is a physical simulation: the learner marks and incises the skin, splits the muscle, clamps and ties vessels, and can cause bleeding that shows on the patient monitor and can kill the patient. In mixed reality, Presage reads the volunteer's real pulse and breathing through a phone camera and uses them as the patient's baseline vitals. When the case ends, a recap explains what happened and why, and a web dashboard follows the session live through SpacetimeDB. The learner's controller motion also becomes a demonstration for a simulated robot arm and hand, which learns the incision-marking step from those demonstrations and is graded with the same checks as the learner. We also built an agent skill that turns any FinchNode chart into a new playable case.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The headset app is Unity 6 on OpenXR with the Meta XR SDK, shipped as one APK that moves through four scenes: the patient board, the office, the operating room and the recap. Voice runs through an ElevenLabs Agents WebSocket client we wrote in C#, so the patient and the coach stream audio and call tools directly from the headset. Both agents run on Claude Sonnet through ElevenLabs. In the office, spoken answers go through ElevenLabs Scribe and then a Claude Haiku classifier that maps what the learner said to one of the four options. The case service is TypeScript on Hono. It reads FinchNode's demo API and derives the risk flags with deterministic rules; no model touches the chart. It then combines the chart with an authored plan and a procedure to produce the case the headset plays. The same service scores the interview and runs the coach, which follows the live state of the operation and decides when a hint is worth giving. Safety warnings are pre-rendered with ElevenLabs Flash, so a warning plays immediately instead of waiting on the model. The surgery runs on a reducer that turns measured tool actions into tissue facts: where the blade crossed the skin, how deep it went, where a clamp sits relative to an injury, how fast the learner pulled. Each step of the operation is a set of checks over those facts. The coach needs this logic on the server and the headset needs it for grading, so it exists in both TypeScript and C#, and both versions must reproduce a shared 41-action golden log exactly. The physiology model that turns blood loss into vitals exists in four places for the same reason, with parity tests between them. SpacetimeDB holds the shared state. Our module has 25 tables and 52 reducers covering sessions, attempts, the coach transcript, commands to the headset, WebRTC signaling for the dashboard and robot results. A scheduled reducer ticks the patient's physiology inside the database, so every client sees the same patient at the same moment. The robotics side is Python. During the incision-marking step the headset records both controllers' poses and grip and posts them as demonstrations. A worker retargets them onto a simulated Franka Panda arm with a Shadow hand in MuJoCo, trains a behavior-cloning policy, grades each rollout with the checks the learner faced, and returns a replay video to the recap. Presage SmartSpectra runs as a separate small service that reads pulse and breathing from a phone pointed at the volunteer.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Keeping two engines in agreement was the hardest constraint. The coach needs the state of the body to talk about it, and the headset needs the same state to grade the learner, so the surgery logic exists in both TypeScript and C#. Small numeric differences broke parity in ways that were hard to spot: a bleed rate of 0.3 ml/s stored as a float drifted from the TypeScript value, and a 0.8 threshold compared differently once a float was widened to a double. We now quantize every measurement to whole millimeters and degrees where it enters the engine, keep rates as doubles, and require both engines to replay a 41-action golden log with identical results. The voice coach was hard to make useful rather than noisy. Our first version routed every mistake through the language model, which took one and a half to three seconds and turned an unsteady hand into a running commentary. Safety warnings now come from pre-rendered clips that interrupt whatever is playing, rough handling is capped at one mistake per tool and tissue every three seconds, and the model only speaks for explanations and hints. The Quest surfaced problems the editor never showed. Tools trailed behind the controllers on the first headset build. The VR patient rendered as a translucent ghost at 13% opacity. The pause menu ignored the pointer, because physics doesn't step while time is frozen, so the new buttons had no colliders yet. And the app wouldn't start over adb until we launched it through the launcher intent. Presage gave us 50 minutes of live measurement for the whole event. After a first test spent 45 seconds without a single reading, we built a guard around it: demo mode by default, sessions that end themselves after five minutes, a cutoff when no face is visible for 15 seconds, and a log of every live second. The guard earned its keep. The next run failed because the terminal had no camera permission, and the one after that returned black frames because the phone was face down. We used about 11 minutes in total.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Getting the voice agents to work in real time was the first big milestone. The patient holds a conversation in character, answering from what's actually in their chart and reacting to whatever the learner does. The coach knows where the learner is in the operation and can be interrupted mid-sentence. Its tool calls also act on the scene: it can highlight a structure or hand over an instrument while it talks. The surgery became something you can actually get wrong. Cutting off the marked line, skipping a tie or nicking the bowel all have consequences, and bleeding you don't control shows up on the monitor and can end the case. The headset and the coach run the same model of the body, so what the coach says always matches what the learner sees. The chart carries through the whole case. A risk found in FinchNode data shows up in the office as something to ask about. At the Time-Out it becomes a check, and in the operating room it changes the coaching at the step it affects. We got real vitals into a simulated operating room. Presage read a volunteer's pulse and breathing from a phone, and Scalpal used them as the patient's starting point before the simulated blood loss takes over. The robot learns from the same practice the learner does. In simulation, a policy trained on demonstrations clearly outperformed replaying them, including when we moved the instrument mid-task, so the recording turned into something more than a playback. Anyone can build on it. The case-authoring skill let an agent with no context write a new, valid case from a FinchNode chart on its first try.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Language models are the wrong tool for anything that has to be fast or exactly right. We started by sending the coach every event and letting it decide what to say, and it was too slow for a warning and too inconsistent for a grade. The version that works keeps the model for conversation and explanation and puts everything else in deterministic code: the risk flags, the scoring, the safety warnings. The model got better once it had less to do. Two codebases that have to agree need a shared test, not shared intentions. The TypeScript and C# engines drifted apart several times before the golden log, and the same lesson applied to the JSON passing between the service and Unity: a field one side forgets about doesn't throw an error, it just disappears. Contract tests that check both directions caught bugs no one would have spotted by reading the code. Being honest about what's real made the product better, not weaker. Every value in Scalpal is labeled as chart data, authored teaching content, a measured reading or a simulation, and keeping those apart forced clearer decisions. The volunteer's real heart rate, for example, can't respond to a virtual bleed, so it became the baseline and the simulation adds to it. And a headset changes the problem more than we expected. Things that worked in the editor failed on the Quest for reasons we couldn't have guessed from a desk, so the earlier something ran on the device, the cheaper it was to fix.

sections.heading: What's next for scalpal.
sections.text: The robot needs real data. Right now it learns the incision-marking step from scripted demonstrations, and the pipeline from the headset to the training worker is in place. The next step is to collect demonstrations from actual learners and see whether a policy trained on people practicing outperforms one trained on scripts. That's the claim the whole project rests on, and we haven't tested it yet. We want more operations than the appendectomy. The cholecystectomy already exists as a procedure the coach can run, with the anatomy modeled. Making it playable in the headset means building the gallbladder region of the operating room and treating the critical view of safety as a hard gate before any clip or cut, the way current guidelines recommend. Hand tracking would replace the controller-driven gloves. A port of MediaPipe's hand model that runs on the Quest already exists on a branch, and real hand motion would make both the practice and the robot demonstrations closer to surgery. Presage could do more than set a baseline. The volunteer's breathing could move the teaching anatomy with each breath, which is the same respiratory motion problem image-guided surgery has to solve. The case library should grow without us. The authoring skill already turns a FinchNode chart into a valid case. What's missing is clinician review, so the cases that reach learners have been checked by people who actually perform these operations.

title: Tab: Groupchat Accountant
tagline: Tab is a friend in your iMessage group chat who keeps track of shared expenses. Say "got pizza, $48" or snap a receipt; Tab splits it, nudges people, and settles up with one 👍. No app needed.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every trip, house, and dinner group has the same problem: someone pays, someone keeps a spreadsheet, and three weeks later nobody remembers who owes what. Splitting apps exist, but they make everyone download something and type every expense in twice. The money talk already happens in the group chat. We wanted the tab to live there too.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Tab is a member of your iMessage group chat. Text expenses: "got groceries, $63" → Tab replies "Groceries, $63.00. Split 4 ways, that's $15.75 each." If something's off ("jake only had a $3 diet coke"), it re-splits. Receipts: send a photo. Tab reads the items, tax, tip, and fees, checks that the math adds up, and lets people claim what they had ("1 and 4", "same as Kian", "we all split the fries"). Asks instead of guessing: missing amount? "How much was the Uber?" Unknown name? "Who's Dhabush?" Tab never invents a number or a person. Settling: by default Tab keeps a running tab. Say "settle up" and it posts one message with who owes whom. Each person taps 👍 to pay their part. A typed "yes" never moves money. Questions: "what do i owe" gets just the amount. "why" gets a one-line breakdown. "@tab ledger" posts a private link to a live web ledger with balances and a money-flow graph. Corrections and disputes: "actually it was 44" updates the expense; 👎 on a settle request opens a dispute that changes only that person's share.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: iMessage client: a Mac bridge that reads enabled group chats and sends Tab's replies, threaded replies, and tapbacks. SpacetimeDB (Maincloud) is the single source of truth. Every write goes through typed reducers; the backend, client, and web ledger read role-gated views. The split math (an even, custom, or itemized split, with tax and tip spread proportionally and exact cent rounding) lives in the module. Settlement is a scheduled reducer that completes simulated transfers. A two-stage AI pipeline: A fast classifier gate (TypeSafe's Jev) sees every message and decides whether it's about money. Only messages that pass go to Grok (xAI) for structured extraction: expenses, claims, corrections, and receipt reading with Grok vision. Chatter never reaches Grok, and its text is cleared from the database. Numbers come from code, never from the model. Every amount Grok extracts must appear in the original message ("thirty two fifty" counts). Receipts must add up, or Tab asks the payer. Even Tab's free-form money answers are checked in code for who owes whom before they're sent. Capital One Nessie: demo accounts are seeded with Nessie, and completed settlements are mirrored there. Web ledger: React + Vite + React Flow, live-subscribed to SpacetimeDB, opened by an unguessable per-group link. Tests: a simulated group chat runs the real backend against an in-memory copy of the database module, with scripted Grok responses. That's 250+ backend tests, plus a browser playground for driving Tab with fake phones.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Real receipts are messy. One of ours printed the card payment as "Credit −$227.66" and "Amount Due $0.00". The first version read the payment as a discount and the total as $0, and the math still "added up". We added code-level guards (payments aren't discounts, a $0 total is never accepted) instead of trusting the prompt. Checking an LLM's numbers isn't enough. Our first check confirmed every dollar amount existed in the data, but "you owe Jake $26 and Joe $6" passed when it was the other way around. Balances are now answered from templates, and the AI path checks direction too. Group chats are chaotic. Several people answer at once, someone's "ok" is to a different conversation, and iPhones send curly apostrophes ("I’m Tanuj") that broke name parsing. We built a tracker for Tab's open questions so the right person's answer goes to the right question. Timing for a live demo: real objection windows are hours long, so a demo mode compresses them, without shrinking how long Tab waits for people to type.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Money only ever moves on an explicit 👍 from the person paying. Tab feels like a friend in the chat: short, lowercase when the group is lowercase, and quiet unless it's about money. Three people and their coding agents shipped 40+ reviewed pull requests in a weekend, with the agents reviewing each other's PRs on GitHub.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Put a cheap, privacy-preserving gate in front of the expensive model. Let the LLM read language, but let code own every number. "Ask, never guess" is a better product than a smarter guess.

sections.heading: What's next for Tab
sections.text: Real payment rails (Venmo/Zelle-style), netting debts across expenses into fewer transfers, multi-currency, and running Tab on its own number instead of a team member's account.

title: Traycer: Food-waste Intelligence
tagline: See what food gets wasted, then waste less.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: It started at our college dining halls. We kept watching trays come back to the dish return with food still on them, meal after meal, and nobody could say what was being thrown away or why. The scale. The world wasted about 1.05 billion tonnes of food in 2022, 19% of all the food available. We throw away more than a billion meals' worth every day ( UNEP Food Waste Index 2024 ). The climate. Food loss and waste generate 8-10% of global greenhouse gas emissions, and are a particularly large source of methane (UNEP). Every uneaten portion carries the emissions and water it took to grow, move and cook it. Hunger and health. About 645 million people may have faced hunger in 2025, and 2.69 billion could not afford a healthy diet ( FAO, State of Food Security and Nutrition 2026 ). The cost. UNEP estimates food loss and waste costs upwards of $940 billion a year. For any kitchen, an uneaten portion is food it bought, prepared and paid someone to cook.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Traycer turns the trash bin into data. It shows a kitchen which foods people leave uneaten, how much, and what that waste costs the planet. Then it lets the kitchen test a smaller portion or a different menu in a simulated service before cooking anything, so it can cook and serve less of what ends up in the trash. 1. A camera reads every returned tray. A phone camera spots each tray and plate and recognizes the food on it using computer vision. A separate vision model works out how much of each food is left, tray by tray, as it happens. 2. Every gram becomes carbon, water and cost. A real-time dashboard totals leftovers by food and converts them into estimated carbon, water and cost, with everyday comparisons like miles driven and showers. 3. Change the menu before you cook it. Choose a change, like a smaller portion of the food that keeps coming back, and the simulator runs a full service with the same simulated diners based on past data, showing leftovers and CO₂e. Every diner is its own AI agent, deciding what to take, who to sit with and how much to eat. 4. Two AI characters you can call. A chef and a food waste consultant on Relay answer texts and take voice and video calls. The consultant explains which foods are being wasted most, while the chef suggests recipes and portion changes to address them. Both can look up tray data and saved simulation results, so kitchen staff can ask questions, talk through recommendations and understand how a proposed menu performed in the simulation.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built Traycer around a connected workflow: capture food waste, understand the patterns, propose menu changes, and test them in a simulated cafeteria. We turned a phone into a live camera that streams frames over WebSockets to a Python FastAPI backend. YOLO-World and OpenCV detect food and containers, while ByteTrack and our tracking logic help prevent the same tray from being counted twice. OpenAI vision refines food identification and estimates leftovers, with a review interface for staff to accept or reject captures. We store tray observations and photos in SpacetimeDB and display them in a dashboard showing waste by food, estimated cost, and environmental impact. Gemini summarizes the capture data into readable insights. We also built a 3D cafeteria using React, Three.js, and React Three Fiber. A Node.js worker uses OpenAI to drive individual simulated students’ food choices, eating behavior, and conversations, while shared TypeScript rules and SpacetimeDB manage the world and waste accounting. To make the findings actionable, we created two fictional AI assistants on Relay: LeBron, a food-waste consultant, and Gordon, a chef. Shared tools let them access camera reports, save recommendations, and retrieve simulation results. Pipecat and ElevenLabs support voice conversations, while SQLite preserves the evidence and links recommendations to their tests. Finally, we built a workflow to compare baseline and proposed menus using the same seeded student cohort, with repeated baseline runs to measure variability. The simulation helps explore potential changes; the camera provides the real-world evidence to verify them at the next service.

sections.heading: === SPONSORS ===
sections.text: Best Use of SpacetimeDB SpacetimeDB is the backend powering each and every component of Traycer. Three systems interact with two Spacetime modules across 25 tables: Computer vision writes what the camera sees. Our Python vision service sends every tray observation to the traycer-camera module. One reducer replaces that tray's food rows and recomputes the per-food and per-service totals for grams, carbon, water and cost in a single transaction, so the totals always match the trays. The tray photos live in the database too, as JPEG bytes in their own table, and the dashboard reads both straight from Maincloud. The agent simulation runs inside the database. A scheduled reducer ticks the world every 200 ms, handling movement, queues, seats, conversations and waste. When a student needs to decide something, the module writes a job row. Relay agents read both. Our video agents, LeBron and Gordon Ramsey, query the camera database and use that information to run informed simulations themselves. When LeBron says bagels are the biggest leftover, he is quoting the same rows the dashboard shows. The value for us was having one source of truth without building a backend for each system. Reducers gave us transactions, subscriptions gave us real-time sync for the simulation, and the worker and the 3D view can disconnect and reconnect without losing the world. Traycer architecture showing SpacetimeDB camera storage, authoritative cafeteria simulation, AI decision workers, live subscriptions, and the evidence bridge. Relay Interactive Agents We used Relay's agent audio and video calling capabilities to implement both an agent Gordon Ramsay, the world famous chef, and a commercial food waste agent consultant named Lebron into our cafeteria simulation. Lebron is able to read the food wastage CV data and the agent people's pattern data to figure out the Pareto-optimized simulation that has the least food waste, the least carbon emissions, and the most cost-savings via an agentic research loop. Gordon is able to read the agent people's opinion data on the menus to figure out the best recipe to serve to the agent people which would lead to the least food wastage. Talk to Gordon and get your recipes figured out. Best Use of Notability We used Notability as Traycer’s working notebook throughout the entire project, connecting handwritten product sketches and architecture diagrams with build checklists, debugging notes, and real detector outputs and dashboard screenshots that we annotated directly on the page. During a late-night team meeting, we also used recording + note sync to keep our discussion connected to our notes, bringing the proposed design, missed food detections, stale dashboard totals, and next tests into one place where someone else could follow our thinking. We absolutely loved collaborating on Notability! Our handwritten engineering plan in Notability: the proposed camera, vision, review, store and live UI pipeline, with the event contract, CO2e math, build gates and open decisions. A real photo test of the detector, annotated by hand in Notability: the boxes pick up the paper beside the plate and miss the pizza label, so we noted trying a tighter crop. Notability's audio recording and live transcript beside our handwritten test notes: 14 of 17 vision-model tests passed, and the same 3 failed until we forced the provider in a scratch run. Best Use of ElevenLabs We used ElevenLabs to animate our Relay agent chef Gordon Ramsay and commercial food waste consultant Lebron and also used it to give them a voice when they talk. For Gordon Ramsay, that means his signature angry British voice using the British preset voice "George" from ElevenLabs and for the consultant, we decided to have it speak in a professional, calm but also authoritative manner using the American preset voice "Eric" from ElevenLabs. For the agents speaking, we used the eleven_v4_turbo model and for the agents hearing, we used the scribe_v2_realtime model. [MLH] Best Use

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Across the team, we tackled three very different kinds of real-time systems. The camera needed to recognize leftovers without counting the same tray repeatedly. The simulation needed to coordinate independent AI diners while keeping movement, queues, conversations, and waste totals consistent. Our voice and video agents brought another set of challenges: calls could connect without carrying audio or video, and interruption detection sometimes cut off replies before they finished. We worked through tracking rules, agent validation, network routing, and turn-taking to address those problems. Bringing everything together also meant giving the dashboard, conversational agents, and simulation shared records so they could refer to the same findings, recommendations, and test results.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're proud of how much we built together: a live camera and waste dashboard, a 3D dining simulation, and two AI characters people can text or call with voice and video. In the simulation, diners have distinct personalities, choose their food, talk to one another, and leave different amounts behind. The dashboard turns tray captures into estimated cost, carbon, and water impact, with Gemini summarizing the findings. We also connected our food-waste consultant and chef to shared evidence, saved recommendations, and simulation results, creating a workflow from identifying waste to proposing and testing a menu change. Seeing each teammate's work contribute to that shared experience was one of the most rewarding parts of the hackathon.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned how to bring computer vision, real-time cloud data, and AI agents together into a working product. Building Traycer taught us how to track objects across video frames, give vision models clearer instructions, and keep a dashboard synchronized with incoming captures. Creating the dining simulation also gave us experience coordinating individual AI agents within a shared world. Beyond the technical work, we learned how much product design matters: translating food waste into carbon, water, and cost makes the data easier to understand, while pairing it with a suggested action gives kitchens a clear next step.

sections.heading: What's next for Traycer: Food-waste intelligence
sections.text: Next, we want to give Traycer new ways to prevent waste. It will forecast how much of each dish a kitchen should prepare, nudge cooks mid-service when a pan is running too full, and route surplus that was never served to food banks and compost instead of the trash. It will track every kitchen's carbon, water and savings over time, so a restaurant group, hotel chain or caterer can compare sites and report real progress, and it will steer menus toward lower-carbon swaps that people actually eat. Our goal is a kitchen that knows what it would waste before it cooks, and cooks less of it. P.S. Spot the Easter egg: our simulated diners are rocking sponsor merch and U-M gear. Go Blue!

title: AI-powered Investment Portfolio Creator
tagline: By answering a few simple prompts, the app creates a stock market investment portfolio based on key criteria. Leveraging powerful technologies such as React, Flask, and data from Yahoo Finance.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We know investing can be really daunting for new investors, so we wanted to make a quick and easy way for beginner investors to start by giving them a personalized portfolio.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: The app generates a tailored portfolio based off of user responses to the given prompts.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built it using react for the front end and flask for the back end of the web app. We also used Yahoo finance for real time and historical data from the stock market.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Connecting front and back end, deploying the web app

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Integrated an LLM,

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Having a clear initial scope for a project helped save time. Writing tests. Learned to find resources online.

title: RxSolve
tagline: Supporting America's independent pharmacies.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We realized that it wasn't necessarily just potential patients that were potentially getting the bad end of the stick from many health insurance cos. it could also be independent pharmacies. Pharmacy Benefit Managers, or PBM's are insurance middlemen that routinely deny a pharmacy its full claim for a given set of medication for no valid reason. CVS and Walgreens may be able to muscle around the PBM's, but your local pharmacy may heavily struggle with such a procedure.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our customers just see their own portals where they submit claims from. However, now RxSolve comes in between our customers and the PBM's to ensure that the PBM's cannot rip off our customers. Our AI agents fight with the PBM until we can figure out a path to being fully reimbursed for our claims. Our agent is only satisfied after recovering as much cash as possible from the PBM for a given claim.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built RxSolve as a TypeScript/Bun monorepo with three main pieces: an API orchestrator, a standalone PBM simulator, and a dashboard. The API checks paid claims for underpayment, gathers evidence, and routes appeals through simulated portal, email, or fax channels. Gemini helps with evidence extraction and negotiation, while deterministic rules handle clear underpayments and PBM decisions. The dashboard shows the claim journey, evidence and communications, ledger activity, and recovery chart. A separate PMS mock demonstrates that the pharmacy can keep using its existing workflow. TigerData stores claim and event data, and Capital One Nessie provides the sandbox ledger.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: PBM appeals don’t follow one universal process: each channel can require different evidence, and a seemingly small omission, like an invoice number or wholesaler attestation, can block a claim. We had to make those differences visible while ensuring the agent never files with incomplete evidence or invents missing facts. At the end of the day minor imperfections in the agent could cost our client pharmacies huge repayment potential. Integrating with the Nessie sandbox also required adapting our logical transfers to the API’s actual transaction behavior.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We built a working end-to-end demonstration of a paid claim being identified as underpaid, routed through an appeal, supplied with missing wholesaler information, and recovered. The demo covers three distinct appeal channels, such as portal, email, and fax and shows their artifacts alongside each claim’s status. We’re also proud that the pharmacy PMS stays separate from RxSolve: the claim enters through the pharmacy’s (mock, we dont have access to a real pharmacy) system, while recovery work happens alongside it. This means that our agents operate independently of a certain pharmacy's system, and the pharmacy does not need to use our application all the time, rather just setting up once and being able to rely on us.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that automating a workflow is more than just guiding models to their next steps. It always needs clear rules about what the system may decide, evidence for what it does, and a safe path to stop and ask a person when information is missing or uncertain.

sections.heading: What's next for RxSolve
sections.text: We’d expand support for unfamiliar PBM forms, with strict limits on which fields an agent can fill, and further test the optional browser-based portal and voice features. Long-term, we’d validate the workflow against real pharmacy and PBM requirements before moving beyond a simulated demo environment, and see how we can scale out solution to those pharmacies.

title: CrediWise - Use the right card, every time.
tagline: Crediwise is a Chrome extension that auto-detects checkout pages and recommends the best credit card to maximize cashback and rewards, while tracking savings and giving AI-powered smart suggestions.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every checkout feels like a guessing game: “Which card should I use?” Most of us don’t know which of our cards gives the best rewards or cashback at that moment. Studies show that people miss out on millions in rewards because they don’t optimize card usage. We wanted to solve this problem in a way that’s effortless — no manual lookups, no entering merchants. That’s how Crediwise was born: a Chrome extension that’s always there at checkout, making sure you swipe smart and save more.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Auto-detects checkout pages across domains (Amazon, Spotify, Delta, etc.). Instantly recommends the best card to maximize rewards/cashback, factoring in base rates and public offers. Provides a savings summary dashboard: How much you’ve saved so far, What other cards would have offered, Category breakdowns and overall performance Tracks lifetime savings and generates AI-powered insights about spending patterns.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Extension (MV3): Detects checkout flows, extracts domain/total, and injects a non-intrusive banner with the best card recommendation. Backend (Flask, Python): Scrapers (Bright Data MCP) pull public offers and rotating categories, normalize into structured data, and refresh every few hours via GitHub Actions. Database (Supabase, Postgres): Stores offers and user profiles. Redis (Upstash) used for fast caching. Dashboard (React + Tailwind): Shows savings summary, category breakdown, card comparisons, and AI-powered insights. Designed for auto-visualization: line charts for trends, pie charts for proportions, bar charts for comparisons. LLM Integration (LLama): Used for parsing unstructured offer terms & conditions into structured rules (merchant, min spend, expiry). Also powers AI-generated insights in the dashboard (e.g., “Most of your savings this month came from streaming — consider adding a dining rewards card next”).

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Offer scraping: Card issuers format offers inconsistently. Normalizing them into one schema required careful parsing. CORS and extension security: Communicating between extension, backend, and UI meant carefully managing Chrome MV3 permissions.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Built a full-stack system in a short timeframe: Chrome extension + backend + scrapers + dashboard, all working together seamlessly. Ensured the system is privacy-first — no sensitive card data stored, only issuer/rewards profiles.

sections.heading: What we learned

title: LoadCheck
tagline: LoadCheck helps owner-operator truck drivers uncover the true profit behind every load, build better routes, and prevent cash shortfalls before the wheels move.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Independent owner-operator truck drivers often receive load offers through texts, emails, and screenshots and must decide quickly whether a job is worth accepting. The advertised dollars per mile can look profitable, but that number may leave out deadhead miles, fuel, maintenance, fixed operating costs, dispatcher fees, and upcoming bills. We created LoadCheck because a load that looks good on paper can leave a driver with very little actual profit—or even create a cash shortage before payment arrives. We wanted to give drivers one place to answer a practical question: Should I accept this load, negotiate a better rate, skip it, or build a stronger route?

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: LoadCheck turns a basic load offer into a complete trip decision. A driver can paste an offer or upload a screenshot. Gemini extracts information such as the pickup location, destination, rate, mileage, and delivery times. Before any calculations happen, the driver receives an editable confirmation screen to correct or approve the extracted information. After confirmation, LoadCheck: Calculates the load’s true estimated profit after expenses Includes loaded and empty miles in the analysis Compares the advertised rate with the true net rate Suggests a counteroffer based on the driver’s target profit Searches combinations of up to three loads Considers pickup windows, delivery deadlines, driving limits, and rest periods Identifies stronger home-to-home routes Combines trip expenses with upcoming bills to predict cash shortages Shows whether a delivery advance could keep the trip funded Instead of only showing numbers, LoadCheck explains what those numbers mean and gives the driver a clear next step.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built the frontend with React and TypeScript , creating separate interfaces for offer confirmation, profitability results, route comparison, and the cash-flow timeline. Our backend uses FastAPI and Python . We separated the main calculations into dedicated modules: profit.py calculates load economics and counteroffers optimizer.py searches for feasible multi-load routes cashflow.py simulates balances, expenses, bills, and advances geo.py estimates mileage and caches location data We used Gemini to read unstructured offers and explain completed results in plain language. However, Gemini does not control the financial calculations. Every number shown to the driver comes from deterministic Python code. We also integrated the Capital One Nessie API to supply sandbox banking activity, upcoming bills, and advance information. Cached cities, recorded sandbox data, and offline map support help keep the main demo functional if an external service becomes unavailable.

sections.heading: Challenges we faced
sections.text: One of our biggest challenges was extracting consistent information from load offers because they can appear in many formats. Screenshots may have missing labels, shortened city names, or information arranged differently. We addressed this by requiring the driver to confirm and edit the extracted fields before calculations begin. Another challenge was separating AI-generated explanations from reliable financial calculations. We wanted the convenience of AI without allowing it to invent mileage, costs, or profit. Our solution was to let AI handle extraction and explanation while pure Python functions handle every calculation. Route optimization was also challenging because the best-paying loads do not always form a realistic trip. We had to account for pickup windows, delivery deadlines, travel time, empty miles, simplified hours-of-service limits, and whether the route returned the driver home. Finally, combining profitability with cash flow required us to distinguish between earning money eventually and having enough money to complete the trip today . A trip may be profitable overall but still become impossible if a major bill arrives before the carrier pays the driver.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that good AI integration is not about giving AI control over every part of a product. It is about choosing where AI is useful and where predictable code is safer. We also learned that profitability and cash flow are different problems. Calculating that a driver will earn money is not enough if the driver cannot afford fuel, food, or a truck payment while waiting to be paid. From a technical perspective, we gained experience connecting a React frontend to a FastAPI backend, processing image-based input, designing optimization logic, integrating external APIs, and creating fallbacks for unreliable services.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud that LoadCheck connects several decisions that are usually handled separately. It can read an offer, verify its details, calculate its true value, find a stronger route, and identify a possible cash shortage in one workflow. We are also proud of making the system transparent. LoadCheck clearly labels simulated and sandbox information and explains its assumptions, including estimated road mileage, average driving speed, and simplified hours-of-service rules. To validate the project, we completed: 100 passing backend tests 15 out of 15 end-to-end demo checks Testing with 60 simulated load-board offers A three-load route search designed to complete in under one second

sections.heading: What's next for LoadCheck
sections.text: Our next step would be to replace estimated mileage with live commercial-routing data and expand the hours-of-service model to include more federal regulations. We would also like to connect LoadCheck to real load boards, fuel-price services, accounting platforms, and authorized banking data. Long term, LoadCheck could learn a driver’s preferred routes, operating costs, home-time goals, and risk tolerance. This would allow it to provide more personalized recommendations while keeping the final decision in the driver’s hands. LoadCheck helps owner-operators make the decision before the wheels move.

title: Runway
tagline: See the dip before it happens. Get help without the spotlight

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Payday is Friday. Rent is due Thursday. For millions of people living paycheck to paycheck, that one-day gap is the whole problem: an overdraft fee, a declined card, or the text nobody wants to send: "can you spot me $100?" When we talked through it, two things kept coming up. People avoid looking at their balance until it's too late, and asking for help is the hardest part : it's embarrassing, and it invites questions about your spending. Being asked can be just as hard: the person helping might be stretched too. Banking apps warn you after you're low. We wanted a bank feature that sees the dip coming and quietly arranges help from people who already said yes, without anyone seeing anyone else's money.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Runway forecasts your checking balance day by day, 30 days out , from your Capital One accounts, and tells you in one sentence when you'd run short: "You're fine until Thu, Oct 22." What-if: tap "$100" and the forecast updates instantly. Ask Runway: a Gemini assistant answers "Can I afford concert tickets Friday?" with real numbers. The AI picks the tool; a deterministic engine does the maths. Quiet Support Agreements: family or friends agree, in advance, to cover short gaps. Both people must say yes. Network Guardian: when a dip is coming, Runway checks each supporter's own forecast for the whole time the money is out, works out what each can give safely, and moves real Nessie money, split across supporters if needed. Repayment when safe: it goes back automatically after a verified paycheck, never in a way that causes a new dip. You can also pay back early, in full or in part. Circles: named groups (Family, Weekend crew) with invite links and pop-up invitations. Send or request money ("$40 · 🎉 Festival"). An activity timeline explains every decision from your side. Privacy by design: supporters see only what they covered and when it comes back. Never your balance, spending, or why. Every sign-in and approval goes through Auth0. In our demo, Maya (20) would be $135 short on Thursday. Sam agreed to cover up to $150, but a loan payment lands before Maya could repay, so his safe amount is $90. Jordan's mortgage is due that week, so his is $0, and he isn't even told. Emma covers $45. $90 + $45 = $135. Runway protects the protector.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Capital One Nessie API: customers, accounts, bills, merchants, purchases, deposits and transfers (8 endpoints). Every money move is a real sandbox transfer plus a deposit. FastAPI backend with a deterministic forecast engine : recurring-payment detection, a bootstrap range, and a calibrated cautious low. The AI never does the maths. Tiger Data (TimescaleDB): transactions as a hypertable, daily spend as a continuous aggregate, plus agreements, decisions and the transfer journal. Google Gemini for Ask Runway, with tool calling and a grounding guard: any dollar figure that doesn't trace back to the engine is discarded. Auth0: PKCE sign-in, verified tokens, owner-only money moves, and approvals. Expo (React Native) for one codebase across web, iOS and Android. Vultr + Caddy: every merge to main deploys itself after lint, tests and a build. Claude as our engineering partner throughout: design, code, reviews and security fixes. How the Network Guardian decides a safe amount. For each supporter, it takes the smallest of three limits, rounded down to the nearest $5: Their cautious lowest balance (5th percentile) over the whole time the money would be out, minus the cushion they keep. The room left in their agreement with this person: their limit minus what's already out. The room left under their total cap across everyone they support. If the supporter's forecast isn't confident yet, nothing is automatic. When several people are short at once, shared supporters are split fewest options first .

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Nessie transfers don't carry a recipient , so every move is a transfer on the sender plus a deposit on the receiver. Nessie also truncates cents, so we store integer cents. Never paying twice. A bank call can time out after the money moved. Every transfer is written to a journal before it's sent, tagged, and an unclear result is reconciled against Nessie rather than retried. Postgres advisory locks and compare-and-set updates stop two decisions from racing. Privacy leaks in unexpected places. A "support on hold" notification would have told a supporter when someone was short, and a one-sided offer could have made someone reachable. We ran about 20 security reviews and fixed every finding. Consent without assumptions. Old limits were migrated with no consent; support only becomes active once both people agree. Production surprises: a 5-connection database pool ran out under real traffic, which made the assistant fall back to rules. We raised it to 15 and made it fail fast.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Real money, not just recommendations: every cover, repayment and send is a verified Nessie sandbox transfer. Evals we can show: Privacy: 15/15 attacks held (including prompt injection) with the guard switched off . Network Guardian: 0 unsafe transfers across 2,000 simulated networks, and it catches deliberately broken versions of itself. Agent: 100% tool selection, 97–100% correct answers across three runs, and 100% of dollar figures grounded on live Gemini (63 questions). Forecast: 66% lower balance error than bills alone ($138 vs $408 across an 18-fold backtest), with 81% of real days inside the predicted range. 570+ tests run on every push, and dozens of small PRs reviewed and merged by a team of three.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: The hardest part of fintech isn't the AI. It's consent, idempotency and privacy : who agreed, did the money move exactly once, and what is each person allowed to see. Letting an LLM pick tools but never do maths made the assistant both useful and trustworthy. A forecast should say how sure it is. Planning for the cautious low, not the average, is what keeps supporters safe.

sections.heading: What's next for Runway
sections.text: Test with real users (our early research used a simulated panel) and partner with a bank sandbox that proves account ownership. Phone push approvals for over-limit help (Auth0 CIBA), and Guardian MFA required for every money move. Smarter repayment plans, and support networks that grow beyond family and close friends. Bringing it where it belongs: inside the banking app people already use, free and with nothing to link. One gap for the AI prize: this write-up never mentions the custom models, and that's what those judges look for first. I'd add these two bullets under "How we built it", right after the Gemini line: Custom models on outside data: we calibrated the forecast's cautious range (split conformal) on IBM TabFormer, a real UK bank account and 4,500 real Czech accounts. How often it's wrong went from up to 43% to about 5%. A LightGBM spending model lost on new data, so we didn't ship it. A formality model trained on 11,000 human-rated sentences, so Ask Runway's tone follows how you write, on top of your age (replies matched how people wrote 19/24 times vs 3/24 with age alone).

title: Dristi
tagline: Have you ever imagined a world where navigation is effortless, safety is guaranteed, and health is monitored- all with just a backpack?

sections.text: Inspiration Imagine navigating your daily routine blindfolded—simple tasks become daunting, and the world feels unpredictable. This is the reality for approximately 245 million individuals living with visual impairments. Every step they take is fraught with challenges, from avoiding obstacles to ensuring personal safety. Inspired by their resilience, we developed "Dristi," a smart bag designed to empower visually impaired individuals, making their journeys safer and more confident. What it does We built a smart bag designed to assist visually impaired individuals. With a simple tap of a button, it sends an emergency alert to a designated contact. The bag monitors posture, measures environmental and body temperatures, and detects obstacles using a webcam and ultrasonic sensors. All information is relayed through a connected web application that provides real-time vocal guidance, enhancing the user's safety and confidence. How we built it with We combined hardware innovation with intuitive software design: Hardware: Software: Challenges we ran into Merging multiple sensors into a cohesive, reliable system proved to be more challenging than anticipated. Coordinating diverse data streams required solutions, especially when our ultrasonic sensor intermittently failed to operate as expected, undermining real-time obstacle detection. Additionally, capturing and reliably saving analog data signals was a persistent struggle due to noise and instability. Accomplishments that we're proud of Successfully integrating diverse sensors into a unified system that performs reliably in real-world conditions. Developing an accessible web application that offers clear, real-time audio guidance. Creating a solution that not only addresses safety but also enhances everyday confidence and independence. What we learned Every test and setback taught us the value of iteration. Continuous feedback from real users helped us quickly identify issues and refine our approach, making the end product more reliable and user-friendly. Bringing multiple sensor technologies together into one cohesive system highlighted the complexity of system integration. We learned that careful calibration and robust data management are essential to ensure every component works in harmony for a safe and confident user experience. What's next for Dristi Looking ahead, we envision integrating advanced technologies to further enhance "Dristi." Incorporating artificial intelligence could enable real-time scene descriptions and object recognition, providing users with a comprehensive understanding of their surroundings. Advanced haptic feedback mechanisms could convey information through touch, such as obstacle proximity or navigation cues, enhancing spatial awareness. Additionally, developing wearable components, like smart glasses or wristbands, that sync with the bag could offer discreet alerts and information, promoting seamless assistance. By embracing these innovations, "Dristi" can transform into a comprehensive, solution, significantly improving the quality of life for not only visually impaired individuals but also for those who want to live a enriched lifestyle.

title: FirstWave

sections.text: Spearphishing remains one of the most pervasive security threats, and standard training often fails to replicate modern social engineering tactics. sections.heading: What it does

AI-Driven Engagement: Our advanced AI agents generate convincing, fake LinkedIn profiles using only publicly available data. These agents then engage with your employees, mimicking real-world phishing interactions. Performance Analysis: After each campaign, receive a detailed report outlining how the target engaged, highlighting vulnerabilities, and providing actionable insights to strengthen your defenses. Proactive Training: By exposing employees to realistic phishing scenarios, FirstWave equips them with the knowledge and resilience needed to protect sensitive data against actual malicious actors.

sections.heading: How we built it

Data Privacy: We rely solely on publicly available LinkedIn data, ensuring that our simulations respect privacy boundaries while remaining effective. Analytics Dashboard: A secure, real-time dashboard tracks key performance metrics, offering clear insights into each campaign’s outcomes and guiding targeted follow-up training.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: The journey of building FirstWave taught us valuable lessons: Realism is Key: Immersive, realistic simulations are essential for effective cybersecurity training. Ethical AI Design: It's possible to deploy potent AI solutions without compromising ethical standards. Data-Driven Improvements: Continuous analysis and feedback are vital for evolving and strengthening security protocols.

Broader Integration: Expand our campaign capabilities across additional social media platforms and communication channels. Automated Training: Develop integrated training modules that automatically adapt based on each employee's performance, ensuring ongoing improvement and readiness against real threats. By turning the tables on cyber threats, FirstWave sets a new standard in proactive cybersecurity—arming your organization with the insights and skills needed to keep sensitive information safe from modern phishing tactics.

title: AffectLink
tagline: AffectLink provides real-time multimodal emotion insights for tele-health with HP AI Studio. Uncovers hidden cues via facial, audio, & text analysis, boosting clinician understanding & patient care.

sections.text: HP AI Studio Project Story (Reworked) AffectLink: Bridging the Empathy Gap in Tele-Healthcare with Multimodal AI

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The rapid shift to tele-health has brought convenience but also a significant challenge: how do clinicians truly understand a patient's emotional state when nuanced non-verbal cues are often lost through a screen? Traditional tele-health lacks the rich emotional context present in in-person interactions. This inspired AffectLink , a project aimed at empowering mental health professionals with deeper, data-driven insights into patient emotions during virtual sessions, ultimately improving care.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: AffectLink is a real-time, local-first AI application designed to provide comprehensive emotional analysis by processing three key modalities: facial expressions, speech tone (audio emotion), and spoken content (text emotion) . Our core innovation, the Emotional Consistency Index (ECI) , synthesizes these independent emotional streams, highlighting when a patient's verbal message might diverge from their non-verbal cues. For example, a patient might say "I'm fine," but their facial expression or tone suggests underlying distress. AffectLink surfaces these critical discrepancies, acting as a powerful tool for clinicians to identify unexpressed emotions and guide their therapeutic approach. All processing occurs securely and locally on the HP workstation, ensuring patient privacy and HIPAA compliance.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: AffectLink was built from the ground up to showcase the power and security of HP AI Studio for real-time, on-device AI inference. Our technical workflow is as follows: Data Capture: Live video and audio streams are captured from the user's webcam and microphone. Orchestration ( main_processor.py ): This central component manages the overall pipeline, distributing data to specialized AI modules and aggregating their results. Facial Emotion Analysis: Video frames are sent to a Video Emotion Processor which utilizes DeepFace (running locally). While we aimed for full AI Studio integration, due to specific complexities encountered during the hackathon timeframe, DeepFace is currently executed directly via its Python library to detect and classify facial expressions in real-time on the local machine. Audio Processing: Audio chunks are sent to an Audio Pre-processor . This module prepares the audio for the deployed AI models. HP AI Studio Integration (Swagger API): This is a core highlight. Our Whisper (ASR) model for speech-to-text transcription, our Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) model for vocal tone analysis, and our Text Emotion model (for analyzing transcribed text) are all successfully registered and deployed locally via HP AI Studio's Swagger API . This ensures secure, high-performance, and on-device inference without cloud dependency for these critical AI components. Multimodal Fusion: The main_processor.py receives results from all modalities (facial, audio emotion, text emotion, and transcription). It then calculates the Emotional Consistency Index , providing a unified view of the patient's emotional state. Data Visualization (Streamlit): All processed data, including live video frames and emotion metrics, are written to local temporary files ( affectlink_emotion.json , affectlink_frame.jpg ). This method of inter-process communication was chosen for efficient real-time updates. The AffectLink Streamlit UI dashboard then reads these files, providing an intuitive, interactive display for clinicians. MLflow Tracking: Throughout the development process, MLflow was leveraged within HP AI Studio to track experiments, manage model versions, and log metrics, ensuring full reproducibility and control over our AI models.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Real-time Performance: Balancing complex multimodal AI models with real-time performance on local hardware was a significant challenge. We optimized frame processing rates and experimented with different model sizes (e.g., Whisper 'tiny' or 'base'). Synchronization: Ensuring accurate synchronization between video frames, audio chunks, and their corresponding emotional analyses was crucial for the ECI. We implemented robust timestamping and buffering mechanisms. DeepFace Integration with AI Studio Deployment: We encountered integration complexities with the DeepFace library within the hackathon's compressed timeline. This led us to handle facial emotion analysis locally via direct Python library calls rather than deploying it via AI Studio's Swagger API like our other models. HP AI Studio Deployment: Configuring and deploying other models (ASR, SER, Text Emotion) to the local Swagger API within HP AI Studio required careful attention to environment dependencies and API endpoint definitions.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Successful Local-First AI Deployment with HP AI Studio: We successfully registered and deployed our Whisper (ASR), Speech Emotion Recognition (SER), and Text Emotion models locally via HP AI Studio's Swagger API, demonstrating secure, high-performance, and on-device inference without cloud dependency. Novel Emotional Consistency Index (ECI): Developed and implemented the ECI to synthesize multimodal emotional streams, providing unique insights into discrepancies between verbal and non-verbal cues. Robust Real-time Multimodal Pipeline: Built a functioning real-time pipeline integrating facial expressions, speech tone, and spoken content analysis on local hardware. Effective Inter-process Communication: Implemented efficient local file-based communication for seamless data flow between AI processing modules and the Streamlit UI, achieving real-time visualization. Strong Privacy and HIPAA Focus: Delivered a "local-first" design directly addressing ethical concerns in healthcare AI by ensuring no sensitive patient data leaves the device. MLflow Integration: Leveraged MLflow within HP AI Studio for comprehensive experiment tracking, model versioning, and metric logging, ensuring reproducibility.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Diverse Model Packaging Requirements: The DeepFace integration challenge reinforced our understanding of diverse model packaging requirements and the importance of a clear, iterative development process within HP AI Studio to overcome such hurdles. HP AI Studio Deployment Best Practices: We learned best practices for packaging models and managing their lifecycle within the platform, including the efficiency gains from consolidating audio-related models into a single environment. Optimization for Local Performance: Gained insights into optimizing frame processing rates and model sizes for real-time performance on local hardware. Ethical AI Design: Reinforced the importance of a "local-first" design as a key strategy for ensuring patient privacy and HIPAA compliance in sensitive AI applications like healthcare.

sections.heading: What's next for AffectLink
sections.text: AffectLink has the potential to significantly impact the healthcare industry by providing clinicians with a vital "sixth sense" in tele-health. Beyond mental health, the multimodal analysis framework could be adapted for sales training, customer service, or even remote education, providing real-time feedback on emotional engagement and comprehension. Its secure, local deployment model makes it highly attractive for sensitive enterprise applications. Future enhancements could include exploring more advanced fusion techniques for the ECI, integrating more deeply with Electronic Health Records (EHR) systems, and potentially expanding to other biometric signals.

title: AgentBIM
tagline: RAG enabled BIM authoring and processing using natural language

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: I was inspired by the challenge of making BIM data more accessible and interactive. Working with BIM models can be tedious, often with multiple back-and-forths. I wanted to create a tool that would allow them to query and explore building information using natural language, simplifying decision-making and collaboration.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: AgentBIM is an intelligent agent that leverages natural language processing and graph databases to provide interactive access to BIM data. Users can ask questions about building elements, relationships, and spatial properties using plain English. AgentBIM translates these queries into AQL for an ArangoDB graph, which is built from parsed IFC data using IfcOpenShell and NetworkX. It then returns the relevant information, visualized or in text, making BIM data intuitive and actionable.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: I started by developing a Python script using IfcOpenShell to parse IFC files and extract building elements and relationships. This data was then transformed into a NetworkX graph for analysis. I used ArangoDB to store the graph data, leveraging its graph database capabilities. The "ArangoGraphQAChain" was implemented using LangChain, which connected the natural language interface to the ArangoDB database. I also incorporated a front-end interface built with Gradio to enhance user interaction.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Parsing complex IFC files and accurately mapping them to a graph database proved challenging. I struggled with handling various relationship types and ensuring data consistency. Developing a robust natural language processing pipeline that could accurately interpret diverse queries was also difficult. Integrating all these components into a seamless workflow required extensive debugging and optimization.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Created a system that allows users to query BIM data using natural language. AgentBIM demonstrates the potential of AI to revolutionize the construction industry.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: I gained valuable experience in working with IFC files, graph databases, and natural language processing. I also discovered the power of natural language interfaces for making complex data accessible.

sections.heading: What's next for AgentBIM
sections.text: I plan to expand AgentBIM's capabilities by incorporating more advanced natural language processing techniques, including intent recognition and context awareness. I'll also focus on improving the visualization of query results and adding support for more complex queries. I am going to add more robust error handling and increase the amount of IFC properties that are parsed.

title: AskStreets: Querying and Visualizing Street Networks
tagline: An agentic AI app that uses OpenStreetMap data to answer queries and generate insights into geographic street networks.

sections.text: 🛣️ AskStreets: Query and Visualizing Street Networks using OpenStreetMap, ArangoDB, and LangGraph Author: Adam Munawar Rahman, March 2025 Using powerful open-source libraries like OSMnx, we can retrieve geographic features and street network datasets from OpenStreetMap and persist them as graphs and collections in ArangoDB. Then, via a LangGraph ReAct agent, we feed natural language queries to LLM-based tools to execute complex lookups, run GPU-backed graph algorithms, and visualize geospatial coordinates. This agentic app enables meaningful insights into the network properties of the desired geographic location, and empowers us to address real-world infrastructure challenges.

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.text: Python 3.10 An ArangoDB instance, e.g. a local Docker container (for GPU acceleration) Nvidia CUDA toolkit, a compatible NVIDIA GPU, and RAPIDS (follow the install guide here ) A credentials.yml file with API keys for your desired AI platform (see sample file in repo)

sections.heading: Running the Code
sections.text: Clone the repo, then in the askstreets directory: python3.10 -m venv env source env/bin/activate pip3 install -r requirements.txt Ensure your ArangoDB instance is running, e.g. to startup the local Docker container: docker run -e ARANGO_ROOT_PASSWORD=<root_password> -p 8529:8529 arangodb/arangodb Then startup the Jupyter server and load the desired notebook: jupyter-notebook askstreets-gpu.ipynb There are two versions of the AskStreets notebook: askstreets-gpu.ipynb which is the hackathon submission with GPU acceleration and fully answered query samples askstreets.ipynb which has cleared cell output and does not have GPU acceleration askstreets-gpu.ipynb also contains output for additional queries that were not demo'd in the video submission.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: During my internship at UNICEF Innovation in NYC, I used OpenStreetMap, OSMnx, and NetworkX to calculate distances between schools and health facilities in UNICEF programme countries using national street and road networks. By writing code to execute graph algorithms, I was able to generate data to address a real-world issue. I would like to generalize this challenge towards a broader use case: if you're a city planner, business owner, architect, etc., you may wish to ask questions about street networks (e.g. accessibility of services, routed distances between landmarks, crowded intersections, etc.) without needing to code lengthy algorithms. This is where AskStreets comes in: by providing the ability to translate natural language queries into street network analysis.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: The Jupyter Notebook submission contains the proof-of-concept for AskStreets. The agentic app uses a LangGraph ReAct agent that accepts user queries and calls multiple tools that can geocode, generate and run AQL, generate and run OSMnx/NetworkX code, and visualize points on a Folium map. By passing a query to the query_street_network function, it will invoke the ReAct agent to run these tools to interpret the query, execute code, and provide a natural language response or map visualization for the specific question.

sections.heading: How I built it
sections.text: I used OSMnx to download street network graphs and geographic features for certain locations, prepared this data to load into ArangoDB, then wrote the LLM-based tools and ReAct agent code for the agentic app.

sections.heading: Challenges I ran into
sections.text: Prompt engineering was a large aspect of this project; I needed to revise the prompts per tool multiple times as I continuously tested and analyzed the output of the ReAct agent, so that I could provide the AI models with more context to accurately interpret user queries and assemble the correct code. Modifying the tools to work in tandem with each other to generate the correct intermediate queries to pass between them was also challenging, but ultimately rewarding.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that I'm proud of
sections.text: I particularly enjoyed seeing the outcome of these tools, which are able to accurately interpret user queries about street networks and correctly identify the geographic attributes to filter or run algorithms against. I especially appreciated that by loading additional datasets like OpenStreetMap features and health facility data into ArangoDB, along with the graph network, the AQL tool was able to pull data across these sources to answer user queries with a higher degree of specificity.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.text: I learned how to work with the LangChain and LangGraph libraries, how to invoke LLMs and prompt engineer to improve answers to queries, and how to prepare OSMnx data to load into ArangoDB.

sections.heading: Citations
sections.text: Boeing, G. (2024). Modeling and Analyzing Urban Networks and Amenities with OSMnx. Working paper. https://geoffboeing.com/publications/osmnx-paper/

sections.heading: What's next for AskStreets
sections.text: Working with geospatial data has so much potential! In the submission notebook, I demonstrate at the end how health facility data can be overlaid with the street network graph and OpenStreetMap features data so that it can also be queried by AQL. By overlaying and combining even more data sets, we can enhance the app's ability to answer many different types of queries. Due to joining the hackathon late, there were tools I would have liked to fully implement but lacked refinement time. For example, a tool to dynamically pull in more data from the OpenStreetMap API based on a user query, a tool to more accurately translate location names, or updates to the visualization tool to draw paths between points. The tool prompts could also be further tuned to be more precise and avoid redundant operations. Different models could be deployed for each tool for their particular use case, with more lightweight models assigned to easier tasks. This app can be further enriched with a UI that can not only accept queries, but also automatically download OSM road networks and features from a user-specified location. It can even be integrated with a sophisticated mapping tool like kepler.gl that offers more visualization options for large geospatial datasets.

title: Codence
tagline: Codence is an AI agent that turns meeting decisions into enforceable specs by syncing Jira tickets and validating GitLab code against agreed rules.

sections.heading: 🧠 About the Project
sections.text: What inspired us Modern product development moves fast, but alignment often lags behind. Now, with AI tools writing code faster than ever, we’re seeing an ironic gap: speed has increased — but product quality hasn’t. Teams can generate code in seconds, but if that code doesn’t reflect the latest meeting decisions, it's just fast wrong work. We were inspired by this growing mismatch between decision-making and implementation . PMs spend hours manually checking Jira tickets. Developers unknowingly violate specs that were never updated. We asked: What if an AI could watch over these processes and enforce alignment? That’s how Codence was born — to make sure product consensus becomes code reality. What we learned We learned that: Meeting notes are messy, but full of hidden structure. Developers don’t ignore specs—they often never see them. The gap between decisions and delivery is often process, not intent. We also realized how powerful LLMs can be when paired with source-of-truth systems like Jira and GitLab. How we built it Frontend : A minimal web interface for uploading meeting notes and reviewing suggestions. Backend : Python + FastAPI with GitLab webhook integration. AI : GPT-based models extract decisions and rules from unstructured meeting notes. DevOps : GitLab Webhook triggers Codence to validate PRs against extracted rules. Jira Integration : Syncs ticket updates through REST APIs after human approval. Challenges we faced Parsing casual, non-standard meeting notes into structured intent. Mapping natural language decisions to specific Jira tickets and code actions. Avoiding false positives in code rule checks while keeping responses fast. Making the AI explain why something violates a rule in human-readable terms. Despite the constraints of time and scope, we’re proud that Codence brings alignment closer to automation.

title: Data Engineer's Buddy
tagline: Using ArangoDB & NetworkX for AI-powered management of enterprise data

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Problem Statement Data in large organizations is spread across multiple DBs on several different DBMS This results in a significant cost of operation from a data engineering standpoint. Proposal Over the course of this hackathon, I've explored how ArangoDB & NetworkX can be used to aid AI in the management of enterprise data. A variety of tasks such as data cataloging, lineage tracking, day-to-day data operations which traditionally requires the collaboration of several teams could be done within minutes by storing the metadata in a multimodal DB such as ArangoDB. Packages & libraries such as NetworkX & CuGraph can then be leveraged by AI agents to deliver insights & perform data engineering tasks within minutes. The multimodal offering of ArangoDB allows for metadata to be stored in such a way that a variety of data engineering tasks can easily be performed withing minutes.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Note: For this hackathon, I've focused on the data engineering tasks that can be performed by AI agents as that is universal & applicable to all enterprises. The delivery of insights is specific to the data & hence won't be applicable to everyone so I've chosen to focus on that at this stage. DEBy - Data Engineer's Buddy is an intelligent agentic app that assists with Data Operations in Enterprises At this stage, DEBy is able to: Identify upstreams & downstreams Assist with ETL Refresh scheduling Intelligently calculate refresh delays Perform impact analysis resulting from changes in a data model

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Data - I've stored the relationships between data structures in the form of Arango Graph & metadata such as refresh details in the form of Arango Collections App - Created using Python, LangChain, LangGraph & OpenAI API

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Identifying the best way to leverage multimodal features of ArangoDB to capture the structure of enterprise data Agent had to learn the relationships between enterprise data structures & the nature of dependencies Teaching the agent data operation tasks

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Using ArangoDB to capture the relationships between SQL objects & storing metadata critical for Data Operations Agent can identify upstream & downstream dependencies & intuitively understand the implications of dependencies with minimal prompting. Agent can perform easily perform tedious Data Operation tasks such as refresh scheduling & lineage tracking The agent can create visualizations for all of the above features

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: ArangoDB's multimodal features can be easily used to capture information about enterprise data structures. Using NetworkX & CuGraph, the data can be parsed in realtime by AI agents to extract insights & automate complex Data Operations tasks.

sections.heading: What's next for DEBy
sections.text: Create an enterprise ready solution leveraging ArangoDB to simplify management of enterprise data Additional features for DEBy that aims to automate complex Data Operation tasks Leverage the multimodal features of ArangoDB to make DEBy the one-stop solution for all of enterprise specific requirements of a Data Engineer
