title: UtiliTrack
tagline: An app that empowers facilities to automate maintenance scheduling, track customer feedback, monitor energy usage, and helping businesses reduce costs. Potentially saving $111 billion in the US.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: UtiliTrack was inspired by a friend’s struggle to manage energy costs in his family-run restaurant. During peak summer months, he was losing between $3,000 to $5,000 monthly just on air conditioning. The toll on his business was severe—not only in expenses but also in wear and tear, leading to vent leaks and damage. His experience opened our eyes to the widespread infrastructure inefficiencies many businesses face. With an annual $370 billion energy waste in the U.S., we set out to create a solution to combat this issue.

sections.heading: What it Does
sections.text: UtiliTrack provides businesses with a powerful tool to manage energy usage and streamline maintenance. It continuously monitors energy consumption patterns and detects inefficiencies, allowing systems like HVAC to operate only when necessary. By integrating automated scheduling and sensor feedback, UtiliTrack adjusts power usage dynamically. This solution not only saves costs but also reduces the strain on equipment, which means less frequent breakdowns. Businesses can now manage operational efficiency from a single dashboard, reducing waste and boosting customer satisfaction.

sections.heading: How We Built It
sections.text: We developed UtiliTrack from the ground up, utilizing programming, data analysis, and integration with sensors to build an effective system. We started by coding functions that track real-time energy consumption and programmed algorithms to identify patterns of waste. The backend was built to support easy integration with existing infrastructure, while the front end offers a user-friendly dashboard for business owners. We also incorporated machine learning to optimize settings based on usage data, making UtiliTrack smarter over time.

sections.heading: Challenges We Ran Into
sections.text: Building UtiliTrack presented technical and logistical challenges. Integrating seamlessly with varied business infrastructures required deep customization and testing. Ensuring accuracy in energy data collection, especially in real-time, was another hurdle. We also had to refine our predictive algorithms to operate reliably across different systems and industries. Finally, creating a balance between automation and user control took careful design, ensuring that business owners can trust UtiliTrack’s insights while remaining hands-on if needed.

sections.heading: Accomplishments That We’re Proud Of
sections.text: One of our biggest achievements with UtiliTrack is its ability to make a real impact on energy costs and operational efficiency. We’re proud of the user-friendly dashboard that allows non-technical users to navigate data insights effortlessly. Testing UtiliTrack in real scenarios and watching it detect and prevent unnecessary energy expenditure was a major accomplishment. Knowing that it has the potential to save businesses thousands in costs while benefiting the environment is something we’re especially proud of.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: This project gave us insight into the intricacies of energy management in commercial spaces. We learned just how much energy and operational budgets are wasted due to inefficiencies and the limitations of traditional maintenance methods. We also gained technical knowledge in data monitoring and predictive analytics, as well as valuable lessons on user needs across different industries. Most importantly, we understood the vital role of sustainable energy practices in helping businesses thrive financially and environmentally.

sections.heading: What’s Next for UtiliTrack
sections.text: In the future, we aim to expand UtiliTrack with advanced predictive maintenance features, allowing businesses to proactively address potential issues before they cause breakdowns. Additionally, we plan to integrate IoT for real-time responsiveness, enabling businesses to adapt instantly to energy usage needs. Our goal is also to tailor UtiliTrack’s features to specific industries, creating customizable options to help businesses further reduce costs and lower their environmental footprint in ways that make sense for their unique needs.

title: Ingineer
tagline: Effortlessly plan events with friends

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Making plans with friends should be easy. Instead, it often turns into a long group-chat loop: “Are you free this weekend?” “Maybe.” “Where should we go?” “I don’t know.” “Someone pick something.” The plan usually dies before anyone decides on a time, place, ride, reservation, or food. Ingenium changes that by letting personal agents coordinate for people. Instead of waiting for every friend to reply, Ing can communicate with each person’s Ing to find when they are free. The group gets a real time to meet, then the right agents help turn that time into an actual plan. All designed around the app people already use to make plans: iMessage

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Ingenium turns a group idea into a scheduled plan. Text Ing something like: “Find a time for dinner this week,” “Plan Maya’s birthday,” or “What should we do Saturday?” Ing can Ask your friends’ Ings when they are free. Each person’s personal agent responds with availability, so the group does not need to wait for every person to manually check and reply. Find the best shared time. Ing compares everyone’s availability and proposes a time the group can confirm. Create the event. Once a timeslot is found, each person's Ing adds the event to their calendar Call in specialists to make the plan real. Find food options. A DoorDash specialist can return delivery options, estimated delivery times, group pricing, and direct links. Plan rides. An Uber specialist can compare ride types, estimate costs, and create a link with the destination ready. Find venues, reservations, tickets, flights, gifts, or supplies. Each specialist returns a few relevant options with the details needed to decide. Build the final itinerary. After the group picks its options, Ing summarizes the plan: what is happening, when it is happening, where to go, and what each person needs to do. Research anything that needs a browser. Users can ask Ing to compare restaurants, research events, or look up options. Ing works in its own cloud browser and sends screenshots and results back through iMessage.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: iMessage coordinator with Photon: We built Ing as the main agent users text. It understands the request, decides what help is needed, starts the group chat, and combines agent responses into one final plan. Specialist-agent system: Ing can call in specialist agents for food delivery, rides, venues, restaurant reservations, tickets, shopping, flights, and itinerary planning. Each agent has a focused job and only responds when it is relevant to the conversation. Real-time group coordination: Ing waits for the agents it called in to respond, then turns their results into a clear group plan instead of leaving users with scattered recommendations. Calendar scheduling: We connected Google Calendar so Ingenium can check free/busy availability, find shared time slots in 30-minute intervals, and create an event after the group confirms. Cloud computer: We gave Ing a sandboxed browser through E2B Desktop and OpenAI computer use. When a task needs deeper research, Ing can browse, compare options, send screenshots while it works, and return a short answer with links. Privacy boundaries: All data from group chats are encrypted and only used by Ing. Calendar details are not shared with the group. Personal connected tools are only available in a user’s private conversation with Ing. Web experience: We built Ingenium’s landing page with Next.js and Tailwind CSS.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: A group chat with multiple AI agents can quickly become overwhelming if every agent replies to every message. We addressed that by giving each specialist a narrow role and a strict reply rule: agents only answer when they are directly relevant, named, or responding to their own earlier message. Otherwise, they return PASS and stay quiet. Ensuring user's data is safe, making sure what is sent in messages is encrypted and only used by Ing How do we learn an individual's boundaries and preferences. ie. are they vegetarian? do they want to go out at 8am on a Monday just because their calendar is open?

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Built a working iMessage flow where a user texts one coordinator and that coordinator can add other agents to the group chat Made specialist agents behave like focused collaborators rather than a pile of generic chatbots. Created dynamic roles for food delivery, rides, venues, reservations, tickets, shopping, flights, and planning. Built calendar availability matching that finds shared free time without revealing private event details. Added event creation and invitation sending after the group confirms a plan.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: the hard part of multi-agent systems is not only getting agents to produce answers. It is deciding who should answer, when they should stay quiet, and how to turn several partial answers into one decision a group can act on. trust matters more than having an agent do everything. Users should be able to see where recommendations came from, inspect links themselves, and keep the final decision for anything involving money, reservations, or personal information. we learned that “social good” does not always need to look like a massive platform. Helping people overcome the small coordination barriers that keep them from seeing friends can be meaningful on its own.

sections.heading: What's next for Ingineer
sections.text: Improve the planner so it can account for travel time, group size, dietary needs, budgets, and event timing in one final itinerary. Test Ingenium with real friend groups to measure whether it actually reduces back-and-forth and leads to more completed plans. Move from prototype-scale agent seats to a more reliable production architecture that does not depend on teammates’ laptops staying online.

title: Safeword
tagline: Most safety apps scream. Safeword whispers. Behind a casual chat, it calls your emergency contact and hands them your location and a word-for-word 911 script.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: 4 in 10 Americans say they would be afraid to walk alone at night within a mile of home, the highest share since 1993. Among women it is 53% , double the 26% of men ( Gallup ). On campus the fear has a basis: in a survey of 181,752 students at 33 universities , 13% reported nonconsensual sexual contact since enrolling ( AAU 2019 ). Panic buttons need a free hand and an unwatched screen. Shared location needs someone to be looking. Phone calls need you to speak out loud, which is exactly what you can't do when the person you're worried about is behind you. And every one of them ends the same way: one person gets notified, and nobody coordinates the response. We are students at Georgia State in downtown Atlanta, and most of us have taken that late walk home. So we asked: what if one ordinary sentence could bring in everyone who cares about you, tell them exactly what to do, and put a human on the line with 911, without the person next to you noticing anything at all? Safeword is our answer. Say it once. We take it from here.

sections.heading: What Safeword does
sections.text: Safeword is a personal-safety agent that lives in the two places you already are: your messages and your phone calls . It runs two conversations at once , and each one is a different technology. The conversation in your pocket: iMessage, powered by Photon. You text Safeword like a friend. Photon Spectrum puts a single agent behind the thread, so there is no app to install and nothing to open under stress. It is where you say "walk me home," where the check-ins arrive , and where the people who love you get the whole story as it happens . The conversation in your ear: voice, powered by ElevenLabs. Some moments are not for typing. ElevenLabs Agents gives Safeword a calm, natural voice that picks up when you call, stays on the line, and keeps you company all the way home. It listens for one thing in particular: your duress phrase . Say "can you water my plants?" and the agent fires a silent escalation while replying with a perfectly ordinary answer. Nobody next to you can tell. Level 1: Stay With Me. You are uneasy, not in danger. Safeword stays with you and checks in. If you go quiet for 15 seconds , it sends follow-up texts . If there is still no reply after 15 more seconds , it escalates and alarms your emergency contact . Say the duress phrase and it escalates immediately. Level 2: Help Me Now. One phrase, said once. Safeword hands you off to people: A phone rings. Your emergency contact gets an automatic call that says who needs help and where. A WhatsApp message lands with everything: your name, your location, what happened, what to do next. A human calls 911, reading a ready-made script so the dispatcher gets the facts in seconds. The software never calls 911 itself. Take Photon away and Safeword has no front door : no thread to text, nobody to loop in. Take ElevenLabs away and it has no voice : no company on the walk, no way to say the phrase out loud. Remove either one and what is left is a panic button. Together they are a response . A night with Safeword Maya is walking back to her car after a late shift and feels someone following her. In iMessage, she texts Safeword: "walk me home." The agent answers over Photon and starts checking in. A block later she calls, and the ElevenLabs voice picks up like a friend on the line. The footsteps get closer. She says, casually, "can you water my plants?" The voice replies, "Of course, I'll remind you tomorrow," and that is the alarm . Her emergency contact's phone rings, a WhatsApp message arrives with her location and the details, and a person who knows her calls 911 with a script in hand. Maya never had to explain, and the person behind her never knew. The rule that shapes everything Software never calls 911. A person who knows her does, with our script. That keeps the system honest, avoids faking a dispatch path, and still gets a human response in minutes.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Safeword has two levels. In Stay With Me , an AI companion talks with you by text or voice like a friend while it quietly listens for a duress phrase or a silence. After 15 seconds of inactivity the agent sends follow-up texts, and after 15 more seconds with no reply it escalates and alarms your emergency contact. In Help Me Now , there is no conversation: it escalates immediately. Either way, the emergency contact gets two things at once, a phone call and a WhatsApp message with all the details. Photon Spectrum ( spectrum-ts ) is the messaging layer. One agent loop reads messages from any provider, so the same logic runs in iMessage and the terminal. The first message returns a menu: 1 for Stay With Me, 2 for Help Me Now. ElevenLabs Agents powers the voice version of Stay With Me. A custom escalate webhook tool fires the instant it hears the duress phrase, while the spoken reply stays normal. Twilio places the automated call to the emergency contact. The call says it is an automated safety alert from an AI assistant, gives her name and address, and tells the contact to check WhatsApp and call 911. WhatsApp (via Twilio) delivers the full alert: her name, address, a map link, the time, and a word-for-word script to read to 911, including "I am not at the scene." Node and Express hold session state, the inactivity timers and the escalation logic. The alert is fire-and-forget, so the companion's reply never lags. A Cloudflare tunnel lets ElevenLabs' servers reach our local webhook. Architecture User (iMessage or voice) | v Photon Spectrum --> Safeword agent (Node) | +-----------------+-----------------+ | | 1. Stay With Me 2. Help Me Now (companion; listens for (no chat; escalates duress phrase and silence) immediately) | | +-----------------+-----------------+ v Escalation +-----------+-----------+ v v Twilio phone call WhatsApp message to emergency contact with all the details Stack Layer Tool Job Messaging Photon Spectrum One agent loop across channels Voice ElevenLabs Agents Companion and duress detection Calls and alerts Twilio Phone call and WhatsApp message Server Node, Express Session state and escalation Tunnel Cloudflare Lets the voice agent reach the server Safety by design Never calls 911; the emergency contact does, with the script. Contacts opt in, and every automated call says it is an AI safety assistant. Location is shared only for the alert. The reply a person sees and the alert that fires are independent, so the screen stays innocent while help is on the way.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: SMS was blocked. US carriers silently drop unregistered business texts, so the alert text came back undelivered. We moved the script into the voice call and added WhatsApp. Calls need permission. Twilio's default geo-permissions blocked the first outbound call until we enabled US and Canada. The voice agent didn't fire. Our escalate tool failed to save at first (a required description was empty), and a dead local server looked identical to a working one. Webhooks and tunnels. ngrok's warning page blocked the webhook, so we switched to a Cloudflare tunnel. Voice over SIP is hard. We chose ElevenLabs plus Twilio instead of routing a call through Spectrum's SIP line. Designing around real emergencies. We cut a simulated dispatch path and kept a human in the loop.

sections.heading: What we're proud of
sections.text: A voice companion that stays natural while silently triggering a real phone call and a written 911 script. An alert that tells the emergency contact everything in one WhatsApp message, with nothing faked or hidden. A clear line between what software does and what a human does. What we learned: the first version of safety is deciding what the software must not do. Carrier rules, consent for AI voice calls, and false-alarm control shape the product as much as the model does.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: What's next: Atlanta first with verified dispatch numbers, then campus pilots with campus safety teams, then a national directory of local dispatch numbers. Later: an evidence mode with photos and Tracks to select: Cox Social Good (main), Photon, MLH ElevenLabs.

title: Dollar Dash
tagline: Turning classrooms into live markets: Where kids trade, learn, and master their financial future

sections.heading: Dollar Dash — Impact Summary
sections.text: Dollar Dash turns financial literacy from an abstract concept into a lived experience. By transforming the stock market into a fast-paced, interactive classroom game, it gives students something most never receive: early, hands-on exposure to how money actually works. Instead of lectures, students learn through consequences — watching portfolios rise and fall, reacting to news, and experiencing concepts like diversification and compound growth in real time. This approach makes financial education intuitive, memorable, and accessible within a single class period. Its zero-friction design — no downloads, no accounts, just a phone — ensures it reaches the students who need it most, particularly in underserved communities where financial education is often absent.

sections.heading: Impact:
sections.text: Empowers students with practical financial literacy from an early age Closes education gaps by bringing investment concepts into underserved classrooms Builds instinctive, experience-based money habits instead of theoretical knowledge Creates a foundation for long-term financial confidence and independence

title: Redreemer
tagline: Redreemer turns text messages into a step-by-step path from shelter to savings and with caseworkers in the loop.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every financial app assumes you have a smartphone, email, and a bank account. 582,000 homeless Americans and 600,000 people released from prison each year have none of that. Financial exclusion is a design problem; so we redesigned it.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Redreemer lets anyone text a single phone number from any phone; even a flip phone get real local resources, real phone numbers, and a guided 8-step ladder from survival to financial independence. It intercepts predatory lenders in real time, checks benefits eligibility, finds fair-chance employers, and celebrates every milestone with a human voice message.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Node.js + React + Supabase backend, Twilio for SMS, Gemini 2.5 Flash for AI responses, and ElevenLabs for voice milestone clips. Every incoming text runs through a 20-layer detection pipeline before AI ever responds, with Auth0 protecting the caseworker dashboard and Vercel handling deployment.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Getting the detection pipeline sequencing right was critical; a crisis message that also mentions a job keyword must hit the suicide layer before the employer layer. Calibrating Gemini's tone was equally hard; every response goes to someone in a genuinely difficult situation, and the line between helpful and patronizing is razor thin.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We built the first SMS platform to intercept predatory lenders in real time ; 23 scam attempts blocked so far. We're also proud of delivering behavioral finance psychology via flip phone, and a caseworker risk-scoring system that tells social workers who needs help before they disappear entirely

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Trust is the hardest design problem in financial inclusion, not the technology. Every decision has to earn it incrementally: plain language, no judgment, free forever, and resources that are actually local, accurate, and actionable.

sections.heading: What's next for Redreemer
sections.text: Expand the local resource database beyond Phoenix to cover major metros nationwide. Partner directly with shelters and reentry organizations to integrate Redreemer into day-one intake workflows. Pursue nonprofit status and CDFI partnerships to keep it free forever.

title: Farsight
tagline: Explore a building through a rescue rover: live camera and person detection, LiDAR-guided indoor autonomy, and a dense room you can walk through in VR.

sections.text: Demo video

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: A responder should be able to inspect an unfamiliar room before entering it. We wanted more than remote steering on a small screen: a live view of the rover's surroundings, help finding people, and spatial context that stays available as the rover moves. VR telepresence and a measured room map bring those views together. Our demonstration is a controlled indoor rescue scenario.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Farsight lets a responder explore a room from a Meta Quest instead of entering it first. An ELEGOO rover carries a LiDAR iPhone and an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano. The headset shows the live camera: move the right joystick to drive, press A for autonomous Explore, and press B to stop and return to MANUAL. In AUTO, the joysticks move your viewpoint through the map while Nav2 navigates the rover. YOLO11n-pose finds people and derives face boxes from head keypoints. The mission report keeps encounter snapshots and draft SBAR notes. A responder can type on the laptop, or hold the left trigger in VR, to ask about the live view. Local Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct answers, Whisper base.en transcribes, and Piper speaks replies or preset survivor phrases in English and Spanish. The models run locally; remote driving still needs the cellular link. After the run, the Mac pulls the posed photos and measured LiDAR seed, then trains a Gaussian-splat reconstruction with Brush on Metal. Walk the room in a browser, replay the rover's route, or open the splat in the Quest. Dechante's face-enabled browser walkthrough puts red dots on the minimap; clicking a face jumps to its recorded viewpoint and opens the real camera frame with the face boxed. These are observed face locations, so a moving person may leave more than one spot.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Swift and ARKit on the iPhone supply synchronized RGB, measured depth, camera intrinsics, and poses. The Jetson runs the Python/FastAPI rover server, YOLO11n-pose through TensorRT, Nav2 integration, and serial commands to the Arduino Uno. Two phone bridges carry the cellular/Tailscale connection. The Mac operator relay serves the TypeScript/Three.js/WebXR app to the Quest over USB using ADB reverse. Our local assistant uses Hugging Face model artifacts: Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct GGUF with its vision projector through llama.cpp, Whisper base.en through whisper.cpp, and Piper voices. The same vision-language service drafts SBAR notes from encounter crops and metadata. The post-run pipeline selects a continuous drive, preserves its posed photos, seeds Brush with measured LiDAR points, trains on the Mac GPU, and prunes the output for Quest. A watcher waits for captures to stop changing before a SSH pull. Face processing runs on the CPU alongside GPU training. The browser walk combines the reconstructed room, recorded route, and face-pin evidence. The immersive Quest splat page provides stick walking and snap turns.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: We had to make camera streaming, perception, navigation, and motor control share a small computer and an uneven cellular link. Mapping and reconstruction also belong on different schedules: a detailed post-run room should not delay the live camera or control path. A convincing reconstruction needs coherent camera poses and useful views. Parked stretches repeat images; malformed JPEGs can stop Brush; an oversized LiDAR seed can make a short training budget much slower. Reducing splat count for a headset can also introduce visible streaks even when the original training score looks good. We kept measured LiDAR, learned reconstruction, simulation, and replay distinct. A face location is evidence of a sighting, not proof of a unique person, and a model-generated note still needs a responder's judgment.

sections.heading: Accomplishments
sections.text: Connected headset driving, live onboard perception, autonomous navigation, and mission evidence in one search-and-rescue prototype. Built a local vision/voice assistant with spoken answers and bilingual survivor phrases on the rover's Jetson. Turned real rover captures into walkable Gaussian-splat rooms with a Mac pipeline based on Dechante's LiDAR-seeded Brush method. Built a room and its face evidence in 114 seconds locally on an M5 Pro from a saved 60-second / 119-photo capture sample. Brush took 112 seconds at 5,000 steps, with 62 seconds of CPU face processing in parallel. A 10-second idle allowance and local-copy stand-in bring that to 124 seconds , excluding real Jetson transfer and browser loading. The sample reuses a longer run's LiDAR seed; it is not a live short-drive end-to-end timing. Added a browser walkthrough that connects face pins to the original boxed camera frames, making the room useful for reviewing what the rover saw.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Give each device the work that fits it: the phone captures depth and pose, the Jetson handles perception and navigation beside the motors, and the Mac trains the post-run room. Capture quality and seed size matter as much as training steps. Measure the final pruned viewer result as well as the training score, and compare settings on the same held-out photos. A useful search record connects a location to the actual observation. A red pin becomes much more informative when it opens the camera frame that created it. Keeping those links also makes it easier to spot duplicate sightings and model mistakes.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: Improve room quality within a predictable end-to-end build budget, including transfer, face processing, and publication. Bring the browser's face-evidence interaction into the immersive Quest viewer. Evaluate localization, detection, and operator performance across repeated physical search-training runs, and make multi-room review easier.

sections.heading: Sponsor tracks
sections.text: Hugging Face — Best Use of Open Source AI: local vision, speech recognition, and synthesis use Hugging Face-distributed models for a responder's workflow. NVIDIA — Best Use of Jetson Nano: the Orin Nano runs onboard perception, local AI, navigation integration, camera streaming, and motor control. Encompass — Data Capturing Hardware: a rover-mounted LiDAR iPhone turns synchronized real-world observations into encounter records and a 3D room. Full Sail — Pathways & Perception: pathfinding, face detection, timed rescue drill scoring, and room walkthroughs support a search-training scenario. Team: Aziz Umarov, Saicharan Ramineni, Dechante (Chang), Mehdi Chraibi .

title: Fireline
tagline: Satellites see a wildfire once it is big. Fireline sees the first smoke.

sections.text: Fireline Tagline: Satellites see a wildfire once it is big. Fireline sees the first smoke.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: From January 1 to April 13, 2025, the Florida Forest Service counted 1,300 wildfires and 57,025 acres burned ( FOX 35 ). Much of that land is remote: no power lines, no cell signal, nobody watching. Satellites can't close that gap on their own. The ones sharp enough to see a small fire pass over a few times a day: VIIRS has about 375 m pixels and 3 to 4 looks a day at mid-latitudes ( NASA Earthdata ). Ground cameras see smoke sooner, but they need a tower, grid power and an internet connection. We wanted a camera box you can strap to a tree in the middle of nowhere that decides on its own whether it is seeing smoke, and that sends only what matters.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Fireline is a flock of tree-mounted camera units and a live console for the crew that manages them. Each unit runs a smoke detection model on its own NVIDIA Jetson, wakes up only when the weather says fire is likely, and sends a single alert packet of 340 bytes or less over a satellite link. The console puts every unit on a map and sounds the alarm the moment one of them confirms smoke. Smoke detection on the device: Pyronear's open YOLO smoke model runs on the Jetson's GPU. Smoke must appear in at least 4 of the last 6 frames, which filters out clouds, fog and dust. Weather-gated wake-up: a cheap humidity sensor on an ESP32 sets a fire-risk tier. The Jetson scans every 30 minutes when it's humid, every 5 minutes when it's drying out, and continuously in critical fire weather. Satellite-sized alerts: every message fits the 340-byte limit of an Iridium short burst data message. In our tests a smoke event is 178 bytes. Images never cross the satellite link. A live console: a fleet map with markers colored by state, an alarm and desktop notification that fly the map to the unit, weather charts for each unit, and a link log showing each packet's size and satellite delay. Plain-language write-ups: each incident gets an instant summary ("Smoke seen by gw-14 in 5 of 6 frames during critical fire weather (34 °C, 22 % humidity). Likely early wildfire."), which Gemma 3 then rewrites for the crew. Gemma also gives a second opinion on the smoke crop. The demo: we point a hair dryer at the sensor. Humidity drops, the status LED goes from green to orange, and the Jetson starts scanning. We hold a smoke video up to the camera. A few seconds later the console sounds an alarm, the map flies to the unit, and the alert card shows the packet that crossed the simulated satellite link.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: DHT11 → ESP32 sets the fire-risk tier → MQTT wakes the Jetson → smoke model + 4-of-6 frame check → interest score → 340-byte packet over the simulated satellite link → FastAPI on Azure → WebSocket → every open console Field unit (hardware) NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano runs the smoke model on its GPU with TensorRT , through Ultralytics . It idles with the model loaded until the ESP32 asks for a scan. ESP32 (Arduino) is the always-on sentry. It reads a DHT11 , averages 3 readings, changes tier only after 3 agreeing readings, and drives the status LED and buzzer. MQTT with a Mosquitto broker on the Jetson connects the two inside the box. AI/ML Pyronear's YOLO wildfire smoke model from Hugging Face (Apache 2.0), trained on Pyro-SDIS, a dataset of labelled smoke images from fixed ground cameras. No training needed. An interest score: average confidence × (frames with smoke / 6) × fire-weather weight . Smoke in critical weather outranks a faint blob on a humid day. An alert fires at 0.5. Gemma 3 (4B) served by Ollama writes each incident up and checks the smoke crop. Backend and infrastructure FastAPI + SQLite ground station: a satellite simulator (340-byte limit, 5–20 s delay, optional drops), incident grouping, offline detection, and a WebSocket for live updates. Azure VM running Docker Compose : the app, Gemma on Ollama, and Caddy for automatic HTTPS (browsers only allow notifications on secure sites). Frontend React , TypeScript and Vite , with Leaflet for the map on Esri satellite imagery.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: A satellite link delivers out of order. With a 5–20 s random delay, an older heartbeat can land after a newer one. The ground station only lets the newest packet set a unit's state. It treats a packet as a duplicate only when the unit, counter and timestamp all match, because a rebooted unit restarts its counter. 340 bytes is a tight budget. We used short keys and rounded numbers, and kept images off the satellite link entirely. The unit refuses to send anything over the limit. A Jetson is slow to boot. Power-cycling it for every scan wasn't practical, so the cheap ESP32 does the always-on watching and the Jetson stays idle with the model loaded until it's needed. AI write-ups on a CPU-only server. Gemma on a CPU VM can take a while. The console shows a template summary instantly, and Gemma's version replaces it when it arrives. If Gemma never answers, the alert still works. We changed the architecture mid-build. We started with a Raspberry Pi ground station and an installed desktop app, and merged them into one hosted website. That meant fewer devices at the judging table, and anyone on the crew can open the console.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Detection never leaves the forest. The decision "is this smoke?" happens on the box. Only a small verdict crosses the satellite link, which answers the reason ground cameras need towers and internet today. The whole chain, end to end: weather sensor, wake-up, on-device detection, satellite-sized uplink, live alert on the map. A console built for the crew, not the demo. Alerts group into incidents, units that go quiet turn grey, and every packet's size and delay is on screen. Honest about what's real. The satellite link and most of the fleet are simulated, and the console labels every simulated unit on screen.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: How to deploy a YOLO model to a Jetson and export it to TensorRT How to design a message format around a hard 340-byte limit How to keep state consistent when messages arrive late, out of order or twice How to split work across embedded, ML, backend and frontend lanes by agreeing on a packet contract in the first hour

sections.heading: What's next for Fireline
sections.text: Tap to place: an NFC tag on each tree holds its name and coordinates, so a crew sets a unit's location with one tap. Locate the fire: two units seeing the same smoke from different angles can triangulate where it is. One modem per flock: units relay to each other over LoRa radio, so only one carries the satellite modem. Field-ready power: cut the Jetson's power completely between scans, with solar and a LiFePO4 battery. Test on Florida scenery: Pyronear's model was trained on other regions' landscapes, so it needs testing against local false alarms like dust and prescribed burns. We haven't measured our false-alarm rate or detection range yet; that is what a pilot is for.

sections.heading: Built with
sections.text: nvidia-jetson, tensorrt, ultralytics, yolo, hugging-face, pyronear, esp32, arduino, dht11, mqtt, mosquitto, python, fastapi, sqlite, websockets, gemma, ollama, azure, docker, caddy, react, typescript, vite, leaflet

title: Permanence
tagline: Intelligent Spatial Awareness & Object Permanence

sections.text: Hydrogen bomb (Astra, Fable) vs. coughing baby: who understands object permanence?

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Frontier models like Fable seem more intelligent in almost every way. They write software, explain advanced mathematics, and work through hard problems. But on one fundamental concept, a roughly one-year-old baby has something to teach them: object permanence . Object permanence is understanding that things keep existing when we can't see them. It lets us remember what's behind an obstacle, follow where it went, and look for it again. Babies show it long before they can explain it. This isn't a claim that babies beat AI on a benchmark. It's the gap that interested us. A model can explain object permanence, but a robot still needs a way to keep it in a changing physical world. A detector losing sight of something shouldn't mean the robot forgets it exists. We built Permanence to turn "I detected it" into "I still know where it is."

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Permanence gives a robot a persistent 3D memory of objects. The rover scans the table by itself, identifies the objects, and keeps track of where they are as they get hidden or leave the camera's view. Our clearest demonstration is a shell game. Show the robot colored balls, cover them with cups, shuffle the cups, then reveal. Permanence tracks which cup holds each hidden ball and checks its answer against the real reveal. You can also: Talk to it. "Hey rover, the cup next to the green ball": a 3D vision-language model picks the object from the scan and shows how confident it is. See its memory. A live 3D dashboard show hidden objects through the cups covering them. See what's seen versus remembered, including how long each object has been out of sight. Send it to a remembered target. "Hey rover, drive": the rover plans around the other cups and goes to its target, even when nothing on camera shows where the ball is. The cups are a demonstration, not the whole idea. The goal is a robot that acts on what it knows, not just on what's in frame.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Two brains, one Jetson. Everything runs on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (8 GB) . An iPhone on the rover is only the sensor: it streams color, LiDAR depth and its own position over USB through Record3D. The reasoning: Qwen-3D , a 3-billion-parameter 3D vision-language model. It reads 18 views of the scan and turns language like "the cup next to the box" into a specific object, in about 4.5 s. Three identical cups have no names; only a model that understands language and space can tell them apart. The fast reflexes: YOLOE. It's prompted with words (no training on our props) and compiled to a 22 MB TensorRT FP16 engine that keeps up with the camera's 15 fps. The memory between them: a 3D tracker we wrote. It matches detections across frames, follows each object through occlusion, and knows that a ball under a cup moves with the cup. Fitting it in 8 GB. CPU and GPU share the Jetson's 8 GB, and Qwen-3D alone was 7.1 GB . We wrote our own 8-bit quantization in plain PyTorch, loading the model one tensor at a time so the full-size version never exists in memory: 4.5 GB . The pipeline allows one memory peak at a time. Qwen-3D picks the target, hands it to the tracker, and its process exits to free its memory before tracking starts. A full run peaks at about 6.1 of 7.4 GB. Interfaces. A Three.js dashboard shows the robot's calibrated view, a top-down memory map, the camera feed, the confidence behind each pick, and live Jetson memory. Voice commands use Chrome's speech recognition. Movement. The Jetson drives an Arduino Uno and L298N motor driver and steers from the phone's position. The rover scans by stop-and-shoot: turn, stop, take a sharp view, roll, repeat. It learns how much power its cheap motors need to start moving, and stops on its own if commands stop arriving. We also built a separate head-steering interface with a Pico W and GY-521 motion sensor .

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: 8 GB is small for two models. Loading both crashed the board, and an earlier run left behind can eat the room. We added the handoff, our own quantization, and cleanup of leftover processes. A wobbly camera. With the phone mounted high on the rover, scanning while moving gave blurred frames. Stopping for each shot fixed it. Cheap motors. They stall when started too gently and hum instead of turning, so the rover measures its own speed and adjusts power. When its left and right turned out to be swapped, it detects that and corrects it in software. Disappearing isn't the same as hidden. A missed detection doesn't mean the ball went into a cup. We needed geometry, motion and containment checks, and matching in 3D so identical cups don't swap identities when they cross. Freshness over completeness. An overlay that shows where the world was seconds ago is useless, so every stage takes only the newest frame.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: The full loop on a palm-sized edge board: perception, memory, language, visualization and physical action, with a 3B vision-language model and a real-time tracker together in 8 GB. The reveal. The robot commits to where the hidden ball is, and we lift the cup to check. Nobody has to take our word for it.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Recognizing an object is only the beginning. Useful intelligence needs continuity: what was there, what changed, and what should still be there when you can't see it. Memory is a design constraint, not an afterthought. Deciding what runs when mattered as much as which models we picked. The strongest demo is a claim you can check: show it, hide it, move it, reveal it.

sections.heading: What's next for Permanence
sections.text: Prediction: a learned world model that guesses what happened out of view, instead of only remembering what it saw. Bigger hardware: Jetson Thor, so the language model can stay loaded and answer at any time. Better hardware and integration: wheel encoders, and ROS 2 / Isaac ROS. Beyond the tabletop, with clearer uncertainty when memory gets old. Longer term: assistive robots and glasses that help people find misplaced things. The coughing baby had this figured out in its first year. Now our robot does too. Out of sight should not mean out of memory. title: BetterBill
tagline: Don't pay what you don't owe. Snap your hospital bill: BetterBill finds the charges worth questioning, shows the proof, and makes the call once you say yes.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: A $12,000 hospital bill arrives. Questioning it means learning billing codes, price files and charity care law, then losing an afternoon on hold. Close to half ( 45% ) of insured adults ages 19 to 64 got a medical bill in the past year they thought insurance should have covered (Commonwealth Fund, 2023 Health Care Affordability Survey). Most people just pay it. They don't need another opinion; they need proof they can hand to billing. AI should do the reading, writing and waiting. Code should do the math. The patient should make the call.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: On our $12,000 sample bill, BetterBill finds $1,916.85 less than billed , every item with its source: MRI billed at $6,900 ; Cedars-Sinai's own published cash price is $5,143.15 An $84 duplicate blood count A $76 units error on blood draws How it works: Snap a photo or paste the text. Confirm every line, fix misreads, mark care you never got. Proof: rules check duplicates, CMS unit limits, the bill vs your insurance statement, and the published price. Every amount carries its source. Help paying: the app screens for financial assistance under the hospital's policy, federal rules and several state laws; Browser Use finds a missing policy live. Act: a letter is drafted in about 2 seconds on production . The patient approves the exact text, then it is sent and an AI advocate calls billing. Share a redacted evidence packet. On the sample bill, results show up in about a second . Free to check; we keep 10% of confirmed savings only, capped at $1,000.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Applied intelligence, split on purpose: AI where it is strong, code where it must be right. AI does the reading, writing, talking and browsing: StepFun step-5-preview reads photos (transcribing only), Gemini drafts letters, an ElevenLabs agent calls over a Photon line, Browser Use captures real price files and policies. Code does the parts that cannot be wrong: A TypeScript rules engine computes every flag and dollar, in integer cents. A claim checker rejects any dollar figure Gemini writes that is not in the bill or the evidence. A browsing agent's quote is kept only if it matches the source PDF word for word. On calls, a Python LiveKit controller, not the prompt, decides when the advocate may speak. Our newest call design, a prototype, is our first where the patient never leaves the line : they join a 3-way call and verify their own identity, and the advocate, never pretending to be them, asks for a hold on the account, the itemized bill, records and a reference number.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Testing without real patients. Real bills are private, so we built 11 realistic sample bills with known mistakes and compared them against real, public hospital prices, policies and laws. We traced it, then fixed it. A demo photo took 26 seconds. Sentry's invoke_agent bill-reader span showed a live StepFun call despite a saved reading. Saved reads now return in under a second . A flag is a question, not a verdict. CMS allows up to 4 blood counts a day, so BetterBill asks billing; it never accuses.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: One workflow from photo to approved call , on web, iOS and Android, from one design in Paper. 22 of 22 seeded errors caught on 11 synthetic bills, 0 false flags on 3 clean bills. We built the eval harness before the demo. 88.8% line recall on 35 phone photos, including angled, crumpled and dim shots. 28 of 28 assistance findings cite their source. Seven sponsor tools doing real work: StepFun, Gemini, ElevenLabs, Photon, Browser Use, Sentry, Tiger Data. We publish our misses. On 5 recreated KFF Health News "Bill of the Month" cases we caught 1 of 3 in-scope findings. Most other findings were coding judgments, device prices and prior authorization, which our rules deliberately do not guess at.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Trust comes from showing the work. A source on every amount beats a bigger number. Let the model talk; let code enforce money, approvals and speaking turns. Measure before you demo.

sections.heading: What's next for BetterBill
sections.text: A pilot with health plans and employers. More hospitals' price files and more states' assistance rules. A security review, then real bills from consenting patients. The 3-way call tested with consenting patients and billing professionals. Don't pay what you don't owe.

title: Henomaly
tagline: More than a bird’s-eye view.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Egg prices over the last few years made it obvious to everyone: diseases like avian influenza move through commercial flocks incredibly fast , killing birds in the hundreds of thousands. By the time a farmer notices something is wrong, the disease may already have swept through an entire house. That disrupts farms, cuts the egg supply, and drives up prices for everyone. So we asked: how can we give farmers an early warning system that: watches the flock constantly , for long periods, keeps working when the internet drops or part of the system crashes, and turns what it sees into something a farmer and a veterinarian can actually act on ?

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Henomaly is a camera-based edge AI system running on QNX that monitors the relative health of different groups of chickens. Instead of streaming video to the cloud, it processes everything locally , because barn internet is anything but reliable. It watches behavior (inactivity, panting, eating, drinking, movement) and looks for visible changes in droppings . It compares each pen against its own normal baseline , not a fixed rule, because behavior depends heavily on bird age and time of day. When something is unusual, it creates an alert with the pen, the time, an evidence image , and an explanation of what changed . The alert reaches the farmer through Photon and iMessage . The farmer can ask questions, request the image, and decide whether to share it with a veterinarian. Nothing is automatically diagnosed, and nothing is escalated without the farmer's permission. Conceptually, the baseline check for a signal x (for example, the share of inactive birds in a pen) is a standardized deviation from that pen's normal for the same hour of the day: $$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$ An alert fires only when z stays above a threshold for several consecutive windows, so a single odd frame never pages anyone.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The edge: QNX 8 on a Raspberry Pi 5 The core system runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with QNX 8.0 and a Camera Module 3 . Nine separate processes , each with one job and its own priority, talking over native QNX message passing . Large camera frames move through shared memory instead of being copied between processes. The camera is driven through QNX's Sensor Framework in C. Full-resolution frames land in a shared-memory ring that other processes read without copying, protected by a sequence counter. Only small summaries travel as messages. Real-time priorities: the camera and the farmer's alert link run at the highest priority, and heavy model inference runs at the lowest. Inference can never starve an alert. On-device AI from QNX's open-source ecosystem: ONNX Runtime 1.24.4 from oss.qnx.com , installed completely offline (106 packages, no internet on the Pi). QNX's Python package for it turned out to be broken, because its compiled module was missing, so we wrote a small C bridge straight to ONNX Runtime's C API and drafted a fix for QNX's package recipe . Fault tolerance: a supervisor restarts any process that dies. We can deliberately crash one part, watch the rest keep running, and see the failed part come back and rejoin. After a power cut, the whole pipeline starts itself on boot. Measured on the Pi 5 itself, our detector runs in 168 ms at 320 px , versus 618 ms at 640 px. Compute scales roughly with input area: $$\left(\frac{320}{640}\right)^2 = 0.25$$ so we expected about a 4x speed-up, and measured 3.7x . The intelligence: open-source YOLO11, trained on Veri We started from open-source YOLO11 models and public poultry datasets , and trained every model on Veri's GPUs . Veri is built mainly for language models, so we used its custom-script mode to run full computer-vision training. Hardware: AWS nodes with 4x NVIDIA A10G (24 GB each), 48 vCPUs and about 180 GB RAM. At peak we ran two nodes at once: 8x A10G . Behavior and chicken models (Big Broiler dataset, Cardoen et al., 2025): We turned 33 GB of research video (102 clips, about 900k frames, about 6.7M behavior labels) into about 130,000 labeled bird crops across 7 behavior classes, plus 18.4k detector frames with 92.6k bounding boxes , shipped to Veri as one 9.4 GB volume . We split by video, not by frame . The 10 test clips were never seen in training, so the scores are honest. We trained three models in parallel on one node : a chicken detector on 2 GPUs with distributed data-parallel training (NCCL) , and two behavior classifiers on one GPU each. Held-out test results: Chicken detector (YOLO11n): mAP50 0.927 , recall 0.93 Behavior classifier (YOLO11n-cls, Pi-sized): top-1 accuracy 0.686; panting recall 0.80, inactivity 0.82 Behavior classifier (YOLO11s-cls): top-1 accuracy 0.701 ; panting 0.83, drinking 0.87 Droppings model (YOLO11n, Machuve fecal dataset, CC BY 4.0): mAP50 0.854 on 679 held-out photos (mAP50 is the mean average precision over classes, counting a detection as correct when it overlaps the true box by at least 50%.)

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Making a language-model platform train vision models. Veri's sandboxed containers originally had only 64 MB of shared memory , which crashed PyTorch's data-loading workers and multi-GPU training. We patched the DataLoader to pass batches through pipes as NumPy arrays , keeping 12 data workers per GPU alive. We reported the cap with logs , and the Veri team raised it to 16 GB, which unlocked multi-GPU training. We also reported custom scripts failing on one GPU provider and a crash about 20 minutes into jobs, and Veri shipped fixes during the event . Expensive failures. A job marked "failed" made even its finished models undownloadable, so we made our training jobs: time-boxed , sizing training to the remaining budget, always exit cleanly , so trained models survive, check multi-GPU communication in 10 seconds before paying for a 30-minute download, and resubmit automatically through GPU capacity and quota errors. Data at scale on bad Wi-Fi. Downloading 33 GB of video inside cloud jobs stalled, so we moved video processing to a laptop and uploaded only the compact prepared dataset. QNX packaging. The ONNX Runtime package had to be installed offline, and its broken Python binding forced us to call the C API directly.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A full edge AI pipeline on QNX : camera, detection, alerts and a self-healing supervisor, running on a Raspberry Pi 5 with no cloud dependency . Models trained end-to-end on Veri , including multi-GPU training, on a platform designed for language models. Honest numbers : every score is on held-out data, split by video, not by frame. A working farmer loop : alerts with evidence over iMessage, with the farmer in control of what reaches the vet. Real contributions back : a drafted fix for QNX's ONNX Runtime package, and platform bugs reported to Veri that were fixed during the event.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: The most important lesson was where our models do not work . Our droppings model performed well on close-up photos but failed on distant, crowded barn footage . On real held-out pen frames, 0 of its 34 detections were actually droppings : they landed on feathers, dye marks, wall screws and drinker parts. A synthetic benchmark had suggested it worked; only a check on real held-out footage showed it didn't. Even at full 2688-px resolution, individual droppings weren't visible. So instead of hiding it, we changed the design : Wide cameras handle flock-level behavior, where our models are validated on exactly that kind of footage. Droppings analysis needs a closer, controlled camera position. In the demo we simulate that path: after the dropping-finding step, the close-up analysis model receives droppings we'd expect from that camera position, at the simulated anomaly level. We also learned that honest evaluation is a design tool : splitting by video, scoring on held-out data, and auditing real frames changed our architecture more than any extra training would have.

sections.heading: What's next for Henomaly
sections.text: Real, veterinarian-confirmed barn data , with better-placed cameras for droppings. Temporal behavior models for short signs like sneezing and head shaking, which single frames can't capture. Field testing on a working farm , with baselines learned per flock, age and time of day. Henomaly can't diagnose bird flu or tell a farmer how to treat an animal. What it can do is keep watching, notice changes earlier, preserve the evidence, and bring the farmer and the veterinarian in before egg prices start climbing again . GitHub: https://github.com/RishitRai/Henomaly

title: SproutPass
tagline: SproutPass connects nearby moms through AI agents that match outgrown baby clothes with growing babies - turning everyday encounters into easy secondhand trades.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: An unexpected spark: During an Uber ride from UCLA to a friend’s apartment, we passed a Lakeshore Learning Store. Its playful, dimensional images of children reminded us of a game world. A friend had also been playing Pikmin, inspiring us to imagine everyday encounters that could be both playful and useful. A short lifecycle, lasting value: Parents buy baby clothes knowing their children may outgrow them within months—even when the clothes are still in great condition. Reselling can help recover some of that cost, but photographing items, creating listings, finding buyers, and coordinating exchanges takes effort. Our “what if”: Two moms are shopping at the same store. One has clothes her baby has outgrown; the other needs that size next. What if their companions could discover the match and suggest a trade? Our goal: Make it easier for families to find the next home for outgrown clothes—and the next size for their growing children.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Starts with a photo or conversation: Parents upload clothing photos in the web app or send them through a connected private iMessage conversation. AI suggests garment details, and parents confirm missing or uncertain information. Understands shopping needs: Parents describe the clothing they need. AI extracts explicitly stated sizes, categories, and budgets, then asks for confirmation before saving the need. Helps discover relevant items: The nearby encounter flow checks shared listings against confirmed needs, using size, category, budget, and fit rules to identify compatible offers. Presents a clear decision: The buyer reviews the garment details and listed price. Sharing a listing authorizes the seller’s side; the buyer retains final approval. Connects the steps: After approval, the app records the ownership update and a simulated payment receipt. Photon connects configured iMessage conversations to offers and receipt notifications. Adds a playful companion: Pixel pets, flowers, and sound effects give the experience personality and celebrate progress. Makes prototype boundaries visible: Payments are simulated; no real money moves and no Visa API is connected. The demo supports simulated locations and named demo profiles. Rack-level positioning and production account access controls remain future work.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Designed before implementing: We developed the idea and sketched the system architecture, then used Codex and Claude to critique assumptions and identify gaps. Used AI throughout development: AI coding tools helped implement the framework, cross-review code, and handle repetitive frontend work while we directed product and integration decisions. Started with an encounter: We first built two people meeting on a map, then connected that interaction to a useful workflow: discovering a match between one family’s available clothing and another family’s needs. Built the frontend in React and TypeScript: The interface combines clothing inventories, pixel companions, and a Leaflet-based map experience. Built substantially on Base44: Base44 hosts the application and persists garments, needs, listings, encounters, proposals, ownership histories, and feedback. Backend functions implement the trade workflow, while realtime subscriptions update the interface. Integrated generative AI through Base44: The Core.InvokeLLM API analyzes clothing photos and extracts structured needs from messages. We validate outputs and request confirmation rather than treating every model suggestion as fact. Connected messaging through Photon: Photon brings the companion into private iMessage conversations, connecting incoming photos and messages to the same backend used by the app. Separated AI interpretation from transaction rules: Application logic validates matches and approvals. Buyer approval triggers the simulated payment flow and saved ownership update.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Choosing a feasible platform: This was our first time building primarily for a mobile experience. We initially explored an installable native app, then realized it exceeded what we could complete in the remaining time. Changing direction: We shifted to a Base44-hosted web app accessible from phones, allowing us to focus on the core experience. Connecting messaging correctly: Registering a family in our database did not automatically connect their iMessage conversation. We had to configure Photon shared-line assignments and establish the conversation connection. Handling location failures: A location timeout initially pushed users into demo mode. We added clearer permission handling, retry guidance, and an explicit demo option. Distinguishing appearance from evidence: An in-app message mirror did not prove that an iMessage had arrived. We separated send-submission status from actual delivery verification.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Starting again at midnight: Within twelve hours, we explored two other ideas before finding SproutPass’s inspiration during the ride from UCLA. We did not begin implementing this direction until midnight. Delivering a connected prototype: We built a workflow spanning clothing inventory, confirmed needs, matching, offers, buyer approval, and ownership updates. Connecting conversation to action: Messages and photos can feed into the product workflow, giving the companion a practical role beyond answering questions. Combining utility and play: We connected an expressive pixel world to a concrete household problem. Finding a shared purpose: After a discouraging start, we delivered something the whole team felt excited about and proud to share.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Persistence can mean changing direction: Moving on from ideas that did not feel right helped us find a problem we wanted to solve together. Reduce repeated decisions: Once a seller has shared a listing, asking them to approve again adds friction. We simplified the flow so the buyer makes the final approval. Confirm what AI cannot know: Photo analysis can suggest details, but uncertain information needs confirmation. Clothing needs use explicitly stated sizes and budgets rather than inferring size from a baby’s age. Verify actions beyond the interface: A message accepted for sending is not proof of delivery. Our demo distinguishes submission status and requires checking physical phones before claiming receipt arrival. Separate testing from validation: Engineering tests and teammate feedback help improve the prototype, but they do not establish that parents want the product. That requires testing with the intended users.

sections.heading: What's next for SproutPass
sections.text: Put it in parents’ hands: Start with an existing preschool or neighborhood parent community. Observe whether participants can add an item, express a need, and understand an offer without coaching. Measure practical value: Learn whether SproutPass reduces listing effort, helps families find suitable clothes, and leads to completed handoffs. Use actual feedback to guide improvements. Strengthen trust: Improve authentication, per-family access controls, and consent settings before expanding beyond demo profiles. Connect real payments: Integrate a supported payment provider and handle payment failures and recovery before supporting real purchases. Explore more precise encounters: Our long-term vision is two moms shopping beside the same rack, with both choosing to enable nearby matching. Their companions could discover a compatible listing and suggest a trade. The current prototype does not support that level of location accuracy. Make invitations welcome: Test when and how nearby suggestions feel useful, while keeping participation optional and the purchase decision with the buyer.

title: TaskChain
tagline: TaskChain lets you stake ETH on tasks with deadlines. Complete them on time to get your ETH back; miss the deadline, and your ETH goes to a charity of your choice. Stay Productive!

sections.heading: Introducing TaskChain:
sections.text: A platform that combines productivity with stakes at hand. With TaskChain, users can create personal tasks, set deadlines, and stake your own Ethereum as motivation. If you complete the task on time, you get your ETH back. But if you miss the deadline, your ETH is donated to a charity of your choice. It’s a win-win: stay on track and help others, all while supporting causes that matter to you. TaskChain turns your goals into meaningful actions, incentivizing productivity while making a positive impact on the world.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We used a programming language called Solidity that allowed us to create and deploy smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain. We developed two smart contracts: TaskManager and TaskManagerFactory. TaskManagerFactory acted as a user database, storing the addresses of all users and their respective TaskManager smart contracts. If users were new to the app, it would create a new TaskManager contract for them. TaskManager contract held each user's tasks, including the task name, description, due date, and managed the allocation and storage of ETH for task completion. For our frontend, we used React.js, which provided an interactive and user-friendly interface for users to easily manage their tasks and ETH staking. The backend was implemented using Node.js and Express, which was used to handle the user wallet and address with API endpoints for frontend.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Smart Contract Efficiency: Optimizing our code to reduce gas. Handling User Data: Securely storing user data and their respective TaskManager contract . Frontend Integration: Accessing smart contracts with the frontend. Unfortunately, we were not able to achieve this within the time constraints... Security: Protecting the smart contracts and preventing outside access to smart contracts. User Experience: Creating an intuitive interface for easy task management and ETH staking.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We’re proud of creating large-scale smart contracts for the first time and successfully adapting to the challenges of Solidity. While linking the smart contracts to our React.js frontend was a challenge, we still take pride in challenging the unknown.

sections.heading: What's next for TaskChain
sections.text: We plan to continue developing TaskChain, with a focus on finalizing and publishing the frontend. Our goal is to enhance the user experience, improve scalability, and ensure seamless interaction with the smart contracts. We also aim to add more features, such as the ability of linking your own Canvas to improve user convenance.

title: Lease Saving Plan
tagline: Calculate car lease payments, insurance, and track savings in one tool! Tailored for your budget, with support for English/Spanish. Simplify car leasing and budgeting with ease!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: I was inspired by the complexity of car leasing, particularly how overwhelming it can be to understand lease payments, insurance costs, and budget planning. I wanted to create a tool that simplifies this process, allowing users to manage car lease decisions with ease and confidence.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Lease Saving Plan calculates monthly lease payments based on user inputs like down payment, lease term, and car selection. It also estimates insurance costs based on age, driving history, and location, and helps users track savings toward their down payment goal. The app supports both English and Spanish for accessibility.

sections.heading: How I built it
sections.text: I built Lease Saving Plan using Python, incorporating the CustomTkinter library for the interface, SQLite for database management, and Matplotlib for visual representations like pie charts. The program integrates dynamic lease and insurance calculators, providing real-time results based on user inputs. A language toggle feature was also implemented to switch between English and Spanish.

sections.heading: Challenges I ran into

sections.heading: Accomplishments that I'm proud of

sections.heading: What I learned
