title: SmartCards
tagline: SmartCards is a user-friendly addon for your budgeting app to help you better categorize your transactions and find investing opportunities from each purchase.

sections.text: SmartCards SmartCards is a user-friendly addon for your budgeting app to help you better categorize your transactions and find investing opportunities from each purchase. Simply upload a picture of any receipt and our GenAI technology will organize your purchases while providing insights to help your financial future.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: SmartCards was inspired by real-world problems we've encountered with split transactions in popular budgeting and cash management applications like YNAB (You Need A Budget). We noticed that these apps typically don't integrate or inspire their users to invest in stable (or unstable) opportunities while using the app. While some may offer learning resources on their websites, this information isn't readily presented to users within the app interface. SmartCards was also conceptualized because of the growing need for financial literacy in our world. Many people are unsure about investing, and we want to help provide the tools to show them the many alternative places a dollar can be outside of the bank account.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: SmartCards is a user-friendly addon for budgeting apps that helps users better categorize their transactions and discover investing opportunities from each purchase. Our key features include: Intelligent transaction categorization using GenAI technology Investment opportunity identification based on spending patterns and other user information Seamless integration with existing budgeting apps User-friendly interface for easy receipt scanning and financial management Users can simply upload a picture of any receipt, and our GenAI technology organizes purchases while providing insights from spending patterns and cashback opportunities to help their financial future.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built SmartCards using a combination of modern web technologies and AI: Frontend: React+Vite and Tailwind CSS for a responsive and intuitive user interface Backend: Node.js for serverside management & Flask to run our local classification model (trained on a Kaggle dataset of 42,000 different products, 83% accuracy) AI Integration: Leveraged OpenAI's API for intelligent transaction categorization and investment insights Version Control: Git and GitHub for collaborative development Development Workflow: npm for package management and running development servers

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: First time using OAuth2, there were a few different ways of integrating it and so we needed to find what worked for us We decided to use a classification model to separate the products / services into categories, but this model needed to be run using Python libraries. Therefore we had to set up and create a parallel Flask server for the model. Huge mixup with the localhost v 127.0.0.1 involving incorrect redirects and other shenanigans. hour long setback Using context provider with react is a pain, since there is no simple way to transfer information from siblings for some horrible reason.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Nice looking landing page and elegant branding / presentation (more for the readme and devpost Fully connected front and back end using 2 servers (This was insane!) Use of chartjs to give cool-looking visuals and a working MVP! WIP database to store user transactions and itemized purchases.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Always remember to keep it simple, we want the MVP here, we're not trying to recreate the entire banking system Starting with some boilerplate is not cheating, know how to set that up easily so that you're ready to roll Don't try to learn a new framework in 24 hours it won't happen. Use your unfair advantages, but also recognize learning does come quite quick Be willing to change project ideas and incorporate company challenges into your project, they have the bigger perspective. Used new libraries like chartjs, and figured out context providers, and first time using a classification model in a full-stack project.

sections.heading: What's next for SmartCards
sections.text: We have exciting plans for the future of SmartCards: Implement machine learning models for even more accurate transaction categorization Integrate with major financial institutions for real-time transaction updates Develop a mobile app for on-the-go receipt scanning and financial management Improve investment opportunity detection algorithms Introduce social features for comparing anonymized spending habits with peers We're committed to continuously improving SmartCards to help users make smarter financial decisions and discover new investment opportunities.

title: Treasure Keepers
tagline: We help first-generation students and people with low income learn about finance through gamified challenges and quizzes. Meet fantasy instructors and learn how to unlock your financial skills.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Financial literacy is an important factor to the success of a student. We wanted to make an immersive and fun way for low-income students and immigrants to improve their financial situation, using gamification and a more approachable fantasy-themed website.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: We offer many different ways for people to improve their finances. We offer tailored AI advice to each person. In addition, we have quizzes to solidify understanding, and a budgeting application to help the user understand their finances.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We used the Streamlit framework as a base to calculate budgets, build a quiz, enter user information and layout our pages. We styled it with lots of CSS. We used ChatGPT to generate advice from our custom characters.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Streamlit splits each page as a python file, so links between pages can only be done through streamlit compnents. While streamlit has many builtin components, trying to override its look and feel was difficult. Referencing a python streeamlit component in CSS was difficult. One of our members momentarily lost their work when pushing to main and didn't save locally. The work was recovered but the project could not have been completed without it.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We created lots of custom assets, which helped us achieve a cohesive fantasy look. We managed to integrate ChatGPT using the OpenAI API in a fun way, using the different character personalities. We managed to work together effectively, splitting the tasks and accomplishing much of what we planned.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Save a local copy of the repository, pull from main often. Agreeing on the purpose of the website sped up the work and allowed us to work on parts of the project separately.

sections.heading: What's next for Treasure Keepers
sections.text: The ability to chat with the advisors and integrate the context of the budgeting into the AI agent. Personalize the questions of the quizzes. Offer something to spend the coins you earned on.

title: Agent Zero
tagline: False and duplicate invoices cost AP teams money. By routing extraction, matching, and anomaly checks to our best fit model, our benchmark-driven AI provides proof/confidence for acceptance review.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Day and night people constantly get scammed by sly, cunning people that are willing to sacrifice their dignity for an extra buck. It comes in all shapes and sizes, but scammers frequently prey on the weak and less fortunate. Those that are unable to afford financial/legal professionals to protect them. In light of this tragedy, AgentZero is designed to serve as last resort of financial warning for unknowing individuals and small businesses.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: AgentZero is an AI tool that is made up of an array of specialized agents pretrained on financial data to uncover malicious invoices before they make it to a bank statement. Depending on the task, an orchestrator agent decided which specialized agents to summon and begin assessing invoices. Each agent focuses on distinct subtle signs of fraudulent invoices and provides individualized risk scores for each metric depending on a predetermined rubric and the User's context. The results are aggregated behind the scenes in order to provide an intuitive and concise output on the predicted reliability of an invoice.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Frameworks: Frontend: Node.js, Express.js, React, TypeScript Backend: Python (FastAPI, BigQuery, Gemini, TensorFlow, YOLOv11, PyArrow) Most of the brunt of the project was in developing a research framework from which to maximize our accuracy. We determined which models would provide the best accuracy/time ratio in order to improve the user experience which boasting great results. We also sourced invoice data with computer vision (YOLOv11), fraudulent transaction data from the IEEE and financial anomaly data. This data was then used to make our out in-house agents that were specialized at picking out malicious invoices.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Accuracy and response time was a big concern when starting this project. Base models were not effective at picking out fraudulent invoices and mostly guessed even though they sometimes loaded for extended periods. We overcame the accuracy problem by pretraining our models and summoning multiple agents that focused on doing just one task very well. We also parallelized our agents and run up to 6 agents at a single time with some invoices.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud of leaving our comfort zone and push ourselves to learn about technology with our friends. We ran on nothing but caffeine and group morale all night to create a project that we can be excited to talk to our friends/family about.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learnt many new technologies and libraries together and taught each other along the way.

sections.heading: What's next for Agent Zero
sections.text: AgentZero is a monetizable tool that many individuals and small businesses could use to close the gap between the wealthy and the poor and give everyone an even playing field when it comes to financial scams. With more financial data and fine-tuning AgentZero could actually break into the market and become a product that people wished they'd had earlier. We truly believe in the potential behind this idea and will continue to develop it further after this hackathon.

title: GreenLight
tagline: GreenLight turns dashcam footage into a learning tool. Incidents become 3D simulations in Three.js with a quiz to boost your driving score, reinforce learning, plus tips on safe driving and insurance.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Between 20 and 50 million people are injured or involved in road traffic accidents globally each year, highlighting the massive scale of reckless driving and other unsafe driving practices. We were inspired to create GreenLight after recognizing that many drivers develop unsafe habits; therefore, we reimagined how people can learn safer driving practices by combining AI, simulation, and gamification into one seamless experience.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: GreenLight is an AI-powered educational platform that helps users become safer drivers through immersive, personalized learning. A user can upload a dashcam footage containing an instance of unsafe driving (e.g., following too closely, sudden lane change, failed stop). Then by using Gemini AI, we analyze the video as well as generate 3D simulations in Three.js that recreate the unsafe driving scenarios from the uploaded footage, allowing users to visualize the incident and understand how different actions could have mitigated or even prevented it. After each simulation, users complete targeted quiz questions specifically designed around the identified safety issues, reinforcing proper driving practices through active learning. We also included a dedicated quizzes section to further educate users on safe driving practices and insurance. Correct answers earn safe driving points, gamifying the learning experience and reinforcing positive driving behavior.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We started by designing our user interface in Figma and researching the best technologies and libraries for our stack, including shadcn/ui components and an icon library for the frontend. We then developed a comprehensive web application using React and Tailwind for the frontend that interfaces with a Python backend integrated with Gemini AI to analyze dashcam footage and identify unsafe driving behaviors. For the backend we used Python with FastAPI as our server which made it really easy to connect logic to the frontend. Using python came as an advantage to us since it has so many libraries that we were able to use such as pydanic. We were also able to use Firebase which was able to store all the data we needed including user, incident, quiz data, and more. We also used Gemini with Gemini ADK for the three.js simulation generation.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Project Scope: Our initial vision was overly ambitious, specifically including a feature that allowed a phone to be used as a live dashcam for instant analysis. We quickly realized the time constraint required us to pivot and focus purely on file upload and the core simulation logic. 3D Simulations: Creating smooth, realistic 3D simulations that accurately represent driving scenarios required careful optimization of Three.js performance, especially for complex traffic situations Google ADK: Navigated the complexities of integrating the new Google ADK framework, resolving a series of dependency conflicts and low-level errors between the asynchronous API and the library's transaction management. AI Analysis: The initial agent architecture created a significant performance bottleneck due to its slow, sequential processing, and the AI's inconsistent JSON and simulation outputs required extensive prompt refinement to ensure reliability.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Developed a functional video analysis pipeline that transforms dashcam footage into educational content. Created an intuitive and fully responsive user interface that effectively teaches safe driving practices through simulations and personalized quizzes. Fostered collaboration and teamwork under tight deadlines, leading to a cohesive final product. Successfully engineered an end-to-end, AI-driven pipeline by Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) that transforms raw dashcam video into interactive 3D driving simulations and personalized safety quizzes. Optimized the system's performance by re-architecting the agent's workflow from a multi-step process into a single, efficient command, reducing the total processing time by approximately 50%.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Effective prompt engineering techniques to get consistent results from AI models like Gemini. The value of providing immediate feedback in educational applications to enhance user engagement and reinforce learning. The importance of setting clear milestones and checkpoints during development for efficient workflow The agent's architecture directly impacts performance, and that a single, highly-structured command (a "one-shot" prompt) is far more efficient than a multi-step, conversational approach. Correctly configuring Python versions and dependencies is critical to mitigating complex integration issues.

sections.heading: What's next for GreenLight
sections.text: Some goals we have for the future include developing mobile integration with seamless upload capabilities for dashcam footage, and enhancing our 3D simulations by refining the accuracy, realism, and visual quality of our driving scenario recreations. Ultimately, our long-term vision is to transform GreenLight from a post-incident review tool into a proactive safety co-pilot, implementing real-time dashcam analysis that provides immediate preventative alerts during actual driving.

title: Next Step
tagline: Learn how to take your Next Step in insurance education by practicing in high pressure scenarios

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We found that many people are uninformed about how insurance works and how to navigate difficult insurance related situations. Current insurance education relies heavily on static learning through dense textbooks, missing the crucial aspect of real-time application. After recognizing this issue, we created Next Step , which forces you to learn in a realistic , interactive environment .

sections.heading: What Does Next Step Do?
sections.text: Next Step uses AI-powered conversational scenarios to transform insurance education. Users engage with realistic, time-sensitive situations across three domains that they can select from: Auto , Home , and Health insurance. Each scenario challenges the user, requiring immediate responses that will be graded on a scale from 0 to 100 based on the application of these. Safety Awareness - Prioritizing personal and others' safety first Insurance Knowledge - Understanding coverage, procedures, and timing Procedural Understanding - Following proper steps and protocols Decision-Making Quality - Making choices that minimize risk and cost

sections.heading: How We Built It
sections.text: Next Step was developed with a modern full-stack architecture that allows for powerful AI to blend with our web technologies. On the frontend , we utilized Next.js with React , TypeScript , and Tailwind CSS to provide an interactive and responsive user experience. The backend is powered by Flask and Python , ensuring efficient processing and seamless integration with our AI. Fundamentally, Next Step makes use of Vapi , our AI voice agent that drives conversational scenarios to make insurance learning realistic and interactive.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: One of our biggest challenges was the creation of the idea itself, it took us hours of brainstorming together to finally come up with a solid plan. Another issue was setting up the python virtual environment for the whole team, we ran into technical issues with discrepancies between what commands were needed to activate them on our own machines. We also ran into issues with dynamic page routing since none of us had previous experience with Next.js before. There was also an hour-long problem of trying to track down a connection issue between backend and AI integration . The error being that the API key was never set 🤦. Fortunately, we were able to overcome all of these challenges with the power of teamwork, persistence, and lots of energy drinks.

sections.heading: Accomplishments
sections.text: We successfully accomplished our goal of transforming the old-fashioned insurance education system into an interactive conversational experience for users to prepare themselves for real-world scenarios. We also were able to learn and adapt to technology we were unfamiliar with on the spot, a crucial skill that we will continue to develop over time.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: We learned the basics of NextJS and React , as well as implementing the voice interface design learning how these interactions require different design patterns to focus on conversation flow and context retention . We learned even more about git and github, especially the first time hackers in our team. Most importantly, we learned the power of scenario-based learning over traditional textbooks.

sections.heading: What's the next step for Next Step?
sections.text: Try saying that again 10 times fast! We plan to add more types of insurance to truly test your knowledge, such as life, business, pet, renters, and more! Enabling you to learn more about different types of insurances and how you can correctly find your through difficult scenarios.

title: The Rat Race
tagline: The Rat Race

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: In a world where the corporate “rat race” is all too familiar, our game, The Rat Race, offers a fresh, creative take on the grind of everyday work life—specifically through the lens of insurance. Built as an interactive web application, our project combines the excitement of gamified storytelling with the practical need for insurance education. Developed for the State Farm and Netflix Challenges, this project is designed to entertain, engage, and educate—without taking itself too seriously.

sections.heading: The Concept
sections.text: The Rat Race takes players on a journey through a whimsical, yet insightful corporate world, where the player assumes the role of a new intern at Snout Farm Insurance. The aim? To navigate daily tasks, build relationships with coworkers, and understand the ins and outs of insurance policies while climbing the corporate ladder. Players can expect a dynamic, choose-your-own-adventure style narrative where every decision counts. Will you rise to the top or get eaten by a metaphorical cat? In this satirical take on corporate life, your success is determined by how well you handle customer claims, engage with coworkers, and make informed insurance decisions.

sections.heading: Core Features
sections.text: Gamified Experience: Players engage in quirky yet educational tasks, from fetching coffee for the elusive "King Rat" (the boss) to handling customer claims with empathy and professionalism. Every action is tied to a set of consequences—boosting your "Sales" and "Coworker" points or risking a trip to the corporate abyss. Dynamic Storytelling: The narrative is non-linear, with multiple paths and endings based on player decisions. Every choice—whether it's making a new friend at the office or getting a claim wrong—impacts the storyline, leading to one of several possible outcomes (including, but not limited to): Promotion: If you excel in your duties, you get promoted, advancing through the ranks of Snout Farm Insurance. Article Written About You: If you are bad enough at your job, the local community will take note. At least you still might be a good person at heart… Fired and Broke: Make poor choices, and you’ll face the grim fate of not being able to make rent. King of Ratopia: If your karma, sales, and coworker relationships are stellar, you can rule the office as the "King of Ratopia." A Tasty Snack: Bad rats get eaten by the cat. Don’t be a bad rat :( The Ratator: Some are drawn to benevolent goodness and care about supporting the lives of others. Some want to watch the world burn from their penthouse office while they eat cheese. Insurance Education: Interspersed throughout the narrative are moments where players must make informed insurance decisions. From selecting the right insurance plans for customers to understanding policies like deductibles, premiums, and risk assessment, the game introduces educational elements in a way that feels natural and engaging. Interactive Customer Support: The game features multiple customer service scenarios where players must respond to inquiries with accuracy and empathy. Whether it’s guiding a college student through insurance options or helping someone file a claim after an accident, your ability to communicate effectively and understand insurance jargon impacts your sales and coworker scores.

sections.heading: Why It's Creative and Fun
sections.text: What sets The Rat Race apart is its blend of humor, creativity, and critical thinking. It tackles a serious topic—insurance—by wrapping it in an office-based, satirical storyline where players are forced to navigate a series of ridiculous, yet relatable, corporate situations. Through the use of decision-making, humor, and multiple branching storylines, we’ve created an interactive experience that’s both entertaining and educational. The incorporation of outlandish claims—like UFO damage and stolen cheese—adds an element of surprise and whimsy, making learning about insurance feel like a fun adventure rather than a dry lecture. It’s a lighthearted critique of corporate America, where every decision feels important, and the stakes are always high—even if it’s just about getting the right coffee for your boss.

title: VL-ADK
tagline: A "psuedo" VLA model leveraging a fleet of autonomous ADK agents.

sections.heading: 💡 Inspiration
sections.text: Over the past few months, agents have taken the world by storm - in the digital space as software agents, and now in the physical space as embodied intelligence. We wanted to get our hands dirty and earn the capabilities of combining the two, with a fleet of software agents piloting their physical agent vessel.

sections.heading: 🕹️ What it Does
sections.text: A robot, a control panel, and a group of Google ADK AI agents controlling its every move. Ask the agents to find something, guide you, or just make you laugh. The Director, Pilot, and Observer agents will do their best to pilot the Jetson Orin Nano to victory.

sections.heading: 💻 How we built it
sections.text: We used SSH tunnels to connect between our hosts and the Jetson Orin mounted on top of our Jetbot. We wrote Python API endpoints that we can call to control the robot remotely, and these endpoints would also be the basis of using ADK for controlling the robot. We created a control panel with react and typescript to analyze the view of the robot live using web sockets and to quickly be able to interact with it. YOLOE was used as a middle layer for image identification to reduce context bloat and token costs when interacting with Google Gemini, and made for some fun optimizations that found the right balance of abstraction with these highly complex and generalized models.

sections.heading: ‼️ Challenges we ran into
sections.text: It was a challenge getting ADK to be precise in the actions it takes for autonomous robotics. Specific implementations of robotic movement were also difficult, and a lot of networking issues came up along the building process. Additionally, some more impactful hardware components like Lidar were out of our budget, so we were limited by what we had. We were able to tweak issues out by the end.

sections.heading: 🏆. Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're proud that we were able to build a proof of concept and a minimal version of a natural language autonomous robot, just like SOTA VLA models dropping lately. It is by no means industry-grade, but it is accessible to us as students and didn't cost the same as a new car.

sections.heading: 🦾 What we learned
sections.text: Networking protocols, working with NVIDIA hardware, and Google ADK.

sections.heading: 🤖 What's next for VL-ADK
sections.text: A Humanoid Robot (after we sell all of our belongins)

title: Halo
tagline: Protection beyond the helmet.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: In 2022, 1,105 cyclists were killed on US roads, the most since 1975. Florida, where we built this, is consistently one of the deadliest states in the country to ride a bike. Many of these crashes start behind the rider: a driver who doesn't see them, or who passes far too close. Cars have had blind-spot monitoring for years, and a Waymo sees 360° with fused sensors. The cyclist next to it, the most exposed person on the road, has a mirror the size of a coin. We built Halo to give riders the awareness a modern car has, inside the one thing every rider already wears.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Halo is a smart bike helmet that watches the road behind you and warns you about what's coming before it reaches you, so you don't have to turn your head. A rear camera and side ultrasonic sensors track vehicles approaching from behind and beside you. When a car enters your blind spot, cuts into your lane, or closes in fast, Halo warns you on the side it's coming from : an arrow on a transparent OLED in your peripheral vision (outline = caution, flashing = danger) a beep panned to that ear in your earbuds a spoken callout like "Car left!" Close passes are measured, not guessed . The side sensor reports the real gap ("passed at 0.32 m"), which is the number that matters under Florida's 3-foot passing law. Every serious alert becomes an incident report . The helmet saves a clip from 6 seconds before to 4 seconds after, attaches the measured gap and warning time, and Gemini writes a short summary of what happened. The Halo iOS app tracks your ride, shows the helmet's live safety state and a 3D "rear-view mirror", and keeps your safety history. A front camera adds a forward BRAKE warning demo for obstacles ahead.

sections.heading: Technical Deep Dive
sections.text: Our core rule: nothing that keeps the rider safe waits on the internet. Detection, alerts and fail-safes all run on the helmet. AI only runs off the critical path. Perceive: YOLO26n, exported to NCNN at 320 px, runs on a Raspberry Pi 5. The rear camera is mounted upside down, and the camera rotates the image itself at no cost. Track and measure: each vehicle is tracked. Time-to-contact comes from how fast its bounding box grows, so no depth sensor is needed, and it stays correct when the box is cut off at the frame edge. Lateral position and velocity predict each car's path, so a car cutting into your lane is flagged before it arrives. Fuse: side ultrasonic sensors are median-filtered, and a wall or parked car fades into the background. When a tracked car leaves the camera's view beside you, the side sensor takes over and measures real clearance. A danger alert requires the camera to confirm it's a vehicle. An echo alone can only raise a caution, because it can't tell a car from a pole. Decide: a tiered alert policy (tracked → approaching → blind spot → danger) with hysteresis keeps alerts from flickering. One shared state drives the OLED, earbuds and phone, so every output always agrees. Fail safely: the Pi sends the Arduino a heartbeat every 250 ms. If it goes silent, the rider feels a warning buzz and the helmet falls back to a plain bike light. If the camera drops, the OLED shows an X, Halo says "rear camera offline", and the side sensors keep warning. Gemini calls are async, budgeted, rate-limited and circuit-broken, so if Gemini is slow or down, the helmet keeps working. Record and explain: frames sit in an in-memory ring buffer. A danger alert writes an H.264 clip in a low-priority background thread. Gemini receives 6 key frames plus the measured facts and returns structured JSON (classification, severity, vehicle, maneuver, summary). It's instructed to treat the sensor numbers as ground truth, and the API key never leaves the helmet. Show: the Pi streams ~700-byte JSON snapshots over server-sent events, and a bundled three.js scene renders the 3D mirror on any phone, even on a hotspot with no internet.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built Halo from scratch: hardware, firmware, the vision pipeline and the app. Hardware Raspberry Pi 5 (main compute) 2× Raspberry Pi cameras (rear, mounted inverted, and front) Arduino Uno (sensors, haptics, fail-safe watchdog) HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensors, angled back on each side 1.51" transparent OLED (SSD1309) as a heads-up display Vibration motors and Bluetooth earbuds for audio alerts Software Python perception pipeline: YOLO + NCNN, OpenCV, Picamera2/libcamera Camera + ultrasonic sensor fusion with camera-to-sensor hand-off Serial protocol between Pi and Arduino with a heartbeat watchdog Gemini for incident analysis and "what's behind me?" voice questions three.js 2.5D rear-view mirror, streamed live from the helmet SwiftUI iOS app with MapKit navigation, ride tracking and safety history A traffic simulator that runs scripted scenes (close passes, cut-ins, tailgaters) through the real pipeline, plus test suites for every module

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Our biggest challenge was speed on a tiny computer . A warning that arrives a second late is useless, and everything, including detection, tracking, sensor fusion, the 3D view and incident recording, has to run on one Raspberry Pi strapped to a helmet. Our first attempts couldn't keep up. We had to make every millisecond count. We shrank the detection model and converted it to a format built for the Pi's processor. We rotate the upside-down camera image in the camera hardware instead of in software. Video encoding runs at low priority in the background, and the phone gets tiny data snapshots instead of a video stream. Gemini was the biggest trap: an AI call can take seconds. So we moved it off the safety path entirely. It never delays an alert, and if it's slow or offline, the helmet keeps working without it. Another unique challenge we faced happened before we wrote a line of code: we threw out our idea. We came to ShellHacks planning a fintech project, a pair of smart glasses that read price tags as you shop and showed your budget in your field of view, like "Honey for the physical world." Once we saw the challenge tracks, we realized a camera, a transparent display and on-device AI could do something far more important than save money: keep someone alive.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A working helmet that detects and warns about cars behind you, fully on-device and offline Measured close passes, not estimates One safety state that keeps the OLED, earbuds and phone in agreement Incident reports where the AI explains the clip but never overrides the measured numbers Layered fail-safes: watchdog, camera fault handling and graceful AI degradation A simulator good enough to develop and demo without a single car

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned how different real sensors are from the ideal version: noise, latency, mounting angles and cables all change behavior. We also learned: Which numbers to trust, and how to design around the ones you can't Why safety-critical logic has to be separated from AI and the network How to fuse sensors that are each wrong in different ways How much hardware integration there is, from camera numbering to audio drivers

sections.heading: What's next for Halo
sections.text: Road testing, and a proper integrated shell with battery and weatherproofing A wider-angle rear camera and radar for better range at speed GPS-tagged incident reports riders can share, and an anonymized close-pass map to help cities find dangerous roads Full incident video playback and reporting in the iOS app The goal is to take Halo from a hackathon prototype to something every rider wears without thinking about it.

sections.heading: Built With
sections.text: Raspberry Pi 5 Raspberry Pi Camera (OV5647) Arduino Uno HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensors SSD1309 transparent OLED Python C++ (Arduino) OpenCV Ultralytics YOLO NCNN Picamera2 / libcamera Google Gemini API ffmpeg three.js Swift / SwiftUI MapKit / CoreLocation

title: Heard!
tagline: A meeting dashboard that joins the conversation.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: At 10 pm on the first night, we had two ideas and no decision. We wrote a design doc for each, half-built a demo for each, and every time one of us pitched, the other two pulled out their phones to check whether it was done. It usually had. We realized we kept going back to whichever project we had sunk the most hours into, and none of us could look things up and argue at the same time. We looked at the AI meeting tools first. All of them are competent secretaries: they transcribe, they summarize, they send you the action items. None of them will sit in the meeting and think with you. We wanted a teammate who would sit in that meeting with us, take the notes, do the research while we talked, and tell us when we were about to rebuild someone else's project. So we built Heard!, the thing we wished had been in the room.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Heard! is an ambient agent teammate that sits in a working meeting. It writes down the ideas and the threads of discussion, looks things up, brings information to the table, answers questions, and joins the discussion when it has something to add. Takes the meeting notes, live, as people talk. Sorts what comes up — ideas, projects, points of discussion — into cards on a shared board. Investigates when needed: researches an open question and brings back supporting information and options. Speaks up when it should, joining the discussion with an opinion of its own. Answers questions from the room, in real time.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We started from the demo, 、wrote out the two-minute meeting we wanted Heard! to sit in, worked backward from what had to happen on screen and when. The first thing we measured was speed. We benchmarked Nemotron models on NVIDIA NIM with reasoning on and off, and the numbers set the design: a card has to be on the board within five seconds of someone naming an idea, so nothing slow can be on that path. Next we designed the architecture from the measurements. A fast Nemotron classifier (Super 120B, reasoning off) reads every few seconds of speech and sorts it: new idea, question, someone talking to Heard. A second Nemotron agent runs in the background and rewrites the meeting notes every twenty seconds. A Claude front desk, running as one long-lived Claude Agent SDK session, makes every decision the room can hear: answer, dispatch a research sub-agent, or stay quiet. Speech in and out is ElevenLabs, Scribe v2 for transcription, and streamed TTS for the voice. Then we built the harness because the model always tries to say something, which is annoying during a real meeting. Finally, we wrote most of the code with Claude Code and tested the whole pipeline. During development, humans wrote most of the docs, architecture designs, implementation specs, and locked down code behavior with tests, while Claude Code implemented the code.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: It's all about ideas. We keep pushing back ideas and coming up with new ones with our own biases. But we are proud that we finally turned this big challenge into the whole project.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are surprised that the NVIDIA Nemotron classifier works so well that during our testing, most of the unrelated chats and debugging chats are well filtered out, and the AI agent doesn't respond to those at all! But everything related to a real project discussion, decision-making, and new ideas is all correctly flagged and recorded. We are proud of the response speed Heard! has. We can reach near real-time asking and answering questions, investigating, and getting a reasonable result in 30s, Nothing to the codebase itself, but our previous AI harnessing experiences make the whole project extremely easy to implement and very robust.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Learned to use Nemotron APIs and ElevenLabs from scratch. Learned to use the Claude Code SDK. Dive deeper into agent loops and architecture design for an agentic system.

sections.heading: What's next for Heard!
sections.text: Maybe persist past memories and make a personal database for all the meeting histories. Potentially rewrite and refine the project to publish as open-source software. Build start-ups that actually solve people's needs.

title: SurrealEstate
tagline: Local Housing Expertise, Accessible Anywhere.

sections.heading: Inspiration: Our Unique Backgrounds
sections.text: Our team has lived across five countries—Switzerland, China, South Africa, India, and the United States—so we know firsthand how difficult it can be to find a home somewhere you don’t know. When Hrehaan’s family moved to South Africa, his parents had to fly back and forth from the U.S. just to make sure the homes they were considering were in safe, active communities. Lucas’s family faced an even bigger challenge: while living in Shanghai, they had to buy a house in the United States without ever seeing it in person. That made us ask: What if you could become an expert on any property, from anywhere in the world, in minutes? Instead of spending hours researching neighborhoods, schools, parks, safety, amenities, and the property itself—or traveling just to meet with an agent—buyers could instantly understand what living there would actually be like before ever stepping through the door.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Once you paste in the Zillow link of a listing you’re interested in, SurrealEstate connects you with Sir Real Estate—an evidence-backed virtual agent that guides you through the home, helps you explore each room, and answers the questions that actually matter to you. Whether you want to know where the closest Starbucks is, whether there are good squash courts nearby, or what the surrounding schools and neighborhood are like, SurrealEstate pulls together verified property and local data into one interactive experience. Instead of opening ten tabs and researching everything yourself, you can tour, ask, understand, and compare, all in one place.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built SurrealEstate to be first and foremost evidence-grounded. A user starts with a Zillow listing or U.S. address; the system gathers neighborhood data from public sources like Census, OpenStreetMap, FEMA, NCES, Yelp, and Reddit, while NVIDIA Nemotron orchestrates follow-up research and keeps every claim tied to source evidence. For the property itself, we convert the 3D-home tour into a structured HouseGraph, using floor plans, room IDs, and panoramas, with Nemotron vision labeling rooms so buyers can navigate the home digitally. The final experience combines the house model and verified research into an interactive walkthrough where buyers can explore rooms, see concise source-backed insights, ask questions to Sir. Real Estate, and export a simple one-page review sheet to compare listings later.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Our main challenge was project direction - specifically, we knew we wanted to make SurrealEstate, but weren't sure the most effective way. While developing draft one of SurrealEstate, we deduced that our intent for the first version was right, but our execution was wrong. We knew we wanted to make the home-buying process more informative and intuitive, but early on, we were too focused on showcasing the technology itself rather than solving the buyer’s actual problem. That gave us something technically impressive, but not necessarily something that felt useful. In our second iteration, we changed the way we approached the project. Instead of asking, “How can we use this technology?”, we asked, “What does a buyer actually need? What did our parents need?” From there, we focused directly on reducing the friction of researching, touring, and comparing homes—even if that meant cutting features or sacrificing some of the initial “wow factor.” That shift in direction is what ultimately shaped SurrealEstate into a much stronger, scalable product.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We’re proud of fighting off the sunk-cost fallacy and choosing the customer over the concept. When we realized our first execution wasn’t matching the problem we actually wanted to solve, we scrapped nearly 10 hours of work and started over. That decision forced us to get much clearer on SurrealEstate’s value proposition: not building the flashiest demo, but building something buyers would actually care about and use. It taught us that strong product development means being willing to let go of good work when it isn’t serving the story, the market, or the customer. One of the technical accomplishments we’re most proud of is how far we pushed NVIDIA Nemotron. We initially challenged it with extremely ambitious tasks, including ideas around 3D reconstruction, and that process helped us learn where the model was strongest and how to use it more effectively. From there, we built a broader agentic system around it: Nemotron helps label floor plans, select relevant facts, orchestrate research, and verify AI-generated responses, while our backend connects multiple external APIs and keeps everything grounded in source evidence. More than just integrating an AI model, we learned how to build a reliable system around it and push the technology to its practical limits.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: One of our biggest lessons was to start small and make the value obvious. William Hill from NVIDIA challenged us with ideas like “try to do more with less,” “give us a reason why we should care,” and, most importantly, “know your story.” We took that seriously. Instead of trying to win through sheer technical complexity, we focused on what makes SurrealEstate meaningfully different: bringing the home, neighborhood research, and buyer questions into one evidence-backed experience. We learned that strong technology only matters if the customer immediately understands why your product should exist and why they should choose you over what’s already on the market. On the technical side, we learned a lot about agentic orchestration and keeping AI systems constrained. Rather than asking one model to do everything, we built a backend pipeline where different components have specific jobs: research providers collect evidence, Nemotron helps select and verify information, Gemini turns that information into buyer-friendly language, and ElevenLabs handles speech. Our API layer ties those pieces together while preserving source IDs and failing safely when information cannot be verified. We also learned that model capability is about more than a benchmark number. Pushing Nemotron toward ambitious tasks helped us understand where it performed well in our actual workflow and where a more focused role created better results. That same lesson applies to API integration and GPU-backed AI infrastructure: the challenge isn’t just getting a model running—it’s designing the orchestration, latency, reliability, and verification around it so the technology actually serves the product.

sections.heading: What's next for SurrealEstate
sections.text: The next step for SurrealEstate is getting it into the hands of real buyers and real estate professionals. We want to explore pilot opportunities with platforms like Zillow and with local Pittsburgh real estate agencies to see how the product performs in actual home-search and showing workflows. That hands-on feedback would help us understand where SurrealEstate creates the most value, refine the experience around real buyer and agent needs, and validate how well our combination of interactive tours, neighborhood intelligence, and evidence-backed AI can fit into the existing real estate ecosystem. From there, the goal is to turn SurrealEstate from a hackathon prototype into a product people can actually use while making one of the biggest decisions of their lives.

title: Weave
tagline: Making the Internet Collaborative

sections.heading: Weave
sections.text: Inspiration We've had countless calls with our parents and grandparents, helping them use complicated technology for things they need access to like medical bills or banking information. Screen sharing is hard to set up, and most webpages aren't built for accessibility. We wanted to make a platform where people can work together on the same pages, and make it as easy as possible to use the internet regardless of who you are. What it does Weave is a desktop browser built on Electron. Multiple people can open the same website together. Each person gets their own view of it: larger text, bigger targets, a clutter-free rebuild of the page, plain wording, or the whole page in many different languages, all as personal settings that follow their account. Cursors, annotations and a hand-drawn lasso from the helper appear on the other person's page, anchored to elements rather than pixels, so different layouts still line up. Webb, a small jumping spider, is the in-page assistant: ask it where to click and it circles the element and explains, in your language, with voice if you want it. How we built it A pnpm TypeScript monorepo: shared zod contracts, an injectable overlay for extraction and adaptation, a synthetic patient portal for a safe demo, a Fastify coordinator, and the Electron shell. The overlay extracts a sanitized page model from the DOM (labels, roles, sections, table rows) with deterministic element ids, classifies sensitive content with rules, and rebuilds a personalized view per person. NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning via NIM powers Webb's answers, element targeting and per-person layout proposals. Gemini handles page translation and simpler wording. ElevenLabs gives Webb a voice in and out. Every model call only ever sees sanitized labels, and every outbound payload is audited. Co-browsing runs as host simulation plus guest intents, sequenced by the server like a game engine, with field claims and a host pause switch. Challenges Hosted model latency has a long tail: one call in three sat for 10 to 30 seconds. Disabling reasoning tokens, hedging requests after 3 seconds, and falling back across providers brought replies to about a second. Small models echo JSON schemas back instead of filling them, and answer poorly in Hindi. We pivot: question in through Gemini, reasoning in English, answer back out. Rewriting page text changed element ids and broke the next translation. The extractor now reads original text through rewrites. Venue Wi-Fi blocked Google's API hosts at the DNS level, which cost an hour of confusion before a resolver change. Keeping two teammates' work merging cleanly all night on one branch. What we learned Privacy and accessibility are the same problem: both are about showing each person exactly what they need and nothing else. And a demo is a product feature. Every "just for the demo" shortcut turned into a real setting someone would want.

Next.js renders the dashboard; React-Leaflet, Zustand, and custom hooks layer in events, calls, social hotspots, and polygons while triggering Gemini-backed (or heuristic fallback) forecasts. title: Pennywise
tagline: Budget smarter, not harder

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Our team wanted to make an impact in the financial technological field. The idea came from our own experience of planning events and struggling to stay within the budget. So we wanted to combine a budgeting app with the friendliness of an AI chatbot.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our web application has a user-friendly form that asks users about the event type, event date, and expense they are expecting to make. Users also have access to an AI financial advisor that can help them plan the budget for their event accordingly. The key features are smart budget allocation according to event type and size, the chatbot that offers personalized financial advice, and visual analytics to track spending patterns. People can also update their names and pronouns at any time, and an additional feature where people can select what accommodation they want so that a diverse range of people can use the web application.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We developed our project using React.js and AntDesign(AntD) for the front end to design a clean interface. This setup allows users to navigate the platform effortlessly, accessing the insights with ease. Building Pennywise within the tight timeline was challenging, but with our team's dedication and collaboration, we were able to create a working platform that empowers users to take control of their finances.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Most of our team members did not know react nor any backend programming. The learning curve was huge. We tried to use MLFlow AI but could not find any pre-trained AI. Then we tried to connect our react with Flask to extract data and incorporate back-end programming, but there were very few readily available resources to learn from. Finding an OpenAI was equally hard, since none of them were free, and none of them had comprehensible documentation. We had to redirect and rethink our project at times to meet the needs in the limited timeframe and considering our lack of experience.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud that we were able to create a user-friendly design that makes it easier for people to keep track of their finances. We are also proud of how we worked as a team. Even when things didn't go as planned, we communicated well and were able to progress. We were able to reevaluate our skillset and rethink our project keeping in mind the short time frame.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: This experience taught us about collaboration and adaptation. Our team had members from various levels of experience, and it was a learning experience to work with people from diverse skill sets. Each person brought something valuable to the table, which made our final product better. We also learned new programming languages like react and flask.

sections.heading: What's next for Pennywise
sections.text: Our plan for Pennywise ahead is to strengthen the backend to extract relevant data and make financial analyses based on the data provided. This will help us handle more data and provide smoother performance for the users. We also want to develop our own AI model and train and design it according to our users' needs. This will allow Pennywise to offer more personalized advises and help in making better financial decisions.

title: Atlantis - The Long Night
tagline: The city sinks at the end of the year. Your money decides if you're on the last ship.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Finance is a very daunting subject. A lot of games have tried to make it fun, but none of them seemed to click for us. So, we decided to create our own finance game that's actually fun, not just looking through spreadsheets and technical analysis, and it still actually teaches you how to make good financial decisions.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Atlantis is a 2D pixel-art game set in a sinking underwater city. The 'Council' has read the tides: Atlantis sinks after the Long Dark. One ship will leave, and Passage on it is sold for coin, only to people who owe nothing to anyone. You have one year to get on that ship: Four seasons: Spring, Summer, Autumn and the Long Dark. Six tides each: every tide is one move. You work, trade at the Market, invest at the Harbor Exchange, borrow, save and pay down debt. A rising price: Passage costs 1,200◈ in Spring and climbs every season. Coin that just sits there falls behind. About ten minutes for a full run. Everyone starts somewhere different. Each of the four classes is built on a real financial barrier, and none is labelled by identity: The Newcomer: no credit history, so no card or loans until they build one with a secured card. First of Their Line: no family wealth, and starts 500◈ in debt to the guild. The Caretaker: care duties cost tides and coin every season, but they have a community lending circle. The Tidewalker: pay swings between 0 and 120◈ a shift, and the Bank won't give them a savings account at first. Every mechanic is a real money concept. Inside the game everything uses in-world names. Then the Modern Mirror , a gilded mirror button in every building, reveals the real thing behind it: Purse / Vault → Checking / savings account Leviathan Credit → Credit card (30% a year, minimum payments, late fees) Standing (300–850) → Credit score Harbor Exchange → Stock market The Tide Index → S&P 500 index fund Deepcoral Salvage → Penny stocks and lottery tickets The Council's debasement → Inflation Grin at the Black Reef → Payday lender Old Maro's lending circle → ROSCA (tandas, susus, chit funds) The Pearl Exchange → Ponzi scheme Nerissa's games at the Drowned Bell → The house edge The game teaches by consequence: Market shocks: one unexpected event hits every season, such as a crab raid on the granaries, a kraken in the shipping lanes or a pearl divers' strike, so you feel volatility. Event cards with real choices: dispute a fraudulent charge, walk away from a "guaranteed" 40% return, or take Grin's easy money. A season report card on a parchment scroll: how close you are to Passage, A–D grades on your choices, where every tide and coin went, how your investments did, and three blunt feedback bullets from Chelo, a 300-year-old turtle. 13 Scrolls: earned for good and bad play, like The Debt Spiral , Siren Song and Read the Ledger , so even losing teaches something. Endings with a lesson: escape with wealth, escape with nothing, get rescued by your lending circle, or miss the last ship. The final Modern Mirror then explains what happened in real-world terms.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Capital One Nessie is the money layer. Every coin movement in the game is a real banking record: Accounts: each class is its own Nessie customer with checking (Purse), savings (Vault) and a credit card account. Loans: the guild loan, the lending circle and Black Reef advances are loan records, kept current with PUT updates. Money movements: wages, sales and dividends are deposits. Market, Exchange and Passage spending are purchases at in-world merchants. Moving coin between Purse and Vault, and paying the card, are transfers. Confirmation: each money effect is queued, POSTed to Nessie, then read back with a GET to confirm it landed. Responses are cached locally, so the game keeps running if the API lags. The in-game Ledger: shows every Nessie record with its status and checks the Purse and Vault against Nessie's balances. A deterministic game engine (Python): Pure and seeded: its seeded so every run in different and unique. It makes the game much more fun to replay. One config file: every number in the game lives there. A balance simulator: bots play thousands of seeded years per class with different strategies (wages only, saver, gambler, kelp trader, diversified, thoughtful) so we can measure what numbers are actually fair to keep. The rest of the stack: Backend: FastAPI and Pydantic, with SQLite storing runs, actions and the Nessie queue. Frontend: React and TypeScript, plus Phaser 3 for the clickable underwater city: three rings of land and water, caustic light, swaying kelp and fish schools. Gemini API. The engine calculates every grade and number. Gemini writes only Chelo's three feedback bullets. Every reply is checked automatically: filler phrases are rejected, length is limited, and any number that didn't come from the engine fails the check. Hosting: the frontend is on Vercel and the backend on Render.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Making it fun and honest at once. Balancing took a lot of simulator runs. Early on, a few hundred coins invested earned less than the shift it cost to trade, so investing lost to saving. We made the first Market and Exchange visit each season free. We also found that money owed to the lending circle wasn't counted as debt, which let one class buy Passage in Spring, so we closed that loophole. Nessie in production. Some resources behaved differently from the docs. Bill reads returned errors, and transaction records didn't update account balances. We built a sync layer that confirms every record with a GET, holds later records behind unconfirmed ones, and only sends loan and bill records once they're verified live. Explaining a deep game quickly. Playtesters were lost at first. We added Chelo's guided tour, short plain explanations in every building, and the Modern Mirror. That way the real-world lesson arrives after you've felt the mechanic, not before.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A complete game: a full year, four classes, 14 market shocks, 13 Scrolls, a season report card, four endings, and a hand-built beautiful pixel-art city. Real banking behind every coin: each move is posted to Nessie and confirmed. Real barriers, not stereotypes: the classes change where you start, never the rules. Teaching by consequence: real-world finance terms appear only in the Modern Mirror. Everywhere else, you learn by playing.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: People remember what happened to them far longer than what they were told. A credit card that snowballed, or a fraud charge they forgot to dispute, sticks better than any definition. A deterministic, fully tested engine made balancing possible. We could change one number and see its effect across thousands of games in seconds. Building on a real banking API forces you to handle the messy parts: failures, retries, confirmations and records that don't behave as documented.

sections.heading: What's next for Atlantis - The Long Night
sections.text: A classroom mode with a shared seed, so a whole class plays the same year and compares choices. More starting classes based on other real barriers. Business ownership and bank loans. Both are already built in the engine and switched off until they're balanced. Sound, and a more dramatic Long Dark.

title: Treasure Dive
tagline: 9 in 10 people never claim money they may be owed. Treasure Dive’s Gemini scout finds open class action settlements, matches them to your Capital One purchases, and shows the proof.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Treasure Dive finds currently settlements, matches them to you, and tells you in plain words when you may qualify . Capital One connect and live scan. You agree to read-only access, and your real accounts and purchases come in from Capital One's Nessie API . You watch the scan happen: messy bank lines ("WHOLEFDS P ST 10180") become real store names, then 26 stores are checked against 44 open settlements. The reveal and your Treasure. A pixel-art chest opens on what you may be owed, clearly labelled an estimate. The Treasure tab lists every match with its deadline countdown, match strength and a verified or unverified badge. Receipts. Paid cash, or did a friend pay? Snap a receipt. Gemini vision reads the store, date and items, and the scout checks them against open settlements. Claims map. Your purchases on a map, with gold tags for claims limited to one state. Tap a state or ask the scout about a place. The daily dive. Every day the scout searches for newly opened settlements, checks each official claim site in code, and matches the new finds to your history. A sonar sweeps and a Search → Verify → Match pipeline lights up as it works. I got paid records a real Nessie deposit, and your chest fills with money recovered.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: App: Expo SDK 58 with Expo Router and React Native Paper. One codebase runs on the iOS Simulator and the web. Animations use Reanimated. The pixel art is drawn from letter grids. The claims map uses react-native-maps (Apple Maps). Notifications, speech and the camera come from Expo's libraries. Every color, spacing value and font lives in one tokens file, and a script checks every text color pair against WCAG AA. Server: Node, Express 5, TypeScript and SQLite (better-sqlite3), with node-cron running the daily dive. Every external payload is validated with zod. Scout agent (Gemini): Discovery runs with Google Search grounding , then a second call turns the prose into structured JSON . Our own code then verifies each claim site: the page loads, it isn't an aggregator, and it names the company and the deadline. When a site blocks bots, Gemini reads it through URL context . Our code checks that Google really fetched the page and that the quoted company and deadline match. That earns a Checked via Google ✓ badge.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Bot-walled claim sites. Many official settlement sites block automated checks with a bare 403. We didn't want to trust the AI's word, or bypass anything. So Gemini reads the page through Google's URL context, and our code checks the quotes it returns before showing a verified badge. Keeping the AI honest about money. Language models love saying "you qualify!" We made "may qualify" a rule in code: summaries pass through a rewrite step in English and Spanish, and every total is labelled an estimate.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: It runs end to end on real APIs : real Nessie accounts and deposits, real Google-grounded Gemini research, and real verification of official claim sites. It also has a full mock mode for offline demos. An agent you can watch think, with every search and source visible, that says "no" when a settlement doesn't fit. Responsible design enforced in code: no filing for users, no fees, "may qualify" wording, sources on every settlement, and scam tips everywhere. Accessibility: English and Spanish, a simple reading level, read aloud, Dynamic Type plus a Larger text option, Reduce motion, screen-reader labels and WCAG AA contrast. 145 automated tests covering the matcher, scout parsing, verification, dedupe, scam rules, nudges, receipts and Nessie.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Grounding is only half of trust. The other half is code that checks the AI's claims before a user sees them. Showing the agent's work (plan, searches, sources) made it feel far more trustworthy than a polished one-line answer. Hard product rules ("never file for the user", "never promise money") are easiest to keep when they live in code and tests, not just in prompts.

sections.heading: What's next for Treasure Dive
sections.text: Real sign-in and connecting real bank accounts beyond the Nessie sandbox. Remote push alerts when a new settlement matches your history, plus deadline reminder.

sections.heading: Credits and acknowledgements
sections.text: Google Gemini API. It powers the scout and the Ask agent: Google Search grounding, structured output, URL context and vision. Models: gemini-3.8-flash and gemini-4-argon , through the @google/genai SDK. Capital One Nessie API. Sandbox banking data (customer, accounts, merchants, purchases) and deposits.
