title: Drigil
tagline: Smart glasses that coach workers with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) through a new job in their supervisor's own voice, then step back as they learn.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Many people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) want to work, and can. But the first weeks at a new job are the hardest. Only 22.7% of people with a disability were employed in 2024, against 65.5% of people without one (US BLS). The support that helps most, a job coach standing next to you, is scarce: the direct support workforce turns over at about 40% a year (National Core Indicators, 2023). A coach might visit twice a week. The other days, small and fixable mistakes add up, and small mistakes cost jobs. We asked: what if the coach never had to leave? Glasses that teach a task step by step, in the voice of the supervisor the worker already trusts , notice mistakes the moment they happen, and step back as the worker learns , because the goal is independence, not dependence.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: drigil is a job coach in a worker's glasses. Our demo worker is Jordan, at a café counter. Teach once. The supervisor records a short narrated video of the task. Claude turns it into 4–8 plain steps. Each step has an instruction, what "done right" looks like, the likely mistake, a gentle correction, a reason, praise and a short cue. With the supervisor's consent, their narration becomes a Cartesia voice clone . Coach live. Jordan presses Start. The glasses camera streams face-blurred frames. Claude checks each one against the whole task and says done , mistake or in progress . Jordan hears the next step, or a fix like "Almost. Turn the sleeve so the words face out." , in his supervisor's voice, with a box drawn around the problem. Talk. An always-on mic hears "Is this right?" , "Why?" , "I'm stuck" or "What am I holding?" and answers out loud, using what the camera sees right now. Remember. Moss keeps short notes about each worker. Next time, before the tricky step: "Remember: turn the sleeve so the words face out." Fade. Every finished step is recorded. As Jordan masters a step, its coaching shrinks from full instructions to a short cue, to alerts only, to silence. Level-ups are celebrated out loud. Steps back are never announced. Re-teach (Factory Droid). If one step keeps causing trouble, Droid rewrites that step of the task in a sandbox, for example splitting it in two or writing a clearer correction. The supervisor sees Droid's work live and approves before anything changes. A person is always one tap away. "Help" pages a coworker buddy first. Two buddies race and exactly one wins. After 20 s it escalates to the supervisor. A hold on the wristband calls the supervisor directly. The supervisor's dashboard shows who is working now, who needs help, who is getting more independent and which steps need re-teaching, all live.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Browser (React + TypeScript): MediaPipe hand tracking and face blurring before any frame leaves the device , an always-on mic with voice detection, and live views for the worker, supervisor and buddy. Edge app (Python, FastAPI): the coaching brain. It handles the live checks, the dignity rules, voice, memory, and the trigger and runner for Droid. Anthropic Claude: Opus 5.5 writes the steps from the teach video. Sonnet 5.5 checks every live frame (the whole step list in one call) and answers Jordan's questions using the live image. Cartesia: sonic-3.6 speech in the cloned supervisor voice, with instructions pre-recorded so playback is instant, ink-whisper speech-to-text, and consented voice cloning from the teach video. SpacetimeDB: the shared, live workplace. It holds sessions, step outcomes, per-step mastery, help requests with an atomic claim race, wristband calls and Droid's job stream. Reducers enforce the rules: only the edge app can record outcomes and only supervisors can override levels. A scheduled reducer escalates unclaimed help after 20 s. Every screen updates through live subscriptions. Moss: a per-worker memory, recalled in about 1.4 ms, before each step and when Jordan asks a question. Factory Droid SDK: the re-teach engineer. It is triggered by data (2 corrections or help requests on one step within an hour) or by the supervisor. It runs at medium autonomy in a per-job sandbox holding only the task, the evidence with names removed, the rules and a validator. Our runner re-validates the output itself, every event streams to the dashboard, and nothing goes live without the supervisor's approval. Bitdeer AI Model Studio: we used it to benchmark and tune the vision check across catalog models (GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-27B) on our labeled test set. Hardware: a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Logitech Brio 100 is the glasses camera, streamed over USB-C. An Arduino Uno Q with a touch sensor is the wristband (hold to call the supervisor, short touch for a quiet note). The fading rule lives in one SpacetimeDB transaction. Support level $\ell \in {0,1,2,3}$ goes from full help to on their own: $$ \ell_{t+1} = \begin{cases} \min(3,\ \ell_t + 1) & \text{if the last 3 runs of this step were clean} \ \max(0,\ \ell_t - 1) & \text{if } \ge 2 \text{ of the last 5 runs had an error} \ \ell_t & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ Dignity is a rule in the code, not a slogan A wrong correction hurts more than no correction: Automatic corrections: they need two mistake answers in a row, wait out a 3 s grace period after each new step, and come at most once every 10 s. Silence when unsure: "unclear" or low-confidence answers say nothing. Never backward: the coach never sends a worker back to an earlier step. Plain language: every line is at a first-grade reading level, one action per sentence, and corrections start with "Almost." Measured, on our 30-frame labeled set (coffee-sleeve task) Live check Accuracy Mistakes caught False corrections Median latency Claude Sonnet 5.5 (live) 73% 44% 6.7% 2.2 s GLM-5.3-Flash on Bitdeer 77% 56% 3.3% 4.4 s Other components: Moss recall p50 1.43 ms / p99 2.68 ms · Cartesia first audio 723 ms. Droid: a real re-teach run took about 35 s with 35 streamed events and passed validation.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Speed vs. accuracy. Bitdeer's GLM-5.3-Flash was our most accurate checker but took about 4.4 s per look, too slow to keep up with a worker. Claude Haiku was fast but missed every "sleeve on backwards" mistake. One model, Claude Sonnet, seeing the whole step list, was the best balance. Never send a worker backward. Finishing step 5 can hide step 4's result, and the model would ask the worker to go back. We mark earlier steps as done in the prompt and clamp progress in code. The app hearing itself. With no echo cancellation, the always-on mic heard the coach's own voice. We pause the mic while speaking and drop anything that matches what the app just said. One voice, always. A stock voice kept slipping in between cloned lines. Every phrase now routes through the consented clone. Prompts that leaked. Example steps in our teaching prompt showed up in unrelated tasks. Short, generic prompts that use only what is in the video fixed it. Real-world networking. Phone cameras need HTTPS, and event Wi-Fi blocks device-to-device traffic. We added a local certificate and fell back to a hotspot. Letting an agent edit the lesson safely. The Droid sandbox, the runner's own validation and the approval step came from asking "what's the worst thing it could do?"

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: The whole loop runs end to end on real hardware: teach from a video, coach live in a cloned voice, catch a mistake, answer a question, fade support, page a buddy, call from the wristband, and re-teach with Droid. Dignity is built into the code (debounce, silence when unsure, steps back never announced), not left to the model. Privacy by design: faces are blurred in the browser, no video of the worker is stored, and teach videos are deleted after analysis. Every number we quote is measured, and we label what is simulated.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Supported-employment research already has the playbook: task analysis, prompt fading and coworker supports. The best AI design here was to follow it, not reinvent it. For this community, "when to stay quiet" matters as much as "what to say". Agents in a real product need boundaries more than intelligence: a narrow sandbox, independent validation and a human approval step.

sections.heading: What's next for drigil
sections.text: Pilot with a supported-employment program and a few job coaches. Move the speaker to bone-conduction earbuds on the frame, and route the glasses mic into live talk. Grow the task library by letting coaches share and remix lessons. Run the check on-device to cut latency and keep more data local.

sections.heading: Real vs. simulated
sections.text: Real: the camera checks, cloned voice, speech answers, memory, fading, help routing, wristband, Droid re-teaching and every dashboard number. Labeled "Sample": the landing page's week-by-week journey. Seeded examples: the three café practice tasks. Voice clone: a teammate playing the supervisor, recorded with consent.

title: Eve: event finances handled
tagline: post-event finances, on autopilot

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Evan won a prize at TreeHacks earlier this year. The organizers first tried to ship him the physical prize, then found out they couldn't because he's Canadian. So they switched to a wire. The payment had to go through Stanford's accountants, which meant every step passed between the organizers, the student government's finance office, and Evan. Forms got requested, sent, and requested again. Emails sat on delivered. Nobody was sure what the next step was. It took about 9 months for the money to arrive. No one really messed up. The organizers just had no way of knowing, right when he won, that a Canadian winner needs a W-8BEN, a withholding decision and an international transfer. Jin co-directs Hack@Brown, so this is the part of running a hackathon we already knew from the inside. When we talked to other organizers, everyone had a story like this. Someone waited weeks on a reimbursement because of one missing receipt. A prize got announced before anyone checked if it could be shipped to the winner. Tax forms got chased down months after. It doesn't help that most student hackathons don't hold their own bank account, so every payment means asking the university or a fiscal sponsor to send it. So we asked: what if one agent with limited permissions did the work of the travel coordinator, the accounts payable clerk and the tax preparer, while a person still decides when money moves?

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Eve handles the money side of a hackathon or any large-scale event: travel reimbursements, expenses, cash and physical prizes, and even the cross-border tax work. Organizers set budgets and rules, attendees submit receipts and claim prizes in a portal, and Eve prepares every payout with its evidence. Overview. Organizers see the budget left, payouts waiting for release, what's blocked and why, and the prize pipeline before the closing ceremony. Travel claims. Attendees upload receipts in a portal. Eve reads them, converts currencies, checks them against the event's caps and policy, looks for duplicates, compares the fare with what other attendees paid and what that route actually cost, and either pays it or flags it for a person. Prizes. For each item prize Eve compares shipping it, buying it locally and paying a cash equivalent, and checks whether it can be shipped to the winner's country. Team splits requires each member to confirm. Eve collects the W-9 or W-8BEN and works out withholding, fees and FX before anything is approved. Fraud guards. Boosted fares get flagged. Travel claims from hackers with no project on record get escalated. A bank account change right before payout freezes the payment until it's confirmed through the original contact channel. Approvals. Every proposal shows the gross, withholding, fees and expected net. Only a controller can release a payment. Organizers can't release payments, and nobody can approve a payment they asked for. The agent doesn't get special access either. It's just another role with limited permissions. Controllers can approve straight from a Slack DM, and organizers get channel alerts and digests. Sponsor portals. University finance portals don't have APIs, so normally a student retypes every sponsor packet by hand. Eve opens the portal on a sandboxed desktop with computer use, fills it out, fixes errors the portal throws at it (like a missing W-8BEN), and stops before Submit, where a person has to press it. Eve also reconciles the sponsor's remittances afterward. Books and filings. Every payment goes into a balanced double-entry ledger that can't be edited after the fact, and every number traces back to the decision that produced it. At the end you can export a journal for QuickBooks and generate 1099 and 1042-S worksheets. We seeded a fake 300-person event with 160 travel claims and 25 prizes, and planted 40 problems in it: underage attendees, expired tax forms, padded fares, a bank account change right before payout, and so on. Eve caught all 40, with no false positives and no wrong payouts.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Frontend: Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui, Base UI and TanStack Table. Backend: Server actions and route handlers, Postgres on PlanetScale with Drizzle, Better Auth for accounts and roles, Zod, and pdf-lib for documents. Long-running jobs like the nightly review and payout proposals run on Vercel Workflow so they survive restarts. AI: Claude, through the Vercel AI SDK and the Anthropic SDK, reads receipts with structured extraction and runs the event review agent. Sponsor portal entry runs on an E2B Linux desktop with Claude computer use. The code decides when to Submit, not the model. We purposefully kept the AI out of the math. Caps, tax rules, withholding and ledger entries are all plain deterministic code with tests, and the model never decides an amount. If Claude isn't sure about something on a receipt, it goes to a human instead of guessing. Money movement is simulated and the tax forms are drafts, not real filings.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Autonomy without a superuser. The agent's limits are enforced in code, not in the prompt. It can propose and hold a payment, never release one. Numbers that don't match. The same payment can look different depending on where you check. The receipt might say one amount, while the card charge another after currency conversion, and the sponsor's records a third. Eve has to pick which number to trust and explain why. Tax rules are messy. They change all the time, and we're builders, not accountants. We couldn't verify every rule we implemented, so we marked the ones we weren't sure about as unverified. Keeping the ledger correct while lots of things happen at once. Duplicate releases and half-finished jobs scared us most, so we wrote tests that try to pay the same claim twice. Getting computer use to recover from the portal's errors without letting it click things it shouldn't.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: 40 out of 40 planted problems caught on the demo event, zero wrongful payouts. Payments that need a controller really do need one. Not even the organizer or the agent can push them through. A balanced ledger that can't be edited afterwards, where every number traces back to the decision that produced it. Watching Eve run into a W-8BEN error on the sponsor portal, attach the form and keep going was a pretty good moment.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Paying people wasn't the hard part. The hard part was knowing what you need before you pay: which form, which country, whose sign-off. If you know that the moment someone wins or uploads a receipt, the rest is mostly bookkeeping. We also got more careful about where the model goes. It's really good at reading messy receipts and web pages. We just don't want it deciding how much tax to withhold.

sections.heading: What's next for Eve
sections.text: Real payouts through Stripe and wire providers instead of the simulated rail, plus verified flight booking through Duffel Verifying the Canadian rules and treaty handling with an actual tax professional Official IRS and CRA forms and e-filing instead of drafts Email verification and invitation emails so real organizations can sign up Trying it on a real event, starting with Hack@Brown, and ideally one where someone is still waiting on their prize

prize_badges: [Hyphenate] The Hyphenated Enterprise: Autonomous Systems for Finance

title: GroundTruth
tagline: An autonomous dispute and billing analyst for satellite ground stations.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Ground stations are the toll booths of space. A satellite passes overhead for a few minutes, an antenna tracks it, the data comes down, and someone sends a bill. AWS Ground Station charges by the minute. KSAT, the world's largest commercial ground-station operator, reported NOK 2.361B (about USD $234M) in 2025 group revenue across about 2.1 million contacts on about 375 antennas . At that volume, every dropped pass, partial downlink, or "the storm ate my data" email turns into a billing dispute. Right now a person settles each one by hand. They pull the pass log, check space weather, check maintenance notices, read the contract's SLA, and decide whether to issue a credit. It's slow and inconsistent: two analysts can rule differently on the same claim. It's also easy to game. If you know the analyst skips the weather check, you'll blame a storm. We modeled Ground Truth on that operating profile and asked Hyphenate's question: can a finance team hire an autonomous system for this corner of the books, with limited access, a clean record, and the sense to ask when it should?

sections.heading: Is it real enough?
sections.text: Realistic data, a messy problem, and proof that it works. The company. A mid-market ground-station operator in the shape of KSAT: hundreds of antennas, millions of contacts a year, minute-based billing, and a flood of customer credit claims when a pass fails. The messy problem. Sources disagree. The customer's claim says "storm," the pass log says the antenna tracked cleanly, space weather says the band was quiet, and maintenance was announced three days earlier. Time matters: a March decision should change what the system does in June. Approvers are busy; the controller sometimes says no. Whoever proposes a credit cannot be the one who promotes the rule that allows it. What's real vs simulated. Real: CelesTrak orbital elements + SGP4 for live satellite positions; a handful of Starlink satellites with their own marker; KSAT-scale revenue anchors from the 2025 annual report ( NOK 2.361B / ~$234M , ~2.1M contacts, ~375 antennas); AWS Cedar as the real policy engine; SpacetimeDB Maincloud as the live system of record. Simulated: the claim stream, pass telemetry features, space-weather bands, and maintenance notices that feed each dispute, generated so we can plant known-good and known-bad cases. How we know it works: Break It is our planted-error suite with an answer key. Each attack (inflated amount, duplicate claim, forged station log, fake storm excuse, insider raising their own limit, and more) is run against the old policy and the current policy side by side. Policy versions also carry a full replay against decision history : escalations fell from 3,406 at v4 to 1,660 at v6 while precision went up , with zero regressions allowed before promote. Finance KPIs (billed, revenue at risk, credits paid, recovered) are computed from the same SpacetimeDB ledger every screen reads, so the demo cannot contradict itself.

sections.heading: Would you hire it?
sections.text: For which seats, and would it earn them: limited access, a clean record of its work, and knowing when to ask? Seats. Dispute analyst (settles routine SLA credits) and controller (reviews escalations, approves or rejects proposed policy). Limited access. System 1 and System 2 can only propose . AWS Cedar has the final say. Anything above a confidence or dollar threshold, or outside the rulebook, escalates to a human. The agent that proposes a credit is not the process that promotes a new rule, segregation of duties is baked into the reducers. On Finance → Ledger, the same identity that approved a credit cannot submit it to ERP, the bar shows “SoD blocked” and Submit stays disabled until a different reviewer acts. Clean record. Every decision writes an audit trail : claim features, System 1 score + SHAP drivers, System 2 citations (pass log, weather, maintenance, contract), Cedar permit/forbid, and the human override when one happened. The ledger is append-only . Anyone reviewing a paid credit can see why it paid, months later. Knowing when to ask. System 1 only auto-settles at 95%+ confidence . Below that, System 2 investigates. If Cedar doesn't cover the case, or the amount is material, it stops and waits for the manager , with the evidence already gathered. After the human decides, the system learns: when at least 3 consistent decisions agree and none contradict, it drafts a new Cedar rule, replays it on the full history , and only offers promotion if it would not have overruled a single past human decision . The controller still has to click promote.

sections.heading: Did we see something new?
sections.text: A company, problem, or approach we haven't seen made autonomous before. The company / problem. Ground-station SLA credit disputes at operator scale , usage-billed space infrastructure where a few minutes of antenna time become revenue, cash, and next quarter's forecast. Not another SaaS refund bot. The approach. Two-speed autonomy, not one big LLM. A cheap tabular model (System 1) clears confident claims on structured features; an LLM (System 2) only reads sources on the hard cases. Most claims never need the expensive path. Deterministic policy on top of probabilistic models. Cedar is the rulebook finance can read and audit. Learned rules show up in plain English ("Dropped pass + maintenance announced in advance → deny") with support and contradiction counts; raw Cedar stays for auditors. Learning with a ratchet. Human decisions mine into new rules, but replay-before-promote with zero tolerated regressions means automation can rise without quietly paying claims a human would have denied. Adversarial by design. Break It assumes customers and insiders will try to game the desk, and proves the current policy catches what the old one let through.

sections.heading: The moment
sections.text: When it catches what others missed, recovers from something going wrong, or defends a decision when questioned. Open the demo video here. A pass looks fine on the Overview globe, then the claim escalates. System 1 isn't sure; System 2 cites the real sources; Cedar refuses to auto-pay. A human decides. That decision joins the labeled set. Over the weekend the rulebook moves from v4 to v6 : escalations drop from 3,406 to 1,660 , precision holds or rises, and Break It shows the new policy catching inflated claims, fake storms, and an insider limit-raise that the old policy missed. Catch. Fake space-weather excuses and forged station logs that would fool a tired analyst fail Cedar + source checks. Recover. A bad auto-path doesn't ship: low confidence and missing rule coverage escalate instead of guessing. Defend. Click any decision and you get SHAP drivers, System 2 citations, and the Cedar statement that allowed or blocked it, the controller's "why did we pay this?" answered in one screen.

sections.heading: SpacetimeDB
sections.text: SpacetimeDB is not a cache in front of our app, it is the app's system of record. Passes, claims, decisions, ledger entries, policy versions, and the simulation clock all live in SpacetimeDB tables on Maincloud. The frontend subscribes with the official SDK; when a claim is decided or a policy is promoted, Overview, Decisions, Policies, Finance, and Break It update together with no polling . Revenue, credits, recoveries, and escalation counts are derived from those same tables, so the finance numbers and the operational pipeline cannot drift . What only SpacetimeDB made easy in a weekend: One live world for the whole company simulation, not REST stubs glued to a separate DB. Reducers as the control plane: the AI proposes; Cedar-checked reducers decide what actually commits; humans promote policies through the same path. Append-only ledger + audit log that every screen reads, so a credit that hits Finance is the same credit that left Decisions. That real-time agreement is the difference between a demo that tells a story and a demo that is the books .

sections.heading: SpaceX
sections.text: Space gives you more to work with than almost any other field, we used it. Real space data in. CelesTrak general perturbations + SGP4 drive the Overview globe. A focused set of ~10–15 Starlink satellites carry a distinct SpaceX/Starlink marker (not the full constellation), beside KSAT-style ground stations and a severity-colored storm band. Every dot is a pass someone will be billed for. Legendary product out. Ground Truth turns that orbital layer into a finance system: dispute intake, dual-speed AI, Cedar policy learning with replay, a red-team harness, and a live earnings/ledger view tied to the same clock. Built end-to-end with Cursor (cloud agents + local) and Grok Bot for planning, demo scripting, branding, and Devpost media, the SpaceXSI eligibility path, used heavily.

sections.heading: What's next for Ground Truth
sections.text: ERP integration: real ERP connectors, sync-status per row, and richer audit on each push. More live data: real space-weather feeds and operator maintenance calendars in place of simulated inputs, plus more satellite constellations, including Starlink, on the globe. Per-customer contract parsing, so System 2 reads each customer's actual SLA terms. Pilot conversations with ground-station operators to test against real dispute history. Generalizing the pattern: any usage-billed infrastructure with SLA credits (telecom, cloud, energy) has the same dispute problem.

prize_badges: [Hyphenate] The Hyphenated Enterprise: Autonomous Systems for Finance

title: half full
tagline: AI-powered, personalized news that spotlight progress and keep you informed without the doom scrolling. Because the glass is half full, and the news should show it.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Somewhere along the way, our generation stopped watching the news. It wasn’t apathy. Most of today’s coverage is written from a doomsday angle: crisis after crisis, framed in ways that leave us stressed, overwhelmed, and helpless about massive world issues we have no power to fix. So we tuned out, not because we don’t care, but because we couldn’t keep absorbing it. The format hasn’t helped either. Traditional news platforms feel built for another era, and social media chops complicated stories into sensational headlines and disconnected clips. Neither fits how we actually consume things today. We started asking: What if staying informed felt less like doomscrolling and more like listening to your favorite playlist? We took our UI/UX inspiration from the applications our peers use most, and set out to build an app that brings young people back to the news. Instead of overwhelming users, it helps them stay informed in a minimal, manageable way, focusing on pressing topics that are hopeful or at least within reach, in an experience that feels native to how Gen Z already engages with technology, without sacrificing the substance or credibility of journalism. That's how half full was born. The world is a lot. The news doesn't have to be.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: half full transforms the daily news into an immersive, swipeable, illustrated experience you can read, watch, or listen to. Instead of throwing hundreds of headlines at users, half full curates a small daily edition of 3–5 meaningful stories. Think of it as a daily playlist for understanding the world. Each story comes with an accessible explanation, original AI-generated illustrations, and natural-sounding audio narration. We're also exploring AI-generated animated explainers that bring illustrated stories to life, making complex concepts easier to visualize. Users can swipe horizontally between stories, listen with their preferred narrator, and explore the supporting evidence behind the reporting. But half full is more than a news reader. See the Receipts: Readers can explore the sources supporting a story rather than simply trusting an AI-generated summary. Your Jar: Users collect their reading history and express how stories made them feel through original illustrated reactions: Interesting, Insightful, Hopeful, and Stressed. The Mini: An optional daily crossword offers a playful way to engage with the news. Your Daily Catch-Up: Previous editions are accessible through a calendar, allowing users to revisit stories from other days. And when you've finished your edition, half full tells you something most news apps never will: You're caught up. No infinite feed. No pressure to keep scrolling. Just a little more understanding of the world.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built half full as a mobile-first Progressive Web App using Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Firebase , connecting several AI services into one news-to-media pipeline. Apify — The research engine Apify powers our news retrieval and source investigation. We developed a custom News Receipts Actor to help gather reporting, investigate supporting material, and track evidence provenance. Published editions and their supporting data can be reused, allowing readers to access the same curated edition without regenerating everything. Anthropic Claude — The editorial brain Claude examines retrieved reporting, compares supporting evidence, and helps select a small set of stories worth understanding. It also transforms complex reporting into accessible explanations and plans visual storyboards. We added structured validation and evidence requirements to reduce unsupported claims and reject stories when sufficient reporting isn't available. Recraft — The visual identity Recraft generates original, story-specific illustrations using a consistent half full art direction. We wanted visuals that felt warm, expressive, and approachable rather than generic stock imagery. We also experimented with Runway's image-to-video technology to explore how AI-generated motion could bring illustrated explanations to life. Cartesia — The voice of half full Cartesia powers our audio narration. Users can listen to news stories through natural-sounding voices, choose their preferred narrator, and control playback. Firebase — The personal experience Firebase Authentication and Firestore support optional Google sign-in, saved reading progress, and reactions. Guest reading remains available. Next.js, Motion, and GSAP — The interactive experience We built a responsive, gesture-driven interface with horizontal story navigation, fluid transitions, and interactive visual elements. Our design combines Spotify-inspired media navigation with Tiimo-inspired warmth, expressive typography, and textured, dithered gradients. Vercel — Deployment Vercel hosts our application, while our external AI services support news discovery, editorial processing, illustrations, and narration.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: 1. Making AI-generated news trustworthy Generating a summary is easy. Making sure the summary reflects credible reporting is much harder. We had to think carefully about source independence, publication dates, evidence quality, and what should happen when a story doesn't have enough supporting information. Rather than forcing the system to produce an edition at any cost, we built safeguards that allow it to reject insufficiently supported stories. 2. Turning articles into compelling visual explanations One of our biggest lessons was that a moving image isn't necessarily an animation that helps someone understand something. Our early attempts used static AI illustrations with programmatic motion layered over them. They worked technically, but they didn't achieve the storytelling quality we envisioned. This pushed us to experiment with actual AI image-to-video generation and rethink how illustrated scenes should be designed from the beginning. 3. Making complex technology feel effortless Behind a simple swipeable interface are multiple services handling retrieval, editorial evaluation, illustration, audio, storage, and user progress. Coordinating those systems while keeping the experience responsive was a significant engineering challenge. 4. Building for real mobile use We worked through touch navigation, portrait layouts, audio synchronization, persistent preferences, PWA behavior, and the realities of different screen sizes. We learned quickly that passing automated tests doesn't automatically mean an interface feels good to use.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're proud that half full is more than an AI chatbot summarizing headlines. We built an evidence-assisted editorial pipeline with a custom Apify Actor, structured source review, and a behind-the-scenes Studio that helps make the process more transparent. We connected real news retrieval, AI-assisted editorial analysis, custom illustrations, and voice narration into one consumer-facing product. We created an original visual identity with illustrated reaction characters and a playful approach to reading progress. We built a swipeable daily news experience, an optional crossword, historical editions, and personalized reading features. And we began turning our illustrated stories into actual AI-generated video, moving toward our vision of short, animated explanations. But the accomplishment we're most proud of is the idea behind the product: We designed a news experience that doesn't measure success by how long it can keep someone scrolling. Instead, we want people to leave feeling a little more informed, a little less overwhelmed, and ready to get on with their day.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Building half full taught us that the most powerful AI experiences aren't necessarily the ones that generate the most content. They're the ones that make complicated things feel simple without losing what makes them important. We learned how to orchestrate multiple AI services, build evidence-aware workflows, design around external API limitations, and create interactive experiences that work across different devices. We also discovered how much thoughtful design matters. The difference between a collection of technically functioning features and a product people actually want to use comes down to how everything feels together. Most importantly, we learned that accessibility, accuracy, and engaging design don't have to compete with one another.

sections.heading: What's next for half full
sections.text: We want to take half full beyond a hackathon prototype and make it an everyday companion for staying informed. Our next steps include expanding our AI-generated animated explainers, improving video and narration synchronization, making visual storytelling more consistent across every edition, and continuing to refine our mobile experience. We also want to strengthen source verification, improve historical news coverage, and make the experience even more accessible to different reading and listening preferences. Long term, we imagine half full becoming a new kind of news platform: one that makes understanding the world feel natural, approachable, and even enjoyable. Because staying informed shouldn't mean staying overwhelmed. half full — The world is a lot. The news doesn't have to be.

title: Silent Voice
tagline: Cancer can take your voice, but we can give it back.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Imagine you go into surgery able to talk, and when you wake up you try to say your kid's name and nothing comes out, not even a whisper. That's a laryngectomy, the surgery that removes the voice box, usually to save someone from throat cancer. Every year close to 190,000 people around the world find out they have cancer of the voice box, and more than half a million are already living without one. But did you know losing your voice box doesn't take your words with it. Your lips, tongue, and jaw still move exactly the way they always did, so you can still mouth "I love you" or "I'm scared" or a bad joke at dinner, but nobody hears it. The tools people get today, like a buzzing device pressed against the neck, give back a sound, but almost never the voice their family knows. The loving words are all still there. Only the sound is missing. That felt like something we could fix. If a machine could read those movements fast enough, it could give people their own voice back in real time as they speak.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: That's what inspired us to build Silent Voice. We want to help people reclaim their voice, so they can talk to the people they love again, face to face or even over the phone. The people who feel it most are their families. A mom who hasn't heard her son since his surgery picks up the phone, and it's him, in his own voice, telling her about his day. Or a grandfather reads a bedtime story again, and his grandkids hear the same voice they grew up with. Now their families get to hear them again with Silent Voice. Really hear them, again!! Silent Voice turns silent mouthing into speech in your own voice, while you're still mouthing. Our demo is a live phone call. Austin, our teammate, calls you on an ordinary phone line, so there's nothing for you to install. You talk normally, and your words show up in his live captions. He answers by mouthing, mouth open and no sound at all, and you hear him in his own cloned voice, carrying the emotion on his face, about 0.7 seconds after his lips start each word. Each word plays the moment the system is sure of it, so he never waits for the sentence to end. When it can't tell what he said, it says "Please repeat" into the call instead of guessing, because putting the wrong words in someone's mouth is worse than a pause. For the person on the other end, it sounds just like Austin, just a beat slower.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Any singular method here is unreliable on its own. For example, if you say the words "bat", "mat" and "pat", they look identical on camera, and it can't tell which is which. So Silent Voice has three readers, each covering what the others miss, combining them into the best possible answer live. Lips. Auto-AVSR, an open-source lip reader, reads finished video clips. We re-read the sentence every 100 ms, with a lightweight add-on trained on the user's face. Muscles. Four sensor pads on the face and under the chin pick up the electrical signals of the muscles that move the lips and tongue, which the camera can't see. They feed an Arduino at 1,000 samples a second. Our muscle model, SVR-1, learned from Berkeley's silent-speech recordings, before being further fine-tuned on Austin's recordings. Conversation. Claude hears both sides of the call. Claude Haiku predicts Austin's next words before he mouths them, and Claude Opus fixes look-alike mix-ups in the captions as they happen. Our code only accepts a swap of one word for a look-alike the readers already considered, so Claude can never put words in Austin's mouth. We also trained our own language model on 72 million words of real dialogue, and it predicts conversation three times better than the audiobook model used in previous research, at a ninth of the size. Voice. We cloned Austin's voice with Cartesia and streamed it to Sonic 3.6, using both his expression and his facial muscles to portray his emotions. A smile will make his voice happier, and clenching his jaw will make the voice louder. Sonic outputs phone audio straight into Twilio, and Cartesia Ink transcribes what you say from the same call. Everything runs on one laptop (RTX 5060), with every message logged and replayable. We built it with Claude Code .

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Making Auto-AVSR read silent speech live Auto-AVSR is one of the best open-source lip readers, but it was never built to be live. It looks through the whole video before answering, which makes it completely unusable for us. Every other real-time lip reader gives up accuracy for speed instead, like LiteVSR, which has an error rate of 46% on its own benchmark. We needed both, so we optimized it wherever possible. To make it live, every 100 ms we reread the whole sentence so far with a fast greedy pass that reuses the work on frames it has already seen, so each pass takes under 40 ms. To improve speed and accuracy, we dynamically crop the footage to only the user's mouth and retrained the lip tracker on Austin's face. In the end, on a brand new test session, our error rate fell to 9.8%, down from Auto-AVSR's 20.9% on the same test. Making Claude think ahead The words "bills" and "pills" look identical to a camera, so you need an LLM to follow the conversation and correct it. The difference between us and other models is that we stream every word live and can't wait 7 seconds for Claude like they can. So, we turned Claude into a forecaster instead of an editor. While the caller is still talking, Cartesia Ink streams their half-finished sentence to Claude, and with two predictions always in flight, a fresh guess at Austin's reply lands perfectly on time, reaching our decoder before Austin's lips even move, tipping close calls toward words that fit the conversation. Making word-by-word speech sound human Cartesia needs to know where the sentence is going to properly add emotion, but our lip reader is live and hands over one word at a time to read immediately. With Sonic's buffer on, it held 14 of 15 words until the sentence ended, and the caller sat through 4.9 seconds of silence. With words sent one by one, it treated each word like a sentence, with a heavy pause between them. So, we taught Silent Voice to phrase like a person. It waits for Austin's natural pauses and sends a few words at a time into one continuing stream, so Sonic carries the melody from phrase to phrase. To keep it fast, we trim Sonic's padding as the audio arrives. The caller hears him about 0.7 seconds after he starts a word, making it as seamless as possible.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A live phone call where one side only mouths, and you hear it as speech while it's being mouthed. Speech starting about 0.7 s after the lips do, in the speaker's own voice, with the emotion on his face. A lip reader that answers every 100 ms and got 90.2% of words right on sentences it had never seen, up from 79.1% for Auto-AVSR out of the box. A muscle model built for just four pads. Given the same four, it picks the right sentence among 10 lip look-alikes 72.3% of the time, against 27.7% for the published model. Claude predicting Austin's reply while the caller is still talking, with a fresh guess about every 0.8 s. Building this all in only 36 hours.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We expected Austin's lip-reading mistakes to be look-alikes like "bills" and "pills". When we went through them one by one, most were short words he'd dropped and contractions like "I'd" read as "I", so that's where our last day went. We switched Claude to Haiku for speed and replayed a test session through it. It changed 31 words, and most of them were right words turned wrong: "sleep" became "slip", "think" became "thank", "creative" became "kind". Opus changed 3 on the same session. So Opus fixes the captions now, and Claude on its own can never put a word in Austin's voice. The emotion reader caught us off guard too. Trained on one session, it called every neutral sentence in the next one emotional. It had learned Austin's resting face from his first three seconds, and he'd started that session with his eyebrows raised. Now it compares him to the last minute of his own face.

sections.heading: What's next for Silent Voice
sections.text: Testing with laryngectomees and speech therapists. Measuring impact in real calls: how often the listener understands on the first try compared with an electrolarynx, how often the system says "Please repeat", and how fast each word reaches the listener. A shorter setup for new users. The lip add-on trains in minutes; the muscle model needs a few recording sessions. Barge-in, so the voice stops when the other person talks over it. Hardware small enough to wear to a coffee shop.

sections.heading: Built with
sections.text: python, pytorch, auto-avsr, mediapipe, hsemotion, kenlm, claude-api, claude-code, cartesia-sonic, cartesia-ink, twilio, zeromq, arduino, bioamp-exg-pill

sections.heading: Team
sections.text: Thai (EMG rig, project manager), Austin (SVR-1, combining the readers, demo speaker), Frank (Cartesia voice, Twilio call, dashboard), Evan (real-time lip reading/auto avsr, Claude predictor). Built on Gaddy and Klein, Digital Voicing of Silent Speech (2020), Auto-AVSR (Ma et al., 2023) and Lipflow .

title: Sophi - The Physical Augmentation Walker
tagline: Sophi is an AI-powered walker with an always-on voice agent for Q&A and GPS navigation, plus a linear lift with robotic arms. Built-in features include collision avoidance and fall detection.

sections.text: Sophi — The Physical Augmentation Walker

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Last year, one of our team members’ grandfathers suffered a serious fall on his way home and spent several months in the hospital. Seeing how a single fall could threaten his life, and how the resulting mobility challenges affected his independence, made us realize how much everyday freedom depends on being able to move safely. We built Sophi for people like him. Sophi is an AI-powered physical augmentation walker designed to help people navigate their surroundings, interact with everyday objects, and stay connected with the people who care about them. Our vision also extends beyond elder adults. It includes the 340 million people who are blind or have low vision, whom our navigation technology can help explore the world with greater confidence. It includes the 1.7 billion people with mobility restrictions, who can use our robotic arms to open doors or pick up dropped objects. And it includes the billions of people who care about an elderly or disabled family member, giving them a way to check in on their loved ones through our companion app.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Sophi combines a walker with a conversational AI assistant, robotic arms, and navigation technology. With a button on the handle, users can speak to a cloud-based agent through a microphone and speaker. The agent can answer questions, display information on a touchscreen, start GPS navigation, and operate Sophi’s SO-101 robotic arms and linear lift. The arms are intended to help with everyday tasks such as opening doors and picking up dropped objects. We use Anthropic’s Claude for the assistant's reasoning and tool-use loop. It can decide when a question needs a fresh distance reading, location, weather, or a screen card, then use the result to answer. We use Cartesia for speech recognition and for Sophi's voice. Distance sensors detect nearby obstacles and trigger haptic feedback to guide the user. Practical additions, including a bike light and bottle holder, support everyday use. Our companion app lets caregivers view the user’s location, check in through Sophi’s camera, and receive messages sent from the walker. To make sure join requests, approvals, membership, and messages can update live, we use SpacetimeDB for the care circle. We also built an AI-guided customization experience that learns about a prospective user’s needs and recommends which modules their walker should include.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Sophi runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 connected to three ESP32 modules. This hardware connects the walker’s sensors, controls, and physical components with the cloud-based agent. We integrated the touchscreen, GPS, microphone, speaker, distance sensors, haptic feedback, robotic arms, and linear lift into one physical platform. To assemble the prototype, we soldered four circuit boards and designed and 3D-printed more than 30 custom parts. The project brought together mechanical design, electronics, embedded programming, AI, and app development. Every feature needed both a physical implementation and a way for the user to access it.

sections.heading: Challenges we faced
sections.text: The central challenge was integrating so many different systems into a single walker. A spoken request needs to travel from the user to the agent and then become an action on the appropriate hardware. Physical integration was another challenge. The arms, lift, sensors, screen, and wiring all had to fit around a walker that someone would hold and move with. Custom-designed parts helped us adapt the components to that shared structure. We also had to consider different accessibility needs. Voice interaction, visual information, and haptic feedback each serve a purpose, and deciding how they should work together shaped the design. Finally, the project required a ton of electrical debugging, including shorted solder joints, overloaded USB buses, and poor connections.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Building Sophi taught us to think about the whole interaction, such as what someone wants to do, how they communicate that intent, and how the device responds in the physical world. We also learned how closely hardware and software decisions depend on one another. Component placement affects usability, mechanical design affects what the software can accomplish, and the interface determines whether those capabilities are accessible.

sections.heading: What’s next
sections.text: We want to turn Sophi into a real product. Our next priorities are refining the prototype, testing reliability and usability, learning directly from potential users and caregivers, and taking it to market. We have already connected with a major prosthetics nonprofit to discuss Sophi’s future. As we continue developing it, our motivation remains the same: to help people who need it most move through daily life with greater safety and independence.

sections.heading: Additional Work
sections.text: To control the robot arms, we developed a custom GPT-controlled harness, tested control with the Dream Labs API, and evaluated some open-source AI models for the SO101 arms. The GPT-controlled harness worked, but was far too slow. The Dream Labs API controlled the arms, but did not seem to behave reliably out of the box. None of the open-source models tested were reliable either. In the end, we developed our own harness which uses IPhones to control the SO101 robot arms.

title: Standard Response
tagline: An AI-powered a platform for emergency services to orchestrate mass evacuations and help people who can't get themselves out.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: On the night of the Eaton Fire in January 2025, Anthony Mitchell, 68, was at home in west Altadena with his son Justin, 35. Anthony used a wheelchair. Justin has cerebral palsy. Anthony called 911 at 6:03am and again at 6:14. The dispatcher told him "They're on their way." Nobody came. Both men died in their home. LA County's paratransit service later said its vans were ready by 4am. Nobody called it. The vehicles existed. What failed was coordination. A UN survey of about 6,000 people with disabilities found that only 1 in 5 could evacuate right away without difficulty. During Hurricane Harvey, fewer than 5% of the people on Texas's disability registry were contacted, because nobody had the staff to call through the list in time. We took that problem to Palo Alto Fire Stations 1 and 6. "We have four dispatchers that sit in the room," one firefighter told us. "You can only answer so many calls." Standard Response is our answer.

sections.heading: In the news:
sections.text: On LinkedIn On Boris Nezlobin's website — read this! It's got pictures and good advice.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Standard Response is an evacuation coordination system: it calls every home in a warning zone, triages who can't get out, routes accessible vehicles and neighbors to them, and keeps every promise to a resident true while the plan changes. A simulated night over the real map of west Altadena. Standard Response has called every home inside the warning zone (white outline) while the fire (top right) moves in. The 1,003 red homes are the ones dispatch has to reach. Ready check: Before any disaster, the agent calls each household (or they sign up at /ready ) and records who needs help and which room they sleep in. A household that would need a ride is paired with the nearest neighbor within 900 m who said they'd drive. Warning calls: A dispatcher draws the zone on the rescue map, or our public Apify Actor starts the calls when a California county issues a warning. The agent calls every home at once and reads each answer back for correction. Life threats jump to the top of the call floor. Neighbors: On every call, the agent asks whether anyone else on the street might not be able to leave, and matches the names people give to homes on file. It calls a resident's named helper first. If nobody is named, it calls the nearest neighbor with a car and says what the pickup takes before they agree. It only asks neighbors the fire reaches first, so helping someone always means driving away from the fire. The ride request stays open the whole time, so a neighbor is a faster first try and never a reason to hold a van. Dispatch: Our optimizer matches each request to a vehicle with the right seats, wheelchair space and crew. A dispatcher approves with one click, and drivers accept on their own phones. Callback: The moment a driver accepts, the resident gets a call with the driver's name and ETA. A home that never answers is called again, texted, then sent to a field crew. The honesty rule: The agent never says help is coming until a driver has accepted. Code enforces that, not the prompt. The agent's constitution: We wrote the call agent 11 principles, taken from how 911 call-takers and crisis lines work, and set them beside Claude's constitution . Claude's constitution asks it never to create a false impression. Ours turns that into one hard rule: never imply help is coming before a driver accepts. The same principles go into every turn's prompt and into the 373 situations Moss retrieves. The Opus judge grades every exam call against them too. Try it at our table: Scan the QR code, claim a house on the map, and Standard Response calls your phone.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Twilio carries every call, Cartesia hears and speaks it, Claude reads each turn and Moss supplies the agency's approved answers. One Convex database connects everything, so no service calls another directly. Each sponsor's part is described below. Dispatch and simulation: Our adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) runs over an OSMnx road graph of Altadena, with OR-Tools and a greedy heuristic as baselines. The night simulator runs on SimPy. The voice server runs on Fly.io and the dispatch solver on DigitalOcean. The dispatch math Every request has a deadline 10 minutes before fire is expected at the home. A rider who boards by the deadline counts zero expected deaths. After the deadline, the count climbs linearly to the household's full risk 600 seconds later. The optimizer minimizes sum over requests (10^7 x expected deaths + need weight x arrival time) + sum over vehicles (driving time) subject to each vehicle's seats, wheelchair spaces and stretcher spaces. One expected death outweighs any amount of driving, and the need-weighted waiting term spreads riders across the fleet. The search ( dispatch/alns.py ) tears plans apart and rebuilds them under simulated annealing. It never moves a run a driver has accepted. On our fastest simulated fire it completes a median of 6 more on-time pickups than the greedy heuristic over 100 seeds.

sections.heading: How we use our sponsors
sections.text: Anthropic: Claude Haiku 5.5 reads every turn of every call and turns what a resident says into record fields, corrections included. In English and Spanish, the two languages fluent speakers reviewed, it also words the agent's short replies. In other languages the agent speaks only fixed lines. Claude Sonnet 5.5 ranks which homes to call first. Claude Opus 5.5 grades every practice call in our voice exam and flags lines that imply help is coming. Code decides what the agent may promise, not Claude. ( interpreter , honesty guard , judge ) Cartesia: Voice is the product, because the people we call often can't use an app but can answer a landline. Every call runs through Cartesia in both directions on Twilio's raw 8 kHz phone audio. Ink-2 hears English, Spanish, French, Hindi and Japanese in one stream and decides when the caller has finished. Ink-whisper covers Mandarin, Korean, Vietnamese, Tagalog and Russian. Sonic speaks each turn with a native voice in each language and stops the moment the caller talks over it. Sonic's delivery also changes as the fire gets closer: speed rises from 1.0 to 1.25, volume from 1.0 to 1.4, and the English emotion moves from calm to determined. A caller who is hard of hearing gets slower speech at full volume. ( voice/phone/cartesia.ts , voice/phone/delivery.ts ) Moss: Before Claude reads each turn, Moss pulls the closest call-taking principles and practice-call moments into the prompt, filtered by hazard and language, within an 80 ms budget. When a caller asks a policy question ("Can I go back in for my cat?"), Claude restates it in English and Moss matches it to the agency's approved answer, which the caller hears word for word in their language. Below a 0.7 match score, the agent says it doesn't know. Across 66 test questions, 61 got the right answer with Moss, including 14 of 18 safety answers, and no dangerous question got an ordinary answer. Without Moss, none of the 54 questions with an approved answer got one. The median lookup took 5 ms. ( voice/knowledge/moss.ts , results ) Convex: Convex is the only way our services talk to each other. The voice server subscribes to the callback queue with onUpdate , so the moment a driver taps Accept, the rider's callback starts with no polling. An accept is one mutation that checks the offer's plan version, and a scheduled function expires the offer after two minutes. Each real rider's retry ladder is a durable Convex Workflow. Triggers update two Aggregate components in the same transaction as each household write, so the call floor's counts are never off. HTTP actions take warnings from our Apify Actor and status from the voice agents, and a daily cron deletes real riders' data 72 hours after an incident closes. ( convex/ ) Apify: We built and published the California evacuation status Actor on the Apify Store. It merges Cal OES and CAL FIRE evacuation zones, CAL FIRE incidents and Caltrans closures from all 12 districts into one record shape. The Actor remembers what it has sent in a key-value store, so each fresh zone reaches our Convex endpoint once per status change. A zone with riders inside starts the calls. Stale zones are never sent: one platform run returned 9 zones that were all old orders, so no one got a false warning call. When Caltrans closes one of our streets, the next plan routes vans around it. ( apify/ ) Mana: We gave Mana the five rules our accept flow must keep and asked it to break them the way a driver tapping fast on a bad connection would. In about nine minutes it read our Convex code, set up a test harness the repo didn't have, and wrote 29 tests. Five failed, exposing three bugs our own red-team runs had missed. A repeated Accept was logged as a stale accept. A driver accepting stops out of order could put a pickup ahead of one already accepted. A late event from the call server could undo a callback the rider had already heard. Mana opened PR #1 with a fix for each ( Mana chat ). Mana found all three bugs 16 to 23 hours b

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Keeping promises while the plan changes: Roads close after a driver accepts, and drivers tap Accept on offers a newer plan replaced. Our Convex stress test fires conflicting writes from dozens of clients at once at a throwaway Convex backend. Its first runs caught four race conditions, and we fixed all four. Mana then wrote 29 adversarial tests against the same flow and found three more bugs, listed under Mana above. Where the agent still fails: Our voice exam, scored like the CritiCall 911 hiring test, still misses its 0.95 bar (the best of three runs scored 0.937). When a caller insists a driver is already coming, only 6 of 64 test calls pass, mostly because the agent skips the status line. Armenian and Farsi callers reached a person within three turns in only 8 of 32 calls. Every result is in the repo's README. Catching soft promises: Claude kept reaching for comforting lines like "we're working on getting help to you." A voice exam modeled on CritiCall, the 911 dispatcher hiring test, caught each one, and every phrase went into the code guard. Rebuilding a whole night: We placed more than 3,300 timestamped UL FSRI records, CAL FIRE damage inspections and LA County's evacuation times on the map, then simulated all 11,855 west-side households.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: On a simulation of the real Eaton Fire night, Standard Response got 16 times as many at-risk households out on time as today's process. On time means everyone is aboard at least 10 minutes before fire is reported near the home. Calls start Vehicles With Standard Response Today's process (modeled) 10:50pm, first fire west of Lake Ave 25 641 of 662 (97%) 39 of 662 (6%) 3:25am, the real evacuation order 50 356 of 662 (54%), 81% of the 442 still reachable 43 of 662 (6%) Each figure is the median of five simulated runs. Twenty-five vehicles is under 2% of AccessLA's paratransit fleet. By the real 3:25am order, fire had already been reported near 220 of the homes, so no fleet could get more than 442 out. The right-hand column is our model of today's process, not the record. In it, 55% of the people who need a ride call 911 about 20 minutes before the fire reaches them. The nearest free unit then takes one household per trip. Both columns assume free-flow traffic and callers who report their needs correctly. Every assumption is listed in data/eaton/night-sim-results.json . Documented requests: Sixteen households west of Lake asked for help that night. Standard Response would have reached 13 of them before they had to ask. Rock-solid promises: In our stress test, 25 ride offers were each accepted by 12 phones at the same instant, and exactly one accept won every time. What our evals show: Across 200 simulated callers in English and Spanish, the agent got every address right. A Claude Opus grader read 2,046 of its lines and found implied promises in 9. Firefighters' verdict: "Honestly, this one is probably the most at the cutting edge of what we're already doing and what could be helpful." (Palo Alto Fire Station 1)

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: The shortage was information, not vehicles: With the same 25 vehicles, 39 households got out on time when people had to reach 911 themselves. When Standard Response called every home first, 641 did. Promises belong in code: Claude reached for the same comfort 911 gave Anthony Mitchell, so every sentence about a ride is now a template code picks. A banned-phrase list caught only 10 of 20 promises it had never seen, while an Opus grader caught all 20. The hardest bugs weren't in the AI: Two phones tapping Accept at once can break a promise faster than any model. Single-transaction mutations fixed all four races we found. Firefighters know what no form asks: "Wheelchair" can mean a 400-pound power chair, crews need a household's language before they knock, and volunteers must drive away from the fire. We shipped every fix the same day.

sections.heading: FAQ
sections.text: Does it replace 911? No. It makes the calls 911 has no staff to make. When a caller reports flames or a medical emergency, the home jumps to the top of the dispatcher's list and the agent tells the caller to call 911. Who runs it? A paratransit agency like LA County's Access Services, on its own rider list. Its dispatcher loads riders from a CSV, draws the warning zone on the rescue map and approves every vehicle plan, and nothing about a ride reaches a resident until a driver accepts. Is it legal for an AI to call people? Since 2024 the FCC has treated AI-generated voices as artificial voices under the TCPA, the federal law on automated calls. An agency calling its own riders about an emergency falls under that law's emergency exception. Agency counsel would confirm this before a real deployment. Isn't the simulator grading its own homework? Its inputs are real records: a census population reweighted to real totals, CAL FIRE's damage inspections and UL FSRI's fire timeline. It tests a dispatch policy against that night, not a prediction of who would have lived. Its assumptions are published with the results. Would it have saved Anthony and Justin Mitchell? We can't say that. The reporting shows vans were ready and nobody called them. Standard Response makes that call.

sections.heading: What's next for Standard Response
sections.text: Drills: A tabletop drill with Palo Alto Stations 1 and 6, then a replay of a night like the Eaton Fire with a paratransit agency's own dispatchers. Shadow mode, then a pilot: Run beside real dispatchers during real warnings, then pilot on an agency's rider list under its authority, deleting rider data 72 hours after each incident closes. Beyond wildfire: Calls and dispatch already work the same for floods, earthquakes and hurricanes. Only the hazard model changes. Every reverse-911 warning today is a one-way broadcast. We want the next one to be a conversation.

title: TouchSpace
tagline: Turning real-world spaces into interactive tactile and audio maps, empowering blind and visually impaired people to explore unfamiliar environments independently.

sections.text: TouchSpace: Making the World Accessible Through Touch

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Imagine entering an unfamiliar building without being able to see its layout. You don't know where the entrances, exits, restrooms, or hallways are. While traditional navigation apps can tell you when to turn, they rarely help you understand the space around you. For blind and visually impaired individuals, independently exploring unfamiliar indoor environments remains a significant accessibility challenge. We wanted to change that. At Cal Hacks 13.0, we came up with TouchSpace , a platform that transforms real-world indoor environments into interactive tactile and audio maps. Our goal is simple: Everyone deserves the ability to understand and explore their surroundings independently, regardless of their visual ability .

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: TouchSpace AI combines spatial scanning, artificial intelligence, conversational voice technology and tactile information to make indoor spaces more accessible. Our system is designed around five core pillars: Scan : A LiDAR-equipped iPhone or iPad to capture an indoor environment. Understand : The scan becomes a floor plan with walls, doorways, landmarks, and a walkable route graph. Share : The whole map is bundled and can be uploaded to a community drive where other devices can download and open. Touch : A interactive top-down view of the floor plan rises as pins on a Dot Pad tactile display, complete with location markers, route highlighting, and braille labels Explore : An AI voice assistant with access to the complete map geometry answers spacial questions, locates objects, and plans routes. Instead of simply hearing "Turn left in 10 feet," users can physically explore a map, understand how spaces connect, and decide where they want to go. *The Dot Pad is a refreshable tactile display with 2,400 pins and a 20-cell braille line, so the same device can show any map.

sections.heading: How We're Building It
sections.text: TouchSpace combines iOS sensors, an accessible web app, and specialized tactile hardware. Apple RoomPlan and LiDAR capture indoor geometry, including walls, doors, openings, and furniture, and structured spatial data. Swift and SwiftUI power the iOS app, where rooms, entrances, and landmarks are labeled and packaged into one .touchspacemap file, ready for sharing or download. Traversal algorithms are used on a navigation graph of walkable connections. Claude-Powered Spatial Understanding help interpret free-form questions. Answers are computed from the map itself, so the AI cannot invent a room or a path. The Dot Pad SDK receives the floor plan as a 60 × 40 pin grid, with raised walls, open doorways, and a pin symbol for each landmark. Room names go to the 20-cell braille line. React and FastAPI provide a web interface for uploading scans, exploring generated maps, and communication to DotPad Our search for tactile hardware led us to the Dot Pad, a refreshable tactile display that already exists. That let us focus on software that fills it with indoor maps generated directly from a scan. Another key decision was keeping AI out of direct route planning. For a blind user, a wrong direction caused by halucination is a safety risk. Instead, the AI agent calls functions that deterministically computes and verifies valid routes.

sections.heading: Challenges We Faced
sections.text: The central engineering challenge is translating complex 3D environments into simple, touch-readable maps . A raw scan can contain hundreds of objects and geometric details. Reproducing everything would make a tactile map cluttered and hard to read. We therefore had to decide which information matters most, such as walls, entrances, obstacles, and key landmarks. The Dot Pad made this even stricter. Its 60 × 40 pin grid leaves room for only the essentials, and its braille line fits just 20 cells. Real scans were also messy. Walls arrived slightly rotated, corners failed to meet, and doors floated off their walls. We also need to ensure that spoken navigation guidance comes from actual map data rather than unsupported AI assumptions. Finally, hardware itself was a challenge. We first tried building our own pin display. Every pin needed its own actuator, which quickly became too much to build within a hackathon. Looking for alternatives led us to the Dot Pad, an existing refreshable tactile display.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: Developing this project taught us that accessibility is not simply about translating visual information into another format. It's about designing information around how people actually experience the world. A detailed visual floor plan isn’t necessarily a good tactile map. Effective tactile navigation requires simplification, clear landmarks, understandable spatial relationships, and consistent representations. We also learned the importance of combining different interaction methods. A tactile map can help someone build a mental understanding of a space, while conversational voice assistance can provide additional context and answer specific questions. Together, these technologies have the potential to create a more inclusive spatial exploration experience.

sections.heading: What's Next
sections.text: Our immediate goal is to complete and validate the full workflow on real devices, from scanning a real room to exploring it on a Dot Pad. Future improvements could include: Automatic multi-room and multi-floor mapping Fuller braille labeling and customizable tactile symbols Hands-free voice interaction, including voice commands to pan and zoom the tactile map Real-time updates for blocked hallways or changed layouts Support for more refreshable tactile displays beyond the Dot Pad Usability testing and collaboration with blind and visually impaired users Ultimately, we envision a future where any building can be scanned once and explored by anyone who needs it. Our Mission TouchSpace is more than a mapping tool. It's an effort to make physical spaces more understandable, accessible, and inclusive. It lets you know the space before you get there. We believe that independent exploration should not be a privilege limited by vision. TouchSpace — Scan a Space. Feel the Layout. Explore with Confidence .

title: MediLedger
tagline: A privacy-preserving drug availability search powered by EigenDA and ZK-PTLS

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Hospital stockouts—the unavailability of essential medications and medical supplies—present a major crisis in healthcare. Patients suffer delays in critical treatments, emergency rooms lack life-saving drugs, and hospitals are forced to ration care. Despite medical advancements, hospitals still rely on outdated, fragmented inventory systems, leading to supply shortages that compromise patient outcomes. The biggest challenge? Hospitals don’t want to share their entire inventory with competitors. Right now, checking stock requires manual calls between hospitals, which is slow, inefficient, and unscalable. The result? Wasted time that directly exacerbates preventable patient harm. Our project is uniquely ambitious in the way we are applying Web3 to a deeply centralized system like healthcare, but we want to reinvent how cybersecurity works in this important industry. We care about using blockchain for social good, so a detailed problem statement highlighting the inspiration for our product is linked below.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: MediLedger is all about collaboration: providing a decentralized platform on which hospitals can more securely and confidently transmit sensitive data. Our system enables hospitals to securely check drug availability at other hospitals without exposing full inventory details on both ends. Instead of storing a simple list of drugs, each hospital stores its own inventory in a Merkle tree, where each leaf node contains a cryptographic hash of a drug name and quantity. The Merkle root (a compact summary of the entire inventory) is then submitted to EigenDA, a decentralized data availability layer. EigenDA allows hospitals to store inventory commitments on-chain without revealing individual stock details and ensures data integrity—any change in inventory changes the Merkle root, which prevents tampering. When a hospital needs a drug, the AI agent first checks the local hospital’s inventory. If the drug is out of stock or the supply is trending low, the AI agent fetches Merkle roots of nearby hospitals from EigenDA using Zero-Knowledge Proofs (zkProof) and the provided Merkle trees. The hospitals that have the requested drug generate a Merkle proof, which extracts the leaf node (hashed drug and quantity) from the Merkle tree, includes all necessary sibling hashes to allow recomputation of the Merkle root, and ensures the proof matches the stored Merkle root on EigenDA. The system then outputs a list of hospitals whose Merkle proofs have been validated, thus proving they have the drug in stock.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The backend server was built with Express.js, Node.js, and TypeScript. For the hashing algorithm, we used SHA256. While configuring the adapter for EigenDA, we used EigenLayer’s extensible agent framework for verifiable AI capabilities and data availability logging. The frontend was built with FlutterFlow, with an initial POC frontend built using Next.js.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The biggest challenge was integration—the backend deployment was not Much of what we worked on also involved repositories and tools with limited documentation, where we underwent educated debugging in a field we had little prior experience in. We initially had two ideas (this one and another more fintech focused on price manipulation) that we pivoted twice between on Friday, so defining the initial feature set for both with a blockchain focus took some time, especially with the crunch time of 36 hours. The biggest challenge was integration as well with FlutterFlow.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: For most of the team, TreeHacks 2025 is our first hackathon ever. We could have played it safe using familiar Web2 tech stacks from classes, we decided to challenge ourselves by diving headfirst into Web3 and cryptography. In a span of 36 hours, we overcame the steep learning curve of understanding and implementing Merkle proofs and trees, which are notoriously complex but incredibly powerful for verification. Despite occasional roadblocks, we were determined to not give up on our ambitious ideas (where else has blockchain been integrated with healthcare?). Our team wore multiple hats—from testing backend deployment to graphic design and marketing. In the end, we are proud of how we built a fully decentralized inventory system for hospitals to use.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: One of our largest takeaways from this weekend is how accessible hacking can be—even to students with limited technical exposure. With the right background and a willingness to learn new tools, we became a determined team that collaborated well on an interesting idea. Blockchain can be used for security and social good, and we hope we proved that through intersecting these technologies with healthcare. For a more technical side, we learned how hash-based data structures allow for selective proof generation. Storing data off-chain in EigenDA was a major shift from Web2 thinking, and now we understand that different decentralization techniques come with trade-offs in performance.

sections.heading: What's next for MediLedger
sections.text: If we had more time, we would love to implement more features related to Web3: Right now, our proof verification happens off-chain in our backend. A great addition would be to store Merkle roots & zkProofs on Ethereum or a Layer 2 (e.g., Polygon, Arbitrum). This would allow on-chain smart contracts to verify zkProofs without a centralized backend. Currently, hospitals only react when a drug is out of stock or if supply has a diminishing trend. We would love to use our AI agent to predict drug shortages before they happen: analyzing historical hospital inventory data to forecast demand surges and sending alerts to hospitals before a stockout occurs. Currently, hospitals authenticate via API keys. Instead, we could use Web3 wallets (e.g., MetaMask) for hospital authentication, where hospitals could digitally sign zkProofs before submitting them. This would prevent unauthorized hospitals from accessing inventory data.
