title: ClearPath
tagline: ClearPath uses AI to connect patients and doctors in one shared workspace, helping care teams coordinate treatment, flag medication conflicts, and streamline prior authorizations.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The doctor has a treatment plan. The patient has hope to get better soon. but, The next step is waiting for a approval. Behind that wait are questions someone must answer: Does this health service require prior authorization? What documentation does the insurance plan need? Which doctor has the missing information? Who is following up? For the patient, those questions become one: “What happens next?” We built ClearPath Health to make that answer clearer. Prior authorization is our primary focus. We turn insurance policy requirements into structured checks, guided documentation, and a review workflow that patients can follow. Supporting that process is a shared care experience where doctors communicate around one chart and patients can participate in their care. A primary care doctor, cardiologist, and endocrinologist may each hold information relevant to the same treatment request. ClearPath creates a place for that context to come together. Our goal is to help healthcare professionals move care forward while keeping patients connected to the people working on their behalf.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Makes prior authorization requirements understandable Our PA engine is grounded in a real 253-page 2026 UnitedHealthcare Dual Complete OH-S3 Evidence of Coverage document. We structured its medical benefits and authorization information into 90 benefit categories : Authorization requirement Categories Required 41 Not required 41 Conditional 8 Each category includes source page references and relevant coverage notes. Conditional requirements preserve distinctions such as diagnosis, service location, and network status. A doctor enters the patient, insurance plan, and requested treatment. The engine checks the policy library and identifies the applicable authorization requirement. An “authorization not required” result answers that specific question; other coverage and payment requirements still apply. Guides a request from documentation to decision When authorization is required, the doctor completes a structured questionnaire and submits the request to a reviewer queue. The reviewer can approve, deny, or request additional information. If more information is needed, the doctor can complete the missing documentation and resubmit. Each action becomes part of a timestamped history. The patient-facing status page reads from the same request record, keeping progress connected to what actually happens in the workflow. Prior Authorization Workflow Enter the request: The doctor selects the patient, insurance plan, and treatment. Check the policy: ClearPath identifies whether authorization is required, not required, or conditional, with source references. Prepare documentation: When needed, the doctor completes the supporting questionnaire. Review and verify: The doctor checks the evidence and answers before submission. Submit: The request is sent through the prototype’s simulated insurer workflow. Track progress: The patient can view the request’s status and recorded history. Brings the care team together around the patient The shared care application brings together conditions, medicines, visit notes, treatment information, and conversations. Each patient has a team room. AI-generated briefings organize shared context around three questions: Who owns the next step? What question is still open? What needs to happen next? The Insights page brings handoffs and team activity into one view. Presence indicators show who is active, and a care-team graph makes the relationships around the patient visible. This shared context supports our broader authorization goal: assembling relevant evidence and helping the right people resolve outstanding questions. The shared-care application and PA engine were developed as separate workstreams. Completing their connection is our next integration milestone. Gives patients a voice through Ava Patients can speak or type to Ava , describe a concern, and answer follow-up questions. They then choose whether to send the conversation summary to one doctor or the whole care team. Doctors receive organized context linked to the patient. They can also use Ava to draft an explanation in everyday language, review and edit it, and send it as text with an optional voice note. A patient can explain what they are experiencing in their own words, and a doctor can respond with the relevant context already available. Supports medication review and explanation Doctors can open a medication panel containing label information, warnings, product details, reported adverse events, and source links. The “Explain to the patient with Ava” action prepares a patient-friendly draft from the retrieved label. Patients can also ask questions about their medicines using that same information. The prescription-checking workflow considers active medicines across prescribers and surfaces potential concerns for clinician assessment. Questions about starting, stopping, or changing a dose remain with the doctor. Adverse-event reports are presented with context explaining that reports alone do not establish causation or an individual patient’s r

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built the shared-care application with a Next.js and React frontend and a FastAPI backend , deployed through Vercel . Policy ingestion and authorization engine We extracted benefit and authorization information from the insurance document into a structured policy library. Rules preserve their classification, conditions, coverage notes, and source references. Policy libraries can move between draft, live, and archived states, with an audit trail recording changes. The PA engine connects those rules to documentation questionnaires and a request workflow. Request history is append-only, preserving earlier actions and decisions. Questionnaire safeguards protect already-submitted answers. How the Policy Engine Works Read the policy: Extract text from the uploaded insurance PDF. Structure the requirements: Organize the policy into authorization rules, conditions, and source references. Validate with Grok: A second-model review flags potential issues for human inspection. Review and activate: A person accepts, edits, or rejects extracted items before activating the policy library. Check the treatment: The engine uses the patient, plan, and requested service to identify applicable requirements. Prepare the request: The doctor completes the documentation, checks supporting evidence, and verifies answers before submission. Preserve progress: The request history records actions and supports the doctor and patient status views. We represented authorization requirements using FHIR-shaped CoverageEligibilityResponse data and documentation through Questionnaire and QuestionnaireResponse . These structures provide a foundation for future interoperability work. The demonstration uses a reviewer queue rather than a live payer connection. AI and data services Each service has a specific responsibility within the experience: Technology Role Policy rules engine Checks structured authorization requirements and conditions FHIR-shaped resources Organize authorization and documentation data Google Gemini Powers Ask ClearPath using available application data and screen context Muse Spark integration Generates care-team briefings with ownership and next steps Muse Voice integration Transcribes audio in the voice workflow OpenAI Supports Ava’s conversations, summaries, and message drafts ElevenLabs Produces Ava’s spoken replies when configured openFDA Supplies medication labels, product information, and adverse-event data NIH RxNav Supports medication lookup and normalization The communication workflow connects AI assistance to a human recipient: Patient speaks/types → Ava gathers context → Patient reviews → Doctor receives → Doctor reviews → Patient gets response We added medication-data caching, preloading, and duplicate-request handling to improve responsiveness. We also refined label matching to reduce confusion between individual medicines and combination products. Explicit rules manage authorization requirements and workflow transitions. AI helps organize and explain information, while people review communication and authorization decisions.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Preserving the meaning of insurance policies. Requirements and exceptions can appear across different sections. We retained conditional classifications and source references so the structured rules remain connected to their original context. Separating different decisions. Whether authorization is required, whether documentation is complete, and whether a reviewer approves a request are different questions. Our workflow represents each explicitly. Making collaboration actionable. Shared information becomes more useful when someone owns the next step. This shaped our briefings, handoffs, and activity views. Matching everyday medication language. Patients may describe a medicine by its purpose, while source data uses ingredient names, brands, and product identifiers. We refined matching around the patient’s chart and the appropriate label. Keeping the application responsive. We addressed blocking AI calls, duplicate Ava responses, and a medication-preloading issue that froze the backend. Integrating parallel workstreams. When a planned extraction branch could not be merged, we built an isolated upload module feeding the PA order desk. That kept the authorization demonstration progressing and clarified the remaining integration work.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We turned a real insurance document into 90 structured benefit categories and built a guided authorization workflow around them: requirement checks, documentation, reviewer decisions, and patient-visible history. Alongside that, we built a shared care experience where patients can explain concerns, doctors can coordinate, and AI can organize information into understandable next steps. Impiricus: Invent the Next Way We Engage HCPs ClearPath’s proposed HCP engagement model begins with work that already matters to a clinician: moving a treatment request forward. The authorization engine helps identify requirements and organize documentation. The shared-care experience supports clarification, medication review, and patient explanations in the context of that work. A clinician can inspect medication information, prepare a patient-friendly explanation, and coordinate with another provider around the same chart. The potential commercial value is a workspace healthcare professionals can return to whenever care requires authorization or collaboration. We would validate that value through documentation effort, request completeness, repeat use, and clinician feedback. Meta: Bringing People Closer Together with AI ClearPath focuses on the relationships between a patient and their care team, and among the professionals caring for that patient. A patient can have several doctors and still feel alone coordinating their care. Our shared experience is designed to help those people work together with a clearer understanding of one another. Ava helps patients express concerns in their own words and share them with a chosen doctor or team. AI-generated briefings help doctors understand shared updates and identify responsibility. Reviewed explanations help patients understand the response. AI plays a meaningful role by organizing conversational and chart information into something another person can use: a concern summary, an understandable explanation, or a handoff with a clear owner. Prior authorization gives that collaboration a concrete purpose. Missing documentation requires coordination. A request for clarification needs an owner. A changing status needs an understandable update for the patient. The connection we aim to strengthen is a patient and their doctors working together through the next step of care. AI/ML: Oracle of the Deep ClearPath combines conversational AI, retrieved medication information, chart context, structured summaries, and task-oriented briefings with an explicit policy rules engine. The engineering challenge is selecting relevant information, preserving its meaning, and producing useful outputs within a workflow. Gemini contributes contextual assistance through Ask ClearPath. Ava combines conversation, transcription, and speech to support communication. The rules engine provides a traceable foundation for authorization checks. Our evaluation priorities include policy-extraction accuracy, summary fidelity, medication-match quality, response time, and whether users can identify and complete the next step. Gemini and ElevenLabs Gemini powers Ask ClearPath, allowing users to ask questions with available platform data and screen context. ElevenLabs gives Ava a spoken interface and supports the voice experience alongside text. Its purpose is practical: letting people hear an explanation and participate through conversation.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that a useful authorization experience begins before a request is submitted. It begins with identifying the applicable policy, understanding its conditions, and gathering information from the people caring for the patient. We also learned that an AI output needs a clear destination. A summary should help a doctor respond. A briefing should help someone take ownership. An explanation should help a patient understand. Traceability matters throughout: a rule needs a source, a status needs an event behind it, and a next step needs an owner. Building ClearPath showed us how administrative clarity and human connection support each other.

sections.heading: What's next for ClearPath
sections.text: Our immediate priority is connecting the shared chart and PA engine into one continuous experience: treatment request, supporting evidence, policy check, documentation, review, and patient-visible status. Next, we plan to: Validate extracted rules and documentation workflows with domain experts. Expand the policy library beyond the initial insurance plan. Replace in-memory demonstration data with persistent storage. Strengthen permission-based sharing and auditability. Integrate real payer submission and response systems. Evaluate task completion, handoff clarity, and patient understanding with users. The current prototype uses demonstration patient data and a simulated reviewer workflow. ElevenLabs voice has been tested locally; the deployed experience uses it when configured and otherwise falls back to browser speech. Our goal is to help healthcare professionals move requests forward and help patients understand the people and actions supporting their care. ClearPath Health: clearer authorization, connected care, and a patient who stays part of the conversation.

prize_badges: Impiricus: Build the next HCP Engagement Tool - 3rd Place

title: DocSpot
tagline: An all-in-one platform for physicians to find specialists and send referrals, making connections between physicians faster and more trusted.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Imagine you’re a physician whose patient needs a specialist. Finding the right person can be difficult, especially when many physicians are digitally dark or hard to reach through the usual industry channels. We wanted to hear directly from an HCP, so we reached out to Dr. Justin Strickland, the owner of a pharmaceutical practice here in Atlanta. He told us, “ Even some of our local physicians who we have known and worked with for years have become increasingly difficult to reach after their practices were acquired. ” Today, 82% of U.S. physicians work for hospitals or corporate entities ( PAI/Avalere ). And in rural areas, finding a doctor can be even harder, as urban areas have nearly three times as many physicians per 100,000 people ( AAMC, 2022 ). To bridge this gap, we looked at how physicians learn about new critical clinical tools and found that professional relationships play an important role. In a survey, 76.4% of physicians named other physicians among their most trusted sources of health information ( Kruger et al., 2012 ). That’s where DocSpot comes in. Built on Impiricus' network of over 1 million opted-in healthcare professionals, DocSpot maps national physician connections so doctors can refer patients, ask clinical questions, and surface telehealth or trial opportunities.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: DocSpot connects physicians based on specialty, experience, and clinical needs, creating a network that introduces more HCPs to Impiricus’ services. An HCP can find a specialist for a referral, explore telehealth and clinical trial options, or find a colleague to answer a clinical question. Drawing from a comprehensive database of physicians and specialists across the US, DocSpot recommends relevant physicians, including those who have not joined Impiricus. For referrals, DocSpot ranks specialists by factors such as specialty, distance, and their relationship to the sender. It then drafts an editable electronic fax (e-fax) with limited patient information. The HCP reviews the recipient, draft, and privacy check before approving it, then tracks the request and response in one place through the platform. A physician outside Impiricus can respond without joining. After that first useful interaction, they can choose to connect with the sender on Impiricus and discover its services through a professional relationship.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Frontend: HTML, CSS, and plain JavaScript power the workflow. SVG draws the network map and groups physicians by specialty, while client-side code generates QR codes for fax previews. Backend and AI: Python FastAPI and Pydantic validate requests. The backend sends limited, structured details to OpenAI’s gpt-4.1-mini model to draft faxes and assist with privacy review. Physician data: We cleaned NPI Registry records in a Jupyter notebook and mapped taxonomy descriptions to DocSpot’s specialties. The demo uses 253 clinician records for sample recommendations. Consent and email: After a specialist accepts, the referring physician reviews a consent form. FastAPI serves the signing page, and the Resend Email API sends the patient a link. The patient confirms their date of birth and signs before DocSpot shares further details.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Our first visual network map consisted of singular, unrelated nodes, and eventually became difficult to read as we added physicians and their connections. To address this challenge, we separated clinicians into specialty groups, made the nodes easier to distinguish, and added a list view. NPI records also used different descriptions for similar specialties, so we had to clean and map those labels before using the records in recommendations. Referrals also required careful handling of patient information. The sending physician reviews the request before it goes out. If the receiving physician accepts, the patient signs a consent form before DocSpot shares any further patient details.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we’re proud of
sections.text: This was everyone on our team’s first hackathon, so we’re proud we turned a physician’s experience into a working prototype under a tight deadline. We're also proud of the network map, which gives HCPs a visual way to see where care is available, and most importantly, helps improve patient care.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Building a healthcare product taught us how much goes into a physician’s decision to contact a colleague. They need to find the right person, protect the patient’s privacy, and review what they send. Because those decisions can affect a real patient’s care, we learned to look at each step from the physician’s perspective and make DocSpot useful in their day-to-day work.

sections.heading: What’s next for DocSpot
sections.text: We hope to explore partnerships with Careset, HealthVerity, or Symphony Health, and GaHIN to improve our physician and relationship data. We also want to integrate a secure e-fax service so HCPs can send and track real requests. We would start with a pilot in one rural Georgia county, learn how local HCPs find specialists and respond to referrals, adjust DocSpot based on their feedback, and then expand to other communities.

prize_badges: Impiricus: Build the next HCP Engagement Tool - 2nd Place

title: DopaMarine
tagline: A study game for dopamine-hungry brains: turn your notes into AI-made levels built for how you learn, beat the final boss, and battle friends in AR and grow from tiny krill into a mighty fish.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We’ve all had those moments where we sit down to study, tell ourselves we’ll focus for an hour, and somehow end up scrolling on our phones five minutes later. As students, we’ve experienced the struggle with procrastination, short attention spans, and just finding the motivation to keep studying. We wanted to make studying feel less like something we had to force ourselves to do. Inspired by Pokémon GO, we created DopaMarine to turn studying into an interactive, real-world adventure where students can move, explore, and learn while also adapting to the way each person learns best.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: DopaMarine turns your lecture slides, PDFs, and notes into a study game made for how you learn. You pick a sea-creature study buddy that matches your learning style. You earn pearls (XP) that allow you to pass levels and eventually beat the boss level — the big bad shark, which is the practice exam. Then take it into AR: open the virtual battlefield right through your phone’s camera and battle solo, against friends, or against players nearby in a Pokémon-style showdown. Each round shows a question from your notes, and you throw the ball with the correct answer to defeat your opponent’s avatar. The people you are competing with can either be studying the same or different things. Everyone starts as a tiny krill, and the more battles you win, the more you evolve into bigger and stronger fish.

sections.heading: How We Built It
sections.text: We built DopaMarine using JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS powering the frontend. We designed the interface in Figma and used custom sea creature designs and artwork throughout the game. Leaflet and OpenStreetMap power the interactive map. The Node.js and Express backend handles authentication, game progress, AI requests, real-time duels, raids, and player presence through WebSockets. We used the Google Gemini API to create structured study decks from uploaded materials, including recall, understanding, and application questions, along with field guides, hints, explanations, and personalized content. Responses are validated server-side before being used in the game. MongoDB Atlas stores accounts, decks, mastery, exams, catches, battles, and other game data, with an automatic local JSON fallback if the database or internet connection is unavailable. Location and creature spawn data are kept in memory rather than stored permanently. We also built several camera-based mini-games using device motion tracking and on-device face detection, with fallback controls for devices without gyroscopes. The game runs entirely in the browser, so there is no native app or installation required.

sections.heading: Challenges We Faced
sections.text: Our biggest challenge was getting the AR features to work consistently across different devices. Recognition and motion tracking did not always behave the same way, so we had to add fallback controls and make the experience more forgiving when something failed. We also ran into occasional Gemini errors and inconsistent JSON responses. We ended up adding automatic retries, fallback models, and server-side validation so one bad response would not break the game. Designing for different learning needs was another challenge because we couldn’t just change the appearance of each fish. We had to actually change some of the gameplay mechanics. We also dealt with file-version and browser-caching issues that caused some changes to not show up correctly during development.

sections.heading: Accomplishments We’re Proud Of
sections.text: We’re most proud that we were able to turn something as messy as raw lecture material into an actual playable experience. Instead of stopping at an AI-generated quiz, we built different game mechanics around the content, added AR, and connected everything to progression, battles, and accessibility features. We’re also proud that we kept the game usable even when parts of the system failed. Building fallbacks and retries wasn’t something we originally planned to focus on, but it ended up being a big part of getting the final demo to work.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: This was our first time building a project with AR, so we learned a lot about how different real-world devices can behave compared to testing everything on our own computers. We also learned that when you’re working with AI, you can’t always assume the output will be consistent or usable, so you have to design around that. We also learned a lot about working as a team under a time limit. Communication mattered more than we expected, especially when multiple people were building different parts of the same system. We had to be more intentional about dividing up work and checking in so we weren’t accidentally doing the same thing twice.

sections.heading: What’s Next
sections.text: We plan to expand the AR experience with location-based challenges, collectible fish, and collaborative exploration. Additional goals include in-game sound effects, natural AI voices, teacher-created study decks, streaming question generation, and full iOS and Android support.

title: FlyBy
tagline: Building smarter ground control for search and rescue - save seconds, save lives.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Finding someone is not the same as reaching them. After an earthquake, people can be trapped under rubble or hidden behind debris while rescuers race to locate them. A published review cites three earthquakes where 85–95% of survivors rescued from rubble were pulled out within the first 24 hours . Time spent sorting information is time a rescue team cannot get back. Source Monish led a high-school drone team that worked on search-and-rescue missions. They could cover ground quickly and use ML to surface leads, but the footage, data, and decisions were fragmented. The drone moved fast, but the workflow around it didn’t. This is personal for us, too. We all come from earthquake-impacted areas of India, where flooding can leave people stranded and difficult to reach. Small drones must navigate cluttered spaces with limited computing power, while responders sort real leads from a flood of detector flags. FlyBy came from connecting those two delays: helping the drone react at reflex speed, assisting rescuers in reaching a decision sooner, and keeping the final call with humans.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: A sighting only matters if someone can act on it. FlyBy combines a fly-inspired visual reflex with AI ground control to move a possible survivor from a drone’s camera to a responder’s decision. In our simulated coastal disaster, a drone searches the area and flags possible people alongside false leads like debris and animals. FlyBy turns those flags into a ranked queue. It weighs each sighting against incoming reports, known hazards, and the latest incident picture, then suggests what to do next: take another look, inspect up close, dispatch a crew, or set the lead aside. Uncertain possible survivors stay visible for human review. New information can change the ranking. Responders can review or override every recommendation, and no crew is dispatched without human approval. The system also prepares a brief so the crew has the location and relevant context in one place. For the close-up search, FlyBy uses a fly-inspired visual reflex that reads camera motion and tells the drone when to brake or turn. A carport simulation lets us watch and test those reactions around obstacles. Together, the reflex and ground control are designed to make the journey from sighting to close-up inspection to human-approved rescue decision one connected mission.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built FlyBy in two layers: Ground control: A Python and FastAPI simulator runs repeatable searches through a flooded coastal neighborhood, streaming possible sightings to a TypeScript and Three.js dashboard. Our fine-tuned Laya model runs locally to recommend the next action for each lead. Grok, through the xAI API, turns messy field reports into a changing incident picture and drafts crew briefs. MongoDB Atlas logs mission events, while code keeps locations and numbers exact and requires human approval before dispatch. FlyBrain reflex: A separate service passes camera frames through the pretrained flyvis visual model. We fitted our own readout to its motion signals so the simulated drone can brake, turn away, and continue toward its goal. We tested those reactions in repeatable flights through a 3D carport, and adapted the MIT-licensed fly-brain viewer to show recorded activity lighting up mapped neurons. We fine-tuned Laya’s scoring layer because the original model could give uncertain possible survivors low or no priority. The fine-tuned model keeps those leads visible for human review while helping responders decide what to inspect next. Together, these layers are designed to carry a lead through one continuous mission, from first sighting to close-up inspection and a human-approved rescue decision.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Defining what makes FlyBy different - Rescue drones with thermal cameras, AI detection, and obstacle avoidance already exist. Our challenge was figuring out how our fly-inspired reflex and AI ground control could help within the same rescue mission. That meant designing the handoff from a flagged sighting to close-up inspection, then returning useful evidence for a human decision. Making the reflex work beyond a clean demo - The pretrained fly model gives us visual motion signals, not a ready-made collision alarm. Our early readout missed hazards and sometimes braked for safe paths, so fitting and testing it against debris, beams, and posts took far longer than expected. Making uncertainty impossible to ignore - Laya needs to help rescuers decide what to inspect next, not quietly dismiss a lead because the evidence is incomplete. The original model sometimes gave possible people low or no priority when it was unsure. Fine-tuning it for drone sightings and incoming field reports took time because we had to make uncertain leads visible for human review while still giving responders a useful order of action.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Building more than a dashboard - Our simulated drone searches a flooded neighborhood and flies back to inspect uncertain leads. New field reports can change the order of the queue, and responders can approve, override, and review each decision. Fine-tuning Laya for rescue triage - The original model could push an uncertain possible survivor to the bottom of the queue or leave it out entirely. We trained its scoring layer for our use case so those leads stay visible for human review, then used the fine-tuned model in ground control. Getting the fly reflex to work in a flight loop - We connected camera frames, fly-vision activity, and brake-and-turn commands, then built repeatable carport flights to test the readout against different obstacles. Making the fly brain visible - Mapping flyvis activity onto tens of thousands of neurons in a 3D viewer was difficult, but it gave us a way to show what the visual system responds to as a scene changes.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: A fly brain does not automatically know what a collision is - flyvis gave us motion activity, but we had to build the part that turns it into a brake or turn. A beam the drone could safely pass under sometimes looked as threatening as one it would hit, while narrow posts could appear too late. We learned that camera view, obstacle shape, and braking distance matter as much as the model. Uncertainty should trigger investigation, not dismissal - The original Laya model could give a possible survivor low priority when the visual evidence was unclear. Fine-tuning helped keep those leads visible, but a model still cannot confirm a person it cannot see clearly. That is why FlyBy combines model recommendations with field reports, another look from the drone, and human review. Autonomy has to fit the reality of a rescue mission - We learned that an onboard reflex is assistance, not permission for an unmonitored drone to search wherever it wants. In the U.S., real operations involve a pilot, visual-line-of-sight and airspace rules, and sometimes emergency authorization . That reinforced why FlyBy keeps dispatch decisions with responders, too. Agentic coding taught us to be precise - This was Rupesh’s first hackathon, and AI agents made it possible to work across a simulator, two models, and a ground-control interface in one weekend. The useful prompts specified what each component should do, how it should connect, and how we would test it. We learned to treat generated code as a starting point to verify, not proof that the system works.

sections.heading: What's next for FlyBy
sections.text: Test the complete mission - We want to evaluate the full workflow, from the first sighting to close-up inspection and a human-approved rescue decision. We’ll compare it with manual review on the same scenarios to see whether FlyBy helps responders act sooner while keeping uncertain possible survivors in view. Test Laya against harder cases - Our fine-tuned model keeps uncertain possible survivors visible, but we need to test it on more varied scenes and field reports. We want to measure missed leads as carefully as response speed, so a faster queue never comes at the cost of overlooking someone. Move the reflex onto a real drone - The carport simulation lets us repeat difficult flights, but real obstacles, lighting, and camera motion will be tougher. We want to improve the reflex and test it on hardware, measuring response time and power use before trusting it in a rescue environment. Build with rescue teams - We hope to test FlyBy with search-and-rescue teams, including teams in monsoon-affected areas of India, and explore compatibility with platforms from companies such as Skydio, DJI, BRINC, and Flyability. The goal is a tool that fits how crews already work and helps them act on a lead sooner.

title: Fourteenth Floor
tagline: The office for AI agents.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Right now, running several AI agents means staring at scrolling terminal logs. The art of programming has turned into babysitting computer bots. Fourteenth makes agent work visible. You can see who's building, who's blocked, and who's handing off to whom. No agent can mark a task complete without receipts, bringing validity and character to vibecoding.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Fourteenth turns any project folder into a 3D office. A manager agent and a team of specialists take their desks and do real work through Codex, while you watch progress, inspect any desk, or walk the floor in first person. The agents operate as a team, not as isolated processes: The manager delegates. Research, test planning, and risk checks go to read-only specialists, while the manager remains the only agent writing code. Agents hand off directly. When one agent finds something relevant, it sends the finding straight to the agent who needs it, and every message is tracked through delivery and acknowledgment. Shared files are coordinated. When two tasks touch the same file, the agents meet and the second task waits its turn instead of overwriting the first. Work is independently reviewed. Completed tasks move to review with their commands, diffs, and test output attached. Agents are replaceable without losing context. A stalled agent can be ejected and replaced, and the replacement resumes from a saved handoff. Most importantly, a task isn't done just because an agent says so. Every acceptance check requires evidence, such as a diff, a test run the system observed passing, or a screenshot that actually exists, before the task can close.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Three.js renders the office, a procedurally generated city, and the agents themselves, whose animations reflect their current task state. Blender MCP was used to build the office interior, with AI driving Blender directly. We used an MCP tool to build the office our MCP-connected agents work in. Codex's app server runs each agent as a sandboxed Codex session on an isolated profile that never touches the user's desktop account. Custom office tools for delegation, status updates, messaging, and acknowledgment enforce the team workflow in code rather than relying on prompts alone. A local-only server handles persistence, replay, and Git checkpoints. The codebase is primarily TypeScript and JavaScript, with Python for the Blender pipeline.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Verifying claims. An agent can report "tests pass" instantly. Confirming that a test actually ran and passed required significantly more engineering than getting the agent to do the work. Coordination without file locks. Without true filesystem locking, we built declared file scopes and a meeting system to keep agents from editing the same files at once. Safe agent replacement. Starting a replacement too early led to two agents competing for the same task. The outgoing agent now has to acknowledge its interruption and save its handoff before the replacement begins. Windows sandboxing proved more difficult than the agent orchestration itself.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: An evidence gate that agents can't talk their way past. A real Codex integration with agents that coordinate as a team. An office that feels like a place worth being in, not a dashboard with a 3D skin. Accessibility built in from the start, including reduced motion, keyboard alternatives, and status labels that don't rely on color. An initial VR mode that runs today.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Making agents trustworthy is far harder than making them run. Clear roles, handoffs, and review requirements improved reliability more than any prompt change. We also found Blender MCP to be a remarkably fast way to build a 3D scene, and that designing a space people enjoy exploring is a distinct skill from building the systems behind it.

sections.heading: What's next for Fourteenth
sections.text: Shared offices , so human teammates can watch the same room and coordinate their agents together. Support for more agent tools beyond Codex and Cursor. Testing on real VR hardware , since the headset path is built but not yet tested on a device.

title: MiiHab: Get Back in the Game
tagline: Physical therapy disguised as Wii Sports, with your physician watching every rep. Recovery that feels like fun.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: For us, MiiHab is personal. We've watched family members go through physical therapy and rehabilitation, and we've seen firsthand how much of a toll recovery can take on someone's mental health and overall well-being. Getting injured is difficult, but the road to recovery can be even harder. Rehabilitation often involves months of repetitive exercises, slow progress, and the frustration of not being able to do the things you once loved. We also know how isolating recovery can feel. A physical therapist we interviewed told us most patients get about one hour a week with their therapist. That leaves 167 hours when they're on their own, with no feedback, no company, and no one noticing when they stop. Physical therapy shouldn't have to be something patients dread or go through alone. That's why we created MiiHab: a Wii-inspired rehabilitation platform that turns physical therapy into an interactive, engaging, and social experience. We wanted recovery to feel less like a chore and more like getting back to the activities that make life meaningful, while giving clinicians a real view of their patients' progress between appointments.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: MiiHab turns traditional physical therapy into an immersive virtual reality experience that is more engaging, motivating, and accessible. Using a Meta Quest headset and the AirPods patients already own as wearable motion sensors, patients enter virtual worlds and play games like golf and bowling with their own physical movements. They also train in a movement studio with guided exercises such as shoulder raises and bicep curls, measured rep by rep. Instead of simply grinding through repetitive exercises, they practice rehabilitation through activities that feel familiar and rewarding. Patients never exercise alone. Alex, an AI physical therapy coach , sits beside them in VR and speaks to them as they move. His brain is Meta's Muse Spark ; ElevenLabs gives him his voice and ears. He coaches only from what was actually measured, such as reach against the target, whether a rep counted, and whether the trunk leaned. He follows the physician's plan and pain rules, and stops the session at a pain score of 7 or more. MiiHab also makes recovery more connected. Patients can rehab side by side with friends in group sessions, play golf and bowling together, and message each other. Muse suggests which friend to reach out to, drafts a reply they can send in one press, introduces two patients working toward the same goal by what they share, and turns a streak into a milestone card they can share to Facebook or Messenger . For clinicians, MiiHab closes the gap between visits. The physician's EHR updates live, rep by rep , while the patient exercises. It shows what the coach said next to the measurements it was based on, tracks movement quality and pain, and can replay the whole program as a timelapse. When the physician updates the plan, the patient's headset explains the change in the coach's voice at their next session. Our goal is to make rehabilitation something patients look forward to, helping them regain their physical abilities, confidence, and independence while having fun along the way.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built MiiHab with Unity, the Meta Quest, AirPods motion tracking, AI, and real-time networking. Motion sensing: we used Swift and Apple's CoreMotion framework to stream orientation and rotation rate from AirPods. macOS only streams motion from one pair at a time, so each pair runs on its own Mac. A relay on the main Mac merges both pairs over a Tailscale tunnel. The Quest's head tracking is the third sensor and measures trunk lean. VR: in Unity and C# we built the golf course, bowling alley, and movement studio in first person. The Mac runs the simulation and the headset renders it, connected over USB. The coach: Alex runs on ElevenLabs Conversational AI with Meta's Muse Spark as his language model, connected through an adapter we built on the Mac. The adapter cleans each request so Muse accepts it and keeps the Muse key local. His audio plays from the coach's position in the headset. Tool calls let him read the care plan and the measured results, log pain, and request a plan review from the care team. Social: a Node coordinator handles friends, messages, anonymous double opt-in introductions, and group sessions, with Muse writing the suggestions. Milestones can be shared through Meta's share dialog. Clinician portal: a React EHR that updates live from the exercise stream and lets the physician sign plan updates that reach the patient's headset.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One Mac, one pair of AirPods. macOS only streams motion from one pair at a time, so a second tracked limb needed a second Mac. We stream both pairs into a relay and merge them there. Solo, both pairs are the patient's: golf follows the stronger swing and bowling follows the throwing wrist. In a group session, each person gets one pair. Venue Wi-Fi blocks devices from talking to each other. We moved the Mac-to-Mac link onto a Tailscale tunnel and run the headset over its USB cable. Then macOS silently blocked the Motion app from connecting over Tailscale, which we traced to App Transport Security. Two sensors, two coordinate frames. Switching the game between AirPod pairs made the club jump, so we realign the orientation at every handover. The camera had to go. We started with MediaPipe body tracking and moved to AirPods plus the headset's own head tracking, which works in a dark room with no camera setup. First-person VR breaks assumptions. 2D menus don't render in a headset's two eyes, so every menu became a board in the 3D world. One sign placed for a third-person view ended up 20 cm in front of the player's face. Making Muse the coach's brain. ElevenLabs sends request fields Muse rejects, so we built an adapter that cleans each request before it reaches Muse.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're especially proud of turning everyday consumer hardware ( AirPods and a Meta Quest ) into a motion-controlled rehabilitation system, without asking patients to buy expensive specialized equipment. We built a pipeline that streams AirPods motion data from two Macs into one system, tells the two pairs apart automatically by which one moves, and lets real movements control gameplay and clinical measurement at the same time. We're proud that the whole loop works: the patient moves, the AirPods and headset measure it, Alex coaches from those measurements, the physician watches it live and adjusts the plan, and the patient hears about the change from their coach. Beyond the technical side, we're proud that MiiHab addresses both the physical and emotional sides of recovery. It doesn't just gamify exercises; it gives patients a coach who is always there, friends to train with, and people who understand what they're going through. Most importantly, we built something inspired by our own families' experiences that we hope could make rehabilitation easier for others.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Building MiiHab taught us that healthcare technology has to go beyond technical functionality. A rehabilitation tool can collect accurate data and still fail patients if it isn't motivating, accessible, or enjoyable to use. We learned a tremendous amount about IMU sensor processing, Apple's CoreMotion framework, real-time data streaming, networking across devices, VR rendering on standalone headsets, and translating physical movement into interactive experiences in Unity. We also learned how to use AI responsibly in a clinical setting: the coach and the social features suggest but never act on their own. Alex can't change a plan, send a message, or share anything; those decisions stay with the patient and their physician. Our biggest takeaway was that recovery isn't just about restoring physical ability. It's also about rebuilding confidence, independence, connection, and the motivation to keep going.

sections.heading: What's next for MiiHab: Get Back in the Game
sections.text: Clinical validation: partner with physical therapists and rehabilitation centers to test our motion-tracking accuracy, evaluate the effectiveness of our VR games, and refine MiiHab with real patient feedback. Meta Horizon Store release: a private release channel so clinics can install MiiHab directly on patients' headsets. The headset's own microphone: so patients can talk to Alex without a Mac nearby. More movements and games: squats, reaching, and balance on the same two-AirPod engine. Clinician tools: alerts when a patient's pain or adherence changes, and plan suggestions from measured trends for the physician to approve.

title: Sky-C2
tagline: AR application that allows plane enthusiasts and air traffic control (ATC) workers to instantly identify aircrafts through Sky-C2's HUD. Aircraft data is generated using OSINT.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: In an airport control tower, identifying the aircraft outside the window is still surprisingly manual. Controllers look out the window, often with binoculars , then look down at a radar display , then cross-reference paper flight strips and lookup tables of callsigns and aircraft types to work out which dot is which plane. All of that happens in a job where every second of attention counts. Watching the constant traffic over Georgia Tech into Atlanta, the world's busiest airport, we asked: what if the information came to the controller's eyes instead of the other way around? Look at an aircraft and immediately see who it is, where it's going, and whether something is wrong, all in one view. That's Sky C2 : a command-and-control view of the sky.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Sky C2 consolidates the out-the-window view, the radar picture and the flight information into a single heads-up display. The prototype runs on a phone in a $10 Google Cardboard. Visual identification without binoculars or lookups. A compass "headband" places every aircraft at its real direction, with plane and helicopter icons. Center one and a card shows its callsign, airline, aircraft type, route, altitude, climb/descent rate, speed and distance. Situational awareness at a glance. Aircraft are color-coded: blinking red for emergencies (including squawk 7500/7600/7700), purple for medical flights, green for military, grey on the ground. A toggle hides ground traffic. Radar built into the view. A heading-up radar mini-map shows the whole airspace around you and rotates as you turn your head, so you don't need to look down at a separate screen. Hands-free queries. Say "Hey Grok" and ask about the aircraft you're looking at ("Where's that flight headed?", "Is that one climbing?"). Grok answers out loud using live data for that exact aircraft. A shared picture. A live view streams what the wearer sees, overlay included, to another screen, so a supervisor or teammate sees exactly what the controller sees.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We didn't use any computer vision. It's all sensors and geometry + OSINT. The headset knows where it is (GPS) and which way it's facing (compass plus gyroscope), and live ADS-B data says where every aircraft is. We flatten the problem to 2D. For each aircraft we compute the bearing from the viewer: $$\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\big(\sin\Delta\lambda\cos\varphi_2,\ \cos\varphi_1\sin\varphi_2 - \sin\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2\cos\Delta\lambda\big)$$ and the signed angle between that bearing and where the viewer is looking, $h$: $$\delta = \big((\theta - h + 540) \bmod 360\big) - 180$$ An aircraft is in view when $|\delta| \le \tfrac{\text{FOV}}{2}$ and "in focus" when $|\delta| \le 7.5^\circ$, a 15° cone. Its horizontal position comes from a pinhole-camera projection, so icons line up with the camera image: $$x = \frac{W}{2}\left(1 + \frac{\tan\delta}{\tan(\text{FOV}/2)}\right)$$ The stack: Web app (Vite + TypeScript): stereo camera view, orientation math, and a canvas HUD drawn identically in both eyes. Flight service (Python/FastAPI): pulls live aircraft from adsb.lol every second, normalizes them, computes bearings and distances, adds routes, and flags helicopters, emergencies, military and medical flights. Voice service (FastAPI + xAI): builds a prompt from the focused aircraft and asks Grok ( grok-4.3 , no reasoning, about 0.9 s per answer). The answer is spoken with Grok's text-to-speech voice , and wake-word detection runs in the browser. Live view: WebRTC streams the composited view peer-to-peer to a laptop, with one-click recording.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: "Heading" isn't where the camera points. The phone's compass reports the direction of its top edge , but in a headset the phone is sideways and we care about the rear camera . We compute the camera's direction from the full device rotation instead: $\mathbf{c} = -R\,\hat{z}$, so heading $= \operatorname{atan2}(c_E, c_N)$. We also correct for Atlanta's roughly 5° magnetic declination. Cardboard is unforgiving. A phone sitting slightly crooked in the headset gave us double vision, and cropping a 16:9 camera stream made everything look zoomed in. We added in-headset calibration (tilt, lens spacing, shift, zoom, field of view), controlled by taps and locked by default so a brushing cheek doesn't change anything. Voice cut people off. Chrome's speech recognition decides you've finished at the first short pause. We switched to waiting for 1.3 s of silence before sending the question. Rate limits. At 1-second updates, adsb.lol started rejecting requests (HTTP 429). GPS jitter made it worse by bypassing our cache. We snap positions to about a 1 km grid, back off when rate-limited, and always fall back to the last good data instead of showing an empty sky. Getting the data right. Helicopters without a type code were described as "slow-moving planes", and a "lifeguard" (medical priority) status looked like an emergency. We derive aircraft kind and status on the server and pass them to both the HUD and the AI.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Geometry and sensors can do a lot of what you'd assume needs computer vision. In a heads-up display, less is more: controllers need the right information in their line of sight, not more screens. Clear contracts between teammates (and their agents) let three people build in parallel with almost no merge conflicts. Always plan for the demo environment: an indoor demo mode, fallbacks for every API, and a live view so others can see inside the headset.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: Sky C2 is a prototype on consumer hardware. Phone compasses drift, especially indoors, and public ADS-B feeds aren't certified for operational use. Next steps would be a proper AR headset with precise head tracking, a surveyed tower position, the airport's own surveillance feeds, and placing labels at each aircraft's true height in the sky, not just its direction.

title: Strider
tagline: Exoskeleton to reduce the strain on your upper legs.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Over 25% of our elderly population has difficult or is completely unable to do activities necessary for everyday life, like climbing up stairs. As you get older, your muscles weaken greatly to the point where, by your 80s, up to 50% of your muscle mass is gone. We developed Strider to bring back the mobility and independence that being able to walk comfortably provides to those who might normally struggle.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Strider uses IMUs to detect different stages of your gait cycle to determine when to apply motor aid. Using its two motors, it can alleviate up to 40 lbs of force in total. The level of assistance can be adjusted, even to negative values, to allow for "progressive overload" of walking, allowing users to become more comfortable walking without aid.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The electronics used include an ESP32, MPU6050 IMUs, REV ION Brushless Motors, SPARK MAX motor controllers, a 3S LiPo battery, and a BEC. Most electronics are mounted on the rear, but the motors are mounted on the sides. The IMUs detect steps by comparing the angle and angular velocities. The ESP32 communicates with the motor controllers via PWM, which control the system's BLDC motors. The two motors are run through a 36:1 compound gearbox to increase the torque and decrease the maximum speed to a more reasonable speed relative to your leg's angular velocity. The battery directly powers the motor controllers and is run through the BEC to provide 5V to power the ESP32. All parts are either cut using a waterjet or 3D printed, to allow for rapid prototyping.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: CAN would have been the communication protocol of choice to direct the motor controllers, but the modules we had refused to send or receive signals. Being able to use CAN and receive motor feedback (position, velocity) would have allowed us to achieve more accurate control over the motors' torque and speed, which would've smoothed the motion. Tuning the motion in general was also so, so tedious.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: The system works! It does reduces the load when walking. Controlling it also doesn't need much getting used to, and does not require any external inputs besides swinging your legs.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: A lot about coding :) Neither of us are CS majors, so getting the system to work right probably took a lot more effort than it should've. It's also a very fine line between natural and unnatural motion, so getting it to feel good enough took a lot of trial and error to determine why it felt "off".

sections.heading: What's next for Strider
sections.text: The biggest avenue for improvement is in the actuators. A greater reduction would be very helpful to allow the motors to be more efficient in the RPM range that a leg moves in (~50 RPM, vs our current max speed of 150 RPM), and a integrated gearbox would also improve the size of the system. Using CAN instead of pure PWM would also help by pulling data from the motors to read the current draw and control the outputted torque. Implementing more robust electronics mounting would also help greatly.

title: Synesthesia
tagline: Visualization of sound in augmented reality to assist the deaf and hard of hearing.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We were inspired by Minecraft’s Sound Subtitles and many video games’ visual sound effects, which show players where important sounds are coming from through on-screen indicators. We realized that this same idea could be used outside gaming to help people who are Deaf or hard of hearing understand the sounds happening around them, and stay more connected to the people they are with.

sections.heading: What We Built
sections.text: Synesthesia is a prototype AR-style sound-awareness system that helps users “see” nearby sound. A siren can appear as a red-and-blue alert on the side it came from, a knock can become a focused pulse in front of the wearer, and a person saying a saved name can trigger a clear visual notification and vibration. By turning sounds into visual, spatial cues, Synesthesia can help users notice when someone is trying to get their attention and participate more confidently in conversations, homes, classrooms, and social spaces.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text: A Raspberry Pi Pico reads three microphone channels and estimates the rough direction of a sound based on relative sound levels. An optional rear-facing sensor provides an additional warning for sounds that may be behind the user. The Pico sends direction events over UART to an ESP32, which forwards them to the phone through Bluetooth Low Energy. On the phone, the web app uses the device microphone and an on-device YAMNet audio-classification model to recognize sounds such as alarms, sirens, horns, knocks, speech, dogs, doorbells, and more. The app pairs the recognized sound with a nearby direction event and displays an animated visual cue using color, shape, iconography, and motion. Users can also save their name and nicknames. Where supported, local speech recognition detects them and creates a more personal alert. The phone camera can provide a live background, creating an AR-style overlay that places sound cues into the user’s view of the real world.

sections.heading: Why AI Is Essential
sections.text: AI transforms raw sound into useful meaning. A simple volume sensor could show that something happened, but it could not distinguish a car horn from a knock, recognize speech, or identify when someone says the user’s name. Synesthesia uses on-device AI sound classification and local speech recognition to turn nearby audio into context-aware visual alerts. This is what makes the system useful for both safety awareness and everyday human connection.

sections.heading: Privacy
sections.text: Privacy was a major design goal. Audio is not transmitted over Bluetooth or uploaded to a server. The ESP32 sends only small direction packets, while sound classification and supported name recognition run locally on the phone.

sections.heading: Challenges We Faced
sections.text: The largest challenge was direction detection. The Pico does not perform true audio triangulation; it compares microphone loudness. This can be affected by echoes, microphone gain differences, distance, overlapping sounds, and background noise. To make the system more honest and useful, we added ambient-noise calibration, event thresholds, clipping detection, an ambiguity score, and a rear-only warning mode. When the system is unsure, it avoids claiming an exact direction. Another challenge was combining the sensor’s direction event with the phone’s sound classification. They do not share a clock, and multiple sounds can happen at once. We built a timing-based fusion layer that assigns a direction only when there is a clear nearby match. Otherwise, the app still shows the sound type without presenting a potentially incorrect bearing.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: Through this project, we learned about MicroPython firmware, analog microphone sensing, UART communication, Bluetooth Low Energy, browser hardware APIs, local machine-learning inference with MediaPipe and YAMNet, Canvas animation, and accessibility-focused interaction design. Most importantly, we learned that accessibility technology should communicate uncertainty clearly. Rather than treating every detection as certain, Synesthesia distinguishes between a confident cue, an unclear direction, and a possible sound behind the user.

sections.heading: Looking Forward
sections.text: Synesthesia is still a prototype, not a safety-certified navigation device. However, it demonstrates how a familiar idea from games can become a meaningful real-world accessibility tool. In the future, we hope to bring Synesthesia to AR glasses, using their microphones and displays to make sound awareness feel more immediate, immersive, and naturally integrated into everyday life.

title: TapChart
tagline: When Parkinson's symptoms mimic a stroke, missing context can mean misdiagnosis. TapChart puts a patient's motor baseline one NFC tap away, giving care teams a vital point of comparison.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: In an emergency, knowing what changed starts with knowing what is normal. For someone living with Parkinson's, tremors and movement difficulties can make that distinction harder. A clinician seeing a patient for the first time may have no record of their usual motor function, leaving a critical gap when evaluating a possible stroke. We built TapChart to make that context accessible. Our starting question was simple: What if a patient's motor baseline could be available with a single tap?

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: TapChart connects routine motor tracking with accessible clinical context. Patients complete a short, camera-based finger-tapping test to record their motor performance over time. TapChart turns those measurements into a personal baseline and charts that help care teams understand the patient's usual movement patterns. An NFC-linked patient profile gives doctors, EMTs, and other healthcare professionals a quick route to that information. When a patient presents with concerning symptoms, their care team can compare recent measurements with their history by tapping their tag. TapChart provides context for clinical assessment. It does not diagnose or rule out a stroke.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We brought together a patient-facing testing experience, movement analysis, stored motor measurements, and an NFC-accessible clinical view. Our movement-analysis pipeline extracts finger-tapping data from a short camera recording. We store the resulting measurements and summaries rather than the videos, associating each patient's records with a unique identifier. The patient experience focuses on completing tests and viewing trends. The healthcare professional experience focuses on quickly finding and interpreting the patient's baseline.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One of our biggest design challenges was serving two very different situations: a patient completing a routine test at home and a care professional seeking context under time pressure. We also had to think carefully about accessibility. An interface for people with motor difficulties needs clear instructions, readable text, large controls, and as few unnecessary steps as possible. Another challenge was defining what our prototype could responsibly communicate. Motor measurements can provide useful context, but translating them into a clinical conclusion requires evidence beyond a hackathon demo.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're proud of connecting a simple patient action to a concrete information gap in care. Instead of treating each test as an isolated result, TapChart builds a picture of the individual over time. Pairing that history with NFC access makes the information easier to reach when it matters. We also made privacy part of our design by keeping derived motor data instead of storing patient videos and ensuring NFC access was only available for licensed healthcare providers.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that collecting data is only part of the problem. Making it accessible, understandable, and relevant to the person using it is just as important. Designing for patients and care teams pushed us to consider accessibility, speed, privacy, and clinical limitations together. It also reinforced the importance of comparing a patient with their own history rather than assuming one baseline fits everyone.

sections.heading: What's next for TapChart
sections.text: Our next step is to gather feedback from people living with Parkinson's, neurologists, and emergency care professionals. We want to evaluate measurement consistency, improve the accessibility of the testing flow, and understand which trends are most useful to clinicians. We would also strengthen provider verification, patient consent, and access controls before any real-world deployment. We also hope to expand the baseline tracking to other degenerative diseases, making this data more available to HCPs for all sorts of conditions.

title: VIGIL: Assistive Eyewear with an Autonomous Aerial Scout
tagline: VIGIL reimagines assistive eyewear via an autonomous aerial scout, extending perception beyond the field of view to help visually impaired users navigate unfamiliar spaces more independently.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: If you cannot see, what happens when you lose something? Maddie, Parth's friend and neighbor, has to experience this struggle every day. Maddie is blind, so losing her phone or water bottle means searching a potentially hazardous room by touch or needing to wait for assistance. We wanted Maddie to be able to just ask where her wanted item is and find it immediately. Hence, we created VIGIL.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Through AirPods, you can ask VIGIL common questions, such as "where's my water bottle?" or "where's my friend Arthur?", and a DJI Tello searches the room, finds your requested item or person, then turns back to find you. After that, VIGIL walks you there with spoken directions, alongside two small pads on the glasses that guide you in the right direction.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The glasses are a regular pair of sunglasses with 3D-printed mounts for an ESP32-CAM, two time-of-flight sensors, and two servo pads on an Arduino Nano ESP32. A laptop runs everything else: Whisper for voice, YOLO and face ID for perception, and a scan-score-hop search that flies the Tello to the target. The drone's steering comes from 1,446 neurons copied from a real fruit fly's brain with standard wiring, while training a 34-number adapter around it with CMA-ES on Modal. Through trial and error of 500+ automated tests, we created VIGIL.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The hardest part was getting everything to hand off in real time, since any command needs to be processed through speech, detection, search, flight, and haptics. The Tello and the glasses each run their own Wi-Fi, so the laptop needs two adapters. The Tello's video running YOLO also wouldn't decode on our Macs at first. Lag was bad enough, so we adapted and integrated it into the simulation we trained in.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: In one weekend we went from an idea to glasses, voice control, and a drone that can find a bottle or a recognized person and guide you to it. The fly brain steers as well: 6.6° of steering error on held-out tests vs. 11.0° with the same neurons wired at random. This progress we made is what we’re most proud of. We're on track for a solution that could improve millions of lives.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Recognizing the bottle was the easy part. The hard part was turning what the drone sees into directions for the user, in relation to the environment. We also found that a real fly circuit steers about as well as a normal PID controller.

sections.heading: What's next for VIGIL: Assistive Eyewear with an Autonomous Aerial Scout
sections.text: Our next step is incorporating feedback from visually impaired individuals. Based on that feedback, we can optimize VIGIL through the eyes of the beholder. Ultimately, we strive to create more compact glasses that function in any environment, solving a problem that Maddie and all visually impaired users face.

title: Delta
tagline: Ctrl+Z for the physical world. An overhead camera version-controls anything you build by hand, so you can see what changed and roll back to the version that worked.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every hardware engineer has lived this. It's 2am, the circuit worked an hour ago, someone changed something, nobody remembers what. Software fixed this in 2005 using Git. Every change is tracked, every state is recoverable, and every "who broke what" answerable in seconds. But walk into any robotics lab or EE classroom today and the state of the art is phone photos, whiteboards, and Slack messages that say "sensor goes in port 3, GPIO is empty except pins 4 and 8." All of us work on hardware. One of us watched a $200 PCB fry because the last tester said "220 ohm" and the docs said "2.2k." We've all lost entire Saturdays trying to reverse-engineer our own prototypes because the last working state was in someone's phone. Software has version control. Hardware doesn't have anything. So we built Delta.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Delta is a Git-style version control system for physical work. An overhead camera watches your workbench. The second anything changes, a wire moves, a resistor goes in, a chip gets rotated, Delta logs a commit. Each commit has before/after photos, a bounding box on what moved, and an AI description of what the part actually is. Live component detection: every component the camera picks up: wires, LEDs, chips, sensors, breakouts, breadboards, jumper cables, screens, buzzers. Specific diffs: not "a resistor moved" but "10kΩ added at F-14 to F-18." Natural-language queries: ask it questions in English. "When did I add the voltage divider?" "What did my circuit look like 20 minutes ago?" "Who placed the STM32?" AI build instructions: hit a button and get a full Markdown build guide so anyone can rebuild the circuit from scratch. Rewind slider: scrub through every state your workbench has ever been in. Checkpoints and works/broken marks: tag states so you can always get back to the last known good version. Compare-two-points view: diff any two moments in time and get a restore checklist. Multi-user sessions: so a whole team knows who did what. GitHub for electronics.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We're running a NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Dev Kit on Ubuntu 22.04 (JetPack 6). A USB webcam at 1280×720 sits above the breadboard on a 3D-printed arm we CAD'd and printed on-site. The Jetson lives in a custom 3D-printed enclosure for thermal management and cable routing. The core architectural decision is that OpenCV handles detection and Perceptron Mk 1.5 handles naming . Each system is responsible for what it does best, which kept detection fast, consistent, and cost-efficient. Change detection pipeline: when a frame arrives, we wait about 1.5 seconds for the workbench to settle so we aren't capturing hands mid-motion. We then mask out 84 pixels (roughly one inch) on every edge of the frame to ignore activity at the periphery. The before and after frames are diffed per color channel with gain correction, which prevents overall lighting changes from registering as real changes. If all three color channels for a pixel scale by the same ratio (spread under 0.12), the pixel is classified as a shadow or glare rather than a new object. We clean the remaining changed pixels with a morphological open and run cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats to isolate each change into a distinct spot. A spot must be at least 46 pixels to be considered real. Camera noise tops out around 21 pixels and a resistor measures about 77 pixels, so 46 is the threshold that reliably separates signal from noise. If nothing qualifies, no API call is made. If more than half the frame has changed at once, the system falls back to the full-scene path and asks Perceptron to re-inventory the entire workbench. Naming the changes: only once a spot passes every gate do we call Perceptron Mk 1.5. We send a zoomed before/after crop of each spot. If the model can't name the component, we widen the crop and retry. If it still can't identify it, we save the entry as "Unidentified part" and move on. When a part is removed in one spot and added in another, those two events are merged into a single "moved" commit. Perceptron configuration: we run reasoning_effort: low , which averages ~5 seconds per call compared to 11-25 seconds on high, and found identical components in our testing. All output is structured JSON with x/y/w/h bounding boxes, with a 30 second timeout and automatic retries. We also use reference-frame diffing: the previous commit's JSON scene is passed back in as context, so the model updates its understanding of the workbench rather than describing it from scratch every call. Perceptron never decides whether something changed. That is strictly the pixel pipeline's job, and that separation is what made detection consistent. Database layer: the backing store is Supabase. Postgres tables hold projects, commits (with a pending → described state so the UI can display an in-progress indicator), checkpoints, capture sessions, and project questions. Supabase Storage holds the before and after JPEGs. Realtime subscriptions push updates to the website as commits are processed. Row Level Security scopes every read and write to project members, the Jetson authenticates with the secret key, and the browser only ever receives the publishable key. All commit IDs are generated client-side, which guarantees that a retried insert cannot create a duplicate row. Frontend: the website is built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, shadcn/ui, and TanStack React Query. It contains the timeline, the before/after viewer, the compare-two-points-in-time view, the works/broken marks and checkpoints, the session recap view, email-based invites, and the Ask AI page. Testing: we wrote 61 unittest cases on the backend covering the diff logic, stabilization, region detection, and a full integration flow using a fake Supabase and a fake AI. The frontend has 12 Vitest cases. A smoke_test.py script exercises the real end-to-end pipeline against the live stack.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Three hours lost to a locked SD card adapter. Pi Imager kept silently failing to flash the Jetson's microSD card, and we spent hours debugging software before realizing the adapter had a physical write-lock switch on the side that none of us had noticed. Once we flipped it, the flash completed on the first try. Perceptron hallucinating components. Our initial prompt was too permissive, and the model would confidently list an Arduino Uno on a completely empty breadboard. We rewrote the prompt from scratch, enforced a strict JSON Schema on every response, and switched to lossless image encoding. Most of the hallucinations disappeared. Thin wires and quarter-watt resistors slipping through detection. Switching image encoding from JPEG to PNG and restructuring the prompt to prioritize finding components over reading color bands significantly improved recall on small parts. Shadows and lighting changes triggering false commits. Early versions logged a commit every time someone walked past the fluorescent lights overhead. We solved it by diffing per color channel with gain correction. If all three channels scale by the same ratio, the change is a lighting shift rather than a new object, and the frame is discarded. Hands constantly in the frame. We built a motion-stability detector that waits for the workbench to settle before capturing a frame, which ensures Delta never commits a half-placed component. Tuning the thresholds. The 84-pixel border mask, the 46-pixel minimum spot size, the 50 percent global-change threshold, and the 1.5 second settle time were all tuned against measured camera noise on the actual hardware rather than chosen arbitrarily.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Delta works end to end. Place a resistor on the breadboard, and within a few seconds a new entry appears in the commit log that reads "Added 10kΩ resistor at F-14 to F-18," with a before/after diff and a bounding box on the exact spot that changed. The full Git metaphor, not a single feature. The system supports log, diff, rewind, user attribution, checkpoints, restore, natural-language Q&A, and automatic build-instruction generation. It functions as a complete tool, not a proof of concept. The hybrid architecture is the part we're most proud of. OpenCV handles the deterministic pixel work directly on the Jetson, which is fast, local, and free of API cost. Perceptron handles the tasks that require semantic understanding: naming components, reading fine text, and writing summaries. A 46-pixel resistor is detected locally without a single API call, and only then does Perceptron identify it as a 10kΩ resistor. Each component of the system is responsible for the work it is best suited to. The results back it up. The detection pipeline produced zero false positives across 100 still frames and correctly handled all eight resistor add, remove, and no-change test cases.
