Tested like a product. 61 unit and integration tests on the backend, 12 on the frontend, and a smoke test that exercises the full pipeline end to end.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Prompt engineering has effectively replaced fine-tuning for projects on this scale. The Perceptron team told us as much when we spoke with them at their booth, and our own iteration confirmed it. With a sufficiently capable base model, careful prompting combined with strict JSON schema enforcement outperforms custom training on any hackathon timescale. Reference-frame diffing is a cheat code. Providing a VLM with the previous frame's output as context dramatically improves consistency. Rather than asking the model to describe each scene from scratch, we give it the prior description and ask what has changed. The difference in output stability is substantial. Image encoding matters more than it appears. JPEG compression artifacts that are imperceptible to the human eye can significantly degrade a VLM's recall on small objects. Switching to lossless PNG encoding noticeably improved detection of thin wires and quarter-watt resistors, and the additional bandwidth cost was negligible. Let the pixels decide, let the model describe. Detection accuracy stabilized the moment we stopped asking the model whether something had changed and began using it solely to identify what the pixel-level pipeline had already isolated.

sections.heading: What's next for Delta
sections.text: Live correction mode: Delta flags wiring mistakes in real time, catching errors while the circuit is still on the breadboard rather than after a board has been damaged. PCB mode: extending the system from breadboards to soldered boards and populated PCBs. Deployment across UW engineering teams: rolling Delta out to Husky Robotics, ARUW, and Formula Motorsports as a shared tool for lab documentation and handoffs. Industrial assembly: expanding beyond electronics to version-control any physical assembly process on a factory or manufacturing floor. Mobile client: a phone app so you can view commits, run queries, and watch the live feed without being at a laptop.

title: Brawlmegle
tagline: Omegle was for talking to strangers. Omoggle was for mogging them. Now there’s Brawlmegle: create your fighter and punch, block, and dodge your way through camera-powered battles with friends.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The developers of this project grew up on Wii Sports boxing and gesturing in front of Xbox Kinect. Next came VR boxing but to us, it felt like it was missing something. With Brawlmegle, we mixed old with new, added the omph which VR Boxing lacks, the effect and impact that classic fighting games, Street Fighter and Tekken, gives.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Brawlmegle is a webcam fighting game where you fight as yourself: Get scanned: stand in front of your laptop camera, and in about 40 seconds our own GPU server turns you into a stylized, rigged 3D fighter. You can even watch it form live. Throw hands: punch, hook, uppercut, block, duck, dodge, kick. The camera reads what you meant to do, and the fight engine decides what actually happens in order to create an awesome strategic and visual experience. And of course it has the flashy arcade stuff we all love like hero entrances, VS screens, and even live AI commentary powered by ElevenLabs.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The game is React, TypeScript, and Three.js in the browser, so there's nothing to install. Body tracking happens via Google's MediaPipe and runs in a Web Worker at around 30 frames per second. Our secret sauce is the intent reader. Instead of mapping your skeleton onto the model, it watches your motion and decides "that was a right hook". The game is online peer-to-peer via WebRTC, with a small matchmaking server and relay hosted on a tiny AWS EC2 instance. The fight engine runs on one of the laptops: it acts as the referee, and the other one just mirrors it and collects input from the second player. For the fighters, we built our own "forge": GPT writes your fighter's backstory and draws a character sheet from your scan. TRELLIS.2, an open-source 3D model we run on our own AWS GPU, sculpts it into a 3D fighter in seconds. Our own Blender auto-rigger gives it a skeleton so it can actually fight. A last step paints your face back on, so it looks a little more recognizable. We were also fortunate to have a talented Blender wizard on our team, who built an incredible Mount Rainier arena so you're fighting right here in the PNW.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The hardest challenge was the intent reader. We kept having issues with fake moves, wrong moves, and even huge delays, which defeated the dream of building something punchy. But as we kept recording fights and running tests, we were able to tune a config system that we believe got to a point where the gameplay is actually fun. The other big one was the 3D fighters. Our 3D generation provider ran out of credits mid-hackathon, so we spun up our own GPU server, which ended up faster. Then the models came out hollow, so dresses and hoodies broke the rigging, and we had to write our own rig checker and fixes until every fighter worked.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Witnessing going from webcam scan to a playable 3D version of yourself in under a minute never gets old. Real fighting-game feel from just a camera: combos, counters, guard breaks Omegle-style matchmaking with live cameras, fully peer-to-peer An AI live commentator that's actually aware of what's going on in the game.

title: Codegraph
tagline: Much code is now written by AI, so developers & beginners often don't understand how their codebase is structured. Existing code-to-graph tools build graphs for AIs to consume. This one is for humans.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: With most code nowadays being AI generated, it's easy for developers to lose understanding of their code. Additionally, long, top-down files of code and codebases with many connecting files can be overwhelming to navigate, especially for beginners. Codegraph aims to solve this problem by providing a better visual experience for fully understanding your codebase.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Codegraph is a VS Code extension that takes a C or C++ folder and lays out the header files, c files, classes, structs, variables, etc. in a graph format. Arrows connect these nodes to show the relationships between files and elements (whether something is a caller, callee, inherits, overrides, etc.). An AI summary of each node is also generated based when a node is clicked, explaining the node's purpose in the context of the program. An 'Ask AI' panel is also available, which can highlight specific affected nodes and trace through the specific nodes in the program in response to questions. For each node, you can also see how big of a risk changing the node in various ways (renaming, deleting, changing behavior, etc.) would have on other methods, and will calculate a risk score for these other methods.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built the graph using the Cytoscape.js library and the cytoscape-elk extension for the library. The AI is built on VS Code's Language Model API, which calls GitHub Copilot Chat or GPT-4o.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Our main challenge was with merging code and overall keeping a clean codebase.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud of getting the graph view to display correctly, even for large and complex C files, and for the AI's ability to understand the codebase and provide targeted, specific help to the user when prompted.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned about development in TypeScript, JavaScript, and the cytoscape library, which we previously had no experience with.

sections.heading: What's next for Codegraph
sections.text: We hope to expand Codegraph to different programming languages, and pick up similar nuances with those languages as we've done with C/C++.

title: Drone Perceptron Relief System
tagline: Multi-drone disaster relief: Perceptron classification model maps live drone footage of moving people to 2D, feeding an emergency relief optimization algorithm (supply-drop vs search vs resupply.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: PLEASE WATCH VID ON 0.75x speed, we sped it up to meet the time criteria. Either way it sounds funny :) Current natural disaster drone relief systems are manual, prone to error in high stress conditions, and hard to standardize due to design flaws and provides poor emergency relief response.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Provides an optimal semi-automatic drone system leveraging live data -> real decisions -> real impact loop. Feeds a drone system responding to a natural disaster.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Drones provide sensor telemetry + footage Perceptron Model classifies people AND estimates distance! Writes time-series data to TigerData Database Renders a 2D map of people in need Feeds Multi-variable optimization algorithm (~8x faster median response over brute force on benchmarks) to decide Next Drone Decision Drone decision feeds back to #1

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: the chronological syncing of the cameras it tough, adding confidence intervals of position is difficult, diluting 3d position of cameras to 2d map is tough, optimization alg is advanced and benchmarking on REAL DATA is tough to nail down.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Shipping an MVP, deriving an optimal alg w latency constraints.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: It is important to build a product that is not simply an instance of the tool (e.g. our first idea we spent ~3+hrs on was an allergen contamination tracker for restaurants) but rather adds technical complexity. We don't want to fall into the trap of a "GPT-wrapper"-esque idea.

sections.heading: What's next for Drone Perceptron Relief System
sections.text: Semi-automatic -> fully automatic using Computer Vision similar to Zoox/Waymo cars. Infrastructure for scalable system

title: dump
tagline: Dump your event photos in one place, find every shot you’re in, and let it all disappear when the weekend’s over.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every group event we go to ends the same way. Someone says "send me those pics," our group chat fills with half the photos, a few of us AirDrop to each other, and the best shot of us lives forever on someone else's camera roll. Google Drive requires everyone to have enough space in their Drive to upload pictures (shoutout Emily), not everyone in our friend group has an iPhone so we can't use a shared album (shoutout Albert 6 months ago), and no one wants to download a separate app (all of us tbh). And even when we do manage to collect everything, finding the photos we're actually in means scrolling through hundreds of blurry crowd shots. We wanted something as easy as tossing photos into a bin. Scan a code, dump our pictures, find ourselves, and let the whole thing disappear after the weekend. That became dump , and each event room is a dumpster .

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: dump is our mobile web app for collecting photos and videos from everyone at an event, with nothing to install and no account to make. Open a dumpster in seconds. We can create one from the site or by texting our iMessage line. We get a link and QR code to share, plus a one-tap Copy Dumpster Link button. Drop everything in. Our friends upload photos and videos straight from their phone's browser. If the signal drops, the upload retries on its own. Find ourselves. We sign in with a name and a quick selfie. Every person in the dumpster shows up in a face gallery, and tapping a face shows only the photos and videos they're in. Search anything. One search bar covers objects, text written in photos, places, and words spoken in videos. We can also tap Ask the dump to describe what we're looking for in plain words. Get texted when we show up. We can opt in to an iMessage when new photos of us land or when someone says our name in a video. Moments and a map. Shots taken around the same time and place are bundled into moments and pinned on a map. Duplicate uploads are hidden automatically. Stickers. We can cut a person or object out of any shot and add it to the dumpster's sticker pack for iMessage. The stage. A live view for a TV or projector at the venue that fills up as photos come in. The Dumpster Fire. We can react with any emoji, but our custom Dumpster Fire reaction powers a leaderboard of the event's funniest moments, ranked entirely by our group's taps. Gone when it's over. Each dumpster burns after 24, 48, or 72 hours, and everything in it is deleted. Our dumpsters have no hosts or admins. Everyone has the same power, including the ability to delete any photo or video.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Frontend. We built dump as a Next.js 15 app with Tailwind CSS, installable as a PWA. Dumpster links. There are no accounts. Each dumpster gets a long random id that can't be guessed, so the link is the lock. Upload pipeline. A background worker processes every upload: it strips camera metadata, makes web-friendly versions, flags duplicates, and runs our models before the shot appears for everyone. AI models. Perceptron is our image understanding service. When someone uploads a photo, the background worker sends it a processed copy and gets back a caption, scene tags, visible objects, text in the image, and the locations of faces. We use those results to organize and search photos. InsightFace detects and groups faces for the people gallery and selfie matching. Selfies are thrown away after sign-in, and face data never reaches a browser. faster-whisper transcribes videos so spoken words are searchable. BiRefNet cuts out stickers on our own server. Backboard powers Ask the dump and replies to free-form iMessage questions. It answers using the dumpster's photo captions, tags, detected objects, visible text, and video transcripts. Each dumpster gets its own Backboard assistant, which is deleted when the dumpster burns. Face vectors and phone numbers are never sent to it. Messaging (Photon 2.0). Photon connects dump to iMessage. From our homepage, we enter a phone number, get assigned a line, and Messages opens with a create command ready to send. From there, Photon: Starts group dumpsters from a text conversation, either with a fixed command like create dumpster "Mt. Si Hike" 48h or a casual message like "open one for the hike, two days," which Backboard interprets. Handles replies in the same conversation, plus sign-in messages using a one-time code that expires in ten minutes and only works from the number it was sent to. Sends opt-in alerts: "new photos of you" (batched about every 90 seconds so we're not spammed), a text when someone says our name in a video, and one warning about two hours before the dumpster burns, with the link. Uses an idempotency key on every send so a retry never double-texts, and never stores a sender's number on the dumpster or passes it to Backboard. Dumpster Fire ranking. Users can react to each photo with emojis, including our special “dumpster fire”, creating our dumpster fire leaderboard. Shots are ranked by their Dumpster Fire count, with other reactions only as a tiebreak. Data and infrastructure. MongoDB holds what the app needs to work right now: dumpsters, guests, media records, face groups, stickers, reactions, and expiration times. Every collection has automatic expiration, so data is deleted even if our worker goes down. TigerData records events about that activity: uploads, views, reactions, and cleanup runs. It powers our uploads-per-minute stats and the cleanup audit trail. Cloudflare R2 stores the photos and videos. Vultr hosts our production backend on a single server running a Docker Compose stack: the Next.js website, the background worker that processes uploads, sends alerts, and burns expired dumpsters, our private face matching service, and our speech transcription service. Caddy sits in front to handle HTTPS, accept uploads up to 150MB, and keep the live photo stream flowing without buffering. The face and transcription services have no public port, so only our own app can reach them. We deploy updates with Docker Compose and run health checks to confirm the site and every service come back up. Domain. We got dumpster.photo through the MLH GoDaddy link, which redirected us to Porkbun to register it. We then pointed it to Cloudflare to manage DNS. Privacy and AI auditing (VEYZL). Our privacy rules are checked on every pull request. The build fails if retention isn't 24/48/72 hours, if data could outlive its dumpster, if face data could reach the browser, or if any creator or uploader identity is stored. We also pointed VEYZL's audits at our public vision endpoint. Based on what i

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Getting VEYZL to reach our model. At first, VEYZL couldn't find or connect to our AI endpoint, so its early audits couldn't test it properly. Once it could, it flagged answers that made unsupported claims, missed instructions, or handled sensitive information poorly. A misleading "PII leak." One flagged leak turned out to be a wording issue, not a real leak. The model hadn't revealed anyone's details, but it said it had no customer contacts instead of explicitly refusing the request. VEYZL also wanted a more helpful answer when an identity check couldn't be verified from the image. After we reworked the endpoint, a later audit passed those probes, though it still saw a few intermittent model errors. Anonymous but notifiable. We never record who creates a dumpster or uploads a shot, but face alerts still need a selfie and phone number. Keeping that opt-in data scoped to one dumpster and deleted with it took careful design. Deletion that actually deletes. Our files, records, face data, and Backboard assistants live in different places, so we built a cleanup worker with database-level expiration as a backstop. Faces that drift. The same person at a different angle kept showing up as a new person until we started keeping multiple examples per face. Never blocking on AI. We made every model optional, so photos still publish even if one goes down. Layering visuals over UI. Our bounding boxes initially covered labels and buttons until we enforced a strict layering order. Writing for our users, not for ourselves as engineers. We rewrote our copy so it describes what dump does, not how it works.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Going from scanning a QR code to uploading photos takes seconds, with nothing to download. Our single search bar finds a face, an object, a word on a banner, or a name said in a video. Stickers are made on our own server, so photos aren't sent anywhere to create them. Our leaderboard is fully community-driven, so the Dumpster Fire reflects what our group found funny. Our vision endpoint went from failing VEYZL's safety probes to passing them before submission. We built a visual identity that feels like ours rather than a template. We integrated Perceptron, Photon, VEYZL, MongoDB, Vultr, Backboard, and TigerData into one coherent product in a single weekend, live at our own domain.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: How to build a background media pipeline that keeps our UI fast while heavy AI work happens behind the scenes. That privacy is easier to design from the start than to bolt on. Not collecting host or uploader identity made many later decisions simpler. That not leaking data isn't enough. A safe AI answer also needs to refuse clearly and explain what's missing, or it still reads as a failure. How to combine hosted and self-hosted models, and when keeping data on our own machines is worth it. How much design restraint matters: removing jargon and generic UI patterns made our app feel more human.

sections.heading: What's next for dump
sections.text: Recap texts: sending a highlight digest of the Dumpster Fire winners before the dumpster burns. Export before expiry: letting each of us save our own photos in one tap before the dumpster disappears. Steadier model responses: tracking down the intermittent errors from VEYZL's latest audit.

title: Formly - the secure, fast form filler
tagline: Formly is Stripe for forms: click “Fill with Formly,” connect accounts like Google Drive, and Formly fills the business’s blank form for you. They get a finished form; your raw data stays private.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every signup, application and checkout asks for the same things: your name, address, ID, income, car, emergency contact. We type them again and again, often from documents we already have sitting in Google Drive or iCloud. Browser autofill only covers a handful of basic fields and stops at anything like an SSN, a driver's license number or a VIN. Businesses feel it too, because every extra minute on a long form is a chance for someone to give up. We wanted something like Stripe Checkout, but for forms: one button a business can drop in, that fills the whole form from the user's own data, while the user stays in control of exactly what gets shared.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: A business adds a Fill with Formly button to its form. When you press it, a secure Formly window opens, and: You connect your data once. Upload files (PDFs, photos, Word docs, text, zip folders), or sign in with Google or iCloud to pull in your profile, contacts, email receipts, Drive or iCloud Drive documents, Apple Wallet and your Health Medical ID. Formly builds your digital twin. It reads everything and keeps a private, organized profile of the facts forms ask for, each one linked back to the file it came from. You can edit any fact or mark it as never shared. Formly fills the form. It matches your twin to the business's questions and fills what it can. If something isn't in your data, it leaves the field blank instead of guessing. You review and approve. Every answer shows where it came from. Sensitive details like your SSN, IDs and card numbers need an explicit yes, and you choose between being asked or sharing automatically. The business gets only the approved answers. Your files never leave Formly. It also handles open-ended questions. On a job application, it drafts short answers in your own voice from your actual resume, and it refuses to make up experience you don't have. To show it working, we built four realistic demo forms styled after the real businesses: a T-Mobile switch and plan signup, a SpaceXAI job application, a Chase Freedom Unlimited card application and a California DMV vehicle title and registration form. Nine made-up people, each with full documents, a resume, and Google and iCloud data, can fill every field on every one of them.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: App: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS 4, with SQLite for local storage of sources, the twin, permissions and fill sessions. Gemini API: Gemini does all of Formly's reading and writing, through Google's @google/genai SDK. Reading files: we send PDFs and photos (like a driver's license) straight to Gemini as inline files, and it transcribes every detail into text. Word files are converted locally, with no AI call needed. Building the twin: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite merges all of a person's sources into one organized profile, and in parallel pulls out typed key facts, each tagged with its source and how sensitive it is. Filling forms: every fill uses Gemini's structured output. We give it a JSON schema, so it can only return a value, a source and a confidence for fields that actually exist on the form. Writing short answers: Gemini 3.5 Flash writes these, since writing quality matters more there than speed. Speed and reliability: we run Gemini with low thinking, which made fills several times faster with the same accuracy on these tasks. If a model is overloaded or rate limited, the request automatically retries on the next Gemini model. Test data: Gemini also generated the realistic email inboxes for our synthetic test people. Backup: with an Anthropic key set, every request can run on Claude instead, using the same prompts. Pipeline: files become text, which then becomes the digital twin. Gemini API looks at the form's fields and fills it in with the Digital Twin's information. Answer Validity: before writing a short answer, the model must quote the exact facts it will use. Code then checks those quotes against the facts in our Digital Twin, and does not let the answer go through if they are not matching. Button: it opens a popup, and results come back through postMessage . If popups are blocked it falls back to a same-page redirect, and it also checks the session in the background, so a result always arrives. Testing: we built a scored test set of synthetic people based on NVIDIA's Nemotron-Personas-USA. Each has a realistic email inbox with traps, such as a relative's details and a gift shipped to someone else. We also used T-Mobile's synthetic data, and you can switch between users within the app. https://github.com/salvobonsma/DubHacks2026

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Getting gigabytes of data into a form, fast. A person's data can run to gigabytes of photos, PDFs, documents and email, and nobody will wait minutes for a form. Sending all of it to a model on every fill would be slow and expensive. So Formly does the heavy reading once, when you connect your data: Gemini transcribes each file a single time and distills everything into a compact digital twin. A fill then only sends that small profile and the form's field list, so it comes back in a few seconds. Building the twin and filling the form each run two Gemini calls in parallel, and low thinking plus structured output kept every call short. Made-up answers. Sometimes it would hallucinate information, so we implemented a fact checking algorithm. Missing data. Google sync first skipped key documents, so some important details were never synced to the Digital Twin Free tier limits. We added automatic fallbacks between Gemini models.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: From one Google or iCloud connection, Formly fills every field on all four demo forms. On our synthetic test set, it got 107 of 108 field checks right. When the data doesn't support an answer, including a written one, Formly leaves it blank. By default, SSNs, IDs and card numbers always ask first, while basic details fill without interruptions. The demo forms look and behave like the real T-Mobile, SpaceXAI, Chase and DMV flows.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Teaching Formly not to answer was difficult. Sometimes we needed no answer, and it would give us hallucinated information. Reading data once, up front, matters more for speed than faster model calls.

sections.heading: What's next for Formly - the secure, fast form filler
sections.text: Real Google and Apple sign-in, plus banks and more data sources. An SDK and browser extension so Formly works on any form. Encrypting the digital twin on your device.

title: Kill-Switch
tagline: Fraud Detection that works for everyone.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1xO3yWOgs9F3zxNz_ngWg5tXuZcaib2phHMvyOp1iq4I/edit?slide=id.h36e91ee2f05074da_0_641#slide=id.h36e91ee2f05074da_0_641 Americans aged 60 and older reported a staggering $7.7 billion in losses to internet-enabled fraud alone in 2025 Fraud detection fails those with cognitive, visual, hearing, and motor disabilities. These groups are inherently more susceptible to scams or risky websites These groups struggle to seek help if they end up in such a situation These groups are vulnerable to psychological manipulation Fraud is a big problem. Online shopping platforms are plagued with listings containing misleading information and counterfeit imitations. It is easy to make a listing look real with a convincing description, pictures of the real item, and a price tag that feels like a bargain, when in reality, an inferior product is waiting to be shipped. While there are some software protections in place, current fraud detection relies on screen-based UI, which inherently fails users with visual impairments, motor limitations, cognitive decline, or other users with disabilities. We set out to make fraud detection and safe online shopping more accessible to everyone. We kept three primary motivators in mind: We need solutions that bypass digital literacy barriers- translating risk into real physical cues that are universal to everyone. Current fraud detection relies on screen-based UI, which inherently fails users with visual impairments, motor limitations, cognitive decline, or other users with disabilities (for example CAPTCHAs) who can’t understand what’s being shown to them For those who are homebound, elderly, or disabled, the physical notify button built in alerts caregivers to potentially dangerous situations For example, say a user clicks on a website, and Google displays an error message about the site being suspicious or potentially dangerous. If the user has some form of impairment that makes it difficult to process this, they may not be stopped and proceed to the risk. Our system would prevent this by visually flagging the site as dangerous.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our system accomplishes the above goals in several ways: Visual Signals via LEDs- we have three LED lights corresponding to different levels of risk. We scan what is currently on the user's screen, asking AI to assess whether or not it should be trusted, and we convert that to a risk score that triggers the physical signal. In addition, we scan the user's current URL via a APIVoid service to get a risk score. Our ESP32 is able to connect to Wifi, which allows us to make API calls from it. Audio signals via a buzzer- we play buzzer noises in addition to the visual signals to correspond to different risk levels. The higher the risk, the more intense and noticeable the signal is. Visual, plaintext cues - we display a specific, simple message for each risk level explaining whether or not the site is safe, suspicious, or risky A "kill-switch"- there is a kill switch button built into the circuit that when pressed, notifies a trusted caregiver or loved one that the user has identified a high-risk situation and they should consider intervening. We use Twilio, a texting service, to accomplish this. This also serves as an acknowledgement by the user that they understand the high-risk activity was detected.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: This project was built using components we had from previous hardware classes here at UW, as well as integrations with C, Python, and Gemini API. We utilized FreeRTOS to simultaneously run the LED, LCD, buzzer, URL, and various other parts of the software. The implementation is currently on a breadboard (as this is all we have access to), as its where all the hardware components live. We pass data back and forth between Python and C through a COM port.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Seeing as we used components we received free from UW hardware classes, this meant we were limited in the types/number of components we have. Thus, our implementation here looks far more trivial than what we would expect it to look like should it become a genuine product. This also means that we were not able to implement as many features as robustly as we would have liked. We also ran into issues with connecting C, Python, and Hardware simultaneously. It was our first time working with the Gemini API and APIvoid, so they required some troubleshooting to work. Given that we were working with multiple programming languages, APIs, and a texting service, this was rather ambitious for us, so there were a lot of minor bugs/quirks to work through to integrate all these services together.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are overall proud of our project. We were in this for the fun of building another hardware project together, and extending our knowledge of how to interface with many different components. Even if it isn't as software-based or as aesthetically pleasing as other submissions we are proud of how much thought went into it and how much care went into the idea.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned how to interface higher level languages (python) with our ESP32, which we didn't know how to do before. We also learned how to connect our hardware to WiFi, and use that to make API calls directly on the hardware chip itself.

sections.heading: What's next for Kill-Switch
sections.text: We're interested in reducing fraud with the device's capabilities, and given more advanced hardware components we believe we can. Our ideal future plans include: Procuring a larger LCD/LED scree, where we can display a clear price breakdown for any item found online, to prevent people from missing hidden fees or shady UI elements Automatic screen capturing/URL detection, so the user does not have to press a button to have their screen analyzed Better identification for large transfers of money or large purchases- require authorization from a caregiver before such actions Extend to scan emails to check for fraud- check for legitimacy

title: KO.rbit
tagline: Fly 31,000 real stars, then KO your rival on Mars

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We wanted the lightsaber duel everyone acts out in the living room, with your real body in the fight and a real planet under your feet. We also wanted space to be real : a universe built from real catalogs, and fights on terrain NASA actually measured. And we wanted to see how far we could get in just 24 hours using AI tools working beside us.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: KO.rbit is a real universe to explore and a full-body saber duel to fight in. Your laptop shows the world and tracks your body. Your iPhone is your lightsaber using its internal gyroscope. Explore a real universe of 31,266 objects: stars, exoplanets, galaxies, planets, satellites, asteroids, comets and SpaceX spacecraft. Fly freely, search every object, jump straight to it and read its fact card. Find the Tesla Roadster, Europa Clipper, Psyche and Hera in their orbits around the Sun. Crew Dragon and Cargo Dragon are docked at the ISS. Speed up the orbits with a 1x / 60x / 600x time-lapse . Ask LYRA to guide you, and see where other pilots are in space. Commission a pilot, jump into a 3D cockpit and challenge a rival. Planetary roulette rolls Mars or Neptune, 50/50 , then a travel cinematic flies you in. Fight with your body. MediaPipe tracks your pose. Scan a QR code, hold to ignite your phone saber, aim by moving the phone, and swipe to step around your rival. Relive the KO. If you opt in, a Perceptron-powered cinematic replay recuts the fight and ends on the finishing blow.

sections.heading: Real space data
sections.text: Exploration catalogs (counted from the JSON files on main ): Stars, 24,835 (460 named): HYG Database v4.1 (Astronexus, CC BY-SA 4.0). Everything within 100 pc, plus named stars out to 3,000 pc. Exoplanets, 5,301 around 3,894 host stars: NASA Exoplanet Archive, PSCompPars table via TAP. Galaxies, 1,034: Gil de Paz et al., GALEX Ultraviolet Atlas, via NASA/IPAC NED. Planets and the Moon, 9: NASA Planetary Fact Sheets. Satellites, 20: the ISS and Hubble (CelesTrak) plus 18 Starlinks (TLEs from a community mirror). Small bodies, 60: 42 asteroids and 18 comets from the NASA/JPL Small-Body Database API. SpaceX spacecraft, 7: Crew Dragon, Cargo Dragon and TESS from CelesTrak, plus four heliocentric craft (Tesla Roadster, Europa Clipper, Psyche, Hera) from JPL Horizons orbital elements. SpaceX fleet facts: vehicles, boosters, capsules and Starship flights from Launch Library 2 . Arena terrain. Mars: real NASA MOLA elevation data for Jezero Crater. It's a 2.5° (about 148 km) crop of the PDS product MGS-M-MOLA-5-MEGDR-L3-V1.0 , resampled to 256 × 256. You fight on the actual heightmap (vertically exaggerated 2.6×). Neptune: stats come from NASA's fact sheet: 11.2 m/s² gravity, 72 K, winds from 0 to 580 m/s, a 16.11 h day. The fight floor is a fictional station platform , and the clouds are procedural. Gravity is shown for each world. It doesn't change combat yet. How we imported it. Python importers (such as crop_mola.py and import-spacex.py ) pull each source at build time. A provenance manifest records SHA-256 hashes and counts, and ATTRIBUTION.md plus an in-game credits dialog list every source. About orbits: satellites and spacecraft use a two-body Kepler solver on real orbital elements from a dated 2026-10-18 snapshot . Not live tracking or SGP4, and satellite altitudes are scaled for visibility.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Authoritative Node + Socket.IO server. It owns the lobby, health and every hit. Camera detections are commands , not proof. The laptop streams pose and the phone streams aim, and a 33 ms tick with 10 substeps checks blade against body, so fast swings can't slip through a guard. Combat rules: 100 health, 15 damage per hit, 0.65 m knockback . Stamina 100: in/out steps cost 14, sidestep dodges cost 24, regen is 28/s after a 700 ms delay, and an empty bar leaves you winded until 40. Guards: a swing within 30° of a held guard breaks it and stuns the defender for 700 ms . After a clash, the defender can't swing back for 250 ms . 3 s countdown , rematch (round resets, devices stay paired), forfeits after a 15 s reconnect grace, and a draw if both players drop. Three.js renders the cockpit, both arenas and the explore universe. Perceptron replay: an opt-in local webcam clip (up to 45 s) with separate upload consent. Director cuts (orbit, low, overhead) add speed ramps, sparks and impact holds, ending on the KO. Audio: a scene-aware CC0 soundtrack, plus a phone hum that follows swing speed. Polish branch: Ally's hit VFX (sparks, shockwave, victory camera) lives on our saturn branch and isn't on main yet. Tech stack Client : React 19, TypeScript, Vite, React Three Fiber, Three.js Body and saber : MediaPipe Pose on the laptop, iPhone gyroscopic sensors as the blade, QR pairing Server : Node.js, Socket.IO. The server owns health, stamina, guard breaks, and every hit AI : Grok Voice for live LYRA, Grok text-to-speech for duel cues, Grok Imagine for her hologram, Grok Bot for research, design, and sound, Perceptron Mk1.5 for the KO replay Data : NASA, JPL, CelesTrak, and HYG catalogs, imported at build time with SHA-256 provenance

sections.heading: Tracks targeted
sections.text: SpaceXAI Grok Voice (Grok API): powers LYRA, our live voice copilot. She can read the match but can't change it. Your own AI companion that walks and guides you through the game, talks to you, answers questions, and narrates. Grok Imagine: built the LYRA you see. We generated portrait options, picked the hologram, and used Imagine for her idle animation. Grok Bot: a whole crew: not one chatbot. Agents ran all weekend beside the programmers. They researched datasets and UI, rated plans, wrote build prompts, designed the brand, storyboarded victory and defeat, redesigned saber setup, curated the sound pack, synthesized jump and landing sounds, audited branches, and drafted this writeup. We wrote the game while they kept research, sound, and previews moving so coding never stopped Cursor: Agent sessions built the camera pipeline, phone saber, 3D arena, catalog explorer, LYRA, and the replay director. Cloud agents audited the repo so planning and code stayed on the same tree Real space datasets: NASA, JPL, CelesTrak and HYG catalogs power all of exploration (31,266 stars, exoplanets, galaxies, planets, satellites, Starlinks and the Tesla Roadster) plus our Mars arena, built on real NASA elevation data. Perceptron A full replay path, not a caption on a video. Opt in and the laptop records a silent clip only while you are fighting, capped at 45 seconds. The arena motion is kept locally too, so the knockout still exists after that cap. Upload is a second consent, and only for the match you just finished. Perceptron Mk1.5 returns the earlier scenes: time ranges, captions, and boxes that follow the player. The game turns those into the cut, with new cameras, slow motion, and sparks. The last shot is always the server-confirmed finishing blow, so the model cannot invent the winner. Proved on the live API with a synthetic silent clip: one movement interval and eight timestamped boxes. MediaPipe tracks the body during the fight and is not this model. This video can be uploaded and saved to the computer

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Two sabers diverged. One line paired body tracking with phone aim, and another made a camera-slash projectile on an older movement grid. We converged on the phone saber, but the rebrand branch still sits on the old line. The contracts drifted apart. Our shared contracts package stayed empty, so every branch edited the server's types directly, and the lines stopped being wire-compatible. The phone gyro needs HTTPS. iOS gates motion data behind secure pages and a permission tap, so we ran self-signed certs and Cloudflare/ngrok tunnels whose hostnames kept changing. Mid-hack pivot from a gesture-based rock and blaster duel to the phone saber. Originally was supposed to be real world position tracking computer vision battle game The replay failed quietly. Stopping the recorder without a flush saved an empty file, and black bars on the result screen made a good take look frozen. Fixing that was recorder engineering plus a new result layout, not a one-line API call.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A two-device, full-body duel where the server decides every hit, with real stamina, guard breaks and rematches. 31,266 real objects from public NASA, JPL, CelesTrak and community catalogs, with SHA-256 provenance and in-game credits. A Mars arena on actual NASA MOLA Jezero terrain . A cinematic KO replay with opt-in recording and separate upload consent. An AI crew next to the coders : research, previews and audio happened in parallel while we shipped code. Favorite moment was the first landed hit between two phones after half the hackathon struggling

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Treating camera input as a request made fights fairer and easier to debug. Agree on shared contracts in hour one. Real data needs provenance. Hashes and attribution make it trustworthy. Short-lived tokens and read-only tools keep an AI copilot safe, and firm shared rules keep an AI crew aligned.

sections.heading: What's next for KO.rbit
sections.text: Gravity that matters: make Mars and Neptune gravity change how combat feels. Replay QA on a full recorded duel and phone browsers. Shared contracts and a full two-laptop, two-phone test pass. -** Expand with even more data** **Improve fighting mechanics and add what we wanted in the beginning, blasters, force pushing, terrain manipulation Overall this is the project we are the most proud of creating ever so we hope everyone likes it

title: Lapse
tagline: A local smart rewards optimizer that maximizes savings and minimizes spending by stacking credit card and loyalty benefits, prioritizing expiring offers, and notifying you of available rewards online

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Between credit cards, memberships, and loyalty programs, we all collect benefits faster than we use them. Every store wants you to join its rewards program. Download the app. Make an account. Remember the password. Congratulations: you now have another coupon to forget about. VISA found that consumers hold an average of 17.4 loyalty memberships but actively use only 8.8. In fact, Americans miss out on up to $10 billion in loyalty savings every year ! People are signing up for rewards, earning benefits, and then forgetting they ever existed! So we built Lapse: a browser extension that remembers your rewards and does the checkout math for you, because we're obsessed with our customers.

sections.heading: Innovation
sections.text: It finds coupons, checks your coupons, memberships, and credit card benefits to find the best combination that gives our customers the best deal. We call this "stacking". Lapse also keeps track of what’s about to expire , so a reward you meant to “save for later” will be pushed to the front of the stack so you'll actually get a chance to use it before it's gone. Expiration-aware search brings those offers forward, while checkout recommendations prioritize savings. Lapse does the math for you. Minimum spends, exclusions, and cashback rates all affect the answer, so we built a constraint model using Google’s OR-Tools solver to handle the math.

sections.heading: User Experience
sections.text: Lapse finds your rewards while you shop. Your dashboard keeps the coupons, expiration dates, and savings in one place. We chose an extension because people already have somewhere to shop, and our extension is a friendly aid to save people time, money, and maximize the benefits they already have. Our LapseSense notice brings relevant benefits into that shopping experience. Live updates arrive through server-sent events, so a newly received reward can appear without a manual refresh. A reward alert needs a recognizable identity across very different shopping pages, which is why we went with a brutalist style UI. Bold colors, thick outlines, and our brutalist visual direction make Lapse feel distinct and unique. On the dashboard, individual rewards look like real little coupons to add a fun touch.

sections.heading: How We Stand Out
sections.text: Lapse connects your personal offers to the cart in front of you. That means checking eligibility, comparing combinations, selecting a payment card, and recording the resulting savings. Our custom merchant tags and term-to-category map also help connect everyday shopping language to rewards. So, searching for “shoes” should not need to remember the exact wording of a footwear email. The distinction is the decision process. A large discount can block another benefit. A smaller compatible offer can produce a better result. An impressive cashback rate can be irrelevant at the wrong merchant. Lapse puts those conditions into the calculation.

sections.heading: Commerce Impact
sections.text: Picture a $500 cart, a fully eligible 10% voucher, and a card that earns 5% cashback on the remaining purchase. Here is the math with that example: Voucher: $500 × 10% = $50 Checkout price: $500 − $50 = $450 Cashback: $450 × 5% = $22.50 Total benefit: $50 + $22.50 = $72.50 You pay $450 at checkout. The $22.50 cashback is a separate benefit. We keep that distinction explicit. For shoppers, easier access to existing benefits could mean fewer forgotten offers and less comparison work. For merchants, easier redemption could support return visits and stronger loyalty engagement. These are potential outcomes, not measured conversion results. 85% of surveyed consumers say loyalty programs make them more likely to continue doing business with brands, according to the 2025 Bond Loyalty Report, produced in partnership with VISA. Lapse helps turn that loyalty into action by bringing forgotten rewards back into the shopping experience. Shoppers get more value from their purchases, while merchants get another reason for customers to come back. Lapse helps people access the value they have earned, while helping businesses deliver on their loyalty promises.

sections.heading: Technical Execution
sections.text: Our backend uses Python, FastAPI, and Pydantic, with PostgreSQL for persistent storage, pgvector for vector search, and pgcrypto for encrypted reward codes. The intake pipeline gives users dedicated reward inboxes and deduplicates messages using both Message-ID and content hashes. Our merchant console sends real emails through that pipeline. We fine-tuned SetFit on labeled emails using our training script, running training locally on a MacBook. It classifies whether an email contains a reward. Our custom extraction cascade then tries JSON-LD → regex rules → GLiNER , merging results with confidence scores for individual fields. GLiNER, Presidio, and the optional MiniLM search fallback use pretrained models. Checkout is a constraint problem We express our stacking rules in Google OR-Tools CP-SAT. Each reward gets a binary variable: xᵢ ∈ {0, 1} Selecting a reward sets its variable to 1. Constraints enforce minimum spends, exclusions, membership requirements, and compatibility. Two incompatible rewards satisfy: xᵢ + xⱼ ≤ 1 Code-bearing rewards satisfy: Σ xᵢ ≤ 1 The objective combines immediate discounts and eligible cashback: maximize cart total − checkout price + reward cashback + card cashback Percentages apply to the appropriate remaining balance. Two compatible, sequential 10% discounts produce: 1 − (0.9 × 0.9) = 19% The engine handles rounding and caps, then constructs an explanation from the selected benefits and calculated amounts. A 200-millisecond solver budget keeps the interaction responsive; a greedy fallback provides a feasible recommendation when that budget is exceeded, without promising global optimality. Search has its own math Our custom ranking combines: score = match × value × urgency Merchant tags and category mappings determine relevance. The urgency component raises the priority of approaching expirations: use it before you lose it. Redemptions feed an itemized ledger and cumulative savings: S(t) = Σ savedᵢ for redemptions recorded through day t. The chart has receipts behind it.

sections.heading: Security, Trust, & Responsibility
sections.text: Trust and security are built into Lapse from day one, because making commerce easier means earning people’s confidence. Our dedicated rewards inbox keeps personal inboxes private , while lightweight ML extracts reward details without relying on an LLM to follow instructions in an email. Confidence scores flag uncertainty, and explainable recommendations show where the savings come from. Everything is run locally your device; Lapse doesn’t use any outside services or make any outside calls. Our goal is to connect people and businesses through innovative, reliable, and secure payments. We’re bringing that principle to everyday rewards: helping shoppers use their benefits with less friction and helping businesses deliver on their loyalty promises. Convenience should never come at the cost of consumer trust. Challenges we ran into The hardest part of stacking was defining what counts as a valid combination. With Google’s OR-Tools CP-SAT solver, we had to translate reward terms into explicit constraints: one promo code per order, minimum spends, exclusions, and restrictions on combining offers. When stacking permission was unclear, we took the conservative approach and treated the rewards as incompatible. The arithmetic was another part that we had to spend time thinking about. Two compatible 10% discounts applied sequentially save 19%, not 20%: 1 − (0.9 × 0.9) = 0.19 Cashback also needs the correct base. A $500 cart with 10% off becomes $450, so 5% cashback earns $22.50, not $25. Discount caps, eligible items, and cent-level rounding added further complexity. We also had to separate expiration urgency from maximum savings. Search can prioritize rewards approaching expiration, while checkout optimization prioritizes the best eligible financial result. To keep recommendations grounded, we built explanations from the engine’s actual selections and calculated amounts. The challenge was making every promised dollar traceable to a reward, an eligibility rule, and the arithmetic.

sections.heading: Future of Lapse
sections.text: Here are some future features that we'll implement as we continue working on Lapse: Location-based SMS alerts: With user permission, notify shoppers of relevant rewards when they enter a store. This would extend Lapse beyond online shopping and require location capabilities outside the browser extension. Receipt and confirmation processing: Extract merchant, purchase date, items, and amounts from receipts and order confirmations to populate purchase records automatically. Link purchases to rewards where supported, flag uncertain matches for review, and record confirmed savings without duplicate entries.

title: Noxen
tagline: A night shift for your facility: Noxen scans every room each night, tells routine changes from real problems, and sends an autonomous drone to take a closer look.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: A hairline crack. A tank that's started to stain. A pallet pushed in front of an exit. Problems in a facility start small and quiet, and most facilities only look for them every few weeks, when a certified inspection team walks the floor. Everything that happens in between goes unseen. We're two UW students, one in CS and one in aerospace, who have spent this fall researching autonomous indoor inspection and talking to the people who would use them: construction project managers, facility operators, and site leads. The same theme kept coming up. Inspections are manual, expensive, and infrequent. On construction sites, the question isn't only "is something broken?" but also "was this installed the way the spec says?" So we asked: what if a facility got inspected every single night, automatically? This weekend we built an autonomous drone that is the core of that loop.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Noxen gives a facility a night shift that never gets tired. Learns what "normal" looks like. A LiDAR + camera unit (standing in for our Overseer drone) scans the space once to build a baseline. Scans every night and finds what changed. Each new scan is aligned to the baseline and compared in 3D and in color. Noxen detects objects that were added , removed , moved , or that changed appearance . Triages instead of crying wolf. A vision-language model classifies every change. A relocated pallet is routine and stays quiet. A tank that changed color is flagged as possible corrosion , with a severity and a one-sentence rationale. Sends the Scout. For each flagged issue, Scout, our autonomous drone, flies to the exact spot. It locates itself inside the LiDAR map using only its camera (no LiDAR, no GPS on board) and avoids obstacles that weren't there when the map was made, including a person stepping into its path. Puts an engineer in control, not on a ladder. The morning report pins every flagged issue on a map of the facility with before/after views and the Scout's close-up footage. The engineer marks each one as confirmed or a false alarm , and that feedback is logged so Noxen learns what matters in that facility. Pings you where you already are. Noxen texts the alert ("Possible corrosion on Tank 2, NW corner. Reply LOOK to send the Scout.") and a reply dispatches the drone. Keeps flying. A hot-swap battery mechanism lets the Scout land, swap a drained pack, and take off again without being powered down. Why this is Cook Smarter: Noxen turns inspection from a periodic manual walk-through into an automated nightly operation. The system makes the first call on which changes deserve a human's time, so engineers spend their hours on decisions, not on walking.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Scan → detect → classify → alert → dispatch. Nightly scan: A Unitree L2 LiDAR and a camera capture the facility in 3D and in color. Our ROS 2 pipeline handles capture. Change detection: Each night's scan is aligned to the baseline with Open3D, and Noxen compares the two. It finds what was added, removed, or moved, and catches color changes like rust or stains that shape alone would miss. It also knows that something hidden isn't missing , and that a pallet that moved is one event, not two alarms. Triage with Perceptron: Perceptron's vision-language model looks at each before/after pair and decides whether it's routine or worth flagging, with a severity and a one-line reason. Scout, our autonomous drone: The Scout finds its position on the LiDAR map using only its camera, by matching what it sees to landmarks we tied to the map during scanning. It avoids new obstacles using camera depth estimation (Depth Anything V2), scaled to real distances by the map, with a YOLO-based safety check as a backup. Engineer dashboard: A FastAPI + React app pins every issue on a map of the facility, with before/after images, Scout footage, and one-click feedback that teaches Noxen what matters in that facility. Alerts with Photon: A Photon messaging agent texts the engineer when something's flagged, and replying sends the Scout. Hardware: We designed and built a battery hot-swap mechanism, and the Scout airframe. Demo: Change detection runs on real LiDAR scans of a room captured at different times. The Scout flies live at our table.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Real changes vs. sensor noise. The L2 has ~2 cm of range noise, so two scans of an unchanged room never match exactly. We tuned every threshold from a measured noise test instead of guessing, so Noxen catches small real changes without flagging noise. Not crying wolf. The hardest part of change detection is deciding what not to flag. "No change produces zero events" became a required test. Telling occluded apart from removed took ray casting, and telling moved apart from new + missing took cluster matching. Matching a photo to a point cloud. A camera image and a LiDAR map don't share features, so you can't match them directly. Anchoring visual landmarks into the LiDAR frame during mapping solved it. Depth from one camera. Monocular depth models get relative depth right but the scale wrong. Using the prior LiDAR map as a metric reference turned "closer/farther" into real meters the planner could use. Rethinking avoidance mid-design. We first put obstacle avoidance on a fixed sensor, then moved it onto the Scout's own camera, because that's how the real product has to work.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A complete loop, scan → detect → classify → alert → dispatch → report , built in one weekend by a team of two, spanning software and hardware. Noxen tells a moved object apart from a new one, and a routine change apart from a real one. That's the difference between a useful report and a wall of false alarms. The Scout navigates with just a camera inside a map that a LiDAR built once, which is what lets the inspection drones stay small and cheap.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Most of change detection is deciding what to ignore. Reliability came from the boring parts: registration gates, visibility checks, and the zero-false-alarm test. Build the expensive map once. Once one sensor has mapped the space, every drone after it only needs a camera. Keep perception independent of the robot stack. Because the pipeline is plain Python running on recorded scans, we could develop and test it without the hardware connected. Design the demo for where it will be judged.

sections.heading: What's next for Noxen
sections.text: Put the LiDAR in the air. Putting LiDAR in the air allows the entire facility to get scanned nightly, not just one room. Our Overseer drone will do exactly this, and run our own software on a Raspberry Pi. The full system. A transportable dock that houses the Overseer and Scout and swaps their batteries automatically, so inspections run every night with no one on site. A facility that learns. Every confirmation and false alarm trains Noxen on that facility, building an inspection history that survives team turnover and shows operators where their weak points are. Paid pilots. We have had customer calls with construction company directors and are working toward a paid pilot of the full system this fall. We start with construction sites , where Noxen can flag work that doesn't match the spec, then move to facilities and data centers, sold as a per-system monthly subscription.

title: Octaby
tagline: AI-powered wrist guidance that helps blind and low-vision people safely reach objects using voice, computer vision, and haptic feedback.

sections.text: Inspiration This project essentially started after one of our friends, after using steroid-based eye drops, had trouble seeing for 8 hours after using it. When we looked into assistive technology, we found so many of tools for navigation like smart walking canes, but fewer that focused on smaller tasks like finding an object on a table and reaching for it. We wanted to build something that could help with those everyday movements. Our V1 version at the start of the day used a large 3d printed bracelet with servo motors that physically pushed against the user’s hand to communicate direction. It gave us a starting point, but we wanted to make the device softer, less bulky, and easier to wear. So we then pivoted a couple hours into the competition, and we spent the rest of the day building a new version using fabric and haptic feedback. What it does This project is a wearable assistive prototype designed to help blind and low-vision users locate and reach for objects. The idea is to connect visual information from a camera to physical cues on the wrist, so someone can feel which direction to move their hand. Essentially, there are 4 haptic motors, one for each cardinal direction, and with different combinations of them we can tell them hand positions and objects. We decided to go with haptics instead of servos, so our goal was to make the guidance feel more natural while putting the electronics into something closer to a wearable garment. How we built it We built fabric wristbands and integrated small vibration motors to provide directional feedback. The hardware is positioning the motors and wiring them to a microcontroller using conductive threading, and then figuring out how to package the components without making the wristband uncomfortable or difficult to move in. On the software side, we worked on connecting the camera-based object detection and guidance logic to the haptic output. That meant thinking through how information about an object’s location should translate into a signal someone could actually understand through their wrist. We essentially took audio input, fed it to Perceptron which converted into guidance signals on the haptic bracelet. We also had a memory aspect that saved specific objects. Challenges we faced Moving from a rigid bracelet to fabric changed more than the appearance. Fabric bends and shifts, so component placement became part of the problem. We had to think about how to keep the motors in useful positions while leaving enough flexibility for someone to wear the device. With fabric, we essentially were able to make it an all fits one device. Another challenge was deciding what the vibrations should communicate. Making a motor vibrate is straightforward, making that vibration clearly mean “move your hand this way” takes more thought. We also had to work through the electronics and power constraints of putting multiple motors into a small wearable with a LOT of troubleshooting. So we essentially had to balance sewing, electronics, and coding all at once. What we learned We learned how much the physical design affects the usefulness of an assistive device. The software can identify a direction, but that information only helps if the person wearing the wristband can understand the feedback and comfortably act on it. This weekend also pushed us to think differently about iteration. We already had an approach using servos, but rebuilding with fabric and vibration motors let us explore a different way of communicating the same information.

sections.heading: What’s next
sections.text: It is still a prototype. Our next step is to find out how well this version supports the everyday tasks that inspired us to build it in the first place. Then build better software that is actually scalable and has more use cases so it can help blind people in genuinely every way. Also potentially add more motors or wristbands on each hand so we can have more combinations of haptics to mean different things.

title: OpenCanopy
tagline: Europe's deforestation law was delayed twice because the checks weren't ready. OpenCanopy checks a plot in one click with free satellite data: every forest cleared after 2020, on the record.

sections.text: TL;DR: Europe imports about €126 billion a year of goods that must now prove they weren't grown on forest cleared after 2020. The law has been delayed twice, because the system to check it wasn't ready. OpenCanopy checks one plot in one click, with free satellite data. On our sample plot in Borneo it found 880 hectares of forest cleared in 2023. Try it live: opencanopy.world If previous link does not work, use this alternate.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every minute in 2024, the tropics lost about 18 soccer fields of primary rainforest. That is 6.7 million hectares in one year, a record and nearly double 2023 (WRI / Global Forest Watch). Since 1990, about 420 million hectares of forest have been converted to other uses, an area larger than the whole EU (FAO). A lot of it ends up on our plates and shelves. The European Parliament ties EU consumption to about a tenth of global deforestation, and palm oil and soy make up over two thirds of that share. The chocolate, coffee, leather, tires and furniture we buy are often grown on land that was rainforest a few years ago. Europe wrote a law to stop it, and then couldn't enforce it. The EU Deforestation Regulation says that from 30 December 2026, cocoa, coffee, palm oil, soy, rubber, cattle and wood can't enter the EU market if they come from land deforested after 31 December 2020 . That covers about €126 billion of imports a year (S&P Global). Every shipment must name the plot it came from. Naming the plot is easy. Checking it is the hard part. The rule was meant to start in December 2024. It was pushed back a year, and then pushed back again in December 2025, with the Commission pointing to systems that weren't ready to handle the checks. The European Commission's own estimate of compliance costs was €8.1 billion a year , cut to about €2 billion only by simplifying the rules and exempting more countries and small operators. That money pays for paperwork. It doesn't let a reviewer see the land. Today, to check one polygon by hand, a reviewer needs a 2020 forest map, a loss map for every year since, and a clear satellite picture for each year, all lined up on the same box. So approval leans on the applicant's own description of the land. That is exactly the gap a bad actor walks through. The people who know the truth are the ones who live next to that forest. They watched it get cleared, but the maps that could prove it are written for GIS experts. We built the check a reviewer and a village can both read, in one click, from open data that costs nothing.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Give OpenCanopy one plot: draw a box, sketch a shape, or upload GeoJSON / KML / GPX. It builds the satellite record for that ground back to the cutoff: Two pictures. The clearest Sentinel-2 scene before the cutoff and the clearest one now, plus every year in between to scrub or play. The loss year. Hansen Global Forest Change marks the year each 30 m pixel lost its trees, through 2024. The JRC 2020 forest map marks what was forest at the cutoff. What it became. Perceptron's vision model reads the current image and outlines regions that look converted: blocks, straight roads, planting rows. The cross-check. A region is confirmed only if at least 25% of it shows post-2020 loss. Anything else stays inconclusive and goes to a person. We show the inconclusive region on purpose. On our sample plot in West Kalimantan, Borneo, the record shows unbroken forest in 2019. About 880 ha (20% of the plot) was lost after the cutoff , almost all of it in 2023, and the land now shows plantation rows. The vision model marked two regions. One is confirmed (43% loss). The other is inconclusive (14% loss). Why that matters: a reviewer sees the answer in one screen, without a GIS team, and the inconclusive region keeps a person in the loop instead of letting a model decide. The only sentence OpenCanopy will say is: "This plot shows post-2020 tree-cover loss consistent with plantation conversion." It never says "illegal" or "non-compliant". The government decides. Every check includes its scene IDs, dates and cloud cover, so anyone can pull the same data and see the same thing. The result is a printable case file with numbered exhibits.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Every byte of evidence comes from space. Sentinel-2 photographs the plot from orbit every five days at 10 m. The Hansen loss map is built from 20+ years of Landsat satellite imagery. OpenCanopy turns that space data into one answer on the ground. Imagery: Copernicus Sentinel-2 L2A from Microsoft Planetary Computer ( pystac-client , planetary-computer ). For each year we pick the least cloudy scene in the same season. Loss and forest layers: Hansen GFC-2024-v1.12 loss-year and JRC Global Forest Cover 2020 v4 rasters, clipped to the plot with rasterio and shapely . Vision: Perceptron Mk1.5 is the engine. Every judgment about what the land became comes from Perceptron. It reads before/after Sentinel-2 pairs, it watches a year-by-year video of the plot (one frame per year since 2020, at 2 fps), and it draws boxes around converted areas on a 0–1000 grid. That is how a pile of red loss pixels becomes "this region is now a plantation". See Why Perceptron below. Global search: we didn't stop at one plot. We indexed every 10° Hansen/JRC tile on Earth for 2020 forest that later lost trees, polygonized each clearing over 10 ha, cut a 2.56 km Sentinel-2 chip around each one, and asked Perceptron one question per chip as Slurm array jobs on UW's Hyak cluster. Perceptron flagged 69 clearings as plantation, and we pulled before/after imagery for every one. Cross-check: numpy compares each model region against the post-2020 loss pixels and applies the 25% rule. Built in Cursor: we wrote the pipeline, server and site in Cursor. Web: a small Python server ( /api/analyze ) and plain HTML/CSS/JS: the demo map uses MapLibre GL over Esri imagery, with a year slider, playback and overlay opacity the landing page is a scroll-driven story the case file is a print-ready evidence dossier with a before/after slider, a flicker mode, and a loss-by-year chart with the cutoff marked.

sections.heading: Why Perceptron
sections.text: Without Perceptron, OpenCanopy is just another loss map. The loss map says trees disappeared. It can't say what replaced them : fire, logging, a road, or an oil palm estate. That last step is the whole EUDR question, and Perceptron is what answers it. It works with no training data. There is no global labeled set of forest converted to plantation after 2020; that's the point of the law. A custom classifier would need thousands of labels we don't have. Perceptron worked out of the box, which is the only way this could be built in a weekend, or scaled to the whole planet. It understands time. We give it a before/after pair, or a video of the same ground year by year, and ask about the change , not a single frame. Most vision APIs take one image and describe it. It localizes. It returns boxes, so we can cross-check exactly the region it points at against the loss map, pixel by pixel. That turns a model opinion into evidence. It's cheap enough to point at the whole planet. Perceptron Mk1.5 costs $0.15 per million input tokens. Each question is one small Sentinel-2 chip and a one-word answer, so a single check costs well under a cent. That means the limit on a global sweep is how many clearings exist, not the budget: a hackathon team could afford to ask about every post-2020 clearing we indexed worldwide. For a regulator, that turns satellite review from a specialist service into something you can run on every plot. It's fast. One Perceptron call reads a whole 2020–2026 video of a 10 km tile and answers in about 4 to 8 seconds (6.8 s on average in our benchmark). We fire calls in parallel and only ask about windows where the maps already show loss, which skipped 12 of 25 windows on our test plot. One-word answers with reasoning off let us batch it across every clearing on the planet. We tested it hard. On labeled Sentinel-2 chips from Riau, Sumatra, generic prompts ("are there planting rows?", "is this an estate?") scored 8 of 16, a coin flip. So we studied what oil palm looks like at 10 m and rewrote the question around it: a dense, regular dotted texture inside rectangular blocks. On a 48-chip test set with that prompt, Perceptron reached 100% precision (16 of 16 "yes" answers correct, zero false alarms) at 67% recall. For a tool that a government acts on, zero false accusations matters more than catching everything, and the loss-map cross-check plus the "inconclusive" state catch the rest.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Clouds and smoke. Several years over Borneo are mostly cloud, and 2026 has haze. Scene selection by season and cloud cover mattered more than any model. Not overclaiming. The Hansen loss map ends in 2024, so we can't say anything was "detected in 2026". The newest images show only what the land is now. Writing honest copy was as much work as the code. Models hallucinate rows. A vision model alone will call a mature forest a plantation. Gating it behind the loss map and keeping an "inconclusive" state fixed that. Drawing any shape. Supporting freehand polygons and three upload formats, and still running on a clean bounding box.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: An end-to-end check on real open data, from a drawn box to a printable case file. An inconclusive region is shown front and center, not hidden. A design that a non-expert can follow: one plot, one story, and one allowed sentence.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Open satellite data is good enough to answer the EUDR question for one plot. The hard part is lining it up and explaining it. Restraint is a feature. Every word we banned ("illegal", "score", "fail") made the tool more trustworthy. How the EUDR actually works: the cutoff is not the start date, and the authority, not the software, decides.

sections.heading: What's next for OpenCanopy
sections.text: Attach the case file to the due diligence statement, so the next reviewer and the public can rerun the same check. Plain-language and local-language packs for communities and forest monitors. Batch checks for every plot in a supply chain, with the same per-plot evidence. Radar (Sentinel-1) to see through cloud in the wettest years.

sections.heading: Why it should exist
sections.text: Economic: €126 billion of trade a year depends on these checks. Every day a check takes, a shipment waits, and every unverifiable plot is a risk for importers and their suppliers. Supply chain: honest smallholders get evidence on their side. One public satellite record per plot replaces stacks of self-declared paperwork that nobody can verify. Environment: if checks stay slow, the cutoff means nothing and 2020's forest keeps turning into plantations. Tropical forest loss is already at a record. A fast, public check is what makes the law real. Trust: every number comes from open data with scene IDs, so anyone (a regulator, a buyer, a journalist, or the village itself) can rerun it and get the same answer.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.text: WRI / Global Forest Watch, 2024 forest loss data (May 2025) · FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 · European Parliament EUDR briefing · S&P Global, deforestation rules' impact on supply chains (2023) · European Commission EUDR simplification review (2026) · Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 and its 2024 and 2025 amendments.

title: Pollensight
tagline: Perception layer for robotic pollinators. Analyzes bee-to-flower visits while simulating robotic pollinators that learn efficient routes from real bee behavior.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Pollinators are disappearing, and about a third of the food we grow depends on them. We wanted to turn camera footage into something actionable: which flowers got visited, which didn't, and how a pollinator robot could achieve perception.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Pollensight turns ordinary fixed-camera video into a per-flower record of insect visits. It can aslo forecast where an insect will go next and plans a robot route to the flowers it missed. Video : tracks insects with boxes and trails. Flower boxes light up during a visit, and a timeline shows every visit. Search : plain-English natural-language search across clips ( "when does the bee land on a flower?" ) that jumps the video straight to that moment. Analytics : visits, dwell time, transit time, flight speed, revisits and a heatmap of where the insect spent its time. Forecast : the insect's predicted path for the next 2 seconds, shown as a spread of possible futures, plus the odds for its next flower and how much longer it will stay. Field : on farm clips, flowers are colored by how many visits they still need, with a robot route that covers the most of them within a time budget. Dataset : accuracy across all 48 clips, with the visual audits behind every number. Upload : analyze your own fixed-camera video. Simulations : a bee trained with reinforcement learning flies over a random flower field it has never seen, in interactive 3D. The same flight is rendered in MuJoCo , with a Crazyflie 2 drone standing in for the bee.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Pollensight is a four-stage pipeline. Perception (Python, OpenCV, NumPy): OpenCV background subtraction and connected components find moving blobs, and a dynamic-programming search links them into flight paths. Every half second we send a 160 px crop to Perceptron's Mk1.5 vision model to check that there's really an insect there, and we keep a path only if at least 70% of its crops are confirmed. Mk1.5 also finds flowers in a median frame, which gives us stable flower IDs for detecting visits. Perceptron API layer: we wrote our own client on top of the perceptron SDK. It uses box, point and clip annotations, JSON-schema output and the Files API for video. Every answer is cached under a SHA-256 key, so the whole project replays offline for free . Intelligence: Forecasting (scikit-learn): a k-nearest-neighbors "path fan" for the next 2 seconds, gradient-boosted next-flower prediction and Monte Carlo rollouts. These are trained on 2,335 real insect flights and tested on camera stations the model never saw. Route planning: an orienteering planner (greedy insertion plus 2-opt) that picks the most valuable flowers to visit within a time budget. Simulation: a Gymnasium environment with a Stable-Baselines3 PPO bee, replayed in MuJoCo using the Crazyflie 2 model from MuJoCo Menagerie. Web app (React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8): Canvas 2D and SVG overlays, a three.js 3D Simulations page, and custom Vite middleware that streams video with HTTP range requests and runs the Python forecast, analysis and simulation behind API routes.
