Data: 48 clips from two Monash University datasets (CC BY 4.0): 38 honeybee close-ups and 10 strawberry-farm clips from overhead cameras.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Result Insect tracking (48 clips) 90% of the path covered, median error ≈ 3–4 px Visit detection (farm clips) 90% of detected visits are real ( 64% without Mk1.5) Flower detection 98% precision, 87% recall Next-flower prediction (unseen cameras) right flower in the top 3 picks 79% of the time (nearest-flower guess: 68%) Robot route delivers 39–56% of missing visits in 30 s (random order: 17–33%) We also built a full pipeline that anyone can reproduce: 45 tests run offline and 144/144 data files pass validation . The whole project goes from raw video to a 3D drone simulation in one app.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: This project was our way into physical AI . None of us had built AI that acts in the real world before, and we learned how to do it by using computer vision to turn raw video into data that a forecaster, a route planner and a robot can act on. Pairing a cheap classical tracker with a strong vision model that checks its work beats either one alone. Mk1.5 raised visit precision from 64% to 90%.

sections.heading: Tech architecture
sections.text: Field video ──► PERCEIVE ──────────────► JSON contract files ──► UNDERSTAND ─────────────► EXPLORE (mp4, fixed OpenCV motion tracking tracks/ field/ Analytics (NumPy) React + TypeScript camera) DP path linking plan/ search/ Forecast (scikit-learn) Vite dev server visit detection (validated) Route planner /api/* routes │ RL bee (Gymnasium + SB3) three.js 3D page ▼ MuJoCo replay Perceptron Mk1.5 (cached client: crops, flowers) Layer What it does Tech Capture Clips and public datasets Fixed-camera mp4 (720p, 30 fps), Monash datasets via figshare, GitHub Releases, ffmpeg / imageio-ffmpeg Perceive Insects, flowers, visits Python, OpenCV (median background, connected components), NumPy (dynamic programming) Vision model Confirms insects, boxes flowers Perceptron Mk1.5 via the perceptron SDK: box detection, JSON-schema output, Files API Understand Analytics, forecasts, plans, simulation NumPy, scikit-learn (k-NN, gradient boosting), pandas, joblib, SciPy, Gymnasium, Stable-Baselines3, MuJoCo + Menagerie Crazyflie 2 Explore The web app React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8, Node.js, Canvas 2D, SVG, three.js Quality Keeps it correct and reproducible pytest, JSON contracts + validator, accuracy evals, visual audits

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Tiny, fast insects on busy backgrounds. Plain motion tracking picked up leaves moving in the wind, and running a vision model on every frame was too slow and too expensive. Our answer was a hybrid: cheap OpenCV tracking proposes paths, and Mk1.5 checks samples of them. Measuring accuracy honestly. We compared against each dataset's own reference tracker and visually audited the flower detections, rather than trusting results that just looked right. Four people editing overlapping code at the same time. Agreeing on fixed JSON formats ( CONTRACT.md ) and a validator early on kept everyone's work compatible.

sections.heading: What's next for Pollensight
sections.text: Real hardware: run the planned routes on an actual drone or ground robot in a test plot. Live video: process camera streams in real time instead of uploaded clips. More pollinators: support more insect species and crops beyond honeybees and strawberries. Grower dashboard: pollination coverage across many cameras and over a whole season. Better simulation: move from replaying recorded paths to flight with real physics, and train the RL bee on real farm layouts.

title: ReMind
tagline: A memory-game companion with a robot arm for dementia care

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Nearly half of nursing home residents live with dementia, and the activities that help them, like sorting familiar objects or finishing a proverb, need a staff member sitting next to them. Staff are stretched thin, so many residents spend much of the day doing nothing. Several of us have a family member in this situation. Existing digital tools tend to be fixed, hard for older adults to use, easy to abandon, and thinly evidenced, so we built a memory-game companion you talk to instead of tap, with a real robot arm so the resident does something with their hands.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: ReMind is a voice companion that a caregiver sets up and supervises. The resident talks, a calm screen shows one photo or a few words, and the caregiver reads a plain summary afterwards. The main game is "Remember the Order". The resident says something like "let's play the shuffle game," and ReMind starts it on its own: the robot arm shuffles three keychains on the table in front of them, then waits. The resident is free to put them back in order by hand, at their own pace. ReMind also has three conversation games based on Cognitive Stimulation Therapy: famous faces, finishing a saying, and everyday sounds. If the resident says something worrying, like a fall or chest pain, Gemini decides whether it matters, reassures them calmly, and texts the caregiver a short summary using Photon. After each session the caregiver sees plain notes about how it went, never a score. The AI can't move the robot on its own. It can only ask from a short list, and our server and the robot's software both check every request.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: ReMind uses a Python/FastAPI backend and a TypeScript/Next.js frontend. Voice runs on Gemini's Live API through Backboard, which keeps long-term memory, and our backend relays the audio so the API key stays off the browser. Caregiver alerts go through Photon: its SDK is TypeScript, so a small Node service turns a request from our backend into an iMessage. The robot is an SO-101 arm with two cameras, run through LeRobot. We taught it by demonstration: one person moves a "leader" arm and a second "follower" arm copies, while the cameras film each 35-second try. We recorded 60 tries, 12 for each of five shuffles, and trained policies on Perceptron's cloud platform. A robot worker re-checks every job against its own allowlist and joint limits before the arm moves.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The biggest challenge was getting the arm to grasp. Our trained policies move smoothly and stay inside safe limits, but after 1,000 training steps they can't pick up the keychains reliably. So the demo arm runs taught positions with the camera verifying the result. We verified two shuffles, swap left/right and swap left/middle, in both directions. The other three stall at the empty fourth slot, which the camera can't see. Re-picks there worked 5 times out of 7. The robot is also picky about its surroundings. Table color, lighting and camera angle have to match between recording and use, and even a keychain placed slightly off by hand can make it miss, so we taped everything down and set up the table with a script where the arm points to each slot. On the voice side, default voice detection decides you're done speaking too quickly, which cuts off people who pause mid-thought. We waited 1.2 seconds of silence before answering. A shuffle also takes many seconds, so game start returns immediately and the AI speaks up when the arm finishes. Photon's free tier only texts enrolled phones, and its error didn't say so. We spent an hour blaming our own code before we tried Photon's starter project, which failed too.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Safety enforced in code: The AI can only call a short list of tools, and the rules live in our server and the robot software, not in the prompt, so the AI can't talk its way past them. Camera-verified robot moves: Every shuffle is confirmed by the camera, with an honest account of what works and what doesn't. An end-to-end alert: A worrying sentence becomes a calm reply for the resident and a short text for the caregiver, without alarming the resident. A game with no scores and no "wrong": It's built on errorless learning and Cognitive Stimulation Therapy principles.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that keeping the AI behind a short, validated tool list is what makes it safe enough to connect to a robot. We also learned that real-time voice is mostly about when to stay quiet, and that for vulnerable users a kind tone and no scores matter as much as accuracy. Robot demos fail on the environment more often than on the model, so the setup is part of the product. A scripted fallback with a camera check beat an unreliable learned policy for a demo, and it's fine to say so.

sections.heading: What's next for ReMind
sections.text: A learned policy that grasps on its own: more training steps and more demonstrations. A camera that can see the fourth slot, so the other three shuffles become reliable. More skills for the arm: each new policy we teach it could become a new hands-on game. Games that adapt to each person: today we pick games per person, but we don't adjust difficulty yet. A pilot with a care facility and an occupational therapist, before we claim any benefit. These steps would turn ReMind from a prototype into a companion a care home could try with real residents. Code: github.com/remind-dubhacks/dubhacks-2026

title: Robo-view
tagline: We created a system for cinematic product showcases and ads with perceptron's SO-101 robotic arm.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Many advertisements of smaller products like smartphones, wearable devices, foods, and more showcase in dynamic angles to better appeal to viewers. Seeing how the SO-101 robotic arm moves around with its attached camera reminded us of this, and gave us the idea to replicate that cinematography using algorithms, making the process more streamlined, smooth, and efficient.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: There are two parts to the project, the app and the arm. The app has voice and text input for users to command the arm, and then after the arm moves around and records at various angles, it sends the video back to the user on the app. The arm then is the second part, and it rotates and traverses around any product using 1 of 3 different dynamic movements as it records.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We split into different groups to work on operating the arms, creating the software, and handling the machine learning. After teleoperating the follower arm to the leader arm, we ran trials to replicate movements and recording angles for cinematography, analyzing the motor arm data and then sending it into the Isaac 0.5 model to train on through ML. We recorded 25 different tests per movement, resulting in around 75 tests total. Through that AI model, we then replicated the arm movements to account for different recording angles explained from user audio input put into the app, and also different object positioning.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The main challenge we ran in to was after doing all the recording and training was relabeling all the data with bounding boxes, which took a bit of time to do while navigating the Perceptron API.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Setting the arm up, training it, getting it to run successfully after hours of work.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned various skills such as robot manipulation, combining agents and tool-calling with the physical world, and creating software for video editing as well.

sections.heading: What's next for Robo-view
sections.text: We think it's best to give the robot more movements, and training with arms that have more degrees of freedom. This could allow for my dynamic shots with greater ranges. We'd also like to train it so that it can identify and record a single object within an environment of other objects.

title: SonoRocky
tagline: Narrating the world for the visually-impaired.

sections.heading: I. Inspiration
sections.text: Our inspiration came from a teammate who witnessed his dormmate, who was visually impaired, struggling to navigate campus using only a mobility cane. Although his cane helps detect nearby obstacles, it provides limited information about the surrounding environment, making independent navigation challenging. [Research] shows that 7% of visually impaired and/or blind respondents experienced non-superficial injuries every month due to hazards and trips. Furthermore, 13% of respondents reported having head-level injuries that resulted in stitches and dental care every month. These experiences inspired us to develop technology that helps our community members with visual impairments to detect obstacles, avoid collisions, and navigate campus more safely and independently.

sections.heading: II. What It Does?
sections.text: SonoRocky includes two major elements: 1) Our Vision-to-Language application, and 2) a Mobility Cane System to detect distances. The Vision System gathers data from a phone camera and the Mobility Cane System to generate a visual-to-audio output that uses natural spoken language to warn vision-impaired persons about their surroundings, as UW research has indicated they possess superior hearing and perception. It also allows individuals to prompt the application with questions about what's in front of them and to read text on walls, to which the model can respond with detailed descriptions. The Mobility Cane System uses an acoustic sensor to detect obstacles in surrounding areas. This data is sent to the Vision System, which converts distance measurements into a series of variable-frequency beeps heard by the individual using the app, warning them to slow down in their stride as they approach obstacles.

sections.heading: III. How We Built It?
sections.text: Perceptron's mk1.5 model was used for recognizing still-frame captures taken from the device camera at a dynamic FPS rate, which then returns a natural language description with customizable details and hazard alerts (< 2-second latency) ElevenLabs' TTS model was used for streaming real-time audio readouts of Perceptron's descriptions The backend server handles interacting with both APIs and can route communication with multiple devices each running its own frontend instance. It also receives POST packets from the ESP8266 with distance data and WiFi status info ESP8266 used for processing ultrasonic distance sensor data, which is transmitted over WiFi to the backend server Fusion 360 + Prusa MK4 to 3D print a housing for the prototype, which can clamp onto rods of varying diameters

sections.heading: IV. Challenges We Ran Into
sections.text: Limited access to hardware and tools for building our demo We needed a tilted angle for the ultrasonic sensor on the Mobility Cane System so that it faces perpendicular to the ground Balancing high-speed camera refresh rate while staying within API ratelimits Tuning the speed of generating the natural language outputs from our video feed, along with the level of detail in the descriptions CAD design for a good angle facing forward on the mobility cane

sections.heading: V. Accomplishments that We're Proud of
sections.text: We limit the character for the audio output for every scan for faster processing speed Prioritize possible hazards before introducing minor details of the surroundings Estimate the minimal amount of stairs to prevent accidental trips Hardware costs less than $15 to assemble

sections.heading: VI. What We Learned?
sections.text: Hardware/Software integration Things do not always go as we expected Optimization of features Software advice from our community mentors (huge shoutout to David from Perceptron!)

sections.heading: VII. What's Next for SonoRocky
sections.text: In order to bring our project to the next level, we decide to achieve our goal by improving the two systems. We want to build sunglasses for the Vision System, with two separate cameras, one looking forward and one looking down, a CPU and two speakers for audio output at the hooks of the sunglasses. The cameras were used to scan the surroundings and identify possible obstacles at a refresh rate of 120 FPS to give a safer condition for vision-impaired people. The forward-facing camera uses a wide-angle lens to capture as much information as possible, while the downward-facing camera estimates the steps between the incoming obstacles (e.g., stairs or uneven ground) with motion sensors to warn the person as he walks. Moreover, we want to complete the mobility cane system by making it fit different types of mobility canes with different lengths and diameters. Furthermore, the cane should not have only one sensor; we will implement several ToF sensors to detect the surroundings in multiple directions and angles, like a LiDAR. Lastly, we would also like to implement more features associated with maps and navigation into our project. We wanted our Vision System to be able to communicate with the user, through natural spoken languages, and be able to understand and execute commands. Nevertheless, location synchronisations will also help a lot in creating a map-level navigation system, so we can better locate and predict the possible surroundings of the user.

sections.heading: VIII. Why the Name?
sections.text: The prefix "Sono-" refers to the usage of sonar in navigation; while "Rocky" is a character in the film "Project Hail Mary" who has no eyes and navigates based on sounds, which resonates with the main aim of our project. Rocky also speaks in short, succinct phrases, just like our project 🪨.

sections.text: Mobility-related accidents experienced by people with visual impairment. (n.d.). https://users.soe.ucsc.edu/~manduchi/papers/MobilityAccidents.pdf Park, W. J., Awad, J., & Fine, I. title: Starward
tagline: Starward shows you exactly where on your hike your phone can text by satellite, so you know before you go dark, and someone at home knows if you don't check in.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Living in the Pacific Northwest, we're surrounded by incredible hiking trails and outdoor destinations. Washington has so many beautiful places to explore, but one common problem with hiking in remote areas is losing cell service. Whether you're hiking through the mountains or exploring a trail deep in the forest, it can be difficult to communicate with anyone if something goes wrong. We wanted to address this problem because staying connected shouldn't require buying expensive satellite equipment or worrying about whether your phone will work. With newer phones beginning to support satellite messaging, we saw an opportunity to make this technology more accessible and useful for hikers. This inspired us to create Starward, a platform that helps people prepare for hikes, understand where satellite communication might work, and keep their loved ones informed along the way.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Starward is a hiking safety platform that helps users plan communication before heading somewhere without reliable cell service. Users start by selecting a hiking trail, date, start time, phone model, and carrier. Starward then analyzes satellite orbit data, terrain elevation, and phone compatibility to estimate where satellite messaging is most likely to work along their route. The results are displayed on an interactive, color-coded map showing areas with stronger or weaker estimated satellite connectivity. Starward also recommends check-in locations and time windows so hikers can plan where and when to contact someone. Additionally, Starward includes a wireless recommendation system that determines whether a user would benefit from an additional satellite service, such as T-Mobile's T-Satellite. Instead of encouraging unnecessary purchases, our system prioritizes the most affordable solution, even if that means recommending that the user buy nothing. Users can share their trip plan with an emergency contact through our Photon messaging integration. Hikers can then send a simple "OK" message to check in, allowing their contacts to receive updates. Starward also includes a missed-check-in alert feature to help contacts identify when someone may need assistance.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built Starward using Python, Flask, JavaScript, HTML, and Folium to create an interactive web application. For satellite coverage estimates, we integrated real orbital data from CelesTrak, using Skyfield and SGP4 to calculate satellite positions. We combined this with trail information from OpenStreetMap and elevation data to estimate how terrain might affect satellite visibility. We then visualized this information through an interactive map that highlights different coverage conditions along the trail. We also created a recommendation engine that evaluates users' phone models, carriers, available satellite services, and pricing to identify suitable connectivity options. For communication, we integrated Photon Spectrum through a Node.js messaging bridge connected to our Flask backend. This enables the application to send trip details and check-in notifications through a messaging service. Throughout development, we used Cursor and Claude Code to help implement features, debug issues, understand unfamiliar technologies, and integrate different components. We used these tools to accelerate development while reviewing and testing our code as a team.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One of our biggest challenges was figuring out how to combine several different technologies into one project that would actually be useful. We wanted Starward to be more than just a satellite coverage map, so we spent time thinking about what hikers would realistically need before and during a trip. Another major challenge was integrating Photon with our Flask web application. Our backend and messaging service used different technologies, so we had to build a bridge between them and work through configuration, message delivery, and communication between the services. We also faced challenges with validating satellite coverage predictions. Satellite visibility depends on several factors, including orbital positions, surrounding terrain, and environmental obstructions. We had to combine multiple data sources while recognizing that our predictions could only be estimates rather than guarantees. Finally, coordinating our different components was challenging because the mapping, recommendation, frontend, and messaging systems were developed in parallel. Making everything work together required debugging, testing, and communication across the team.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: One of our biggest accomplishments was integrating Photon into our web application and getting the messaging functionality connected to our hiking safety workflow. Building a system that could connect a trip plan with text-based communication was especially exciting because it made Starward feel like more than just a website. We're also proud of combining real satellite orbital data and terrain information to build an interactive hiking map. Seeing how these different datasets could work together to provide useful information was rewarding. Another accomplishment was building a recommendation engine that doesn't automatically try to sell users something. We wanted Starward to make decisions based on what would actually benefit the hiker, including telling them when their current phone and service are already sufficient. Most importantly, we're proud that we were able to bring together multiple technical components into a working local web application during a hackathon.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: This project taught us a lot about integrating different technologies and turning an idea into a functional application within a limited amount of time. We learned how satellite orbit data can be used to estimate communication opportunities and how geographic features such as mountains and ridges can affect connectivity. We also gained experience working with external datasets, designing recommendation logic, and connecting a Python backend to a separate messaging service. Working with Cursor and Claude Code showed us how AI-assisted development can speed up implementation and debugging, but also reinforced the importance of understanding, reviewing, and testing the code ourselves. One of our biggest takeaways was that creating something useful isn't just about adding more features. It is about understanding the user's problem and designing a solution that is simple enough to use in a real situation.

sections.heading: What's next for Starward
sections.text: In the future, we want to expand Starward beyond hiking to support other outdoor activities such as camping, backpacking, and exploring remote areas where reliable communication may be limited. We also want to expand our trail coverage beyond Washington and the Pacific Northwest so that users can plan trips across different states and eventually other countries. On the technical side, we hope to improve the accuracy of our satellite coverage estimates by incorporating more detailed terrain and vegetation data, expanding device compatibility, and refining our predictions. We also plan to improve our messaging system with automatic missed-check-in detection, more messaging channels, and more reliable trip tracking. Eventually, we would like to make trip information accessible offline so hikers can reference their plans without needing an internet connection. Our long-term goal is to make Starward a useful outdoor safety companion that helps people explore confidently while staying connected to the people who care about them.

title: tensormew
tagline: Reinforcement Learning + LLM agent that plays the Pokémon Crystal video game and wins!

sections.text: tensormew tensormew plays Pokémon Crystal and beats Falkner for the first gym badge. We use reinforcement learning to teach an agent to play Pokémon Crystal, and call an LLM only when the game actually needs a decision.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Pokémon Crystal is a long, stateful game: maps, one-way ledges, scripts, menus, and a gym fight at the end of the first stretch. Calling a language model on every frame is slow and expensive, and a screenshot still does not show collision bytes or event flags. Most steps do not need language. Walking a tile, closing a text box, and picking a damaging move are mechanical. Language is for the moment the agent is stuck and has to choose a goal. The question we measured is how many steps actually needed an LLM on the way to the first badge. Crystal is a hard test of that split: PyBoy has no collision grid for this ROM. The map is a pair (group, number) . Cut is face the tree, press A, confirm . Ledges are one-way. Dialogue is an open script ( wScriptMode / wScriptRunning ), not a single textbox bit.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: An agent plays Pokémon Crystal (US 1.1) inside PyBoy and clears the opening of Johto: leave New Bark, reach Cherrygrove, finish the Mystery Egg quest, walk to Violet City, and beat Falkner. Three actors share one loop: Actor When it runs What it outputs RL policy Overworld, no trigger One of up , down , left , right , A Macros Open dialogue or a routine battle Mash A, or pick a move slot LLM director Cut tree, stuck tile, hard battle, open script One tool call plus a one-sentence reason Tools the model may call: go_to , run_path , use_cut , mash_text , choose_move , switch_pokemon . Every call requires a reason . That sentence is logged for the judges. It is never sent to the emulator as input. There is no town-to-town route table. The policy is paid for new tiles, new maps, story flags, catches, levels, and the maps on the way to Violet Gym. Falkner is the terminal reward on that chain: EVENT_BEAT_FALKNER pays +50 , and wJohtoBadges flips to the Zephyr Badge. Outcome The run starts in New Bark, map (24, 4) , with no badges. It crosses Route 29, Cherrygrove, Route 30, Mr. Pokémon's house, Route 31, and Violet City, map (10, 5) , then enters Violet Gym, map (10, 7) . Dialogue with Elm, the rival, and Mr. Pokémon is finished by macros. Falkner's Flying-types are fought with a type chart, not move slot 1. The episode ends with one Johto badge and EVENT_BEAT_FALKNER set. Demo surfaces PyBoy window of the Game Boy screen, from New Bark through the gym. Live HUD: return, entropy, tiles and maps discovered, badge count. Streamlit thought log ( app.py ) over logs/decisions.jsonl : map, position, actor, tool, reason, tokens, and estimated dollars. Plain walks show actor=rl and $0 . The LLM rows are the stuck, dialogue, and gym moments.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Stack: Python 3.13, PyBoy 2.8.1, the pret symbol file rom/pokemon_crystal.sym , NumPy PPO, PyTorch for the vision policy, Gemini Tool Calling, Pydantic tool schemas, Streamlit, SQLite run log. ROM identity is pinned: SHA1 f2f52230b536214ef7c9924f483392993e226cfb . RAM is read through symbol names and banked WRAM ( pyboy.memory[bank, addr] ). Position is wXCoord / wYCoord . Badges are wJohtoBadges . Story state is the 2,048-bit wEventFlags block. That's how we know the egg was delivered and Falkner is down before the badge sprite even updates. Layer 1: emulator and game state src/emulator.py : loads the ROM, ticks, and saves. src/ram_parser.py : turns RAM into a GameState and a text snapshot for the model. src/collision.py : classifies pret tile IDs: walls, Cut trees, warps, and one-way COLL_HOP_* ledges. src/step.py : moves exactly one tile. src/states.py : a labeled checkpoint manifest, so a gym attempt can resume from Violet instead of the title screen. Layer 2: the RL agent Routine overworld steps are a policy, not the LLM. That's what carried the agent from New Bark to the gym door. Small CPU policy ( src/ppo.py , models/ppo_policy.npz , ~14.5 KB) Linear or 2-layer MLP actor-critic. Five actions. 17 observations: four neighbor tiles, x/y, badges, battle, dialogue, four visited-neighbor bits, party size, max level, caught count, and a story-stage scalar. Story stage is 0 in New Bark, ~0.45 with the Mystery Egg, 0.75 in Violet City, 0.85 inside the gym, and 1.0 once Falkner is beaten. Vision policy ( src/deep_policy.py , models/deep_policy.pt , ~50.5 MB, 13,220,678 parameters ) A ResNet-style trunk on the raw 144×160 frame, an MLP on the 17 RAM features, a 512-wide GRU, then actor and critic heads. Trained with PPO and curriculum resets ( tools/train_deep_ppo.py ) on parallel headless PyBoy workers. Play it with ./run_live.sh . Reward ( src/rl_env.py ) is potential-based shaping (Ng, Harada & Russell) plus one-time bonuses that spell out the Falkner route: Signal Reward Step cost −0.01 New tile +1 (+2 on the current objective maps) New map +10 Waypoints Route 29 +3, Cherrygrove +5, Mr. Pokémon's house +8, Violet City +12, Violet Gym +20 Story flags Starter from Elm +15, Mystery Egg +20, egg returned +20, rival in Cherrygrove +15, beat Falkner +50 Catches 10 / 5 / 2.5 (floor 0.5) Level-ups scaled by 5, so the party is strong enough for the gym before the badge reward dominates Route 29's potential pulls the agent up the one-tile gap at x=31 and away from the south ledge. Layer 3: the LLM director src/triggers.py fires on CUT_BLOCKED , STUCK (same tile for 8 steps), BATTLE , and DIALOGUE . src/llm_supervisor.py sends the state text plus the trigger and forces a tool call. src/tool_dispatch.py runs it. src/agent_loop.py logs map, position, badges, actor, trigger, tool, reason, tokens, and estimated USD. The system prompt holds the facts the pixels omit: no Cut before the badge, ledges don't climb, and the northern highway on Route 29 is the road to Cherrygrove. Layer 4: macros and the gym fight src/macros.py holds dialogue open until wScriptMode returns to 0. That's how Elm, Mom, and the rival actually finish. src/battle.py scores moves by power, accuracy, and the Gen 2 type chart. Ground into Flying is 0×, so Mud-Slap is not what we throw at Pidgey. Electric, Rock, and Ice are 2×. src/saycan.py blocks the gym while the party is empty or under level 10, then lets the fight start.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The screen is not the state. Map ID, event flags, and collision live in banked WRAM. The vision net still needed the 17 RAM features to tell "egg delivered" from "standing on a wall." One-way ledges. Hopping south on Route 29 dead-ends the run before Cherrygrove. Collision became directional, and the reward potential was written around the x=31 gap so the policy takes the northern highway. Dialogue looks like a stall. A long NPC script used to trip the stuck detector and abort the quest. We raised the dialogue and battle streak cap and made mash_text wait until the script closed. That's what got us through Elm and the Mystery Egg handoff. A tiny policy can fake an exit. Early linear PPO showed a high New Bark exit rate in a batch, then failed a single visual run. The 13.2M-parameter GRU is what we trusted for the full walk to Violet. Falkner is not a walking problem. Pressing move slot 1 loses to Flying-types. The fight only landed after move choice used the type chart and the party was gated at level 10. Tokens versus frames. An always-on LLM on this route would have been a call per tile from New Bark to the gym. Triggers-only kept the dollar counter on the decisions that mattered.

sections.heading: Accomplishments we are proud of !!!
sections.text: Zephyr Badge. The agent leaves New Bark, finishes the Mystery Egg, reaches Violet Gym, and beats Falkner. wJohtoBadges is 1. EVENT_BEAT_FALKNER is set. That's the run. A full agent loop where the language model is a tool-calling director. Button presses stay in the policy and the macros, including the gym fight. The early Johto plot encoded as reward: Mystery Egg +20, egg returned +20, rival +15, Violet Gym +20, Falkner +50, plus a Route 29 potential that avoids the ledge trap. Two policies in-tree: a CPU MLP for fast segment tests, and a 13.2M-parameter screen-plus-RAM GRU trained on vectorized PyBoy workers, which is the policy that plays the badge run. A decision log and Streamlit view of the whole route: $0 on walking steps, with a reason and a token count only when the director is invoked. Directional collision, warps, and indoor transitions, so the agent enters Elm's lab, Mr. Pokémon's house, and Violet Gym instead of treating doors as walls. Banked RAM, pret collision, one-tile stepping, a labeled checkpoint chain, and 34 test modules around that stack.

sections.heading: Cool stuff we learned !!!
sections.text: The first badge is a control problem with a few language moments. Wiring the model to buttons made the route unreproducible. Wiring it to six validated tools made every intervention on the way to Falkner inspectable. **Realized that the Pokemon were too low leveled so it had to go back and continue to level up - showcasing long term horizon planning. Reward has to match the map. A generic new-tile bonus hops the south ledge and never sees Cherrygrove. The Route 29 potential is why the policy arrives at the gym. Event flags are the progress bar. The badge bit stays zero until the last fight. EVENT_GOT_A_POKEMON_FROM_ELM through EVENT_BEAT_FALKNER is the actual curve, and the +50 at the end is the only reward that should dominate it. Batch eval is the honest one. A single window can miss an exit the batch finds. We log entropy beside return so a collapsed policy is visible before we claim the gym.

sections.heading: What's next for tensormew
sections.text: The Zephyr Badge is the first checkpoint, not the goal. Bugsy in Azalea Town. Teach the same loop HM01 Cut, stand on a real Cut tree, fire CUT_BLOCKED , and clear Ilex Forest with use_cut() on the way to the Hive Badge. Whitney in Goldenrod. The Miltank fight is the next battle-policy test. Replace "best damaging move" with a search battler (Metamon) once the party can reach her. Publish the cost table for the Falkner run: calls, tokens, and dollars for triggers-only vs always-on, taken from the saved episode rather than a short sample trace. Keep the curriculum moving: resume from post_falkner and pay the same style of waypoint and event rewards through Union Cave, Slowpoke Well, and Goldenrod. Longer term, the research stack in SPEC.md Appendix A: a larger simulator fleet, ghost scouts, and a minimax battler, on top of the mover, triggers, supervisor, and PPO that already earned badge one.

title: Tool Distill
tagline: Agents burn 30+ tool calls finding a path that only needed 5, then forget it. Our library tooldistill turns the path into a verified, reusable tool and keeps it working as the underlying tools change.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Watch an agent solve a real multi-step task and you see the same thing every time: twenty or thirty tool calls of trial and error to find a path that only needed four or five. Then the next run starts from zero and rediscovers it, paying the same tokens, the same minutes, and the same risk of taking a wrong turn. That is friction nobody chose. Several projects already let an agent save such a path as a new tool. What none of them answer is the question an engineer asks before letting generated code run in production: why should I trust it, and what happens when the tools underneath it change? tooldistill is our answer. The agent proposes; the library verifies. Nothing the model claims about a tool is believed; everything is measured.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: tooldistill is a Python library, with a CLI and a Claude Code plugin, that you drop into an existing agent loop with a handful of lines. It records every tool call of a run into a trace . When a run succeeds and was expensive, it nudges the model once to propose a distilled tool : a small Python function that completes the whole task by calling the base tools in a fixed, known-good sequence. The next time a similar task comes up, the agent makes one call instead of thirty, and the work inside that call costs no model tokens at all. In our invoice demo a discovery run of twenty to thirty base calls became a single distilled call with four inside it. Before any agent can use a proposal, it passes three checks: Static : the source is inspected with the AST before it is ever imported. Only a small allowlist of imports and statements is accepted, every base tool call must name a tool that exists and pass its required arguments, and the dependency list comes out of this pass. Replay : the tool is run against the responses recorded in the source run, matching each call on its exact arguments. No side effects, and a proof that the code reproduces the run. Efficiency : with $m$ measured calls, baseline $b$ and a configured reduction $r$, the tool passes only if $m \le b\,(1-r)$. Verified tools move through a lifecycle, draft → verified → active → suspect → deprecated, driven by evidence rather than by what the model says. When a base tool's schema changes, dependents are re-verified. When a tool that was down during discovery comes back, the affected distilled tools are flagged and can be rebuilt into a shorter version. When a distilled tool fails at run time, the agent receives a structured error, finishes the task with base tools, and that very run becomes the source of the next version. Base tools can be plain functions or MCP servers, and inside Claude Code the plugin's hooks record the session while its MCP server offers the verified tools back.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Spec first. A single design document fixed the terminology, the file format for distilled tools, the store schema, the verifier, the lifecycle table and a build order with acceptance criteria, and every step shipped as one commit with its tests green. The library is Python 3.12+, managed with uv, with a SQLite store in WAL mode so the agent process and the CLI can write at the same time. The runtime uses a context variable so the same call() helper runs live through the developer's executor or replays from fixtures. The built-in distiller asks Claude for a proposal with structured outputs, and treats the answer exactly like one from the agent. The MCP adapter runs the async MCP client on a background thread so the rest of the library stays synchronous by contract. The Claude Code plugin is a thin adapter: a SessionStart hook creates the trace, PostToolUse hooks record calls, an MCP server exposes the tools, and a slash command replaces the nudge. We tested without the network (338 tests with fake tools and a scripted model), then ran the four-step demo against the real model and a real Claude Code session, and published 0.1.0 to PyPI.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Replay is unforgiving. A single extra keyword argument the source run never sent makes the fixture lookup fail, so the rules the model reads had to say exactly that, and the hook-recorded outputs inside Claude Code had to be byte-identical to what the live executor records. They are. Incentives leak into generated code. Early runs showed the model dropping a step the task required, a calendar conflict check, because fewer calls read as a better verdict, and proposing tools whose inputs were the answer. Both were fixed in the prompts, not the checks: a tool must do everything the task asked, and its inputs may only be what the request states. A verdict that leaves the model guessing is a bug. "verified: 4 calls vs baseline 6" once led Claude to tell the user to promote a version that was already active. Verdicts now always state what became of the version. Two event loops, one contract. Bridging synchronous library code with the async MCP client and Claude Code's own server loop took care: anyio insists a connection is closed by the task that opened it. Small portability traps : uuid.uuid7 exists only on Python 3.14, so trace ids got a portable, time-ordered implementation; Windows shells treat <name> as redirection.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: The complete loop works end to end in both integrations: discovery, proposal, verification, reuse, recovery of a base tool with a rebuild, and a schema change producing a structured error, a fallback and a replacement version. The library never trusts the model and never calls a base tool on its own. It is on PyPI, and the plugin installs from the repository as a marketplace.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Verification is a product feature, not a safety afterthought: users will only hand an agent generated tools if something other than the model vouches for them. Replay proves reproduction, not generalization, so a runtime safety net matters as much as the checks. And the text the model reads shapes the code it writes more than any rule in the verifier does.

sections.heading: What's next for Tool Distill
sections.text: The problem has a buyer. Every team running agents in production pays for rediscovery twice: in tokens and latency on every run, and in the engineer who eventually hand-writes the tool the agent kept reinventing. tooldistill turns that into a measured saving per task, which is the number a team lead already tracks. Distribution is in place. The library installs from PyPI, the Claude Code plugin installs from the repository as a marketplace, and both are where developers already look for tools. A written walkthrough of the sandbox agent is the first piece of developer-facing content; adapters for the other agent frameworks widen the funnel without changing the core. The product is the shared store. A single developer gets the library for free. A team gets a hosted store where every agent proposes into one registry, one verification pipeline vouches for every tool, and a change in a base API retires or rebuilds the affected tools for everyone at once. That is the paid tier, and it is the same code behind a server. On the roadmap next: a heuristic check that rejects inputs which only appear in the source run's tool outputs, a subprocess sandbox for distilled tools, and an efficiency measure that credits saved model turns and tokens rather than calls alone.

title: BurnoutBuddy
tagline: Burnout Buddy watches your steps, commits, and eye bags to decide if you need a nap, a meme, or to touch grass — all in the name of not losing your mind while coding.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: As students juggling deadlines, hackathons, internships, and side projects, we’ve all felt the creeping burnout that’s hard to name but even harder to fight. Most mental health apps felt too serious or clinical, we wanted something fun, light, and proactive. After too many late nights debugging and forgetting what sunlight looks like, we realized burnout doesn’t announce itself, it just quietly takes over. We wanted to build something that could catch us slipping before we spiral, using the very data we already generate: our steps, our sleep, our GitHub commits, and our tired faces. Burnout Buddy became our goofy, 3D self-care sidekick, combining real-world signals, AI, and playful visuals to remind us to hydrate, vibe, and breathe before burnout hits too hard.

sections.heading: ？What it does
sections.text: Burnout Buddy is a personal wellbeing dashboard that tracks signs of burnout and helps you bounce back. It: Tracks physical and mental exhaustion using Fitbit data, GitHub commits, and real-time webcam fatigue detection. Calculates a personalized burnout score using sleep, steps, commits, and drowsiness levels. Offers timely interventions like hydration reminders, lo-fi Spotify tracks, and AI-generated motivational quotes. Provides journaling and task tracking to support mindful productivity. Visualizes burnout trends over time with interactive graphs. Encourages self-care before self-combustion — because burnout doesn’t announce itself, it just sneaks in.

sections.heading: 🧱 How we built it
sections.text: Frontend: React.js with custom CSS for styling, Chart.js for data visualization, and Spline for 3D embedding. Didn't forget Confetti (because vibes). Backend: Flask API to serve burnout score, quotes (via Google Gemini API), Fitbit and GitHub data. Data Pipelines: Python scripts to fetch Fitbit step/sleep data and GitHub commits, stored in MongoDB atlas. Fatigue Detection: Real-time drowsiness detection using OpenCV, MediaPipe, and dlib for webcam-based eye tracking Database: MongoDB Atlas stores time-series Fitbit/GitHub data and user journal entries securely Spotify Integration: Lo-fi music player powered by randomized Spotify Web Player embeds Burnout Scoring: Custom burnout score calculated from sleep, activity, commits, and fatigue using a weighted formula

sections.heading: 🎯 Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Integrating real-time webcam analysis using MediaPipe and dlib in a way that didn’t crash on multiple machines. Merging data from multiple APIs into a clean and meaningful score (averaging is easy, burnout isn’t). Making sure Flask, Mongo, and React played nice — and in sync — without one ghosting the others. React’s spontaneous desire to break when the camera stream said hello. A major CORS and API communication between Flask and React issue that turned out to be not so major (that we still spent 5 hours debugging) Parsing Google Gemini API responses into usable JSON formats

sections.heading: 🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Built a full-stack wellness app that blends data science, computer vision, and user-centered design Successfully integrated real-time webcam-based drowsiness detection using OpenCV, MediaPipe, and dlib Connected to both the Fitbit and GitHub APIs to gather personal activity data securely Designed a burnout scoring algorithm that combines physical, digital, and visual fatigue metrics Created a clean, fun, and interactive UI with features like Spotify embeds, journaling, and task tracking Visualized personal trends in sleep, steps, and commits using Chart.js ⁠Built a burnout detection tool that we’d genuinely want to keep using after this weekend.

sections.heading: 📚 What we learned
sections.text: How to wrangle health, code, and chaos into a meaningful burnout metric Real-time computer vision can absolutely be combined with soft UX to create something empathetic How to use OpenCV, MediaPipe, and dlib for facial fatigue detection How to integrate and authenticate with Fitbit and GitHub APIs How to process and visualize time-series data using Chart.js in React The value of designing experiences that care for the user, not just inform them Sometimes, you really do need to listen to a dashboard telling you to hydrate

sections.heading: ⏭️ What's next for BurnoutBuddy
sections.text: Scale to companies as a team wellness tool, offering anonymous burnout trends without compromising privacy Add journaling insights, mood tracking, and burnout trend visualizations Push smart alerts for burnout spikes — think “go outside” or “close VS Code” Integrate calendars and build a Chrome extension that nudges users away from doomscrolling Launch internally for dev teams — then gently expand into the wellness SaaS space Offer personalized recovery suggestions using machine learning trained on individual usage patterns and habits

title: Jesture
tagline: Jesture is a magical gesture-based drawing experience where your hands become the paintbrush! Wave your arms about and watch your beautiful (or hilariously terrible) art manifest on your screen!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The inspiration for Jesture mainly comes from popular fiction. The idea started as one one-off comment by a couple of my friends who thought it would be interesting to be able to control your computer through hand gestures like in Iron Man, where Tony Stark uses hand gestures to control devices or interact with virtual environments. This concept felt futuristic and exciting, but we also saw a practical application: making technology more accessible and intuitive. Gesture-based controls can provide an alternative interface for individuals with limited mobility or those who find traditional input devices like keyboards and mice challenging to use. By combining creativity and accessibility, we aimed to create a tool that is not only fun but also empowers users to interact with technology in a more natural and inclusive way. A paint application is the perfect demo for this new idea as it showcases the potential of gesture-based controls in a highly interactive yet fun way. Drawing is a universal activity that doesn't require any prior technical knowledge, making it accessible to users of all skill levels (even kids, in this case). By allowing users to create art with simple hand movements, the application demonstrates how natural gestures can replace traditional input devices like a mouse or stylus. A paint application also highlights the precision and responsiveness of the gesture recognition system. "The artists" can see immediate feedback as their gestures translate into lines, shapes, and colors on the canvas, making the technology feel seamless and engaging. Generally, a paint program provides a solid base to explore features, whether it be the general controls of a gesture-based system or integrating Gen-AI to guess the user's creations.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Jesture is an interactive drawing and guessing game powered by gesture recognition. Users can draw on a virtual canvas using hand gestures, switch between drawing modes (free draw, line, circle), and have an AI guess what they are drawing. It combines creativity, technology, and fun into one seamless package.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: MediaPipe for real-time hand gesture recognition. Raylib for rendering the drawing canvas and UI. OpenCV for capturing webcam input. Google GenAI for generating AI-based guesses of user drawings. Python as the primary programming language to integrate all these technologies. Tensorflow used to train the hand gesture recognition (thumbs up/thumbs down/pointing/etc.)

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Fine-tuning gesture recognition model to ensure accurate and responsive controls. Managing real-time performance while processing webcam input, rendering graphics, and running AI predictions simultaneously. (Some of my earlier implementations were painfully slow)

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Successfully integrating gesture recognition with a drawing application. Creating an "objectively" fun and interactive experience where AI guesses user drawings. Building a smooth and responsive interface that feels intuitive to use.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: How to work with MediaPipe for gesture recognition and its potential for other applications. The power of Raylib for creating interactive graphics in Python. The importance of optimizing performance when working with real-time systems. How to integrate AI models like Google GenAI into creative projects in a fun way

sections.heading: What's next for Jesture
sections.text: Adding more gesture-based controls? A multiplayer mode update where users can collaborate on drawings? Other platforms like mobile?

title: Tariffix
tagline: Tariffs made simple — track, compare, and calculate in seconds.

sections.text: Inspiration With tariffs becoming a popular topic in recent news, we saw a growing gap in consumer understanding of how these hidden costs influence everyday purchases. Tariffix was born out of a desire to make that information accessible, understandable, and easy for the average American shopper. What it does Tariffix is a dual-platform tool a Chrome extension and a website designed to help consumers understand the hidden layer of tariffs behind the products they buy. Browse smarter on sites like Amazon and Walmart with real-time insights into tariff-influenced pricing powered by AI. Look up HTS Codes (Harmonized Tariff Schedule) to understand import taxes on specific goods. Estimate how much companies pay in tariffs , and how those costs might be affecting you. How we built it Tariffix was developed as a monorepo featuring: A Next.js website for tariff education and HTS lookup. A Vite-powered Chrome extension to overlay data on online stores. A shared AI backend that scrapes metadata (product category, country of origin, etc.) and calculates estimates. A ** Pricing algorithm to ensure even with errors you ensure you get an estimate. A MongoDB database to store and update HTS codes and tariff rates. Challenges we ran into Finding accurate, real-time tariff data was harder than expected. We initially planned to use the U.S. Department of Commerce’s FTA Tariff Rate API , but it hadn’t been updated since early 2024. To solve this, we created a custom dataset using web scraping and tariff tables, allowing us to estimate tariff costs across various goods. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built a seamless integration between extension and site. Developed a flexible backend for live tariff estimation. Made a complex economic concept easier for the average consumer. What we learned Tariff data is fragmented and hard to access, centralizing it is valuable. Building for both web and extensions takes planning and modular design. UX matters a lot when explaining dry, complex topics like international trade. What's next for Tariffix Integrate real-time news on trade policy and tariff changes. Expand the database to include country-specific tariff rules. Partner with financial organizations and companies. Add visual graphs and price comparison tools for better insight.

title: Koalafied
tagline: 🐨 Improving the koala-ity of your job search 🐨

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Applying for internships and jobs can be tedious and boring. In a competitive job market, students like us are rushing to apply to hundreds of internships without a proper way to keep track of them. Many have turned to the bland Excel spreadsheets to mindlessly track their applications. This leaves students like us to be disorganized and bored when it comes to applying to jobs. We were inspired by idle games like Neko Atsume, and decided to create a similar mechanism for gamifying job applications.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Enter Koalafied , a gamified way to keep track of your job applications and important information like interviews and offers. As you work towards building a future for yourself, you also work towards building a community of cutesy and unique Koala's deep within a quiet forest. Users can sign up for an account to rise up the leaderboards to a wide range of koala-ity career choices and unmatched fame. They can collect koalas by applying to jobs, interviewing, and receiving offers. Track status updates on their applications and keep track of important interviews or deadlines via a notepad. Most importantly, they can play with their koalas!

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Koalafied is built on the MERN stack, meaning we used MongoDB, Express, React, and Node.js for our application. We first planned out our application by storyboarding and creating mock-ups for interfaces and then collaborated on setting up our database on MongoDB, discussing the structure of our data. We used Node and Express in combination with MongoDB to create users, an encrypted login system with JWT sessions, and store users' applications and of course those CUTE KOALAS. We found using MongoDB to be very efficient and easy to get started with. It made developing our backend a lot easier than we expected. For our frontend, we used React and Material UI to build a login form, a leaderboard, and most importantly the dashboard, which displays all of a user's application statuses, notes, and user statistics (applications, interviews, etc.). And don't forget about those CUTE KOALAS playing around on the bottom of the screen! Finally, we used Photoshop to edit and create graphics for our application, and Postman to test our backend API routes.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Building animations With Pure React : we found it difficult to set up the initial function structure that would allow for smooth animations and movement physics. There was a steep learning curve, but after gaining a better understanding of React's page update structure, we were able to create complex movement for our koalas. Creating Sessions with JSON Web Tokens (JWT) : Allowing users to login, stay logged in, and also be restricted from accessing protect routes without an account proved to be a struggle. This was one of the more difficult and annoying challenges to deal with, not through just it's difficulty, but also through its recurring nature. We learned that in times where you find yourself getting annoyed with problems like these it's important to stay calm and work together. As Always... Styling Everything : CSS is hard y'all. But we did it :)

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Evan Masiello, a second-time hackathon participant, first honed his existing skill for building react pages and creating backend connections when developing the dashboard and Express endpoints. Something that he did not expect to end up developing was the animation for the Koalas, but he found it to be a very fun experience. Evan enjoyed challenging himself by thinking of new ways the Koalas could move or be interacted with and figuring out how to implement them. He definitely strengthened his understanding and skills related to React.js through this process and also gained valuable experience using MongoDB for more intricate data than in the past. Benjamin Johnson learned deeply about how react works and react syntax. A step up from what he was normally accustomed to, which was just HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for building a webpage. Ben expanded on his knowledge of MongoDB which he had minimal knowledge of before Bitcamp to implement the leaderboard functionality. Caleb Holland, a second-time Bitcamp participant traveled from his usual comfort as a frontend developer to explore the backend. He learned how to create an encrypted user system using Node and MongoDB, create sessions with JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and most importantly learned how to have a good time with his pals. In addition, he continued to hone his sense of design by creating a majority of the graphics for the application, and by building some of the components used on the login and dashboard page.

sections.heading: What's next for Koalafied
sections.text: Originally, we wanted to use the Gemini API to generate the sprites for the koalas and create endless quests for the user. Although this was beyond the scope of this hackathon, this is something we'd like to implement as we improve upon the project in the future. We also had aspirations to have this tool auto track your applications after applying for jobs, either through an extension, or an email connection. This would make it much easier for users to organize their applications, as this removes the need to manually add in their applications. In the end, it was a tree-at to create Koalafied. We learned a lot, and we look forward to expanding upon it in the future!

title: Quaran.Tech
tagline: Experience contact tracing in this game (with AI, because why not)

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: During major public health events, the public is often not aware of the duties of public health workers such as contact tracers, decreasing the efficiency of procedures such as public health mandates and "flattening the curve." This game aims to educate the public on various public health risks and how they are dealt with. In addition, Efthimios Papadopoulos is an avid gamer and it was noticed that current games may become boring after the storyline has been exhausted. This game is an experiment in the use of large language models to enhance game experiences through the generation of alternate storylines.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Quaran.Tech is a cross-platform HTML5 game that allows players to experience the life of a public health specialist in a fast-paced environment. When days are shortened to in-game seconds, the more tedious parts of this occupation are eliminated, and we are left with the most intense and nerve-wracking decision-making.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: HTML/CSS/JS/jQuery was used to develop the game frontend which is hosted on Cloudflare Pages The backend runs on Cloudflare Workers ensuring scalability for the long run. Gemini API is used to generate unlimited new scenarios for players to experience. MongoDB stores existing scenarios. The .TECH domain name was utilized.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Making a game without a game engine was more difficult than we thought. Without the abstractions of scenes and sprites, mundane commands such as showing and removing icons sometimes led to strange, difficult, and random errors. Time was a serious constraint. We initially did not think of the LLM integration, but when we started writing the game storyline file, a new appreciation for game development was gained as we realized that writing storylines was extremely time-consuming.Therefore, we decided to integrate the AI story writing into our game, which accelerated development of the storyline, but slowed us down due to the added complexity. ...and finally, CORS issues. A lot of CORS issues.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're proud that we built a game in the short timeframe provided. Efthimios had never written a game before of any sort, and Heng had only experimented with some small games in easy-to-use game engines. In addition, it was our first time integrating Google Gemini into an application.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Efthimios learned a lot of HTML and CSS techniques. From zero to hero type ah learning 😤😤😤. Heng Ye learned the intricacies of developing game software. In addition, he learned how to utilize Gemini API, Cloudflare Pages, and Cloudflare Workers.

sections.heading: What's next for QuaranTech
sections.text: Voice chat with AI characters (doctors, patients, government officials) More reliable LLM storyline generation.
