title: Batman
tagline: Batman is an iMessage contact that watches your back when you meet a stranger. It checks in quietly and alerts the friend you chose if you go silent. Secret code words get you out. No app needed.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: First dates, Facebook Marketplace pickups, apartment viewings: we meet strangers all the time, and most safety apps assume you'll open them at the exact moment things go wrong. We wanted something closer to a friend who knows where you are, checks in only when something seems off, and gets help if you go quiet. Everyone already has iMessage open, so Batman lives there. There's no app, just a contact.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Text Batman your plan ("date at 7 at Lula Cafe"). It asks a couple of quick questions, gets a yes from the friend you chose, and watches your Find My location for that window only. If you leave fast, go dark, or run late, it checks in discreetly. If you don't answer, it alerts your friend with your last location. Two secret code words give you a silent way out: one gets you an excuse to leave, the other quietly alerts your friend.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: iMessage: TypeScript on Node, using Photon's spectrum-ts for messaging and advanced-imessage over gRPC for Find My, Focus status, and read receipts. Plan engine: a deterministic state machine with durable SQLite timers that survive restarts. The escalation ladder is code, not a model. Risk rules: geofences with hysteresis, plus speed checks for leaving by car: $$ r = \max(r_{\text{base}},\ 2\,a), \qquad \text{outside} \iff d > r + \min(0.5\,r,\ 60\,\text{m}), \qquad v \ge 7\ \text{m/s} $$ where $a$ is the GPS accuracy and $d$ is the haversine distance to the venue. Ladder timers tighten at night and for riskier meetups: $$ T_k' = T_k \cdot 0.7^{\,\text{night}} \cdot 0.6^{\,\text{vigilance}} $$ Language: Claude handles plan extraction and reply classification with structured outputs. Code words are matched deterministically before any model call. Hosting and process: an always-on single machine on Fly.io. We built it with parallel Claude Code subagents (core, conversation, integration, test, and safety review), backed by 1,000+ tests and evals.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Safety logic should never depend on a model. The LLM reads messages; it never decides to escalate. Evals matter. Our reply classifier hit 98.7% accuracy with zero distress replies labeled "OK". Code words hit 100% recall with 0 false positives across about 2,000 normal messages. Real platform limits shape the design. On a shared pool, every user gets their own number and has to text first. Calls need a dedicated line.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: Platform limits. Outbound calls were blocked (SIP 403) and native location pins weren't supported, so we built honest text fallbacks. A sleeping laptop. Windows Modern Standby silently paused the server mid-test, so we moved Batman to an always-on host. GPS noise. 300 m outliers were faking departures until we added outlier rejection. Tone. Batman has to feel like a friend, not a form, without ever revealing anything on a lock screen during a meetup.

title: Bazaarly
tagline: Bazaarly helps pop-up apparel vendors track event inventory, accept Solana payments, and use Snowflake and Nessie to analyze sales, monitor cash flow, and make smarter restocking decisions.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: One of our teammates has a friend who runs a flea-market stall selling apparel. From hearing about their experience, we saw how much work goes into running a small pop-up business: keeping track of products and stock, recording payments, understanding expenses, and figuring out how much the event actually earned. These tasks often live in different places, which makes it difficult to get a clear picture during or after an event. A vendor might know that some items sold, but still have to reconcile sales, remaining inventory, transaction activity, and event fees before deciding what to bring next time. That conversation inspired us to build Bazaarly: a tool that connects event inventory and checkout with financial tracking and sales analysis. We want vendors to spend less time piecing together records and more time understanding how their business is performing.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Bazaarly is a React and TypeScript dashboard for pop-up apparel events. Vendors can organize garment inventory by event, review product details and stock statuses, and see sales activity associated with each event. The checkout prototype uses Solana Pay on Devnet. A customer can initiate a payment for an item, and Bazaarly records the sale only after the payment is confirmed on the Solana network. Event sales records and summaries use the item’s USD price, so vendors can review results in familiar dollar values. This is a Devnet prototype; it does not process real-money payments. For each event, Bazaarly summarizes confirmed revenue and sales activity, with product and category breakdowns. It also tracks vendor-fee coverage and provides a sales ledger for reviewing recorded transactions. Vendors can compare completed events to understand how their results differ and use that information when planning future inventory. We also explored using the Nessie sandbox banking API for a financial-management dashboard. The prototype is intended to help vendors review simulated account and customer activity, track money coming in and going out, and get a clearer view of cash flow. Nessie provides simulated banking data, so this part demonstrates the dashboard concept rather than connecting to a vendor’s real bank account. In addition, we developed a separate Snowflake Cortex sales-consultant prototype. It accepts uploaded sales CSV files, calculates metrics such as total revenue, average order value, and category mix, then passes those figures to a language model to support evidence-based recommendations. A vendor could use it to examine which categories contributed most to revenue or whether sales were concentrated in lower-priced items. The Nessie financial dashboard and Snowflake consultant are prototypes; they are not yet connected to Bazaarly’s live sales records. The consultant uses the data in the uploaded CSV and does not claim to have access to live fashion-trend data.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The main Bazaarly dashboard uses React and TypeScript for the user interface, with Firebase and Firestore for application data. Events and inventory are organized so vendors can review products and sales in the context of a specific event. The Solana Pay checkout runs as a separate app and connects to Bazaarly through the checkout flow. We treat a sale as complete only after the Devnet transaction is confirmed; creating a payment request alone does not add a confirmed sale to event analytics. The Nessie prototype uses simulated banking data to demonstrate cash-flow and customer/account activity views. The Snowflake Cortex consultant uses a Node.js backend: it processes uploaded sales CSV data and calculates metrics on the server before sending the structured figures to the model.

sections.heading: Challenges and lessons
sections.text: A key challenge was deciding when a sale should count as a sale. A checkout request and a confirmed on-chain payment are different events. We designed the prototype so event reporting relies on confirmed payments, helping keep the sales ledger and analytics tied to completed transactions. We also learned that QR payment compatibility can vary between wallets and devices. A payment flow that works in one wallet may behave differently in another, so wallet interoperability needs testing as part of the checkout experience. Another challenge was bringing financial activity and sales analysis into a useful view without overstating what the prototypes can do. Nessie’s simulated account data can demonstrate how a cash-flow dashboard might work, while Snowflake Cortex can analyze metrics from an uploaded sales file. Neither prototype currently reads live financial or sales data from the main Bazaarly app.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: Our first priority is letting vendors record what they paid for each item when it’s added to inventory, so Bazaarly can show true profit and margin by item, category and event instead of just revenue. We also want to test with real vendors to see whether the insights change how they stock and price. Nessie is a sandbox, so a production version would need a real financial-data provider and a secure connection to vendors’ accounts.

title: CampusSync
tagline: CampusSync streamlines college life by matching friends' free time, coordinating spontaneous hangouts, and tracking club meetings and dues.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: As a first-year college student, navigating campus life is overwhelming. The lightbulb moment came when my brother asked for my schedule on Google Calendar, and we instantly saw our mutual free times. It made me realize how convenient it is to know when peers are free to grab food or hang out. I wanted to build an app that eliminates the friction of scheduling, alongside the headache of tracking campus clubs and dues—tasks that shouldn't cause students unnecessary stress.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: CampusSync is an all-in-one student platform that centralizes college life. It automatically maps out mutual free time between friends for spontaneous hangouts, tracks course schedules, and unifies campus organization life. It makes discovering clubs effortless for first-years and simplifies tracking meeting times and paying dues, replacing chaotic posters, missed club fairs, and endless group chats.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built CampusSync using a modern mobile-first stack focused on clean UI, real-time schedule overlap visualization, and intuitive dashboard layouts to manage classes, friend statuses, and club directories seamlessly.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Designing a clean interface that could cross-reference multiple complex schedules without looking cluttered was tough. Balancing real-time schedule alignment with club listings, meeting conflict detection, and dues tracking required careful data structuring and UI refinement.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud of creating a solution that genuinely solves a real, daily pain point for college freshmen. Bringing schedule syncing, friend coordination, and club management into one cohesive, beautifully designed app feels like a major win.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned the importance of user-centric design—especially for incoming freshmen who feel lost trying to discover campus culture outside of social media or scattered flyers. Simplifying complex college data into quick, glanceable insights is key to building useful tools.

sections.heading: What's next for CampusSync

title: Ebb
tagline: Ebb is a smartwatch for kids with special needs that senses rising stress, calms them with breathing, scenes and a familiar voice, and learns what works, keeping parents and teachers in the loop.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: For five years I worked as a tutor, and over that time I worked with many students with special needs. I also got to know their parents, several of whom worked as instructional assistants (IAs) in schools. Those conversations stayed with me. They described a community that is deeply committed but often stretched thin: students who get overwhelmed in the middle of a lesson and can’t always find the words to say so, and adults who are trying to notice and respond to many needs at once. They also described how hard it can be to keep strategies consistent between home and school. What stood out most was that none of this came from a lack of care. The families and educators I spoke with cared enormously. What was missing were tools that fit the moment, ones that are personal to each student, discreet, and respectful of their dignity. I kept thinking about how a student might get a quiet, private way to reset, and how an educator might get a gentle way to check in without singling anyone out. That is why we built ebb. It is a wearable and companion app that lets parents and teachers set up a student’s calming preferences, send supportive prompts, and give students a way to ask for help on their own terms. We chose techniques with real support behind them, like slow breathing and predictable routines, and we made privacy and sensory safety central to the design. I wanted to take action instead of only hearing about the problem. Ebb is our first step toward a solution that is built with the community’s voice at its center, and we hope to keep improving it alongside the families and educators who inspired it.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Ebb is a smartwatch, an iPhone app and a website that help kids with special needs calm down before a meltdown, and keep their parents and teachers informed. On the watch Senses rising stress: it reads movement (rocking, hand-flapping) and room loudness, and compares them with what’s normal for this child. It keeps loudness levels only, never audio. Responds in steps: a gentle breathing buzz → a full calm mode (a breathing circle, a calm scene, a soothing voice, light vibration) → a “needs an adult” alert if it doesn’t settle. Starts calm three ways: by itself, when the child taps the watch, or when a teacher or parent taps Start in the app. Asks the child afterwards: three faces for better, same or worse. It learns Measures results: how much agitation dropped and how fast the child settled. Tunes itself: “False alarm” or “Helped” ratings from teachers make it less or more sensitive. Picks scenes: it learns which scene helps this child most at each time of day, and still tries new ones sometimes. Predicts: it forecasts the riskiest hours ahead. For the adults Parent setup: pair the watch with a QR code; fill in an assessment, and AI drafts a calm profile; choose the calm voice (an AI voice or their own cloned voice); approve 6 scenes each week. Teacher tools: start or stop calm, rate each moment, write journal notes. Live view and insights: a live agitation graph, a heatmap of when hard moments happen, what works, and an AI weekly report. Texting: parents and teachers can text Ebb (“How was Sam today?”) and pass notes to each other by iMessage. Location (optional): GPS only if the parent opts in; teachers see it only during school hours. Privacy: the child is known by a nickname only, there’s no audio, the AI never receives names, and data is automatically deleted after a set time.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We got a programmable watch, created a ui for the website, app and watch. Connected the backend and the logins. We used photon for the messaging system. We used gemini for the profile for the assessment for the student done by the parent. We used the Arduino ide to push all the updates to the watch. We also used elevenlabs for the voice feature and voice cloning for the familiar parent/guardian.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: We definitely ran into lots of problems especially connecting the database to the watch, and making the watch usable.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A closed loop on real hardware. The watch senses rising agitation, buzzes a breathing cue, and starts calm mode by itself. It then measures whether the calm moment actually helped and feeds that back into its own settings. We tested this end to end on a LilyGO T-Watch S3 Plus. It learns per child. Each child gets their own movement and noise baseline, sensitivity that tunes itself from teacher “false alarm” ratings, and a Thompson-sampling scene picker. Its reward combines the teacher’s rating, the child’s own check-in, and the measured drop in agitation. A full product in one weekend: firmware; an iPhone app (QR pairing, live graphs, insights, location); a Supabase backend with row-level security on every table; a website; AI calm profiles and weekly reports; a calm voice that can be the parent’s own; iMessage texting for parents and teachers. Privacy from the start. Children are known by nickname only. The watch never records audio. Names are stripped before anything reaches the AI. Location is opt-in, and teachers can only see it during school hours. Old data is deleted automatically. We also fixed every issue our security reviews found before demo day.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Hardware is humbling. HTTPS failed until the watch synced its clock. Venue Wi-Fi was 5 GHz only, and the watch needs 2.4 GHz. A volume setting silently wrapped around to zero. The tiny speaker sets a hard ceiling on volume. Simple statistics carry a lot of weight. A per-child baseline plus z-scores beat any one-size-fits-all threshold. Defaults matter for kids. Auto-start is off until a parent turns it on, and adults always keep control. Security reviews catch real bugs. Ours found that an email-style iMessage handle could pose as a parent, and that a teacher could switch off auto-start by flipping “false alarm” on and off. Both are fixed. Integrations shape architecture. Photon’s iMessage connection needs a constantly running program, so we built a small bridge with a message outbox instead of forcing it into serverless functions.

sections.heading: What's next for Ebb
sections.text: Pilot with real classrooms and calibrate the agitation model with special-education teachers, behaviour analysts and occupational therapists. Add heart rate and skin response on future hardware for earlier, more accurate warnings, plus a louder speaker. Report against IEP goals so progress data supports each student’s individualized education plan. Become compliant: FERPA and COPPA review; school data agreements; deleting a child’s data with one tap; encrypted offline storage. Build an Android app and multi-classroom dashboards for schools. Train an on-device model on labelled moments, so the watch spots patterns before the numbers rise.

title: Klane
tagline: Your next job is hiding in the headlines. Klane turns news, permits, and business activity into contractor leads - on a map or over text.

sections.text: Klane Your next customer is out there. Klane helps you find the evidence.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: A roofing contractor should not have to spend their evening searching permit portals, procurement notices, and expansion announcements to find tomorrow’s work. Useful signals often appear before someone posts a straightforward request for a contractor. We wanted to connect those scattered clues to the right trade, location, and next step, in an interface people could use between jobs. The design combines Carolina blue with Frutiger Aero’s sense of space and movement: an interactive globe, frosted controls, and a transition into a local opportunity map.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Remembers a business profile, trade, and territory. Guest, John Adam, and Maya Chen demonstrate different starting contexts. Runs bounded research across public news, official project pages, permits, procurement notices, and institutional announcements, revealing initial results while additional batches continue. Filters candidates for trade relevance, currentness, source support, and physical location, including checks for competing contractors and expired procurement notices. Opens company dossiers with dated indicators, titled evidence links, proposed scope, timing, and published professional contact research when available. Models materials, labor, equipment, overhead, reserve, staffing, break-even bids, and installation timelines from editable job assumptions. Supports voice search, spoken briefings, follow-up chat, saved prospects, and an account-aware iMessage agent. Records evidence observations over time and shows permit reference analytics. Outreach requires review and approval of the recipient and message. Public evidence indicates a prospect, not confirmed purchasing intention. A bounded search can return fewer results when evidence fails the checks. Contact details require published source support.

sections.heading: How I built it
sections.text: React, TypeScript, Vite, custom CSS, MapLibre GL, and Lucide power the interface. A Node.js HTTP server keeps provider credentials outside the browser, validates data with Zod, and coordinates research, voice, messaging, and database adapters. OpenAI's ChatGPT 6.1 Sol was used for coding assistance.

sections.heading: Technical Toolkit
sections.text: Languages Interface & Development AI & Messaging Data & Platforms Program and data flow flowchart TD A[Web prompt, voice input, or Photon iMessage] --> B[Account context and request budget] B --> C[Trade and territory research plan] C --> D[Gemini grounded research and structured extraction] C --> E[Bounded municipal and institutional feeds] D --> F[Source, currentness, trade-fit, and address checks] E --> F F --> G[Progressive map and company dossiers] F --> H[Tiger Cloud Postgres and Timescale evidence memory] H --> I[Sync outbox] I --> J[Snowflake signal analytics] K[Official Raleigh permit feed] --> J G --> L[Follow-up agent and editable job economics] H --> L J --> L L --> M[ElevenLabs spoken briefing] L --> N[Reviewed outreach draft] Gemini: grounded discovery, structured extraction, account-aware answers, uploaded brief interpretation, and proposed estimate assumptions. The adapters support a Gemini API key or Vertex AI ADC. The development demo currently uses Gemini through Vertex AI; an API-key text request was separately verified, while grounded API-key requests encountered quota limits. Photon: Spectrum powers iMessage. Verified sender mappings connect conversations to contractor profiles. Explicit requests for another trade override the profile default; messaging can launch fresh research without a prior website scan. ElevenLabs: Scribe provides microphone transcription with live partial text through the realtime integration. Flash provides spoken company briefings; alignment timestamps drive word progress when available. Tiger Data: Tiger Cloud hosts operational Postgres/Timescale storage for profiles, discovered companies, signal observations, conversation context, outreach receipts, and the warehouse outbox. Weekly evidence history measures what Klane observed over time; it does not establish market-wide demand. Web favorites currently remain browser-local. Snowflake: receives signal events from Tiger’s outbox and stores official permit reference data. The development warehouse was loaded with 2,000 real City of Raleigh permit records. Issue-week activity, coverage dates, and declared whole-project valuations provide context. A separate comparable-job table supports verified completed-job rates only when enough matching records exist. No verified paid-job dataset is included, and permit valuations are never substituted for contractor prices. .tech: klane.tech is the acquired project domain. Hosting, production authentication, and domain routing remain next steps. Other public services include official ArcGIS permit/address feeds, US Census address geocoding, and CARTO/OpenStreetMap basemap data. Google Search grounding discovers indexed sources; Klane is not an exhaustive crawler of every local record system. Keeping research bounded A discovery run uses up to three batches targeting five qualified buyers, capped model outputs, and a configurable per-minute call budget. Caching, shared in-flight requests, bounded source fetches, and on-demand dossiers reduce repeated calls. Follow-up questions reuse account and company context. Provider quotas and insufficient evidence can still limit a run.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Finding a mention of “electrical” is easier than finding an actual buyer for electrical work. We iterated on competitor filtering, stale bid deadlines, explicit trade scope, source corroboration, and address verification. We also worked through provider quotas, ADC setup, Snowflake network access, and the distinction between permit valuations and completed-job prices. Globe interaction and globe-to-map transitions required careful camera and animation handling. Live microphone text, readable iMessage replies, and evidence presentation each needed their own interaction patterns.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We connected web research and a field messaging agent to the same account-aware backend. We built a progressive map, linked evidence dossiers, inspectable work-package economics, and a real database-to-warehouse flow. We chose to withhold unsupported prices and stale prospects instead of filling the interface with invented data.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Useful research is a chain of checks: who the buyer is, what work is supported, where it happens, when the signal matters, and which source establishes each claim. We learned to use operational storage for memory, a warehouse for aggregated reference data, and deterministic calculations for estimates users can inspect.

sections.heading: What's next for Klane
sections.text: Expand official municipal coverage, add verified completed-contract comparables, improve contact-role coverage, and evaluate opportunity relevance with real contractors. Deploy behind production authentication with stable database egress, connect klane.tech , and add durable scheduled research and approved follow-up workflows.

title: Phish Finder
tagline: Ever received a link that might look suspicious? Well worry no more.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Have you ever gotten a text with a link and thought, “This looks kind of sketchy, but I’m not sure?” That happens all the time. A phishing link might look like a delivery update, a bank alert, or a warning that your account is about to be locked. And when the message feels urgent, it is easy to click before really thinking about it. That’s why we built Phish Finder . We wanted to make checking a suspicious link as easy as texting it to someone you trust. Instead of just giving a yes or no, we wanted Phish Finder to show people why .

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Phish Finder lets you investigate a suspicious link without opening it yourself. Here’s how it works: You forward a suspicious link to Phish Finder through iMessage . Phish Finder immediately lets you know that it is checking the page. The link is opened inside an isolated sandbox instead of on your phone. We inspect the page, domain, redirects, threat-intelligence sources, brand impersonation signals, forms, and other warning signs. Phish Finder sends a screenshot of the page back to you, followed by a verdict like Dangerous , Suspicious , No red flags found , or Couldn’t check . You can open the web dashboard to see the full report, including the evidence behind the verdict and previous scans. If something looks malicious, we also make it easier to prepare the information needed to report it to the FTC. We were especially careful about uncertainty. If one of our checks fails or we cannot confirm something, we show that instead of pretending the link is safe. You can also send Phish Finder a screenshot or photo of a QR code, and it can extract the suspicious link and analyze it the same way.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built Phish Finder as a pipeline connecting iMessage, a cloud-hosted sandbox, our security analyzer, Gemini, and a React dashboard . When a link comes in, our gateway sends it to a Python FastAPI analyzer running on a cloud VM. The analyzer opens the page in an isolated browser environment, captures a screenshot, follows redirects, and checks multiple security signals. We also query threat-intelligence sources and look for things like suspicious domains, brand impersonation, and credential forms. Those findings are combined into our scoring system to produce a final verdict. We use Gemini to help turn the technical evidence into an explanation that is easier for a normal user to understand. The result is then sent back through iMessage and stored so it can also be explored through the dashboard. For the frontend, we used: React for the dashboard TypeScript for safer development Vite for our development and build setup TanStack Query for API requests and scan updates React Router for moving between reports Zod to validate the data coming from our backend We designed the dashboard with a Frutiger Aero-inspired style using blue skies, glassy panels, bubbles, and our clownfish logo.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One of our biggest challenges was safely opening suspicious websites. We wanted Phish Finder to learn as much as possible from a page without clicking buttons, entering information, downloading files, or exposing our own machine. That meant thinking carefully about redirects, network access, browser behavior, and what our sandbox should and should not be allowed to reach. Another challenge was connecting the input, frontend, and backend altogether. A single scan moves through iMessage, the gateway, the analyzer, external security services, Gemini, and finally the dashboard. And we had to be careful about our wording. “No red flags found” is not the same thing as saying a website is definitely safe.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We’re proud that Phish Finder does more than just throw out a warning. It actually shows users the evidence behind the verdict. We’re also proud of: Building an end-to-end flow where someone can text a link and receive a screenshot and verdict back Safely inspecting suspicious pages in an isolated environment Combining multiple signals instead of relying on a single phishing indicator Building a dashboard where users can explore the evidence behind each scan Getting 10/10 correct results in our evaluation Deploying the system to the cloud so the full texting flow still works with our development laptops closed Giving the project its own Frutiger Aero-inspired visual identity and interface (very fun)

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: One thing we learned is that it is important to communicate uncertainty rather than presenting results as pure fact. If a tool gives someone a score or a verdict, they are probably going to trust it, so we had to think carefully about what that verdict actually means. We also learned how important it is to define the communication between different parts of a system early. Even small differences between what the gateway, backend, and frontend expect can cause a lot of problems later. Finally, we learned that because link previews don’t run JavaScript, every report needs its own server-rendered preview image.

sections.heading: What's next for Phish Finder
sections.text: There is still a lot we would like to build. Next, we want to: Test our scoring system against a much larger collection of phishing and legitimate websites Improve visual impersonation detection so we can compare suspicious pages against real brand websites Add more threat-intelligence sources Improve scam reporting and sharing Make the experience even easier for families and people who are less comfortable with technology Our goal is for Phish Finder to become something people can use the moment a message makes them hesitate: Forward the link. Let Phish Finder check it first.

title: Scrub+
tagline: transforming human-computer interaction for surgeons

sections.text: Scrub+ Rethinking how surgeons interact with medical imaging, without touching a computer.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: My father had to undergo an urgent heart procedure because of serious coronary blockages. It was a complicated case, and my family had a hard time finding a specialist who could perform it. Through that experience, I became interested in the practical challenges of surgical workflows and how engineering could help address them. One problem that caught my attention was how surgeons interact with medical imaging during operations. Once surgeons are scrubbed in, they cannot use a regular mouse or keyboard without compromising sterility. Instead, they may need to ask someone outside the sterile field to navigate CT scans for them. Finding a specific anatomical structure, changing the viewing angle, or taking a measurement can require several rounds of verbal instructions. In a 2016 study , completing an image-navigation task by directing an assistant took an average of 246 seconds, compared with 215 seconds using gestures. Touchless medical imaging systems already exist, but many focus primarily on basic navigation, such as scrolling, zooming, and rotating. Surgeons still have to manually search through scans to find specific information, and some systems require specialized hardware.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Scrub+ is a touchless, spatial computing interface that lets users explore real 3D CT scans through hand gestures and voice commands using a regular laptop webcam. Users can rotate medical images, move cutting planes through anatomical structures, measure distances, locate specific anatomy, and compare hypothetical surgical plans. The main feature is an anatomy-aware voice copilot. Instead of manually navigating through a scan, users can ask Scrub+ to find the information they need. For example: "Scrub, show me the tumor relative to the portal vein." Highlights both structures, calculates their closest distance, and moves the camera to show their relationship. "Scrub, show me where the tumor is closest to a major vessel." Searches the available vessel segmentations, identifies the nearest vessel, and displays the measurement alongside a CT cross-section. "Scrub, focus on the left kidney." Automatically locates and frames the kidney. "Scrub, save this plan." Saves the current cutting plane and camera view. "Scrub, compare this cut to the original plan." Compares tumor margin, remaining liver volume, and vessel intersections between two hypothetical resection plans. "Scrub, show me the original plan." Restores the previously saved configuration. Scrub+ also supports gesture-controlled surgical planning. Users can move a cutting plane through a liver CT scan and see measurements update as the plane changes. An optimization algorithm searches 3,751 nearby cutting-plane candidates to identify alternatives based on selected planning constraints. The application also includes a virtual aortic stent-graft demonstration with simplified sizing, positioning, and flow calculations. All anatomical measurements are calculated from the CT data and segmentation masks rather than generated by a language model.

sections.heading: How I built it
sections.text: Medical imaging and preprocessing I used a real liver CT scan from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon and processed the imaging data using Python. I also used TotalSegmentator to generate additional anatomical labels. The processed CT volume and segmentation masks are included with the application, allowing users to explore the demo without running the preprocessing pipeline themselves. Users can also import their own NIfTI CT scans directly into the browser. Imported scans can be viewed and measured, while compatible segmentation masks enable the anatomy-aware planning features. 3D volume rendering I built a custom volume renderer using three.js, WebGL, and GLSL shaders. Instead of displaying a static anatomical model, Scrub+ renders the underlying CT volume together with its segmentation labels. This allows individual structures, such as tumors and blood vessels, to be highlighted within the surrounding anatomy. A movable cutting plane exposes cross-sections through the CT volume and supports interactive exploration of hypothetical resections. Hand tracking and gesture recognition I integrated MediaPipe to track 21 landmarks on each hand using a regular webcam. Scrub+ supports several gestures: Open palm to move and tilt a cutting plane. Pinch and drag to rotate the 3D scan. Two fingers to place distance measurements. Fist to lock the cutting plane. Two-handed pinch gestures to zoom. To make the controls more stable, I implemented landmark smoothing and a gesture state machine to reduce jitter and unintended transitions between gestures. I also experimented with a small neural network trained on synthetic hand-landmark data to improve gesture recognition when fingers overlap. Because a regular webcam cannot directly measure depth, the application estimates relative hand depth from apparent hand size. Geometry and surgical planning I implemented the measurement and planning calculations using the underlying voxel data and segmentation masks. These include: Liver remnant volume, calculated from segmented liver voxels on either side of the proposed cut. Tumor margins, calculated using distance transforms. Vessel intersections, determined from the segmented vascular structures. Anatomical distances, calculated directly from the 3D segmentation geometry. A geometric optimizer that evaluates 3,751 nearby cutting-plane candidates. The planning measurements update as the user manipulates the cutting plane. Voice copilot The voice interface uses the browser's Web Speech API and the wake word "Scrub." Common requests are handled by a predefined command parser. An optional language model interprets less structured requests and maps them to supported application actions. The language model does not calculate distances, volumes, or surgical margins. Those calculations are performed by the geometry engine. The core viewer, gesture controls, measurements, and optimizer work independently of an LLM.

sections.heading: Challenges I ran into
sections.text: Making gestures intuitive My first implementation used palm orientation to switch between rotating the model and manipulating the cutting plane. Although the gestures were technically recognizable, they were awkward to use consistently. I eventually changed the controls to use an open palm for cutting-plane manipulation and a pinch for rotation. This made the interactions more natural and reduced accidental mode changes. Handling unreliable hand landmarks MediaPipe can produce unstable landmark predictions when fingers overlap or become partially obscured. I added filtering and gesture-state logic to improve stability. I also experimented with a lightweight neural network for gesture recognition under occlusion. The neural network showed improvements on synthetic hand data, although real-world validation is still needed. Estimating depth without specialized hardware I wanted Scrub+ to work with an ordinary laptop webcam rather than requiring a dedicated depth camera. To approximate hand movement toward and away from the camera, I used changes in the hand's apparent size. This provides useful relative movement for interaction, but it is not equivalent to precise 3D hand tracking. Rendering and processing large CT volumes Medical imaging data can be computationally expensive to process and render interactively. Combining volume rendering, segmentation overlays, hand tracking, and continuously updating geometric measurements required preprocessing and performance optimization to keep the interface responsive.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that I'm proud of
sections.text: Built an interactive 3D medical imaging viewer that renders real CT data directly in the browser. Implemented touchless gesture controls using a regular laptop webcam. Created an anatomy-aware voice copilot that can locate structures and calculate measurements. Built planning measurements that respond dynamically to changes in the cutting plane. Implemented a geometric optimizer that evaluates thousands of candidate cuts. Verified measurement calculations against independent NumPy implementations. Built the main functionality without requiring an LLM. In one test configuration, the geometric optimizer increased the measured tumor margin from 6.3 mm to 10.2 mm and reduced intersected segmented vessel components from two to zero. This demonstrates an improvement in the selected geometric metrics, not proof that the alternative cut would produce a better clinical outcome.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.text: One of my biggest takeaways was that making an interaction technically possible doesn't necessarily make it useful. My initial goal was to control medical images with hand gestures. But I realized that simply replacing mouse movements with gestures doesn't eliminate the work involved in finding a particular anatomical structure or measurement. That led me to focus more on anatomy-aware navigation and direct information retrieval. I also learned that the most useful role for an LLM in this application isn't making medical decisions; it's interpreting what the user wants and invoking the appropriate deterministic tools. Finally, working with real CT data made me appreciate how much complexity exists between a visually convincing medical imaging prototype and a clinically usable system.

sections.heading: What's next for Scrub+
sections.text: Scrub+ is currently a research and educational prototype, not a clinically validated surgical planning system. My next steps are to test the interface with surgeons and clinical trainees, evaluate gesture reliability under realistic operating-room conditions, and validate the anatomical measurements and planning algorithms more extensively. I also want to expand the planning capabilities with more detailed vascular anatomy, liver segment mapping, and more realistic resection geometries. Ultimately, my goal is to make medical imaging more accessible during complex procedures and reduce unnecessary friction in surgical workflows. With further development and clinical validation, systems like Scrub+ could help clinicians retrieve information more efficiently and spend less time navigating software.
