title: Pyrosense
tagline: a wearable live hazard map that builds itself as you walk

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Firefighters entering unfamiliar buildings have to make critical decisions. This necessitates situational awareness, but enter smoke, heat, darkness, and changing airflow, and it becomes difficult to understand both the structure and how hazardous gases are distributed inside it. Many dangerous gases (VOCs) are invisible and cannot be reliably detected by humans without sensors. Existing gas monitors are essential, but they still rely heavily on manual sampling. Firefighters may need to take readings at multiple locations because concentration can change with airflow, ventilation, vapor density, and sensor response time. These readings are collected at different places and times and thrown away rather than forming one continuous view. As a result, individual measurements may only be seen by the firefighter carrying the monitor or relayed verbally to command. This makes it difficult for the whole team to maintain a unified understanding of where hazards are concentrated, how conditions are changing, and which areas remain unmeasured. GPS is also unreliable indoors, and building plans may be missing, outdated, or incomplete.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our system creates one live spatial view of hazards (past, present, and predicted future) inside an unfamiliar building. The view maps indoor layout, firefighter locations, and gas concentrations. It starts with the firefighter’s helmet . A compact sensing unit is mounted on the helmet. As it moves with them through the structure, it generates a structural map, tracks their position, and links gas readings to where they were collected. These readings form a live gas concentration heat map that highlights hazardous areas, shows changing conditions, and identifies unsampled regions, displayed onto the dashboard for the incident commander or chief on site. The system also visually and audibly alerts firefighters to dangerous conditions such as rapidly rising gas levels or entry into high hazard areas. The incident commander, who coordinates crews and tactical decisions, can add reported information such as victims, blocked exits, entry points, and other hazards directly onto the map. The system must fit into existing fireground workflows. Firefighting procedures with PyroSense keep radio communication and command procedures in place. PyroSense automatically adds mapping and environmental data to tablets or laptops already used for coordination by chiefs and incidence commanders.

sections.heading: Hardware design
sections.text: The wearable prototype is built around a Raspberry Pi 5, which collects and synchronizes data from each sensor. A LiDAR sensor continuously scans the surroundings to generate the building layout and support indoor localization. An IMU measures motion and tilt to help track the orientation of the mapping system and reject unreliable LiDAR scans when the sensor is tilted too far. For environmental sensing, we use a volatile organic compounds (VOC) sensor to continuously measure relative VOC levels. The Raspberry Pi then streams the sensor data to a laptop, where the mapping, hazard visualization, and command interface are processed and displayed.

sections.heading: Software architecture
sections.text: For deployment, we run backend and dashboard on a single Vultr VM with Docker Compose. FastAPI pulls the Pi's stream over Tailscale, and nginx serves the dashboard. Readings go to Tiger Cloud, which turns them into the heat map, so replaying a past walk is just a time-range query. One script deploys everything. Dashboard was made possible with three.js. We render walls from the SLAM map as it fills in, paint the gas field on the floor, and draw the air above it as drifting particles. You can watch from overhead or drop into first person at the firefighter's eye height, looking where they look as they move. Incident command gets layer toggles, follow mode, per-responder exposure history, and one-click marks for victims, fire and blocked exits. Also made a really cool landing page!

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Hardware bring up: Debugging drivers, SSH, and hotspot issues to connect our Raspberry Pi to our laptop. Data streaming latency: Reduced Pi to frontend latency by 50% by transmitting only new sensor readings, cutting traffic by about 10×, lowering SLAM map update frequency, serving live data from memory, and sending map images only when they changed. Data visualization: Designing an intuitive way to display the building map, gas heat map, changing conditions, and unsampled areas.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Full complete prototype: We successfully integrated mapping, localization, and gas sensing into a wearable solution that works in real-time. Hazard mapping and prediction: Used Gaussian Processing to produce accurate gas maps with Good workflow integration: We made sure that our solution integrates seamlessly into existing workflows so that firefighters can adopt it easily!

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: When doing Raspberry Pi setup without a monitor, make sure to install Ubuntu server and not desktop!

sections.heading: What's next for Pyrosense
sections.text: Next, we want to adapt the prototype for real fireground conditions. A key next step is replacing optical LiDAR with mmWave radar , which can continue mapping through dense smoke, darkness, and dust where cameras and optical LiDAR struggle. Thermal imaging could also be fused with radar to improve visibility and detect heat sources. We also plan to integrate certified gas sensors, SCBA air and emergency status, and further tune gas source estimation and short term hazard prediction using real-world data. The next major step would be testing the system with firefighters and fire departments to gather feedback, validate its usefulness in real scenarios, and eventually bring it to market.

title: Soundscape
tagline: A video game-inspired tool that transcribes non-speech audio into captions, giving people who are deaf or hard of hearing more ways to experience sound.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Captions show every word but miss the door slams, the phone ring, the glass breaking, and the keys dropping. People who are hard of hearing have a gap in knowledge of what’s happening around them, with current solutions inaccessible to many. Soundscape captions the sounds that matter , using all the context available. Soundscape is a video game-inspired tool that transcribes non-speech audio into captions, using visual and environmental context to help identify 500+ sounds, giving people who are deaf or hard of hearing more ways to experience sound.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Upload a file to the dashboard or use the extension on a YouTube video. It samples images and audio to determine where each part of the video takes place. It detects sounds such as traffic, animals, and alarms, then uses current environment to help choose the most fitting labels. It turns those sounds into captions that appear when the sounds happen. The extension directly overlays the video with finished captions alongside combined with directional information

sections.heading: 1. Environment analysis
sections.text: FFmpeg and FFprobe extracts audio, video frames, and timing information PySceneDetect and OpenCV divide the video into scene spans labelling each one to an environment SigLIP and CLAP , loaded through Hugging Face Transformers and PyTorch, compares frames and audios to each environment NumPy fusion and YAML settings combine visual/audio scores on a custom weight split to select an environment, while falling back to general if confidence is low

sections.heading: 2. Sound detection
sections.text: SoundFile and torchaudio prepare overlapping audio windows for the models PANNs CNN14 scores AudioSet sounds, which the project maps to its caption vocabulary. Silero VAD identifies speech regions Python post-processing applies custom environment priors (weightings), filters uncertain events, and produces baseline and conditioned results

sections.heading: 3. Captions and viewing
sections.text: Python caption writers turn detected events into timed WebVTT tracks and can merge them with supplied speech subtitles FastAPI and Uvicorn provide the local upload, processing-status, video, and caption endpoints HTML, CSS, and JavaScript power the user side while a Chrome Manifest V3 extension overlays conditioned captions on live YouTube playback yt-dlp, Node.js, and FFmpeg get supported YouTube videos for the local backend along with direction analysis added to the caption display

sections.heading: 4. Evaluation and tuning
sections.text: Versioned JSON contracts and YAML configuration define how the pipeline stages exchange results and how models are configured AudioSet strong-label clips and ESC-50 provide evaluation and tuning data, with Kaggle tooling used to obtain the AudioSet dataset The Python harness, Optuna, and MCP tooling support repeatable scoring and parameter searches pytest, Node's test runner, and Playwright check the Python pipeline, extension logic, and browser behavior

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: - Making captions accurate in early stages of testing, the model (PANN) used to classify sounds produced many plausible but wrong labels of the events happening. We improved accuracy by introducing environment based scoring, class thresholds, and safety exceptions.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Real-time processing We built the project with the use of captioning sound events in real-time as the goal. Our current algorithm uses all context available and would be more accurate with live feed because of additional location like location data. Custom environment priors We have a dozen preset environments used to better classify sound events based on the current scene in the video. Each environment has tuned sound coefficients for accuracy based on a labelled dataset ran through a pipeline to determine which sounds are more likely to be heard in a certain environment, so it is based on real data and not generated! In-house processing : All of the sounds events being classified and the video segmentation with environment labelling is being processed locally on lightweight ML models that were fine-tuned through video datasets and manual inspection.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: From building Soundscape, we had to learn about common pitfalls when dealing with sound and captioning: Scene Context: Sounds are easier to classify and interpret when knowing what is happening around in the video and related context Sounds categorized: Having more sounds with specific information could be counterintuitive to what we're trying to achieve, and having a threshold and a broader sound is more helpful than an inaccurate caption Evaluation data: Datasets of videos we looked at for training the environment coefficients was hard to find and often needed manual correction Synchronizing: The entire process of video formatting, processing video and audio tracks, caching, and displaying it back all had to work in hand to provide the sound captions at the correct timestamps

sections.heading: What's next for sound thing
sections.text: Connecting with hardware : Since we built the processing with real-time in mind, we would love to get our hands on a pair of smart glasses with a camera to test the performance on a live-streamed feed. Custom Mobile Software : To stay aligned with the goal of allowing this project to remain accessible, we plan to implement a mobile app which can connect to a local (or through the internet) server so that many others can use this project without specialized hardware

title: Dream House
tagline: Empowers interior designers to turn 2D floor plan sketches into immersive 3D interiors, in seconds instead of hours.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Interior designers often spend countless hours transforming 2D floor plans into 3D visualizations, a process that’s both time-consuming and technically demanding. Mastery of CAD or 3D modeling software is often required just to visualize a design. Dream House was created to streamline this workflow. It enables designers to sketch, iterate, and generate immersive 3D interiors within minutes, freeing them to focus on creativity rather than technical overhead.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Dream House converts rough 2D floor plan sketches into detailed, editable 3D spaces: The user begins by sketching a floor plan. The system refines it into a clean, formal layout. After customization and adjustments, the finalized floor plan is rendered as a fully furnished 3D environment, all at the press of a button.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The frontend was developed with Next.js, while the backend runs on FastAPI. The initial sketch is processed by Nano Banana to generate a formalized floor plan. The refined plan is passed through SAM (Segment Anything Model) to classify and extract furniture coordinates and dimensions. CubiCasa5K is used to detect and map walls. Using Trellis, we generated a repository of 3D furniture assets. Each detected furniture item is matched to the closest 3D model, which is then rendered in Unity alongside the extracted wall geometry to produce the final scene.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The toughest challenge was achieving reliable extraction of furniture and wall layouts from floor plans. We experimented with Nano Banana masking, coordinate mapping, and YOLOv3 before settling on a hybrid approach using SAM for furniture segmentation and CubiCasa5K for wall detection. Integration across multiple frameworks also required careful pipeline design to maintain data consistency and accuracy.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We’re proud of building a robust, end-to-end system that integrates computer vision, generative modeling, and real-time 3D rendering into a single cohesive workflow. Despite numerous technical hurdles and integration challenges, Dream House consistently produces accurate, realistic 3D representations from simple sketches.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: This project taught us how to coordinate multiple complex tools and ML models within a unified architecture. We learned the importance of detailed planning and system design before implementation, as early oversights often led to rework and communication gaps. Most importantly, we experienced the power of combining AI and visualization technologies to simplify creative workflows.

sections.heading: What's next for Dream House
sections.text: Next, we plan to: Improve segmentation accuracy by fine-tuning or training domain-specific models for furniture recognition. Expand our 3D furniture library with more customizable assets. Add advanced interior customization features, such as materials, lighting, and decor variation. Deploy Dream House as a web platform for interior designers to explore, iterate, and visualize designs effortlessly.

title: NavSense
tagline: Navigation for everyone. Turn directions into haptic cues with smart gloves.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Audio directions occupy hearing in busy streets, and screens pull eyes away from the path, which adds risk for people who rely on those senses every moment outside. Haptics carry spatial cues through touch, so guidance can land even when sound is loud or vision is busy, which supports safer wayfinding for blind or low-vision people and Deaf or hard-of-hearing people. The goal is practical access to route information through a sense that is open and available in motion.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: NavSense pairs two smart gloves to a mobile app and sends turn cues as distinct vibration patterns that map to left, right, forward, pause, and recalculation signals . Each glove carries an ESP32 that speaks Bluetooth Low Energy to the app, which keeps messages small and responsive while preserving battery life in short-burst transmissions. The app pulls a route from the Google Maps Directions API, parses steps, and assigns a clear haptic pattern to each maneuver with consistent timing windows for advance notice and execution. A voice agent handles start, destination, travel mode, rerouting, and quick questions, using ElevenLabs for natural speech and a Gemini model for robust intent and dialogue control. The gloves are rechargeable over USB‑C and include LEDs for pairing, battery status, and quick error signals that mirror haptic states for cross-sensory clarity. We also integrated machine learning models that can detect surrounding noises like sirens. If detected, the gloves will alert users of potential danger and prompt them to pause before continuing their route.

sections.heading: Who does this help
sections.text: People who are blind or low‑vision can keep hearing and mobility tools active while receiving turn cues through touch, which removes the need to split attention between a screen and the street. People who are Deaf or hard‑of‑hearing can move without relying on audio prompts, since navigation arrives as tactile instructions that work in quiet and in noise equally well . Runners, cyclists, and commuters gain a heads‑up, hands‑free option that reduces screen checks and helps keep focus on traffic and terrain in motion . This supports the spirit of UN SDGs including SDG 10 Reduced Inequalities, SDG 11 Sustainable Cities and Communities, SDG 3 Good Health and Well‑being, and SDG 9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure by improving access, safety, and inclusive mobility tools.

sections.heading: How does it help
sections.text: Haptics free eyes and ears by moving guidance into the hands, which preserves situational awareness in crowds, in traffic, and in low‑light or noisy conditions . Each pattern is short and unambiguous, like a left‑hand buzz for left turns, so cues land fast and do not overwhelm . NavSense works alongside canes, guide dogs, and safety apps by adding layered information through touch rather than replacing existing aids

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The iOS app and the voice agent collect the start, destination, and mode by voice, then sends a route request to a server that calls the Google Maps API for detailed legs and steps in JSON form . The app, connected by BLE, can connect to both devices simultaneously and send ASCII to each individual gloves based on the required haptic feedback with small vibration motors connected to the ESP-32. These vibration patterns are pre-coded into the device's hardware (ESP-32). We also custom 3D printed a box to fit on the device and house the components. The LEDs are connected to the pinout of the motors to illuminate when a signal is sent. Additionally, we used a BMS system for our 18650 battery to make it easily rechargeable with USB-C, so the battery can power the device as needed. We used ElevenLabs to provide natural voice for prompts and summaries, while a Gemini model resolves intents, follow‑ups, reroutes, and question answering in a conversational loop over webhooks.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Like any hackathon project, NavSense came with its fair share of roadblocks. Since our app depended on Bluetooth and navigation modules that required Xcode, having only two Macs made development tricky. We had to constantly switch devices and pass around small code changes just to test builds and verify functionality, which slowed us down. On the hardware side, one of our ESP32 boards ran into a bootloader issue during glove assembly, forcing us to reflash and rework parts of the code before we could get it stable again. Time management was another challenge; several team members were balancing midterms and other commitments, so coordinating availability and keeping momentum wasn’t always easy. Despite these setbacks, we adapted quickly, divided responsibilities, and kept pushing forward, which made the final result even more rewarding.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Our biggest accomplishment is building an app that promotes inclusivity and accessibility, a tool designed to support people with disabilities and help them navigate daily life more safely. This mission was central to our project, and seeing it come to life in a working prototype was incredibly meaningful for our team. On the technical side, we’re proud to have created our first-ever iOS app, taking an idea from scratch all the way to real device testing. We also developed smart gloves that use both LEDs and custom vibration patterns, tuned to deliver clear and reliable navigation cues. For routing, we integrated Google Maps so users can smoothly move from their starting point to their destination with step-by-step guidance. Finally, we went beyond traditional maps by adding voice support powered by ElevenLabs and a Gemini model, enabling users to converse with the system and control navigation at their own pace. Together, these accomplishments showcase not just what we built, but the impact it can have in making navigation safer and more inclusive.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: This project pushed us to grow in both technical and collaborative ways. We learned how to build vibration-enabled smart gloves by bringing hardware and software together, making sure the signals were reliable and meaningful for navigation. On the app side, we gained experience designing a React Native iOS app with a clean UI and integrating APIs like Google Maps for real-time routing. Implementing an AI agent was another big milestone, teaching us how to use models for natural voice guidance and interactive navigation. Just as importantly, we learned how to collaborate as a team under pressure, dividing tasks, syncing code, and problem-solving together to meet a tight hackathon deadline while many of us were also balancing midterms. In the end, we not only improved our technical skills but also developed a stronger sense of how teamwork and communication are just as critical as code in getting a project across the finish line.

sections.heading: What's next for NavSense
sections.text: We see NavSense as just the beginning of what wearable-first navigation can become. Our next step is to enhance the haptic smart gloves with a broader range of vibration signals. We want to build a “friends and safety contacts” feature, where trusted contacts can view the user’s live location and route through a web dashboard. This way, if a user is unexpectedly stopped for an extended time, their contacts can step in to check on them. Beyond software, we aim to refine the glove design itself, making it smaller, lighter, and more comfortable to wear for longer periods. Finally, we’d love to expand NavSense beyond accessibility into broader use cases, like runners, cyclists, or anyone who wants a safe, screen-free navigation experience.

title: Plant Hopper
tagline: 50% of water used for watering plants is wasted. With Plant Hopper, we efficiently water plants and result in a 0% waste.

sections.heading: 💡 Inspiration
sections.text: Traditional watering methods like sprinklers waste up to 50% of the water they use. They treat every plant the same, ignoring that some need more or less water, or operate on different schedules. We wanted a setup that’s smarter, healthier for plants, and massively more efficient. Plant Hopper solves this by individually targeting plants using computer vision, optimized schedules, and soil moisture readings. The system scales across multiple plants using a database-driven model instead of fixed hardware zones.

sections.heading: ⚙️ What We Built
sections.text: ✅ Hardware + Firmware Custom CAD turret with 2 DOF (pitch + base rotation) AprilTag detection to locate each plant and calculate distance and offset PID alignment + trigonometry to compute optimal shooting angle Servo-controlled custom, tunable, water gun for precision watering ✅ Cloud + Web App Firebase backended, Next.js + Vercel webapp Robot publishes soil moisture sensor data and CV images for analysis to the database Web app sends commands (e.g., water now, do plant scan, get current moisture health) Commands are executed in real-time through a Python threaded controller This lets users monitor and control their plants from any device, anywhere, with no local setup. ✅ Python Control Layer A multithreaded Python script ties everything together: Runs computer vision Manages serial communication with the Arduino Handles Firebase reads/writes Oversees timing, alignment, and command execution

sections.heading: 🧠 What We Learned
sections.text: Building Plant Hopper forced us to combine multiple disciplines at once: Systems Integration: Hardware + web app + database + serial communication Hardware control: PID and apriltag calculations to accurately track plant movements. Real-Time Syncing: Keeping commands and sensor data properly timed Firebase Architecture: Structuring live robot–app communication Camera Calibration: Fixing lens distortion using a YAML calibration file for AprilTag accuracy Multithreading Parallelism: Utilized the CPU's multithreaded architecture to communicate between many sources of information. Cross-System Debugging: Managing both hardware constraints and web-side logic

sections.heading: 🚀 Next Steps
sections.text: There’s lots of room for growth: 📱 Add new UI features (analytics, reminders, plant profiles) 📦 Create DIY kits for scalable deployment 💧 Upgrade to a high-pressure water system for range and accuracy 🌿 Expand to greenhouse or multi-plant environments 🤖 Development towards wheeled turrets

title: FlowBoard
tagline: The ergonomic way to storyboard. Turns rough sketches into videos by drawing on a canvas.

sections.heading: 🧐 Inspiration
sections.text: Traditional animation is slow. You have to redraw every frame and refine motion by hand. We built FlowBoard to automate that process. You sketch once, refine your image with AI, write a quick prompt, and AI generates the moving sequence for you.

sections.heading: 🤯 What it does
sections.text: FlowBoard is an AI-powered storyboard tool that turns sketches and text prompts into context-aware connected video clips that extend forever. Users can: Draw directly on 16:9 frames on an interactive canvas Add written prompts to generate video clips from each frame Connect frames with arrows to build a sequence Enhance frame drawings with AI Merge multiple clips into one final output It turns rough visual ideas into coherent videos of any length in minutes.

sections.heading: 👷‍♂️ How we built it
sections.text: Frontend: React + TypeScript Tldraw 3.15 for the interactive canvas and custom frame shapes Tailwind CSS 4.1 and Radix UI for styling Vite for development and builds IndexedDB storage Backend: Python (BlackSheep async web framework) Gemini AI Veo 3.1 for video generation Nano Banana Pro Flash for frame enhancement Google Cloud Storage for file output Redis for job queue and caching Uvicorn ASGI server

sections.heading: 🤦‍♂️ Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Enhancing images and creating accurate videos based on user's description Making sure context is saved and preserved across scenes Managing deployment architecture

sections.heading: 😊 Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Seamless end-to-end AI video generation A polished UI that feels like a real storyboard editor A fully functional drawing canvas with custom shapes Video thumbnails displayed directly on connecting arrows Smooth merging of multiple generated clips into a final render

sections.heading: 🧠 What we learned
sections.text: How to manage long-running AI operations using Redis and polling How to orchestrate a full pipeline between drawing → image → video The importance of UX features like loading states, blur overlays, and thumbnail previews

sections.heading: 🤑 What's next for FlowBoard
sections.text: Making UI/UX more smooth to deploy and scale

title: komo
tagline: WHERE IS THAT FILE??? Was it a thread in Slack? Or an import in Notion? komo is here to organize your chat histories and threads for easy retrieval. With komo, easily get into a "flow state".

sections.text: komo helps you get into it!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: As a busy working professional at a growing startup in San Francisco, Alvin has to deal with a ton of data every day to cross reference. Whether it's reallyyyyy longgg slack threads or files imbedded in notion, searching for data takes up so much time. Lots of data gets lost in company work softwares which decreases productivity.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: komo is designed to optimize workflows by seamlessly integrating different workplace platforms together. It's a unified, intelligent workspace that declutters your digital life by letting you search for related documents, messages, and media across multiple platforms—all in one place. Instead of jumping between Slack threads, Notion pages, files, screenshots, and random PNGs buried in conversations, our tool becomes your One-Stop Search Hub. With a single query, it fetches content from your connected services, analyzes it, and presents everything in a clean, organized interface. Along with a search, it provides detailed summaries of where your query was referenced, in what context, and on which service/app. 1. User searches query: “Onboarding slides” 2. Backend performs: • Slack Search API • Notion Search API 3. Each service returns JSON metadata 4. If the result is a file (PPTX, PDF, image): • We call the platform’s file download endpoint (maxing API calls!) • Gather information (texts/messages) around the file to gain contextual references about the file 5. OCR output (clean text) is sent to an AI model for summarization 6. Frontend displays: • Unified Search Results • File/text preview • AI summary

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Frontend • React + TypeScript — Fast UI development with predictable component structure • Next.js — Super-fast dev environment w/ deployment features • Tailwind CSS — Rapid styling and responsive layout Backend • Node.js + Express — Lightweight, hackathon-friendly API server and routes • Custom /search endpoint — Unified search handler for all services • Internal service wrappers (not exposed): • notionService.ts — Notion Search + Page/Block parsing • slackService.ts — Slack Search + File retrieval • Gemini AI integration to summarize search! External APIs & Integrations • Universal search • Slack Web API • Search messages/files • Notion API • Retrieve page content + file blocks

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Connecting API backend to our frontend was very tricky because we were working on different branches that weren't constantly updating. Also, fetching backend calls from frontend took a while to navigate. SlackAPI: documentation wasn't thorough, had to learn how to work with refresh tokens, API results didn't give us the info we wanted so we had to parse data differently. NotionAPI: searches took too long to query, we had to think of loop holes: stored cached db locally so that we didn't have to re-search every single page.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We had a beautiful design from our PM who had never touched design before. She did amazing and the UI looks wonderful. We also have never used Slack and Notion API's, with limited documentation, we were able to seamlessly integrate it into our app through the countless Auth Tokens and Client IDs. Optimizing search times was also one of the biggest feats — our backend dev was able to maximize efficiency while minimizing API load. The goal of bringing down our search times by 96% also helped us not get rate limited!

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: New technologies are always fun to try out and even with limited docs, no issue is irresolvable. With adequate research and concentration, each of our bugs were resolved. We learned how to access different workspaces through a common web app and how to leverage AI to help solve bugs but not take over the whole project.

sections.heading: What's next for komo
sections.text: Full Multi-Platform Expansion Right now we support Slack and Notion, but komo is designed to scale. Next integrations include: • Google Drive & OneDrive • iMessage/WhatsApp/Discord • GitHub issues & PR search • Email (Gmail, Outlook) • Open Source Extension based Developer kit Real Deployment: • Leveraging Cloud Services to reach real users • Storing compute instances and DB setup to manage data • Optimizing search and UX based on feedback Real Authentication (OAuth) During the hackathon we used hardcoded tokens for speed. Next steps: • Implement secure OAuth for Slack + Notion • Add token refresh + encrypted storage • Let users manage connected apps in a “Linked Accounts” panel Smarter AI Search + Summaries We want to develop deeper intelligence: • Automatically detect topics from your workspace • Multi-document summarization (“summarize everything about X”) • Timeline view of past conversations + files • Entity extraction (names, dates, diagrams) Visual & Media Intelligence We plan to extend support for: • Slide decks (PPTX → text + slide previews) • Videos (frame-based OCR + transcript search) • Tables and charts (AI extraction & interpretation) Custom Workspaces + Hotkeys We want to enable: • User-defined “workspaces” for topics like school, work, hackathon • Global hotkey (e.g., Cmd + Shift + K) to open komo anywhere • Spotlight-style popup search on your desktop komo aims to be a one-stop-shop to search through your digital life! From searching through all your services, to boosting productivity by unifying your contextual-search, komo aims to be around by just being a shortcut away ;)

title: Vril
tagline: Vril lets anyone become a physical product designer with the help of AI. It is a product design software that creates and iterates 3D products + packaging just from plain english.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: People have ideas for physical products but lack the 3D modeling skills or time to design them. Even simple items like mugs or boxes require specialized tools, long iteration cycles, and expensive designers. We wanted to make product design something anyone could do. Like how Lovable makes coding accessible for non-technical people.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Vril lets users create and edit full 3D product models and packaging by describing what they want in plain English or uploading a reference. It also includes an editor where users can iterate the shape, materials, and packaging with AI.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Generates editable 3D models from text or reference images. Includes a prompt-driven editor similar to Cursor for adjusting geometry and materials. Generates packaging using AI, including textures, dielines, and artwork that can be edited panel by panel. Supports exporting the product and packaging files in standard formats.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Generating 3D models that are editable, not just static meshes. Building consistent UV maps for textures and packaging artwork. Allowing users to target specific panels or surfaces for localized edits. Keeping the editing workflow simple while still giving users control.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We built an end-to-end workflow from text prompt to full 3D product and packaging export. We enabled non-designers to iterate on shape and artwork without needing modeling skills. We solved panel-level editing for packaging, which is usually difficult for AI tools.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: People want to iterate quickly, so the editing loop must be fast and reversible. Good UV layouts and dielines matter a lot for packaging quality. Natural language is enough for most users to describe designs if the system interprets it correctly.

sections.heading: What's next for Vril
sections.text: Adding physics-aware models for more accurate product dimensions. Supporting multi-material and multi-part products. Integrating with manufacturing partners so users can order prototypes directly. Expanding the editor with finer control for advanced users while keeping the core workflow simple.

title: CARmen
tagline: A web to further understand the incredible capabilities of technology applied to the new Cupra car. Know your car before it is even yours. A solution to the SEAT challenge at HackUPC.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We took on the SEAT challenge because we felt a personal drive to push ourselves and to test the limits of our knowledge, which a project like this one might surely do.

sections.heading: Project Overview
sections.text: We developed an intuitive and intelligent platform that helps potential buyers interact with and explore the Cupra Tavascan. Through a combination of conversational interfaces, image understanding, and immersive visualization, users can get to know the car in a more engaging and informative way.

sections.heading: Key Features
sections.text: Chatbot : Provides accurate, conversational responses to questions about features, specifications, pricing, and more. 3D Simulation : Offers an interactive experience to explore the interior of the Cupra Tavascan. Image Recognition : Allows users to upload photos of the vehicle or specific components to receive detailed information. Object Detection : Automatically identifies and labels parts in images User Experience : The interface is designed with Cupra’s visual identity in mind—clean, modern, and easy to navigate.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text: 1. Data Preprocessing We begin by processing the Cupra Tavascan user manual (PDF): The content is divided into meaningful sections (e.g., safety, dashboard, controls). Text and images are extracted and indexed for later retrieval. Metadata such as section titles and page numbers is added to enable context-aware search. 2. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) To answer user questions, we use a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach: A vector database stores embeddings of the manual's content, including both text and images. When a query is made—either as text or via image selection—the system retrieves the most relevant chunks. A language model (LLM) uses the retrieved information to generate accurate and grounded answers. This system supports both textual questions and interactions based on specific regions within uploaded images. 3. User Interface The frontend is designed for clarity, responsiveness, and ease of use: Users can upload an image and select an area to receive relevant information. A chatbot provides natural language interaction for asking questions about the vehicle. A 3D simulation allows users to visually explore the interior of the Cupra Tavascan. All results are shown in a clear and informative way, maintaining a consistent visual design aligned with the Cupra brand.

sections.heading: Technical Implementation
sections.text: Our system is composed of the following main components: Data Preprocessing : The Cupra manual is parsed, segmented, and enriched with metadata for efficient search. Vector Indexing : Text and image embeddings are stored in a vector database to enable semantic similarity search. RAG Pipeline : Combines vector-based retrieval with a large language model to generate context-based answers. Frontend : A web application that handles image uploads, region selection, chatbot interaction, and 3D visualization. Image Processing : Uses the Canvas API to extract selected image regions and send them in base64 format to the backend. Backend API : Processes inputs, retrieves relevant content, and returns formatted explanations for the frontend to display.

title: CUPRA-App
tagline: Una aplicación interactiva para explorar y aprender sobre las características de tu nuevo CUPRA Tavascan a través de tareas, juegos de aprendizaje y recompensas.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We were inspired by the SEAT Know Your Cupra Challenge in HackUPC

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our project helps recent car owners get to know their new Cupra Tabascan through a gamified app that teaches them one step at a time. It also serves as a pocket manual that contains all the information at a single search.

sections.heading: How we built it

sections.text: During our second day, one of our member's laptops stopped working.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud that we made an app that resembles the original brand.

title: DataCenter-DeCoder
tagline: The intelligent design platform that transforms complex data center planning into a visual, constraint-driven experience, optimizing resources and maximizing performance with drag-and-drop simplicity.

sections.text: DataCenter-DeCoder: Visualizing Optimal Data Center Design

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We created DataCenter-DeCoder to address the complex challenge of data center design, where engineers must balance competing constraints like power, cooling, space, and cost. Traditional approaches rely on disconnected tools and manual calculations, so we envisioned an intuitive visual solution with real-time feedback.

sections.heading: What We Built
sections.text: Our application combines: Interactive drag-and-drop interface for module placement Real-time constraint visualization and validation Resource flow modeling between components Visual representation of design tradeoffs The frontend uses React with TypeScript and Material-UI, while the backend leverages FastAPI with custom optimization algorithms.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: Our biggest hurdles included: Creating a responsive UI while constantly recalculating constraints Developing intuitive interfaces for complex constraint definition Implementing efficient module placement algorithms Balancing visual clarity with detailed information

sections.heading: What's Next
sections.text: Future plans include 3D visualization, thermal modeling, machine learning for optimization suggestions, and integration with vendor equipment catalogs.

title: ECHOLOOK

title: Feel the CUPRA
tagline: Voice AI Assistant and EEG Integration for a Digital Twin Experience of the CUPRA Tavascan.

sections.text: Our project consists on a groundbreaking digital twin representation of the CUPRA Tavascan car so that the customers of the model are able to learn all its cutting-edge functionalities without reading the manual. This allows them to enjoy a full exploitation of the car features before they even get the car. The project consists on a digital twin that includes many state of the art functionalities, such as a 3D model representation of the car integrated with a user-friendly tutorial. In addition to the tutorial, voice interactive Generative AI agent is able to answer any user question based on the oficial car user manual using a RAG strategy . Moreover, we have implemented a electroencephalograpic (controlled with the mind) driving simulator for the Tavascan . The key features of this Project are: Interactive user-friendly digital twin to showcase all car features. When we first open the application, we are presented with a realtime 3D animation of the Cupra Tavascan welcoming the software. This 3D model is the main focus in the application, since it is the digital-twin that will approach the car to the user before even having it, noticing no differences once you see the physical car. A "Know more" button makes the user eager to feel what is like having a Cupra Tavascan after that cinematic introduction, wich when pressed, leads us to a new scene where we can discover every single one of the features that the car offers to us. A "Learn about..." menu pops up, revealing the possibility to go through 6 different visually and voice assisted tours that guide the user through all the amazing features, without needing to read any manual. Some of this tours have the possibility of you to try out a feature, for example, the car acceleration and braking system, in a physically accurate simulation. In every moment, you have the possibility to ask the virtual assistant any question you might have about the car by pressing a button and start talking. The technologies used for this are Unity3D and C#, using every single feature about Unity: Animations, Lighting, Physics, Interactive UI and integration with all the other project parts. Voice interactive AI assistant: it knows all about the user manual and answer the questions the customer has about the car using: Gemini 2.0 Flash Embeddings (RAG strategy) Voice processing Pipeline: Record user audio -> precess audio and answer based on the manual -> output the response audio and transcript to text. Mind controlled physically accurate driving simulation to showcase the acceleration and brakes of the car. The EEG component is implemented using a Muse EEG headband. Although this device is primarily marketed to help users meditate by monitoring their brainwaves, it also provides real-time measurements of alpha and beta wave activity. Since higher beta wave levels generally correspond to increased mental activity, we can infer whether a person is focused or relaxed. The headband uses four electrodes positioned near the frontal cortex to capture raw EEG signals. We acquired these signals in Python, then filtered out noise via a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to isolate the relevant frequency bands. Next, we assembled a dataset from the cleaned EEG readings and manually labeled each sampling period as “focused” or “relaxed.” Using this labeled data, we trained a Random Forest classifier to predict mental state from EEG features. Finally, we integrated the classifier into a simple visualization tool: an orange cube whose behavior—accelerating or braking a simulated car—is controlled by the model’s predictions. We exposed the classifier via a Flask API, allowing the Unity-based simulation to update the car’s speed in real time based on the user’s mental state. Kinematic equations with the real values of power, torque, acceleration curves, mass etc are used to build an unprecedented simulator of the acceleraion and braking phases of the car in the most realistic way in Unity3D using the C# programming l

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: We had the AI voice assistant ready in Linux but when using it in Windows we struggled to integrate it adequately, as some libraries where not compatible. We surpassed it, making use of Docker. Another challenge was to correctly process the voice input sended to the Gemini API. It was hard to make it work and transcript it later to text. We managed to make it work and create a good pipeline and have a working AI assistant.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Above all, our teamwork and task division skills have been greately increased, specially in what it comes to working under high pressure in a project of this dimensions. Furthermore, Inside this team planning that guided us to completing this challenge, every member had to learn and use technologies that were out of their confort zone, such as having to learn and implement the simulation in Unity or using for the first time the Gemini API.

sections.heading: What's next for Feel the CUPRA
sections.text: This project goes far beyond than just a hackathon submission, it introduces a new step between physical user manuals and digital interaction and assistance in Industry 4.0. Additionally, it is intended to be an inspiration for future professional projects inside CUPRA for this purpose, such as introducing this new technologies and paradigms to digitize the process of learning a new car, in such a new way that not only enhances the user experience with the car itself, but also makes them enthusiastic about it to the point of being curious of learning more about it.

title: FlowCore
tagline: “Design, Optimize, and Simulate Sustainable Data Centers — Visually and Intelligently.”

sections.text: 🏗️ Datacenter Designer — HackUPC 2025 x Siemens Energy Welcome to our project for the Siemens Energy challenge at HackUPC 2025 ! In just 36 hours, we built an interactive, intelligent, and modular system to design, optimize, simulate, and monitor sustainable data centers tailored to any region in the world.

sections.heading: 💡 Inspiration

Building these infrastructures is often expensive, complex, and disconnected from real-time environmental factors. Our mission was to give engineers and energy managers a tool that not only simplifies design, but actively optimizes it —both economically and ecologically.

Achieved live data syncing across multiple subsystems. Built a system that’s both fun to use and deeply technical .

sections.heading: 📚 What We Learned

title: IndiSearch
tagline: See it. Find it. Wear it. A Chrome extension that turns any outfit you see online into a shoppable reality.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Imagine watching the latest music video from your favorite band or streaming a movie online when a stunning outfit catches your eye. You want to find it online, but tracking it down can be frustrating and time-consuming. That's where IndiSearch comes in. This project was born from a simple and relatable experience: spotting an outfit you love and having no idea where to find it. Whether it's a scene from a TV show, a post on social media, or a look from a fashion campaign, inspiration can strike anywhere. Unfortunately, access doesn't always follow. With IndiSearch , we set out to close that gap. By combining computer vision technology with the Inditex API, we created a tool that allows users to search for clothing in any moment, turning style inspiration into real-world discovery.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our Chrome extension makes shopping effortless by letting you discover and buy clothing directly from any website. As you browse platforms like Netflix, X or Youtube, the extension automatically detects clothing items within the visuals. When you hover over or click on a highlighted piece, it instantly searches the Inditex database for similar items you can purchase or virtually try on. Whether it's a jacket from a movie scene or a cap from an influencer's post, the extension helps you find and shop the look in just a few clicks. Finally you can try this new outfit using the try on feature. Powered by a diffusion model, this tool lets you virtually try on the clothes you are interested in, giving you a more interactive and confident shopping experience.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We developed a Chrome extension using JavaScript, supported by a Python backend built with FastAPI. The backend integrates multiple APIs and libraries to enable various core functionalities. To begin with, we used the YOLO model to detect people on the screen and draw bounding boxes around them. For product search, we connected to the Inditex API, allowing users to find clothing items related to the selected visuals. To enhance image data, we integrated SerpApi to perform image scraping of Inditex products. Since the Inditex API requires images to be accessible via public URLs, we also implemented a mechanism to generate temporary image URLs. Lastly, we utilized the Try-On Diffusion endpoint from RapidAPI, allowing users to see how clothes would look on them.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Since we had never worked with Chrome extensions before, developing one took more time than we initially expected. One of the main challenges we faced was with the IndiTech API. It does not return actual product images, only purchase links, so we had to implement an additional step to retrieve the image sources ourselves. We also encountered another issue with the Inditex API, which requires publicly accessible URLs for image inputs. To solve this, we created a method to generate temporary URLs for the screenshots we captured during the browsing experience.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We developed a lightweight, user-friendly Chrome extension with a non-intrusive design. Despite a tight 36-hour timeline, we successfully overcame every challenge and completed all the tasks and features we had planned from the outset.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Throughout this project, we gained valuable experience in a wide range of technologies and techniques. We successfully developed and deployed a fully functional Chrome extension capable of analyzing a user's screen in real-time. We integrated advanced computer vision models like YOLO to detect people in images accurately. We also implemented web scraping tools to retrieve product details, using product names, ids and brands (based on on-screen content and the IndiTech api). These images were then displayed to users in a seamless interface. One of the most exciting parts of our project was using state-of-the-art diffusion models. These models allowed us to take an image of a person and an image of a clothing item, and generate a realistic new image of the person wearing that clothing.

sections.heading: What's next for IndiSearch
sections.text: Although we are very proud of our application, we recognize that there is always room for improvement. In the long term, we see great potential in enhancing both the accuracy of clothing search and the quality of image generation. With additional time and development, these features could be further refined to offer a smoother and more reliable user experience. To improve usability even further, there are several features we aim to develop. First, we would like to integrate the extension more seamlessly with Inditex platforms, allowing users to add items directly to their shopping basket without leaving the current page. Another key area for improvement is mobile accessibility. Currently, the Chrome extension is limited to desktop use, but our goal is to make the tool accessible to as many users as possible, including those on mobile devices.

title: Inditex Visual Search
tagline: Find fashion pieces similar to the ones you love with Inditex’s powerful visual search technology. Just upload a photo or snap one with your camera—and discover matching styles in seconds.

sections.heading: 🧠 Inspiration
sections.text: We were really intrigued by the model developed by the Inditex Tech team, which allows users to find similar clothing items from their brands just by uploading an image. What caught our attention the most was the opportunity to experiment with image preprocessing to improve the performance and accuracy of the AI behind it. --

sections.heading: 🛍️ What It Does
sections.text: Our application enables users to: 📷 Upload an existing photo or take one using their device’s camera 🧠 Search for visually similar clothing items using Inditex’s visual search technology 🎯 Interact with a UI designed to closely match the simplicity and elegance of Inditex’s platforms The goal: make the experience intuitive, fast, and enjoyable for any user. 🛠 How We Built It Our development journey involved several stages: 🔄 Started with React + FastAPI , but later migrated to a full Next.js setup for simplicity and better integration 🚀 Deployed the app on Vercel for seamless hosting 🧩 Used Server-Side Rendering (SSR) to protect API credentials and handle secure calls 🖼️ Experimented with multiple web scraping techniques to extract product images 🔐 Implemented token auto-refreshing to ensure API access remained stable in production We also designed a clean, central interface to guide users through the entire process effortlessly. 🧗‍♀️ Challenges We Ran Into This wasn’t as simple as it first seemed. Some key challenges: 📉 Communication hurdles slowed alignment across the team 🕷️ Vercel doesn’t support tools like Puppeteer, so scraping product images became difficult 🛡️ Zara’s anti-bot security blocked us in production (though we bypassed it successfully in local environments!) 🧪 API calls failed due to hidden character issues—solved thanks to help from Alexandre Ortega (Inditex Tech) Despite these setbacks, we kept iterating and found workarounds to push forward. 🏆 Accomplishments We're Proud Of ✅ Built a functional MVP under time constraints ✅ Created real value with a polished user interface ✅ Solved technical obstacles through teamwork and persistence ✅ Delivered a product that matches the challenge’s goal This wasn’t easy, but we’re proud of what we accomplished! 📚 What We Learned 🔄 Refreshed our Next.js and frontend skills 🕸️ Learned advanced web scraping under production constraints 🌐 Gained experience deploying full-stack apps on Vercel 🎯 Improved our ability to scope ideas and prioritize features We started big, but adapted quickly and focused on what really mattered. 🔮 What’s Next for Inditex Visual Search We have tons of ideas we’d love to implement next, such as: 🧪 Image preprocessing to boost AI accuracy 🧍 Virtual try-on or 3D garment previews 🔍 Detecting and selecting individual clothing items within a photo 🏪 Checking product availability in nearby stores (when API access allows) 👤 Adding user accounts for personalized recommendations based on previous searches

title: MMG
tagline: An app to be connected even without connection. (Vueling Challenge)

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We've always been fascinated by projects that involve all kinds of expertise—from hardware to software development, and even IT.
