title: Hey Buddy
tagline: Language shouldn't cut anyone off. Buddy joins any phone call to interpret both sides live and warn people about scams, and gives energy and health hotlines a record of every call.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Many of us have family members who understand English but freeze on the phone: a pharmacist talking fast, a clinic confirming a time, a utility asking for an address. The same people are the ones phone scammers target, with a "grandson" in jail who needs bail and your bank account information, warning you not to tell anyone. The family usually hears about it afterwards. It is the same problem on the other end of the line. A gas utility, a community clinic or a plant's safety hotline gets calls from people who can describe a leak or a symptom perfectly well, just not in English. Those are the calls where a misunderstanding is most expensive.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: For people: Buddy is an interpreter you add to the phone call you are already on. There is no app to install: During any call, tap Add call , dial Buddy's number, and tap Merge . Buddy greets both sides, then interprets turn by turn: the other person hears you in English, and you hear them in your language. It works in English, Turkish, Spanish, Arabic, Hindi (beta) and Mandarin (beta). If the caller starts using scam tactics, such as pressure to pay in gift cards or wire transfers, a demand for secrecy, a request for a code or password, or asking you to install an app, Buddy warns you in your own language right after its interpretation, and sends the same warning on WhatsApp. It quotes the caller's exact words; it never says a call is "safe". Afterwards, the portal (phone number + PIN) shows every call as a conversation thread with the original and the interpretation side by side, the audio of each turn, and a short summary written by Meta Muse Spark . The summary and the warnings are in the user's language, with English versions available on request. For businesses and hotlines: every line (an ad campaign, a website number, a safety hotline) gets its own tracking number. Each interpreted call becomes a CRM record automatically: where the caller came from, what they wanted (booking, pricing, safety report, investor inquiry, …), the outcome, follow-ups, and the full bilingual transcript. Urgent safety calls, like a resident reporting a gas smell in Spanish, are marked escalated . The dashboard shows calls by line, language and intent. The whole web app, including the CRM, works in the same six languages, with right-to-left layout for Arabic.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Telephony: a Twilio number whose webhook opens a Media Streams WebSocket. We segment it into utterances on the server, and Buddy's voice goes back into the same call. Speech-to-text: ElevenLabs Scribe v2 with automatic language detection plus per-language key terms (so "torunum", "kefalet" or "gift card" are not misheard). The spoken language decides who is talking and in which direction to interpret. A low-confidence result is retried once in the user's language. Translation and scam cues: xAI Grok ( grok-4.20 non-reasoning) translates each turn with a glossary for scam-relevant terms, and separately reads the other party's recent turns for six manipulation cues. A warning is spoken only for a strong cue (payment, secrecy, credentials, remote access), at most once per new cue per call. "This is the police" or "your grandson is in trouble" on its own is recorded for the portal but never interrupts the call. Speech: ElevenLabs Flash v2.5 with a native voice per language, straight into the call. The greetings for all six languages are pre-synthesized at startup. Post-call summary: Meta Muse Spark writes two or three sentences in the user's language after the call ends. App: Node.js + Express + Socket.IO server and a React + Vite + Tailwind web app, served from one process on Railway , with a persistent volume for call history and audio, on hey-buddy.tech . Safety by construction: the caller's words are always treated as data, never as instructions, so "ignore the warnings" gets interpreted rather than obeyed. Portal and CRM logins are rate-limited. Each business key only sees its own tracking numbers. A tests-only audit pass found and fixed ways a malformed stream frame or login attempt could crash the server.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Latency on a real phone line. Each turn is STT → translation → speech, and every second of silence feels long on a call. We started with a translation model that spiked to 3–13 s on phone audio and moved translation to Grok, which answers in about 0.6–0.8 s. The pipeline now takes 1.1–1.4 s per turn on a real merged call; from the end of speech until Buddy starts speaking, the median on real calls was 1.4–1.8 s. Warnings that arrive in time. We first ran scam analysis on Meta Muse Spark; on a live call it hit our 8-second budget and the warning never played. We moved live analysis to Grok (1.3–1.5 s, in parallel with the interpretation) and gave Muse the post-call summary, where a few seconds don't matter. Who is speaking? A merged three-way call mixes everyone into one audio stream. We use the detected language plus the user's saved language to decide who spoke and which way to interpret. Merging calls. Buddy used to greet the instant it answered, which collided with the carrier merging the calls and garbled the greeting. It now waits for the merge. Warnings that are useful, not noisy. A lone "this is the police" is suspicious but common. Our first policy warned on it, so we moved to warning only when a demand follows: payment, secrecy, a code or remote access. Carrier rules. SMS from a new local number was filtered until A2P registration, so warnings go out over WhatsApp.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A working interpreter on ordinary phone calls , with no app and no special hardware: verified on real calls in Turkish, with Spanish, Arabic, Hindi and Mandarin tested end to end on phone-quality audio. Scam warnings that show their evidence (the caller's exact words) instead of asking to be trusted. One product for both sides of the language gap: the person calling and the business or hotline answering. The whole experience, including the business CRM, available in six languages.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: For live interpretation, the response time of the translation model matters more than anything else. Put each model where its latency fits: the fast ones inside the call, the slower ones after it. Phone audio (8 kHz, compressed, three people on one line) is much harder than a laptop microphone. Key-term hints and a single retry in the user's language made the biggest difference. Safety features have to be conservative on purpose: quoting evidence and never saying "this call is safe" is what makes them trustworthy.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: Native-speaker review of the Arabic, Hindi and Mandarin experience, and testing with older users and community organizations. Registered SMS alerts, and letting the user pick a trusted family member to receive the warning. Pilots with a utility or clinic hotline, starting with safety-critical calls.

sections.heading: Meta challenge: Bringing People Closer Together with AI
sections.text: Who it is for. People in the US who are not comfortable on English phone calls, often older immigrants, and the families who worry about them. On the other end are the clinics, utilities and other businesses that want to understand them. How it strengthens human connection. Buddy does not replace the conversation; it lets two people actually have it. The user speaks for themselves, in their own voice and language, instead of handing the phone to a relative or hanging up confused. When something sounds wrong, the warning arrives during the call, when it can still change what happens, and it sends the user back to the people they trust: in our demo, the grandparent's answer is "I'll call my son first." The portal lets the family look back at what was said together. Why AI is necessary. Recognizing speech from a short, noisy 8 kHz phone clip in six languages, translating it in under a second while keeping names, amounts and negations intact, and telling the difference between "buy gift cards and read me the numbers" and "never give anyone a gift-card code": none of this works with rules or keyword lists. The models do the language work. The product decides when to speak up, and always shows the exact words that triggered it.

title: Inkling
tagline: The first notes app that learns from your mistakes instead of deleting them. Inkling keeps every erase, pinpoints the second you got stuck, and re-teaches it in your language before the exam does.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Your notes are lying to you. Maya is in a calculus lecture on the chain rule. She writes \( \frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2) = \cos(x^2) \), hesitates, erases it, and rewrites \( \cos(x^2) \cdot 2x \). A few minutes later the lecture compares the product rule with the chain rule. She slows down, erases, and goes quiet while the professor keeps talking. She never writes it again. Her final page looks perfect. That's the problem. The one moment she almost learned something and the one gap she still has were both erased , by her and by every notes app she has ever used. Three weeks later, the exam finds the gap for her. Every notes app on the market keeps the result . The richest signal of how a student actually learns (the pause, the erase, the rewrite) gets thrown away. Inkling is built on one idea: the eraser is the best learning signal in the classroom, and nobody is listening to it.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Every other app deletes your mistakes. Inkling keeps them, and turns them into a study plan. Ghost ink. Nothing you erase is ever lost. Erased handwriting stays on the page as dashed teal ghost ink that you can show or hide. Finds the exact second you got stuck. Every stroke is time-stamped to the lecture. Inkling's own detection engine, Signal Lab , reads four pen signals every 10 seconds (pausing while the lecturer keeps talking, writing slower than your own normal, erasing more than usual, and pen pressure), and flags the moments you got stuck. You're compared with yourself, never with a class average. Pairs every mistake with its fix. Erase, then rewrite in the same spot, and Inkling pairs the before and after as a corrected misconception . Erase and never come back, and it's an unresolved gap that follows you into your next session until you fix it. Re-teaches you in 60 seconds. For each moment, AI reads your handwriting and what the professor was saying at that second , then writes a short re-explanation and one check question. Get it right and the moment turns into a breakthrough . Replay 20s plays exactly what you missed. In your language, out loud. Help in 10 languages (Spanish, Hindi, Mandarin, Arabic, Telugu and more), read aloud by a natural voice. Live lectures too. Press Start in a real classroom and Inkling transcribes the professor live in your browser, so all of the above works without a recording. Built for Notability, not against it. Compare with Notability lays your clean Notability page over everything it hid: 33 erased pieces of ink, and the one gap she never fixed. Export for Notability sends ghost ink and moments back as a PDF you open in Notability. For teachers: an anonymous heatmap of where the whole class got lost , with the three stretches most worth re-teaching. No names, no cameras, and nothing shown for groups smaller than three.

sections.heading: How I built it
sections.text: App: Next.js 16, React and TypeScript, with a pointer-event ink canvas for iPad, Pencil, touch and mouse. Every stroke is stamped with the lecture second, speed and pressure. Signal Lab (built from scratch): a pure-TypeScript engine that scores each student against their own baseline, pairs erases with rewrites by overlap, and classifies moments. It's fully unit-tested and inspectable: every flag shows which signals fired and by how much. Gemini reads the handwriting (what changed between the erase and the rewrite). Groq (gpt-oss) writes the re-explanations, check questions and translations with strict JSON schemas, and answers are graded on the server. ElevenLabs gives it a voice. Tiger Data (TimescaleDB): pen samples live in a hypertable . time_bucket powers per-window stats, and a continuous aggregate ( ink_lecture_hotspots ) finds where the whole class slowed down in a single query. The same code also runs on SQLite with zero setup. Shipped for real: live at inklingapp.tech on Railway, with a public demo mode that can't be abused (no uploads, rate-limited AI, self-resetting demo data). There's also a landing page with an AI assistant that answers questions about Inkling. Tested like a product: 850+ unit and integration tests and 100+ Playwright end-to-end tests, run on SQLite and Postgres. Every build phase was verified end to end before the next began.

sections.heading: How I used Notability
sections.text: Notability Pro was my research and design notebook for the whole build. I imported the MIT 18.01 lecture from YouTube and used Smart Notes to find the chain-rule segment, drew the architecture and the ghost-ink idea on the canvas , and asked Note Chat where students go wrong. It named exactly the mistake of writing \( \cos(x^2) \) without the \( 2x \), which became the heart of the demo. And Inkling gives back to Notability: it compares with, and exports to, your Notability notes.

sections.heading: Challenges I ran into
sections.text: Telling a correction from a mess: scribble-outs, strike-throughs and Undo all look like erasing, so pairing needed overlap thresholds, time windows and special cases. "Slow" has to mean slow for you: fixed thresholds punished naturally slow writers. Per-student baselines fixed it. A demo that can't fail: the full demo runs offline on hackathon Wi-Fi, with fixtures, self-hosted fonts and a browser-voice fallback. AI providers changed mid-hackathon: a Gemini model was retired. The provider-agnostic AI layer made it a one-line config change.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that I'm proud of
sections.text: The full loop works live: erase → flagged → re-taught → breakthrough , in under a minute. A detection engine that's explainable , not a black box. Privacy by design: no cameras, no class averages, k-anonymous teacher views, and keys that never touch the browser. A real product, live on its own domain , built and shipped solo in one weekend.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.text: The process of writing says more than the final page. Even simple signals (slowing down against your own normal, erasing, going quiet while the professor talks) line up with where students got stuck in my demo sessions. And time-series data is the right shape for pen data.

sections.heading: What's next for Inkling
sections.text: Pilot with real classes this semester, and grow the labelled data so detection accuracy is measured beyond my demo set. Native iPad app with PencilKit for richer pressure and tilt signals. Spaced review: unresolved gaps come back as check questions before the exam. Instructor mode: push a re-explanation to the whole class for the stretch everyone struggled with. Deeper Notability integration the moment an API opens up. Inkling: learning is in the process. Inkling keeps it.

title: Lullabuy
tagline: See the recall before your money moves. Lullabuy holds a Visa payment until a camera reads the baby gear's label at pickup and checks it against CPSC and NHTSA recalls.

sections.text: Who it's for: a parent buying used baby gear from a stranger online and paying for it at the curb. What they get: the money doesn't move until a camera has read the item's label and checked it against CPSC nursery and children's recalls, NHTSA car seat recalls and the federal resale bans. If the item is recalled or banned, the Visa hold gets reversed and the parent never paid. Inspiration I spent over four years working with kids ages one to five in child care and camp programs. A lot of parents would show up with a secondhand stroller or a bassinet they got off Facebook Marketplace, and there was really no easy way for them to know if it had been recalled. Most of them had no idea recalls even applied to used stuff. And it's not a small problem. About 100 babies died in Fisher-Price Rock 'n Play sleepers, and at least 8 of those deaths happened after the recall (CPSC, Jan 2023). This year Consumer Reports looked at Facebook Marketplace and found 50 of the first 65 listings it reviewed were banned infant in-bed sleepers, before it stopped counting. Marketplaces filter what they can read in a listing. Nobody reads the label on the actual item when the money changes hands in a parking lot. So that's the moment we built for. What it does The whole idea fits in one line: the money doesn't move until the camera has seen the item. Find it. The parent types or just talks to our shopping agent ("a bassinet for my newborn under $80, pickup in Atlanta"). Gemini turns that into a search over 1662 real listings we scanned, and every result comes back already checked. Red ones can't be bought, amber ones need a look at pickup. You can also do the whole thing by voice with our ElevenLabs agent. Agree and hold. The buyer agrees on a price and types their card into Visa's own Microform fields. Lullabuy asks Visa to authorize it with capture off, so the money is held, not sent. Meet and scan. At pickup the buyer photographs the label. The barcode gets read on the phone, the label text gets read into model, batch and manufacture date, and our own model looks at the photo for product types that are banned outright (inclined sleepers, padded crib bumpers, drop-side cribs). Check. Those values go against 1136 CPSC nursery and children's recalls and 71 NHTSA child car seat recall campaigns. The rules follow the law: a recall only counts for the batch or date range it names, mesh crib liners are allowed, and a car seat always gets NHTSA's used-seat check. Capture or reverse. No match, the hold is captured and the seller gets paid. Recalled or banned, the hold is reversed. Anything uncertain keeps the hold and moves no money. The app never says "safe". It says "no recall match as of" the date it checked. Get the call. This is the part people react to. If the hold gets reversed, Lullabuy actually calls the parent. A real voice (ElevenLabs) tells them which CPSC recall their item matched and that they weren't charged, and they can press 1 to hear it again. It only ever calls a phone that said yes: the first call just reads a 4-digit code that you type back in. Or settle it at a table. At a swap meet or a consignment sale, the seller plugs in a regular USB barcode scanner and opens /checkpoint. One scan of the UPC settles the hold. If the scan comes in broken, or a recall's UPC is off by a digit, it doesn't guess. Nothing moves until a person checks. After the sale. Every captured sale gets an item passport on Solana that anyone can verify, and it's also minted as a Metaplex Core asset. The recall watch keeps checking every sale. If a recall comes out later for something a parent already bought, they get a push notification and the asset's on-chain attributes get updated. Who it helps, and why a marketplace would pay for it This is a big market. GlobalData, in a report for Mercari, valued the U.S. secondhand kids and baby market at $7 billion in 2021 and projected $12.8 billion by 2030 (that covers kids' items broadly, clothing included, not just cribs

title: Nudge
tagline: Nudge

sections.text: 📖 DeepWiki (full code walkthrough): https://deepwiki.com/AlanRoybal/hackgt 🐙 Code: https://github.com/AlanRoybal/hackgt Nudge — call the people you love when you're both actually free

sections.heading: The challenge and who it's for
sections.text: The people we love most are the ones we call least. Not because we don't care — because starting a call is friction: is she busy? is it a bad time? what do I even say? So we default to a "miss you" text, and months go by. Nudge is for anyone with someone they keep meaning to call — a parent in another city, a sibling, a college friend, a grandparent. Specifically the pairs who want to talk more but keep bouncing off the "is now okay?" problem. There are no roles and no group features: one friendship, two phones.

sections.heading: How it strengthens human connection (meaningfully, not metrically)
sections.text: Nudge removes the three things that stop a call from happening, and it does it without turning friendship into a streak or a notification farm: It finds the moment. Both phones share only free/busy blocks from their calendars (never event titles) plus on-device signals — Focus mode, driving, whether the phone is awake. When both of you are free right now , both phones get one nudge. A nudge is a mutual invitation: either person can Skip with a reason, and the other side just sees "Not right now." It makes the call better. During the video call, when you say "remember the hike last weekend?" the photo appears in your own mini window with an Ask first card. Tap Show and it's on Mom's screen. Conversations stop being "how are you… fine" and become show-and-tell. It carries the thread. Afterwards Nudge writes a short summary you both can see and delete. Topics with follow-ups ("physics exam Thursday") seed the next nudge: "Want to ask Mom how the exam went?" Every one of those steps is opt-in and symmetric — nothing happens to the other person without their acceptance. That's the point: the app is a good friend who says "you're both free, want me to connect you?", not a machine that guilt-trips you.

sections.heading: Why AI is essential (and where it isn't)
sections.text: Nudge's core feature — photos that appear because you mentioned them — is impossible without AI, and we built it entirely on Amazon Bedrock first-party models: Amazon Nova Lite reads the live transcript one line at a time and decides is this a reference to a photo, and what would you search for? ("the hike last weekend" → hike mountains last weekend ). It also captions every indexed photo, writes the post-call summary, extracts follow-up topics, and drafts the "in a meeting until 4" auto-replies. Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 puts your photos and the spoken query into the same 1,024-d vector space. Photos are embedded image-only (our eval showed it beat caption fusion: top-1 1.00 vs 0.95). Amazon S3 Vectors stores those embeddings and answers each query scoped to the speaker's own photos only . Amazon Rekognition + Nova gate what ever gets indexed: moderation labels, OCR for documents/IDs/screenshots, and a Nova "is this sensitive?" pass. 9/9 sensitive fixtures were excluded; 0/7 benign ones wrongly excluded. We measured it rather than hoped: the detector scores precision 1.000 / recall 0.896 on a 140-window eval set with 0/30 hard-negative false positives , retrieval is top-1 1.000 on a 60-photo CC0 set, and end-to-end transcript → suggestion runs at ~1.0 s p50 against the deployed stack. Where AI isn't the answer we didn't force it: free-time matching is deterministic interval math, the nudge scheduler is adaptive but rule-based (response history adjusts timing within the frequency you chose), and Amazon Transcribe + Amazon Chime SDK handle speech and media as infrastructure, not "features."

sections.heading: Why it's original
sections.text: Most "stay in touch" apps take one of two shapes: reminder lists / streak counters, or scheduling — put a call on the calendar for Thursday at 7. Scheduling sounds responsible, but it is a high-commitment act: you are promising your future self and someone else's future self, and people quietly resent and abandon those promises (the event gets moved, then skipped, then the app gets deleted). Nudge is deliberately low-friction and low-commitment : nothing is ever scheduled. It waits until you are both free right now, asks each of you with a single tap, and if either says "not now" nothing happened and nobody was let down. Because saying yes costs nothing and saying no costs nothing, people keep using it — the app never becomes a chore you owe someone. Beyond that, Nudge is different in four concrete ways: Mutual availability, not reminders. Both calendars have to be free; both people have to accept. Nobody is ever "reminded" to bother someone who is busy. The camera roll joins the conversation. We haven't seen another calling app that listens for "remember when…" and surfaces the actual photo — privately to the speaker first, then shared with one tap. Ask first, always. Nothing leaves your phone by voice alone. The suggestion appears in your window; the friend sees nothing until you tap Show. Photo indexing is 30-day, resized, private-bucket, and deletable; free/busy is the only calendar data that leaves the device. Tap phones to become friends. Adding a friend is physical: hold two iPhones near each other (UWB / Nearby Interaction, with accelerometer knock detection as fallback) and they link over MultipeerConnectivity — no handles to type when you're already in the same room.

sections.heading: Tools, harnesses, and models — and what each one bought us
sections.text: Product stack Layer What Why it mattered iOS Swift 6, SwiftUI, iOS 18+, XcodeGen, SwiftPM ( NudgeKit package) Strict concurrency caught real races in call/photo state; NudgeKit keeps 60+ pure-logic tests fast without a simulator. Calls Amazon Chime SDK for iOS (0.27.4) — 1:1 video + data messages Data messages carry photo-share offers/acks so photos sync in the mini windows without a media pipeline change. Speech Amazon Transcribe Streaming (SigV4 + event-stream hand-written in Swift; Chime meeting transcription as fallback) No AWS SDK for Swift needed; final segments feed the detector line by line. AI Amazon Bedrock: Nova Lite , Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 ; Amazon Rekognition (moderation, DetectText) First-party only, all covered by AWS credits; see above. Backend TypeScript 5.9, Node 22 on ARM64 Lambda, esbuild, AWS CDK v2 One cdk deploy stands up the whole stack; 0.3–0.8 MB bundles keep cold starts sub-second. API/Auth API Gateway HTTP + WebSocket, Cognito User Pool + Identity Pool, Sign in with Apple Identity Pool gives the phone short-lived creds to call Transcribe directly. Data DynamoDB single table (TTL), S3 (private, resized), S3 Vectors (1,024-d cosine) Serverless vector search with no cluster to run. Async SQS + DLQs (nudge delays, expiry, post-call summary), EventBridge Scheduler Replaced Step Functions with plain delayed messages — simpler, cheaper. Push APNs (alert / background / VoIP) + Notification Service & Content extensions Accept from the lock screen; rich nudge cards. Test & eval harnesses (what made shipping this in a hackathon possible) evals/ — detector (140 two-speaker windows incl. 30 hard negatives + 8 context cases), retrieval (60 CC0 photos), safety (16 fixtures). Every prompt change re-ran these; the detector's "judge only the newest line" fix came straight out of an eval regression. tools/peer-bot — a headless-Chrome Chime client (Puppeteer + amazon-chime-sdk-js ) that plays your friend: accepts nudges, joins the call with a fake camera, answers photo offers. two-bots mode verifies simultaneous shares, queues of three, and p95 ≤ 800 ms show latency without a second human. tools/e2e/ios-e2e.sh — XCUITest scenarios that run the real app in the simulator against the deployed dev stack with the bot as the friend, including the app-terminated → push → Accept → call path. tools/latency-report — pulls CloudWatch metrics for transcript → suggestion timing per stage. Vitest + fast-check (93 unit + 31 integration tests against the live dev stack) and XCTest (62 tests in 16 suites). Screenshot mode — a launch argument that renders any screen with seeded data so ios/scripts/screenshots.sh produces all 212 captures deterministically; also what the design review ran on. Build-process tools Claude Code built the app and backend from a single detailed spec ( prompts/01-claude-code-build.md ) with a decision log ( docs/DECISIONS.md , 50 entries) so every non-obvious call is written down. Devin produced the Figma design system and full screen set in parallel ( prompts/02-devin-figma-design.md ), then adopted the contrast-adjusted tokens we measured ( ios/scripts/contrast.py ) so light-mode "Strong" colors clear WCAG AA. Apple design skill ( emilkowalski/skills → apple-design , pinned in skills-lock.json ) kept the UI restrained: standard system chrome, flat pastel content, labels that name what's inside. DeepWiki (link at top) documents the resulting codebase.

sections.heading: What's real today, what's next
sections.text: Deployed to a dev stage in us-east-1 ; all backend integration tests and the simulator E2E run against it. Two things we could not fully verify in the simulator and want to finish on physical devices: real APNs/VoIP delivery (dev stage logs pushes to DynamoDB so tests can assert on them) and UWB tap-to-add. Before any public launch: a lawyer's pass on the transcription consent language, and splitting the single Lambda IAM role.

prize_badges: Meta: Bringing People Closer Together with AI - Winner

title: PledgeCheck
tagline: Approve at-home iPLEDGE pregnancy tests in one tap, with fraud checks and an audit trail that proves you met the FDA's anti-falsification rule.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Isotretinoin (often known by brand name Accutane) is one of the only medicines that can clear severe acne for good. It also causes serious birth defects if taken during pregnancy. To prevent that, the FDA runs a safety program called iPLEDGE . Every patient who can become pregnant must take a pregnancy test every single month , and then pick up the prescription within a strict 7-day window . Until now, those monthly tests had to happen at a clinic. Picture a college sophomore who drives to her dermatologist every month, sits in a waiting room, and misses class. One month her car breaks down, she misses the window, and her treatment stalls. Many patients simply give up. The rules are changing. On February 9, 2026, the FDA approved changes to iPLEDGE that dermatologists had been lobbying for years: patients may take their monthly pregnancy test at home during and after treatment, if their prescriber allows it (the first, pre-treatment test must still happen in a clinic); a patient who misses the 7-day pickup window can retest right away , instead of being locked out for 19 days; for patients who cannot get pregnant, monthly counseling paperwork is dropped. The formal rollout was moved to November 15, 2026 , so the iPLEDGE computer system can be tested. But the FDA has allowed at-home testing under "enforcement discretion" since 2023, so clinics can rely on home tests today . Here's the catch. The FDA says prescribers who rely on home tests must take steps to minimize patients falsifying the results , and it doesn't say how. Every dermatology practice in the country is now responsible for an anti-fraud process that doesn't exist yet. We built that process!! YAY

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: PledgeCheck turns an at-home pregnancy test into a fraud-resistant, auditable record that a dermatologist can approve in one tap. The end-to-end workflow The patient requests a refill from their patient dashboard. The clinic approves it , and PledgeCheck emails the patient a one-time link . It works once, expires in 24 hours, and is never stored in readable form. The patient opens the link and taps Start. A 40-minute session begins, and only now is a 4-character one-time challenge code revealed. The patient writes the code on the test in clear letters, takes the test, and photographs it. It's live camera only : photos can't be uploaded from the gallery. Voice guidance in English and Spanish is available to walk them through every step, for patients that need it. The photo goes through fraud checks and two independent readers (Grok and OpenCV - details below). The dermatologist sees one card per test : the photo, both readings, any fraud warnings, and the patient's timeline. They approve or reject in one tap . Software never approves anything on its own. Approval opens the 7-day pickup window, and the patient can fill the prescription. Every action is recorded in a tamper-evident audit log, whose fingerprint is regularly stamped onto the Solana blockchain, so no one can quietly rewrite history. Not even us! A drug-maker dashboard shows only anonymous weekly totals , such as tests verified and days from test to fill, with no patient-level data.

sections.heading: The security checks (the heart of the project we're super proud of!)
sections.text: Every check below stops a different way of cheating: Cheating attempt What stops it Sharing or reusing someone's link One-time link: works once, expires in 24 hours, one 40-minute session Guessing a link Each link contains a 256-bit random token, about $2^{256}$ possibilities. Guessing one is effectively impossible Sending an old photo, or last month's test Challenge code: the code didn't exist until the patient tapped Start, so an older photo can't contain it Uploading an edited or downloaded image Camera-only capture: no file uploads, and the server records its own timestamp Resubmitting the same photo (even cropped or brightened) Photo fingerprint (details below) A misread or doctored test Two independent readers must agree, or a human reviews it Editing records after the fact Hash-chained audit log + Solana anchor The challenge code. Codes use 4 characters from a 31-character alphabet (we removed look-alikes like 0/O and 1/I/L, which are easy to misread in handwriting). That gives $31^4 = 923{,}521$ possible codes, and a patient can't know theirs until the session starts. The photo fingerprint. Each photo is turned into a 64-bit "perceptual hash", a fingerprint of what the image looks like . Small edits barely change it. If a new photo's fingerprint differs from any earlier photo's in fewer than 8 of its 64 bits, $$d_{\text{Hamming}}(p_{\text{new}}, p_{\text{old}}) < 8,$$ we treat it as the same photo and block it, across every clinic. Two readers, on purpose. Grok (AI vision) reads the result and the handwritten code. OpenCV (classic image processing, no AI) measures the test lines pixel by pixel. AI can be confidently wrong, and it can even be tricked by text written in the photo. A second method that works completely differently is unlikely to make the same mistake. If the two disagree, or if either is less than 85% confident, the test goes to the doctor for a closer look. The tamper-evident audit log. Every action (link issued, session started, photo received, fraud rejection, approval) becomes an entry whose fingerprint includes the entry before it: $$h_n = \text{SHA-256}\big(h_{n-1} \,|\, \text{entry}_n\big)$$ Change any old entry, and every fingerprint after it stops matching. Someone with full database access could still rewrite all the fingerprints. So every 10 events, and on demand, we publish the latest fingerprint to the Solana blockchain, a public record that nobody (including us) can edit. The Verify button recomputes the whole log and compares it with Solana: green if nothing changed, red (pointing to the altered entry) if anything did. What we're careful to say: the Solana anchor proves the record wasn't changed afterwards . It doesn't prove a photo was real; the fraud checks do that. And only a fingerprint goes on the blockchain , never any patient information. Privacy by design. Photos are deleted after review ; only the fingerprint is kept. Email addresses are never written to the audit log. Emails have a neutral subject line ("Your PledgeCheck link"), so nothing sensitive shows up on a lock screen.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Part Technology Why Web app (patient, clinic and drug-maker screens) Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, shadcn/ui , hosted on Vercel One codebase for every screen; the patient flow works in any phone browser, no app install Database, logins and access rules Supabase (Postgres) Each clinic can only ever see its own patients, enforced inside the database itself AI reader Grok vision (xAI) Reads the test result and the handwritten challenge code Second reader + photo fingerprint Python, OpenCV on a Vultr server Independent, non-AI line reading, plus the reuse fingerprint Tamper-proof anchor Solana (devnet) A public, uneditable timestamp of our audit log's fingerprint Voice guidance ElevenLabs Pre-recorded English and Spanish instructions, so the patient never waits on a live AI call Email Resend Sends the one-time link from our own domain, [email protected] Anonymous analytics Tiger Data (TimescaleDB) Weekly totals for drug makers, kept separate from patient data Domain .Tech pledgecheck.tech for the app, api.pledgecheck.tech for the image service Testing. More than 450 automated tests cover the web app, plus a database test suite (78 checks for access rules and the audit log) and the image service's own tests. We also ran end-to-end tests against a real local database, which issue a link, start a session, and independently re-verify every audit fingerprint. Real-world check. We bought pregnancy tests and photographed them: negatives without code, negatives with code, an unused test, and a random object. On those photos, Grok read every result and every handwritten code correctly . That's a small sample, not an accuracy claim.

sections.heading: Sponsor tracks
sections.text: Impiricus. PledgeCheck is built for clinicians first. It solves a brand-new FDA requirement that makes dermatologists responsible for preventing misread and faked at-home pregnancy tests, and turns it into a one-tap approval with an audit-ready record. It opens a new way to engage healthcare providers without adding to their workload, and it's a platform: iPLEDGE is the first of many FDA drug-safety programs with the same monitoring needs. Identity verification with Persona, which Impiricus already uses, slots into our design at the start of each test. A Marina's Mission (Social Good). Monthly clinic visits are a real barrier: missed classes, lost work, long drives, and treatment that stalls when a patient can't make it in. PledgeCheck lets patients test at home safely, so more people can finish a treatment that changes their lives. Tiger Data. Our drug-maker dashboard reads from a separate Tiger Data warehouse that holds only anonymous events (tests verified, days from test to pickup), never patient IDs. Small counts are hidden to protect privacy. Solana. Every clinic action goes into a tamper-evident audit log, and we anchor its fingerprint on Solana devnet. The Verify button checks the log against the blockchain, so any edit, even by an insider, is caught. Only a hash goes on-chain, never patient data. Vultr. Our image service runs on Vultr. It fingerprints every photo to block reused images, and adds a second, non-AI reading of the test lines as a cross-check. Grok (SpaceXAI). Grok vision is our primary reader: it reads the test result and the patient's handwritten challenge code from the photo, the core check that the photo was taken during this session.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The audit log that froze the whole app. At one point every audit write hung, and the database logged about 100 errors per second. Our database function signalled a conflict with an error code that means "temporary problem, just retry", so the system retried the same doomed request forever until it ran out of connections. We switched to an error code that tells the app to re-read the latest entry first , the only way a retry can succeed, and removed a lock that had made the jam worse. Analytics that could have broken patient care. While writing a test, we found that a single wrong analytics setting would have made every clinical approval fail. We rebuilt it so analytics can fail quietly without ever blocking a doctor's decision. The computer-vision reader meets real photos. OpenCV looked fine on clean test images, but on our real photos it got 4 of 6 wrong. A hand holding the test merged with the test itself, and the pink cap looked like two result lines. Because it's uncalibrated, it's capped at low confidence, so every one of those cases safely went to the doctor. But it showed us that real-world photos are the hardest part. A server that stays silent. When our image server was unreachable, requests didn't fail; they hung , which could have stalled a patient's upload. The lesson: every outside service needs a time limit. Identity verification without a company. The ID provider our sponsor uses requires a registered business and tax ID, which a student team doesn't have, and the alternatives we tried had no free tier. Three people, one night. We each built our part on separate branches and merged them into one working app, keeping each other's code working along the way.

sections.heading: Honest limitations
sections.text: We'd rather tell you what PledgeCheck can't do yet: We can't prove who took the test. The challenge code proves when the photo was taken, not whose test it is. Someone else could take the test and write the code on it. This is an open limitation with no known solution without violating patient's privacy. However, we do our best to minimize fraud. We can't tell what went on the stick. A test dipped in water shows a normal-looking negative. (That's exactly how we made our own demo negatives!) No photo-based system can detect this. The OpenCV reader isn't calibrated yet. It needs dozens of labeled photos across lighting conditions and test brands. Until then, its confidence is capped, so it only adds caution, never speed. Our Grok testing is a small sample: six photos of one brand of test. No government ID check yet. Impiricus already uses Persona for identity verification, so an ID + selfie check before each session fits naturally into their roadmap. We designed the Start step to plug it in, storing only a scrambled fingerprint of the identity, never the ID itself. We couldn't access it this weekend (it's business-only and paid), and Stripe Identity had no free tier either. No connection to the real iPLEDGE system, which has no public API. The clinic still enters the verified result into iPLEDGE; PledgeCheck produces the trustworthy record behind it. Demo data only. Every patient is synthetic. Real use would need a HIPAA compliance review, business agreements with every vendor, and a security audit. It needs a smartphone with a working camera and internet connection. Patients without one still need the clinic. Our timing rules (like the 7-day window) follow published summaries of the FDA changes and need checking against the official iPLEDGE prescriber guide before real use.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Every outside service will eventually fail, so plan for it. Analytics, email, the image server and the AI reader all "fail soft": they add a warning for the doctor instead of blocking a patient. Two different methods beat one clever one. The most reliable safety feature was requiring an AI and a non-AI reader to agree.

sections.heading: What's next for PledgeCheck
sections.text: Government ID + selfie check at Start, through Persona, matching Impiricus's existing stack. Calibrate the OpenCV reader on real photos from clinics, across test brands and lighting, and add an on-screen framing guide for the camera. Automatic photo-quality warnings (blurry, too dark) so patients can retake before sending. Audit PDF export for FDA and program inspections, including the Solana proof. Reminders before a patient's testing or pickup window closes. Confirm every rule against the official iPLEDGE guide ahead of the November 15, 2026 rollout. A platform for more drug-safety programs: iPLEDGE is one of many FDA safety programs with similar monitoring needs. Pilot conversations with dermatology practices.

sections.text: In the product: Grok (xAI) reads test photos and handwritten codes. ElevenLabs generated the voice guidance clips. In development: we used AI coding assistants to help write code and tests, plan, add comments and debug. The team designed the system, the security checks and the workflow; reviewed and tested every change; bought and photographed real tests; and made every product decision.
