title: Optimized Ray-marching algorithm
tagline: Optimizing rendering of perlin-noise generated heightfields using methods such as Sphere Tracing and Illinois method

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: I was inspired to tackle this challenger because it contained a unique intersection of 3D creativity and math which I both love.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: This algorithm renders heightfield meshes that are generated using functional brownian motion.

sections.heading: How I built it
sections.text: I improved upon Huawei's basic raymarching algorithm by making many adjustments. Level of Detail optimizations: The functional brownian motion mesh generator creates a mesh by summing multiple noise maps. I altered the mesh generation to be dependent on the camera location so that smaller details and higher frequency noise maps were not added to the mesh at larger distances. K-Lipschitz Bounded Sphere tracing: I knew I wanted to improve upon the height based ray marching iteration but struggled with finding out how to generate a signed distance function for each point. Instead I came across the K-Lipschitz equation which provides a bound on the distance function based on the fBm parameters. Height Rendering cutoffs: I improved the sky rendering time by simply ending all rays if they reached a height greater than the maximum possible height of the mesh. Illinois method: The most significant and novel method in this algorithm is the Illinois method implementation. To save time with raymarching while close to the height maps surface, the Illinois method checks wether there will be a hit in a certain window and skips this window if there is not a hit. This significantly reduces the number of small steps the algorithm takes by skipping these windows entirely.

sections.heading: Challenges I ran into
sections.text: I ran into multiple challenges in this algorithm. The improvements such as the level of detail and height cutoffs seemed fairly obvious and were quite easy to implement. The Sphere tracing and Illinois method were not however. I suspected that the gradient would be useful in determining the distance function for sphere tracing but trying to devise a method before finding K-Lipschitz bound was extremely challenging. Luckily once I found the K-Lipschitz equation it was an obvious solution to my problem. I was struggling thinking of ways to solve the grazing problem that ray marching has until I considered a root finding method that I was recently studying in a Computational Physics course, the bisection method. Since the height from the mesh is a signed function I realized that I could search for a sign change in a window significantly larger than the iterative step size and probably be able to detect wether a hit was in the window much faster than the brute force method.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that I am proud of
sections.text: I am quite proud of my K-Lipschitz bound distance function as well as the Illinois method implementation. Combined I was able to reduce the step count by 37.8 percent which is far more than I thought I would be able to achieve with in the 48 hour period.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.text: I learned about ray marching and various ways to improve its performance.

sections.heading: What's next for me
sections.text: I hope to continue working in 3D computer graphics and building impactful technology and software.

Summaries: Gemini API receives a structured session JSON and returns a readable report for users/clinicians.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: Lighting/occlusion causing pose jitter, calibrating angles across body sizes, counting reps reliably, and packaging it so it runs smoothly in-browser.

sections.heading: Accomplishments
sections.text: An end-to-end flow: guided drills → real-time overlays → symmetry/ROM scores → auto-generated report . We built clear exercise animations and handle one-side-weaker cases.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Designing stable metrics (not noisy ones), smoothing pose data, writing prompts for medical-adjacent language, and UX that motivates without overwhelming.

sections.heading: What’s next
sections.text: We’re committed to take Rehabit to the next level. In the coming weeks we will: Add personalized baselines , more upper-limb drills, and side-view capture. Launch a clinician dashboard (cohort views, PDF exports, alerts for large left–right gaps). Keep data privacy-first (on-device where possible, encrypted storage, consent logs). Start a commercial pilot with a partner clinic, validate against goniometer measures, add FHIR/EHR export, and align with HIPAA/PIPEDA + RTM reimbursement. If we had more time this weekend: we’d ship auto-calibration for camera distance, richer coaching cues (“slow the right side”), polished PDF reports, clinician invites, and additional drills (reach, grasp, gait). We’re not diagnosing —we make progress visible and actionable , and we plan to keep working on this beyond the hackathon.

title: SFU Grad Map
tagline: Visualize your journey from first year to graduation.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The idea for SFU Grad Map emerged from our shared frustration with the goSFU system’s outdated and unintuitive design. Many students struggle to find prerequisite information, especially for 200-level and upper-division courses, which often requires manually navigating through multiple course outline pages. We wanted to create a solution that simplifies this process by providing a clear, interactive, and visually engaging way to explore degree progressions.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: SFU Grad Map is a web application that allows students to easily visualize their academic journey. By searching for a course, users can instantly see its description, prerequisites, and equivalent courses displayed in a dynamic and interactive graph. This helps students understand course dependencies, plan their future semesters efficiently, and make informed decisions about their academic paths.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built SFU Grad Map using Next.js with JavaScript as our main development framework. The Gemini API powers the course data extraction, transforming unstructured prerequisite information into organized and readable JSON outputs. We used D3.js to create the course visualization graph, ensuring smooth transitions and intuitive interactions. The user interface was designed using shadcn and aceternity component libraries to maintain a modern, responsive, and cohesive design system.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One of the biggest challenges we faced was the Gemini API rate limit, which affected our ability to process multiple courses quickly. Handling course equivalencies was also complex, as certain courses could substitute for others depending on program requirements. We also explored building a manual parser for faster performance, but quickly realized that SFU’s course descriptions used natural language too inconsistently to parse reliably. Balancing accuracy, performance, and maintainability required significant iteration in both logic and system design.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud of building a fully functional prototype that successfully integrates the Gemini API and displays course relationships in a clear, visual format. Our team overcame data parsing challenges, optimized API usage, and created an interface that genuinely improves the student experience. We also developed a scalable system architecture that can easily support future features such as multi-semester planning or integration with student transcripts.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Through this project, we learned how to work with AI-powered APIs for structured data extraction, manage asynchronous API calls efficiently, and design data visualizations that communicate complex relationships effectively. We also deepened our understanding of frontend system design, state management, and the trade-offs between manual and AI-driven parsing. Most importantly, we learned how to collaborate efficiently under time constraints and align design goals with technical feasibility.

sections.heading: What's next for SFU Grad Map
sections.text: Looking ahead, we plan to expand SFU Grad Map by introducing user authentication and personalized degree tracking, allowing students to log in and visualize their progress toward graduation. We also aim to integrate real-time data from SFU’s course outline system to ensure up-to-date information on prerequisites and course availability. In the long term, we envision supporting recommendation features that help students optimize their course load based on prerequisites, semester offerings, and workload distribution. Additionally, we are exploring caching and custom parsing techniques to further reduce dependency on API rate limits and improve system performance.

title: Track2Give
tagline: Track your impact. See the change. Give with confidence.

sections.text: Track2Give

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every year, millions of tons of food are wasted because people forget what’s in their fridge or pantry until it’s too late. We wanted to tackle this problem by creating a solution that helps people track their food inventory and get notified before items expire — turning potential waste into opportunities to give back. Our inspiration came from the idea that small digital actions can lead to big environmental and social impact . By preventing just a fraction of household waste, we can collectively reduce emissions and help feed more people.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Track2Give is a smart food-tracking web app that: Lets users add and manage their food items with expiry dates. Automatically tracks time remaining before expiry. Sends friendly alerts when items are about to expire. Suggests donation options for soon-to-expire items.

sections.heading: How We Built It
sections.text: We built Track2Give using the following technologies: Frontend: HTML, CSS, and EJS templates for dynamic UI rendering. Backend: Node.js and Express.js to handle routes, authentication, and API requests. Database: MongoDB for storing user data, food items, and expiry timestamps. Authentication: Passport.js for secure login and session management. Notifications: Scheduled background tasks to check expiry dates and send alerts. The development flow looked like this: Design & Wireframing – Defined user flows and designed a clean, accessible interface. Backend Setup – Built Express routes for adding, editing, and deleting food items. Database Integration – Structured MongoDB collections to store food data efficiently. Logic Implementation – Used date arithmetic to compute remaining shelf life. Testing – Validated accuracy of expiry calculations and improved performance.

sections.heading: Challenges We Ran Into
sections.text: Building Track2Give wasn’t without its challenges: Date management: Handling date calculations consistently across time zones. Real-time updates: Making sure expiry alerts update automatically without manual refreshes. Database relationships: Linking users with their personal inventories securely. UI consistency: Ensuring the interface was intuitive and responsive across devices. Each challenge helped us improve our problem-solving and debugging skills.

sections.heading: Accomplishments That We're Proud Of
sections.text: We’re proud that we turned an everyday issue — forgotten groceries — into a practical and scalable tech solution. Some highlights include: Building a fully functional, data-driven inventory tracker. Designing a clean, modern interface that anyone can use. Implementing real-time expiry alerts successfully. Promoting food donation and sustainability awareness.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: Throughout this project, we learned: How to structure a full-stack application from scratch. How to implement authentication securely with Passport.js . The importance of clean UI and user experience design. How impactful even small software solutions can be when aimed at sustainability and social good .

sections.heading: What's Next for Track2Give
sections.text: We plan to expand Track2Give with: AI-powered expiry prediction using OCR-based receipt scanning. Donation integration with local food banks and charities. Mobile app version for easy barcode scanning and item tracking. Community leaderboard for rewarding users who donate frequently. Our long-term goal is to make Track2Give a platform that not only prevents waste but connects communities through giving . Developed with ❤️ for sustainability and social impact.

title: Apex FSD
tagline: We trained a neural net on our own racing laps, handed it a real steering wheel, and watched it rip. Embodied AI that learns from pixels and turns a physical wheel to race in a driving game - FH4

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Most AI driving projects end at a function call. We wanted ours to end with a steering wheel turning on its own. Self-driving used to mean hand-built pipelines: one system for lane detection, another for path planning, and another for obstacle avoidance. Deep learning collapsed all of that into one network. In 2016, NVIDIA's PilotNet showed a single convolutional neural net could learn to steer straight from camera pixels. Tesla's modern FSD v12 has since taken the same end-to-end idea onto real roads. One of us is a racing fanatic with a force-feedback sim rig under their desk, and a hackathon is where big ideas get chased. So we asked: could we build that same pixels-to-steering brain in a weekend and have it physically turn a real wheel, one a human can grab back at any moment?

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Model: a CNN based on NVIDIA's PilotNet architecture: 5 convolutional layers that learn road features (edges, lane lines, curves), then fully connected layers that turn them into driving outputs. We added custom late fusion of Forza's live telemetry: the car's speed joins the image features right before the decision layers, because the same corner needs different steering and braking at different speeds. road crop (66×200) ──► 5 conv layers ──► image features ─┐ Forza speed (telemetry) ─────────────────────────────────┴─► FC 100 → 50 → 10 ──► steering, throttle, brake Wheel loop: Forza can only read one controller. HidHide hides the real wheel from Forza, so the game only sees vJoy , a virtual wheel that the neural net can control and also mirror and intake data from the wheel. This allows us to switch between manual driving and FSD without pause, just like on real autonomous vehicles. TMX wheel ──(angle, pedals)──► our runtime ──► vJoy ──► Forza ▲ │ └──── motor turns the wheel ◄──┘ ◄── AI prediction (laptop, over Ethernet) Stack: Python, PyTorch, DXcam, OpenCV, PySDL2, vJoy + HidHide, Forza Data Out telemetry, two PCs over a direct Ethernet link.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Syncing frames with telemetry. Every frame, wheel reading, and telemetry packet is timestamped on one clock. We measured that the screen shows the game 66 ms after telemetry reports it by matching gear changes on screen against gear changes in the telemetry. Hot-lap data doesn't teach recovery. We mostly recorded fast laps, minimizing lap time and chasing apexes. So the model never saw what to do once it drifted off the line, and it couldn't recover after going off the road. It also never learned to use the road markings as guidance but more or less memorized the patterns around each corner. Overfitting. We tuned the driving (steering gain, throttle ramping, and a corner speed limit) and added DAgger : when the AI makes a mistake, we rewind, take over, and drive it properly, and those corrections become new training data. Driving at signs instead of lanes. The network learned a shortcut: steer toward the big "HORIZON" signs rather than follow the lane markings. Crash run-ups in our recordings had taught it that. We cut them from the data automatically. - Lack of Data. We trained all of our dataset during the hackathon, which accumulated up to around 3 hours of driving on one race/map. The model's ability to generalize is poor, but we did try testing it on races it had never seen before, and it was able to steer around some tight corners and perform decently on straights.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: The wheel actually moves. A neural network's steering decision ends up as a real Thrustmaster TMX turning by itself in front of you, driven by a 100 Hz PD loop with static-friction compensation. Getting motor tracking error from 134° down to 9° by throttling commands to the wheel was the moment the whole thing clicked. A real end-to-end pipeline in a weekend: screen capture → telemetry sync → recording → automatic data cleaning → PilotNet-style training → inference over Ethernet → vJoy → Forza → physical wheel → human takeover → DAgger corrections back into training. The human is always in charge. Grab the wheel, tap a pedal, or press a button, and control is yours within a fraction of a second, and every disengagement is logged with its cause. Stale frames, telemetry, or network? The AI backs off on its own. Honest data engineering. We measured the screen running 66 ms behind telemetry by matching gear changes and built automatic crash/rewind/pause detection with adaptive buffers so the model stops learning from our mistakes. A model that beats its baselines on day one. Our first real GPU run cut held-out steering error well below both the always-zero and training-mean baselines, with a live HUD showing the AI's intended path over the game view.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Hot laps don't teach recovery. We recorded fast, clean laps, so the model never saw what to do after drifting off the line. DAgger (rewind, take over, drive it properly, retrain) was the fix, and it reframed the whole project: the dataset is the product. Speed belongs in the model. Late-fusing telemetry into PilotNet made a real difference: the same corner needs different steering and braking at 80 km/h than at 200 km/h. Keep two machines honest. A clean contract between the inference laptop and the game/wheel PC, plus per-failure logging, saved us hours of guessing over an Ethernet cable. In machine learning, the first 99% comes quickly, and the last 1% takes all the work. It was difficult to optimize our inputs and weights through trial and error given the tight time constraints to retrain the model.

sections.heading: What's next for Apex FSD
sections.text: Interactive Voice for Driving Agent . You can command it to drive faster or slower or turn more aggressively in real time as it dampens or strengthens the inference controls inputs. - More advanced inputs . Right now, the model is only trained with the speed and wheel input for every frame. We haven't tried giving it more inputs, like the wheel turning acceleration or feeding it the speed for the past 5 frames, giving it more context. Take it out of the game. The whole stack is already camera-in, steering-angle-out. The next step is swapping Forza's screen capture for a dash cam and the game's telemetry for a car's OBD-II speed, then running the model in shadow mode on real roads: it predicts, the human drives, and we measure the gap. Same recorder, same DAgger loop, real data. From shadow to assist. Once shadow-mode predictions agree with a human driver, the same force-feedback controller that turns the TMX can become a gentle steering nudge, with the same grab-to-take-over logic we already have. Better model, more data. Fix the right-turn underestimation we saw in the baseline, add training-time mirroring, weight steering loss properly, and record on more than one circuit so we're evaluating on routes the model has never seen. Longer horizon. Lane changes, overtaking, and navigation inputs, then a reinforcement learning layer on top of the imitation baseline.

title: Chess without Borders
tagline: Chess is soooo boring and outdated. Introducing Chess Without Borders, a new way to visualize space and strategic game play. Step into a world of non-euclidean space and learn a whole new way to play

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Chess is built around simple spatial rules: rooks move straight, bishops move diagonally, and positioning determines strategy. We wanted to ask a weird question: what happens if the pieces stay the same, but space itself changes? Inspired by non-Euclidean geometry and Escher-like impossible spaces, we created Chess Without Borders to turn abstract mathematical ideas into something players can actually interact with. Instead of explaining curved space through equations, we wanted players to experience it through a game they already understand.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Chess where you can warp the board itself. Players move familiar chess pieces across Euclidean and non-Euclidean space. Pieces keep their fundamental movement rules, but their paths depend on the geometry around them. A rook still travels "straight," for example, but in curved space that means following a geodesic. Players can manipulate the board's geometry, causing attack paths, distances, and strategies to change in real time. This makes warping space part of both offense and defense.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Language: TypeScript Frontend: HTML + CSS + vanilla TypeScript 3D graphics: Three.js for the board, pieces, camera controls, and tile selection Build/dev tooling: Vite 8 Backend: Node.js 24+ Multiplayer: WebSockets, using the ws library Game logic: Custom TypeScript engine shared between browser and server

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Our biggest challenge was separating warping space from simply teleporting pieces or visually bending a normal chessboard. We had to think carefully about what "straight," "adjacent," and "distance" actually mean when the underlying geometry changes. We also needed the game to remain understandable: making space weird is easy; making weird space strategic and intuitive is much harder. Another challenge was keeping the mathematical model and the visuals synchronized so that what players see accurately represents the moves they can make.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're especially proud that non-Euclidean geometry isn't just a visual effect in Chess Without Borders, it's a core game mechanic. The player can directly interact with geometry and immediately see the consequences on the game. Familiar chess pieces provide an intuitive reference point, making complicated spatial ideas much easier to understand. We're also proud of creating gameplay where a player can look at a familiar chess position, warp the space, and suddenly discover an entirely different strategy.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that changing geometry doesn't require changing the fundamental rules of a system. A rook can always move straight, the interesting question is what does "straight" mean in this universe? Building Chess 2 also taught us about geodesics, curved spaces, coordinate transformations, and the challenge of representing non-Euclidean mathematics on a flat screen. Most importantly, we learned that visualization and interaction can make difficult mathematical concepts much more intuitive.

sections.heading: What's next for Chess 2
sections.text: We have several ideas for expanding Chess 2 beyond our current prototype: Chess Bot: Build an automated opponent capable of understanding and strategizing around warped space, not just traditional chess moves. More Polished UI & Customization: Improve animations and visual feedback, with changeable backgrounds and board themes. Spatial Incentives: Add special regions that reward players for exploring the warped board, such as granting additional warps/geometry shifts when a piece reaches certain locations. More Geometries: Introduce spherical geometry and other non-Euclidean spaces with different movement behavior. Ultimately, we want Chess 2 to evolve from chess played in warped space into a game where controlling space itself becomes part of the strategy.

title: Common Ground
tagline: For park-goers to reach park planners and make better parks together. Ever been to a park meeting? filled in a park survey? Exactly. At least this is cool.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: You ever been to a park board meeting? Yeah me neither. This let's green space planners get precise feedback and metrics to figure out what residents want instead of whoever shows up at 3pm on a Tuesday. Don't want to make a design? that's fair, cast vote for your favourite design that other passionate people have created.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Design a real park in 3D. The demo is Jonathan Rogers Park in Mount Pleasant, built from real 1 m lidar elevation, the city's tree inventory, the community garden, and the streets, sidewalks and bus stops around it. Place stuff: benches, native trees (bigleaf maple, Garry oak, western red cedar), playgrounds, ponds, paths and gardens. You can also terraform the ground. Need help? Just describe it. Type "shady play area, loop path, dog run" and Gemini turns it into a layout. Live budget and rules. Cost, tree canopy, hard surface, earthworks and path slopes (for accessibility) update as you build. Vote and review. Upvote or downvote designs with reasons, leave comments on a single bench ("move this"), or walk through the park at eye height. Planners get the good stuff: heatmaps of where people put things, vote reasons, an AI summary of the main themes, and exports to CSV, GeoJSON and DXF.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: How we built it React and three.js (React Three Fiber) for the 3D editor, with the BC Design System for the UI. A TypeScript API on Hono, with Postgres through Drizzle. Locally that's pglite. Terrain from NRCan HRDEM. We search their catalogue and read only the bytes we need fromGeoTIFFs, then project everything into a local metre grid. Site data from Vancouver Open Data, bus stops from TransLink GTFS, and some outlines from OpenStreetMap. Gemini for "Describe it" and the planner summary. A layout solver that picks spots for each item based on how steep the ground is, routes paths with A*, and scatters trees. 3D models are CC0 from Kenney and Quaternius

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: UI/UX pain Map projections. Lining up lidar, city data and OSM in one coordinate system took way longer than it should have. Getting Gemini's structured JSON output to cooperate, and handling rate limits. 3D performance on phones. 3D jank in general.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: It runs on real terrain and real city data It can works completely offline, AI included, thanks to a fairly simple fallback 3D stuff is cool

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Dealing with lidar/satellite/map data 3D Jank How much of a city's data is open if you go looking for it AI is way more useful when it fills in a structured form than when you let it freestyle

title: Cubic
tagline: Cubic is a two-player co-op game where one player walks the outside of a cube and the other is trapped inside, and you solve puzzles together by talking each other through the walls.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We play a lot of "friendslop" co-op games together and wanted to make our own, one where communication (or miscommunication) between two friends is the whole point.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Two players share one cube. One walks the outside, the other is trapped inside, where everything is dark and mirrored. You can't see each other's screens, so you talk through the walls: read codes, count objects, guide each other across invisible paths and pass items to solve all six faces. Solo players get an AI partner.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: TypeScript monorepo: shared game logic, server and client. Node.js + Socket.io: Game state, lobbies, chat, reconnects. Phaser 4 + Vite: pixel-art rendering, keyboard, gamepad and touch. WebRTC: voice chat that gets quieter the further apart you are on the cube. Gemini + ElevenLabs: personality and voice for the solo AI partner. Vercel + Render: hosting.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Getting the 3D cube physics right was tough.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of

sections.heading: What we learned

sections.heading: What's next for Cubic

title: Deceipt
tagline: The better alternative for physical receipts

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every year, 300 billion paper receipts are printed worldwide — and two out of three go straight into the trash. Nobody keeps them. They fade in your wallet, they pile up in junk drawers, and the one time you actually need one — a return, a warranty claim — it's gone or unreadable. Meanwhile that paper trail costs an estimated 3.3 million trees a year in the US alone, plus billions of gallons of water, all for slips of thermal paper nobody asked for. Deceipt started from that frustration: the receipt you can actually find.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Deceipt is a paperless receipt web app. The site opens with an interactive game, "Your Paper Trail" — count your weekly receipts, dodge them in a 20-second arcade round, then watch your yearly pile stretch out in front of you in metres. Then it shows the alternative: digital receipts that are searchable, expense-ready, and never fade. We also built a working in-browser demo of the app itself — dashboard, receipt verification, warranty tracking — so you can feel what "no paper" is like. Live at www.deceipt.tech , fully playable on mobile.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Designed and built with Figma Make (React + TypeScript + Vite), deployed as a static site on GitHub Pages with a custom domain ( www.deceipt.tech ) via Cloudflare DNS. The game is canvas-based with keyboard and touch controls; the demo app is a fully interactive prototype with receipt detail views, export-to-text, and warranty tracking.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The morning of demo day we discovered the landing page didn't render at all on mobile — phones only saw the dashboard shell. We traced it to the responsive branch rendering the wrong view and shipped a fix before judging. We also kept every environmental stat honest, with sourced caveats on each figure, instead of inflating numbers for effect.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A complete working experience in 36 hours: a playable game, a personalized environmental reveal, a fully interactive app demo, and a custom domain live with HTTPS — tested on desktop and mobile.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: How much craft goes into a landing page that has to hook someone in 60 seconds, how to debug responsive rendering under deadline pressure, and that tight constraints (a static site, no backend) force creative in-browser interactivity.

sections.heading: What's next for Deceipt
sections.text: Real receipt ingestion (email forwarding and retailer integrations), OCR for paper stragglers, and the privacy story: on-device-first receipt data that's never sold or used for marketing.

title: Doggin' Around
tagline: Hate how a comic ended? Upload it and we turn its panels into a 3D world you can walk into. Step inside as any character and rewrite the ending yourself.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Everyone has read a comic and wished it ended differently. We wanted to let you step inside the panel and change it. Huawei's challenge provided photographs of two dogs, and the white dog wearing sunglasses, flowers, and a blue bow became the hero of our comic, Storm Night : locked out as a storm rolls in, he's the only one who knows where the spare key is buried. Read it as drawn and the night ends badly. Step into the first panel, play it in 3D, and the comic redraws itself with a new ending. For that to work, the comic's hero needed a little life: a dog that could look around, respond to us, do tricks, and bring a ball back. That meant solving several problems together. A comic page has to be read: who is in it, where one scene ends and the next begins, and which panel becomes a place you can walk into. And the photo showed the dog's personality, but it did not show its complete body or explain how it should move. We needed to reconstruct its appearance, give it an underlying skeleton, and make those pieces work together. This became Doggin' Around , a comic you can walk into, built on image-to-3D research running in the browser. Along the way, we explored two different modelling approaches for its characters: generating a rig and detailed appearance separately, and fitting an anatomical dog model before optimizing its appearance.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Doggin' Around turns a comic page into a world you can step into, and lets what you do there change how the story ends. Read the comic. Upload the page and the pipeline goes to work: it detects the characters, separates the page into its scenes, lifts the hero out of his panel, and builds him from every side into a rigged 3D character. Step into the panel. The dog leaps into panel 1, and the panel dissolves into a first-person 3D world built from that scene, in the rain, with the dog at your side. Change the ending. Get him to dig up the buried key, unlock the cabin, gather firewood and light the fire. Back on the page, the panels after the one you played redraw into a happier ending. Talk to it. Hold F and say "Biscuit, sit!" Inside the comic, your companion is fully interactive: Give it something to do. Huawei's white dog has 29 actions, including sitting, running, digging, shaking hands, high fives, backflips, and Gangnam-style dancing. Play fetch. Throw a ball and the dog turns toward it, walks or runs after it, slows down, reaches toward the ball, picks it up, and carries it home. Catch its attention. The dogs glance around naturally and briefly follow your cursor. Their head movement continues smoothly through animation changes. Inspect how it works. Switch between the detailed Gaussian appearance, the underlying mesh, and the skeleton. Adjust animation speed and rendering density, pause a pose, or compare the source photographs. Try compatible models. Import an animated GLB with a supported skeleton and animation structure. Huawei also provided the seated Tricolor dog photograph. Our local research demo brings that second dog to life with 12 actions. Its licensed research assets are excluded from public production builds. Model generation currently happens offline. The browser loads the prepared assets and handles rendering, animation, and interaction.

sections.heading: From photos to interactive 3D dogs
sections.text: Huawei white dog Before: Huawei's original cropped photograph After: our full-body Gaussian dog Huawei Tricolor dog Before: the original seated photograph After: our standing Gaussian reconstruction

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: From comic page to playable world The pipeline reads the page the way you would: it detects the characters, separates the page into its scenes, and lifts the hero out of his panel, then builds him from every side into a rigged 3D character. Storm Night 's pages and panels were painted with Gemini from our own scene plates and the dog's reference, so every panel is drawn from a scene we can also build in 3D. For the panel you step into, World Labs' Marble turns that scene into a walkable Gaussian-splat world with a collision mesh. Rapier handles the physics, and Spark renders the world, the dog, and the first-person hands together. Gemini also paints the in-between frames that dissolve the panel into the live 3D view. Voice commands use ElevenLabs' realtime speech-to-text. The characters Both dogs use 3D Gaussian Splatting for their detailed appearance. Think of a Gaussian as a tiny, soft-edged 3D shape with its own color, size, and transparency. Tens of thousands of these shapes combine to represent the dog's coat and facial details. The two dogs use different structures to make those shapes move. Huawei white dog Huawei Tricolor dog Body and skeleton AniGen-generated model with 41 joints BITE-fitted D-SMAL model with 35 joints Detailed appearance 50,000 selected TripoSplat Gaussians 37,525 Gaussians from our reconstruction pipeline Animation connection Gaussians follow the skeleton Gaussians follow the deforming mesh The math behind the dogs Several mathematical models connect the photographs, 3D bodies, fur, and animation: 3D Gaussian Splatting represents the coat with soft 3D ellipsoids. Each Gaussian uses a center, covariance, color, and opacity. The renderer projects them to the screen and blends them from front to back. G(x) = alpha * exp(-0.5 * (x - mean)^T * covariance^-1 * (x - mean)) Linear blend skinning moves the white dog's Gaussians with its skeleton. Each Gaussian receives up to four joint influences whose weights add to one. new position = sum(weight[j] * joint transform[j] * position) BITE and D-SMAL fitting describe the Tricolor dog through adjustable shape, limb, pose, scale, translation, and vertex-offset parameters. This lets us change the seated fit into a standing dog while preserving its estimated anatomy. vertices = scale * alignment * SMAL(shape, limbs, pose, offsets) + translation Surface-bound deformation attaches each Tricolor Gaussian to its ten nearest mesh faces. Closer faces receive more influence through normalized inverse-distance weights. weight[k] = (1 / max(distance[k], 1e-8)) / sum(1 / max(distance, 1e-8)) Image reconstruction loss teaches the rendered dog to match the reference views. We combine pixel error with structural similarity, then add geometric penalties that keep the mesh and Gaussians stable. photo loss = 0.8 * L1 + 0.2 * (1 - SSIM) Quintic easing smooths pose changes, head glances, takeoffs, and landings. Its velocity and acceleration reach zero at both ends, which prevents visible snapping. h(t) = 6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3 Approach 1: Build the Huawei dog's rig and appearance separately We began by generating a full-body reference from Huawei's cropped portrait, preserving the recognizable face and accessories while making the hidden legs and back plausible. We used AniGen to generate a textured model and skeleton. We then used TripoSplat to generate a more detailed Gaussian appearance from the reference. Our own binding code aligned the two outputs and connected the Gaussians to the skeleton. We gave the glasses, flowers, head covering, and bow appropriate head or neck attachments so they followed the dog's movement. After comparing several densities, we selected 50,000 splats, prioritizing the face and accessories. Approach 2: Fit Huawei's Tricolor dog anatomy, then optimize its appearance For Huawei's second dog, we started with its seated photograph and used BITE to estimate its body shape and pose through D-SMAL, an adjustable 3D dog model. We converted that fitted body into

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: A panel has to become a place. A comic panel is one drawn moment. We had to build a world from the same scene, line its opening view up with the panel closely enough to dissolve one into the other, and keep the story's cause and effect (the buried key, the cold cabin) playable. One photograph leaves a lot unseen. Our first direct reconstruction of Huawei's cropped portrait produced an eight-joint rig. Creating a full-body reference gave the model enough information to produce a much more useful 41-joint skeleton. The hidden anatomy remains a plausible reconstruction. A detailed appearance still needs a movement system. Generated Gaussians arrive as a static model. We had to align them with an animatable structure and keep the fur, face, and accessories attached during movement. Small motion errors were immediately noticeable. Sliding paws, a floating ball, or a head snapping back to one angle made the dog feel less convincing. We added contact corrections, matched travel speed to gait, connected fetch to the mouth position, and preserved gaze through action changes. Jump also needed a deliberate sequence: front paws lift first, all four paws become airborne, then the front paws land before the hind paws. More refinement did not always preserve the dog. The full DGE edit softened Tricolor's tan markings and eye detail. We kept the original face and body, retained the improved tail geometry, and restored its dark fur color. Research tools needed substantial integration work. We resolved Python, CUDA, and library compatibility issues, checked coordinate systems, and compared Python deformation with the browser implementation. We also had to keep detailed rendering fast enough for live interaction.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We built a comic you can step into and rewrite, and two working modelling pipelines for its characters, connected to the same interactive playground. Huawei's white dog preserves its distinctive accessories across 29 actions. Huawei's Tricolor dog demonstrates our implementation of SMAL-pets' core reconstruction methods, with full mesh animation and detailed Gaussian appearance. Both selected models reached 60 FPS in Chrome at 1440 × 960 on our test Mac . We verified animation transitions, paw contact, gaze, pause behavior, fetch, model switching, and density changes through numerical checks and browser tests. The Tricolor GPU run also stayed within our budget, with a conservative compute and storage estimate of US$2.96 against a US$10 limit. Most of all, we are proud of the small details: the panel dissolving into the world you step into, the ending redrawing itself, the dog noticing the cursor, planting its paws, reaching down for the ball, and smoothly returning to its next action.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned how much work sits between an image-to-3D result and an interactive character. Appearance, anatomy, animation, and behavior each need attention, and their connections matter just as much. We also learned how to turn a research method into a working application. That involved implementing mathematical ideas, adapting older code, checking results numerically, and making deliberate choices when generated outputs changed the dog's identity. Visual inspection and automated tests complemented each other. Tests caught unstable transitions and incorrect transforms. Watching the dogs from different angles caught details that numbers alone could miss. The most useful lesson was to evaluate the whole experience. A seamless step into the panel, a recognizable face, believable paw contact, and a smooth head turn all contribute to whether the story feels like one you are inside.

sections.heading: What's next for Doggin' Around
sections.text: We want to make the whole process live, so someone can upload any comic, choose the panel whose ending they want to change, and play it, with its characters built through a guided workflow. Our next priorities are: Run character detection, scene separation, and world generation live for any uploaded comic. Improve reconstruction across more breeds, body shapes, and poses. Preserve distinctive markings and fine coat detail more consistently. Grow voice control from keyword commands into natural-language direction. Expand interaction with toys and environments through physics and collision handling. Reduce loading time and improve performance on mobile devices. Make a shareable generation workflow using assets and models with suitable redistribution rights. Longer term, we want any comic to become a story people can step into and rewrite, and these dogs to become characters people can bring into their own games, stories, and virtual spaces.

title: DoubleTake
tagline: You never have to go alone to a date again! Double Take allows you to partner up with your friend and find a match in a group setting in hopes of forming friendships or potentially something more!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Our inspiration came straight from the room here at SFU! A teammate in our tram is single, and when a dating event was announced here at the hackathon, our teammate felt super nervous and anxious about the thought of going alone. As we were hyping them up, we joked about how much easier and less terrifying it would be if we could all just go together as a squad to brave the singles scene or better yet, find someone as a team. That sparked the whole idea: why not build a platform that matches people based on shared "vibes" and duos, making dating and meeting new people fun, social, and way less intimidating?

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: DoubleTake is a dating platform that allows you to partner up with your best friend and find a match with another pair. It solves the interview-like process of regular dating apps which focuses more on individual prospects and commonly used (dry) pickup lines. It's safer, less pressure, and a lot more fun, because your best friend comes too. Key Features include : Duo - Create a single profile for you and your friend, finding a shared interest and making Discovery Feed - Find and match your next double date through a single swipe. Search - Search based on common filter types and hobbies another pair may have as well as potential vibes based on TiDB's Algorithm . Matchs - Every duo you like matches you back and you enter the messaging groupchat Your Duo - Your Duo profile with your friend

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Frontend (Jill) : Jill used react for the pages which uses hooks to load the data of the user and to know who the current user is. She created an api.js that either asks the fake back end in mocks or sends the real request through the httpClient.js into a Spring boot API. Components were used as reusable blocks that pages were assembled from and the context folder is shared the the current duo and user on every screen. Jill used tailwind for the CSS with the assistance of Claude Code to ideate and sort out technical bugs and structural plans of the project. Database/Backend (Valerie) : Valerie built some of the backend infrastructure using Java Spring Boot, connecting it directly to a cloud TiDB database to manage our application data and user profiles. She engineered the backend architecture, handled the database persistence layer, and integrated the vector search features so the app could process and match data smoothly. Backend (Annie) : I built part of the backend infrastructure and database architecture using Java Spring Boot and TiDB. I developed the main application logic, engineering the REST controllers and service layers to handle user workflows, while designing, adding, and structuring the database tables to securely persist our application data.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Frontend (Jill): Tailwind's long class lists were frustrating, but Jill saw its value for building quickly without separate CSS files. Her biggest challenge was building a mock API that matched exactly what the real backend would return, including data shapes and error codes. She solved it by working backwards from each screen to identify the functions needed, creating one mock function per endpoint from the team's API contract, and adding a single setting to switch between mock and real data. Database/Backend (Valerie) : Integrating the vector search functionality was a major hurdle, setting up the AI embedding pipeline to translate plain-English descriptions into accurate vector queries for TiDB required careful handling. We also had to troubleshoot cloud deployment networking, resolving CORS blocking between our local frontend and our Render backend. Backend (Annie) : One of our biggest hurdles was successfully bridging the gap between our frontend and backend. Connecting the client-side interface to the live API endpoints required troubleshooting network routing, handling data mapping discrepancies, and ironing out communication bugs so the frontend could seamlessly send and receive data from the server.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Frontend (Jill): Bringing the entire user experience to life by building a sleek, responsive interface that seamlessly translates complex user interactions and smooth navigation into an intuitive, polished client-side app. Database\Backend (Valerie): Architecting the backend services and integrating the cutting-edge AI vector-embedding pipeline (⁠AiEmbeddingService.java⁠) that allows our app to perform intelligent, plain-text semantic "vibe matching" directly inside our cloud database. Database\ Backend (Annie): Engineering the core backend infrastructure, building out robust REST controllers, managing the service layer logic, and structuring and adding the relational database tables to ensure rock-solid data flow and persistence.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Frontend (Jill) : Jill earned how React projects are structured, from reusable components and routing to sharing state with context, and how Tailwind integrates through Vite. Jill practiced hooks, promises and API calls, and adopted better JavaScript practices like centralizing API calls, handling loading and error states, and documenting functions. Database/Backend (Valerie) : Valerie learned that when we set our minds to a goal, we can pick up entirely new technologies and build complex full-stack features in a remarkably short amount of time. Even though I had no prior experience with a lot of this tech stack before starting, this project showed me how fast we can learn, prototype, and ship a fully functional, AI-powered application from scratch. Backend (Annie) : I learned how rapidly we can design, build, and deploy a robust backend system from scratch when diving into new technologies. This project taught me the ins and outs of structuring scalable Java architectures, managing database schemas, and successfully integrating client-server communication under a tight timeframe.

sections.heading: What's next for DoubleTake
sections.text: DoubleTake is in it's earliest stages of development where many possibilities and scopes can be included to better improve the application such as : Customization and filters of potential prospects Your personal profile Messaging feature -Photo Intergration

title: Etika
tagline: etika tells new BC sole proprietors which registrations, taxes and hiring rules apply to them. Three AI agents check official sources, cite every claim, give next steps. Rules decide, AI explains.

sections.text: Etika: Legal Team, Decoded. A friend spent a whole weekend trying to figure out if her candle business needed to register for PST. Four government sites, a Reddit thread, and a phone call later, the answer was "not yet, but close." Compliance info isn't missing, it's fragmented. BizPaL lists permits that may apply, Ownr just registers a name, and an accountant only knows what you tell them. Nobody says what applies to you , why, and what to do next, and the thresholds move underneath you the whole time. So we built Etika.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Etika is a compliance navigator for new Vancouver sole proprietors. You answer a few questions and confirm the facts Etika understood. Three specialist AI agents (Registration, Tax, and Employer, each with its own persona) then check your situation against official government sources. You get a readiness score, plain-English explanations with the official government source behind each one, and a Now/Next/Later plan where every item links to the real form. Mention a change in chat, like "I'm hiring next month," and Etika proposes a fact update. Confirm it and the assessment re-runs live: the employer obligations (WorkSafeBC, CRA payroll account, minimum wage, pay statements, payroll records) move from Later to Now, and the score updates with them.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pydantic v2 Database: TiDB Cloud, holding vectors and relational data in one store AI: Gemini Flash for intake parsing, agent explanations and chat; gemini-embedding-001 for retrieval Frontend: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind The core rule is code decides, Gemini explains. Every profile fact is stored as a value plus a confirmed flag, and an unknown fact is never treated as "no." Skip a question and the requirement becomes "Needs your input," not a guess. A deterministic engine matches confirmed facts against a reviewed registry of requirements, each tagged now, trigger or recommendation, with dependencies (business number before GST or payroll). Tax calculators run the real tests: PST's rolling 12-month $10,000 small-seller line plus the no-premises condition, GST's $30,000 threshold, and a straight-line projection of when you'll cross each one. The score and the order of next steps come from the same code, never from the model. The knowledge base is ours. We collected official BC Registries, CRA, WorkSafeBC, BC Laws and City of Vancouver pages by hand, split them by legal section, embedded them, and stored them in TiDB with metadata for authority, jurisdiction, requirement and retrieval date. Every chunk has a review status, and only approved chunks can be retrieved. Retrieval is filtered by requirement and jurisdiction, and returns "insufficient evidence" instead of a weak match. Each agent owns one area of the registry, receives only the evidence retrieved for its requirements, and returns structured findings with citations. We then validate every citation against what was actually retrieved in that run and drop anything that wasn't. The walk-through screen shows each agent's progress live.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: The law was harder than the code. PST's exemption depends on a rolling window, not a calendar year, so one good month can flip your status, and it also depends on whether you have established premises, which market sales make ambiguous. We flag those cases as gray areas for a professional instead of resolving them. Building the knowledge base from scratch was the other big job. The hardest part wasn't collecting pages, it was narrowing each agent enough that it could only answer from its evidence, so Gemini never filled a gap with something that sounded right but wasn't sourced. Three parallel agents also blew through Gemini's rate limit fast. We rebuilt the pipeline so code prefetches all evidence up front and each agent makes exactly one call, cutting Gemini usage from 8 to 15 requests per assessment down to 3.

sections.heading: What we're proud of
sections.text: The RAG pipeline: we built the whole source-to-citation process ourselves, from scraping and reviewing official sources to chunking, embedding, and gating retrieval so an agent can only cite evidence it actually pulled in that run. Because status comes from code, the same facts always produce the same score, and the model can't talk its way into a different answer. And the hiring moment, one sentence in chat and several legal obligations switching on live, is the best 10 seconds of the demo.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: Pre-filled government forms generated from the saved profile, auto-generated policy documents (privacy, refund, workplace), a renewal and deadline calendar, and expansion beyond Vancouver sole proprietors to other BC cities and business structures.

title: HyperSpace
tagline: Explore knowledge by bending space. Hyperspace maps 2,475 Wikipedia topics onto a hyperbolic disk: what you focus on grows, the rest stays in view. Search by meaning, grow new branches with AI.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Big knowledge collections are hard to explore. Lists hide how ideas connect, and mind maps turn into hairballs once they grow past a few hundred nodes. We wanted exploring thousands of connected concepts to feel like flying through a space instead of scrolling a page. Hyperbolic geometry fits this well. In hyperbolic space the amount of room grows exponentially with distance from the center, just as a tree's number of nodes grows with depth. So the whole tree fits in one view: whatever you focus on is large and readable, and everything else stays visible but compressed toward the edge.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Hyperspace turns 2,475 Wikipedia topics about artificial intelligence into a universe you explore on a Poincaré disk . Click to recenter. Click any topic and the whole map transforms around it, so it glides to the center while its neighbors spread out and distant branches shrink toward the rim. You never lose context. Search by meaning. Type a topic or a question. TiDB combines full-text and vector search, and the map flies to the best match, highlighting related topics along the way. Grow new branches. Hit Expand on any topic. Hyperspace pulls related pages from Wikipedia, Gemini picks and cleans up the best ones, and they grow out of the map as new branches. Results are cached so repeat expansions are instant. Source-backed. Every topic shows its Wikipedia summary and a link to the article. Euclid toggle. Flip to a flat radial tree of the same data, and you can see why the geometry matters: by depth 3 the flat rim runs out of room. Presentation and demo modes. Press P for a clean full-screen view. Demo mode serves cached search and expand results, so the core experience keeps working without network access.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Data pipeline (Node.js) We crawl Wikipedia's category graph breadth-first from Category:Artificial intelligence , grafting in key branches (Machine learning, Computer vision, Natural language processing, Robotics). Breadth-first order means each page keeps its shallowest parent, which also breaks the cycles in Wikipedia's category graph. We filter out maintenance categories, lists, biographies, companies, media and news events, fold articles into their same-named categories, and use article length as a stand-in for importance when pruning. The result is a clean tree: 249 categories and 2,226 articles, up to 4 levels deep, each with a short intro and a source link. TiDB Cloud One nodes table holds each topic with its root-to-node path as JSON, a full-text index on title and summary, and a VECTOR(1024) column with a cosine vector index . Embeddings are computed inside TiDB with its built-in EMBED_TEXT model. Each topic is embedded with its breadcrumb (e.g. Attention (Machine learning > Deep learning) ) so short or ambiguous titles keep their meaning. Search runs a hybrid query that merges full-text hits with vector-similarity hits, with a boost for exact title matches. An expansions table caches every Expand result, keyed by topic and dataset version. Gemini Expand collects candidate pages from Wikipedia (category members or search results), then asks Gemini to choose the 5–8 best children, write 1–2 sentence summaries, and return strict JSON that we validate before it touches the map. Frontend (Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind) The disk is rendered with d3-hypertree . Recentering uses a Möbius transformation, the distance-preserving motions of the disk: $$T_a(z) = \frac{z - a}{1 - \bar{a}\,z}$$ This sends the clicked point \(a\) to the center, and edges are drawn as geodesic arcs. We wrote our own label picker (scored by subtree weight and closeness to the focus, with overlap rejection), because the library's built-in culling only ever labeled the root. To stay fast, we render a pruned set of about 470 nodes and graft new nodes into the live tree as you navigate or expand, instead of rebuilding it.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Wikipedia is a graph, not a tree. Categories have cycles, duplicates and many people, companies and films filed under "AI". Turning that into a clean hierarchy took many rounds of filters. Performance. Rebuilding the hyperbolic layout on every click was too slow, so we wrote an in-place graft that adds nodes to the live tree without starting over. Labels. The library's label culling showed only one label, so we replaced it with our own collision-aware picker. Tooling surprises. One of the visualization library's npm dependencies shipped without its build output, so we vendored a working bundle. Balancing hybrid search. Full-text and vector scores live on very different scales, and merging them so keyword hits don't drown out meaning took careful tuning.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A smooth, genuinely non-Euclidean interface where clicking any distant topic glides it to the center. The side-by-side Euclid toggle, which shows in one click why hyperbolic space is the right fit for big hierarchies. A real data pipeline: thousands of curated, source-linked Wikipedia topics, embedded and searchable in TiDB. A demo that keeps working with cached data when the Wi-Fi doesn't.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Hyperbolic geometry in practice: Poincaré disk coordinates, Möbius transformations and geodesics. How to run full-text and vector search side by side in one database, and why combining their scores is harder than it looks. How to get dependable, structured JSON from an LLM and treat it as a helper inside a pipeline rather than a black box. How much cleanup real-world data needs before it looks simple.

sections.heading: What's next for Hyperspace
sections.text: Smarter hybrid ranking (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion) and search that explains why a result matched. Multi-level Expand, so newly grown branches can keep growing. More universes beyond AI: any Wikipedia category, or your own notes and documents. Collaborative exploration: shared trails and bookmarks through the disk.

title: Ink Habitat
tagline: Draw your creature and watch it come to life!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We were inspired by the farm-related games we've played before. It is a pity that we couldn't create our own creatures because there were some restrictions on the creatures in the game shops – sometimes, they didn't look the way we wanted, and it was boring. So, we asked ourselves why not draw our own creatures. At first, we designed the Grasslands island to be the base world of our game and started drawing our creatures. But after some time we understood that it is a bit dull when you only draw your creatures and watch how they move. And then, we invented the friend system and battles between friends – so that you could go to your friend's farm and battle with them and get one of their creatures.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Ink Habitat is a creature farm where you can draw your creatures, give them names and speech, assign them unique behaviour and voices with AI(Gemini and ElevenLabs), and bring them to life in a virtual environment. You will get an opportunity to explore different landscapes such as Grassland, Desert, and Ocean, visit your friends' farms, and fight them in creature team battles using three creatures. Each battle includes random buff cards that may be helpful or detrimental to your creatures. The winner gets an opportunity to pick one creature from the defeated side. In order to increase the realism of the game, all creatures that took part in the battle must have some rest after it.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We started by sketching the basic island environment and designing our own creatures. We then built the website and developed the different features step by step, including creature creation, farm exploration, friend interactions, and the battle system. We also integrated AI into the project to help bring our hand-drawn creatures to life with animations and attack behaviours, along with voice clips that make each creature feel more unique. We used GitHub to manage our code and collaborate throughout development.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The most difficult part was designing the battle mechanics. It was necessary to consider very thoroughly how the battles were to be conducted, who would be the winner and how to make sure that the result will be surprising but at the same time fair. After adding random buff cards to our game, the process of balancing became even more challenging. It was necessary to consider how one card or another would affect the player’s team of creatures.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Neither of us had experience in game-making before, so creating Ink Habitat became quite a challenge for both of us. In the beginning, we had an easier task in mind that we were more familiar with. But we have chosen to leave our comfort zone and create something unique and innovative. What we are really proud of is that we managed to create an interactive world of creatures with custom-made drawings, different locations, social interactions, and battles. What is even more important, we did not choose the easy way out.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: During the hackathon, we acquired some skills in working with GitHub in terms of collaboration, making changes in the code and integrating various parts of the project. Also, we've understood how we could use AI to our advantage and make our creatures interactive without creating all the animations manually. Moreover, we've realized that game development is not only about developing the concept. Sometimes even something simple may turn out to be quite complex.

sections.heading: What's next for Ink Habitat
sections.text: In the future, we plan to make our creatures more interactive, as opposed to just clicking on them to see how they move. Instead, the players will be able to give food to the creatures, train them, level them up, and establish more bonds with them. In addition, it would be interesting to consider ways to enable the creatures to move from the website to the players' computer screens as their little virtual companions. We would like for our Ink Habitat to be more of a world to live and grow in, rather than a game which people only play.

title: Otter Nonsense
tagline: Otter Nonsense is a casual multiplayer collection game, but the players are all otters!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We were inspired by chill games like WEBFISHING and Sledding Game!

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: It's a game where you dive to collect a variety of trinkets, have meaningful conversations, and buy accessories. Unwind by a campfire, chat with friends or go diving for clams! Chill out and watch the sunrise from the benches by the stream!

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Pushed and pulled frequently, merging changes and waiting for others to finish their work. We used three.js for the main game as well as python for the multiplayer and networking stuff.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: How to integrate AI into our workflow to speed things up and managing an ever-growing and mutating codebase (with 4 people working on it at the same time). We also ran into numerous issues with the 3d animations for the otter characters.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Figuring out multiplayer Simple but robust no-account system Automatic deployment via GitHub Actions The scenery and how beautiful the world looks The trinket collection mechanic

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Network infrastructure Creating a game in Three.js 3D Modelling (Blender)

sections.heading: What's next for Otter Nonsense
sections.text: Improving the performance Adding additional minigames Ability to have multiple servers running and allowing you to join with your friends only Allowing otters to wear other types of accessories or clothing other than hats

title: Phase Escape
tagline: Roll a marble through a hyperbolic maze where the route you take changes which dimension you're in. Tilt a real controller, slip between 4D layers, and outrun the hunters.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Most "non-Euclidean" games use curved space as a visual trick. I wanted the curvature to be the core mechanic. In curved space, walking around a loop and coming back to where you started still turns you: that's called holonomy. We wanted players to feel that with their hands, by tilting a real controller rather than pressing keys. Perspective puzzles in The Witness and Superliminal inspired the 4D side of the game.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Phase Escape is a chase through a maze built on the hyperbolic plane, a space that curves the opposite way to a sphere. It's drawn in the Poincaré disk, where rooms crowd toward the edge because space grows exponentially. The maze also has a fourth dimension: five layers, each with its own colour. Doors only open in their own colour, shards can only be collected in theirs, and hunters can only see and hurt you when you share their colour. You change layer by twisting the controller like a dial. You can also let space itself do it: roll once around a pillar and you come back one colour over. The four rooms around a pillar form a square with 72° corners instead of 90°, so a lap turns you 360° + 72°, which is exactly one of the five layers. One level jams twisting entirely, and loops are the only way through. The tesseract in the corner is your view into 4D. Rifts block some passages, with a four-dimensional plank floating over each one. All you see is the plank's smeared shadow until you rotate your view through 4D, and then it lies flat and becomes a bridge. There are 9 levels, plus tutorial tips, high scores, and music where every layer has its own chord.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Game: TypeScript and Three.js in the browser, packaged as a Windows desktop app with Electron. Geometry: done exactly in the hyperboloid model (3×3 Lorentz matrices in 64-bit floats) and rendered with GPU instancing at 60 FPS. Controller: an ESP32 with a BNO055 orientation sensor on four AA batteries, streaming tilt and rotation at 100 Hz over Bluetooth Low Energy, or over USB. How the code got written: we built it with Claude Code, directing the design, testing every change, and pushing back when something felt wrong to play. Fairness checks: a solver proves every level can be finished, and an autopilot plays every level start to finish with the real physics. In total there are 143 automated tests. Claude code the G.O.A.T.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Coming in without much coding experience. I used Claude code describing exactly what I wanted, reading what it produced, and using tests to catch its mistakes. Making curved-space math fair. Measuring the marble's wobbly path gave inconsistent results, so we carry your orientation room-centre to room-centre instead. That makes every pillar lap exactly 72°. Hardware. The sensor sometimes failed on first start-up until we added a clock-settle delay. Bluetooth on Windows failed silently on slow first searches until we added a "searching…" indicator, a timeout and a retry. My first design was too abstract. Players found tesseract-matching vague, so I rebuilt the game around a chase, with hunters, lives and a timer.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: It works: a real wireless controller drives a game in genuinely curved space at 60 FPS. The geometry is exact, not faked. The 72° per lap comes straight from the math, and the game explains it with a picture. Every level is proven solvable by the computer. Players learn holonomy by doing it, not by reading about it.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: How to run Bluetooth Low Energy on an ESP32 and connect to it from a browser. How hyperbolic geometry works, what holonomy is, and why rotations in 4D happen in planes rather than around axes. How to build software with an AI as a teammate: plan carefully, test everything, and check the output yourself.

sections.heading: What's next for Phase Escape
sections.text: Support standard gamepads, so anyone can play without our custom controller. Publish it properly: host it on GitHub Pages so it runs in any Chrome or Edge browser, and release the desktop app. An endless mode using the level generator, a battery-level readout on the controller, and more levels.

title: Pixel Cat Arena
tagline: -Pixel Cat Arena is a browser cat-battler where you gear up and fight your way through PvE and PvP, and your rarest gear can become a real Solana NFT!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Cats. I like Cats. I also wanted item ownership in a game to mean something more than a database row. Solana gave me a way to let players actually own their rarest gear without breaking the game it lives in. I also like cats.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Pixel Cat Arena is a browser cat-battler: build a cat, gear it up, fight scaling PvE enemies, challenge other players, and trade gear on a fixed-price marketplace. Legendary items can be exported as real Solana devnet NFTs , and the item stays equippable in battle, but in-game selling/listing is permanently disabled once exported, because trading now happens wallet-to-wallet. Whoever holds that wallet can claim the item back into their account.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Pixel Cat Arena is a browser cat-battler: build your cat, gear it up, fight your way through PvE, battle other players, and trade gear on a marketplace. Legendary items can be exported as real Solana devnet NFTs! Still equippable in battle, but once exported you can't sell or list it in-game anymore, since trading moves to the wallet. Whoever ends up holding that wallet can claim the item into their account.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Art :( Also figuring out where the "truth" lives when ownership is split between a database and the blockchain.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Building the whole game solo, and getting a real devnet mint + real wallet-signature claim working end-to-end.

sections.heading: What's next for Pixel Cat Arena
sections.text: Balance updates, new stats, new gear, new cats, new Stuff!

title: PunchCode
tagline: An IDE/game that simulates coding on an IBM 029 Keypunch machine.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The CSSS Historical Track is what inspired us to make this website. When we saw that SFU once had a IBM card-punch machine, we were fascinated by how people used to code this way. So we decided to build our own simulator for others to experience the way coding was back in that time period. The name "PunchCode" was inspired both by the fact that you are literally punching in code to program, and the fact that we included a few LeetCode style problems in our app that let you test your skills. So a combination of punching in code and some inspiration from LeetCode.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: The website simulates and teaches individuals how people used to code with the IBM 029 card-punch machine. They would need to punch the desired Fortran code and then compile it using a stack of punch cards inputted into the machine.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built the web app using NextJS, with TypeScript as our main front-end programming language. On the back-end we used Python with the FastAPI, mainly to compile and run the user's Fortran code.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: We ran into a few challenges during our project. Our first major challenge was figuring out how the IBM 029 card-punch machine worked in real life. We had to spend a few hours doing research as this was a vital part of our project. This was difficult due to the scarcity of reliable info as many sources opposed each other. On top of this we had to learn Fortran because this was the main language people used at the time. Another challenge was finding a solution to make sure the site displays well on varying resolutions, we often ran into bugs in this regard.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud with the level if historical accuracy that we achieved on this project, historical accuracy was one of our mains goals and we wanted to make the experience as authentic as possible. The sound design is something else we are proud of as it adds a nice atmosphere when using the app.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned a lot about punch cards and their use in the past in coding, and especially in regards to how the machines worked. We also learned to code in Fortran.

sections.heading: What's next for PunchCode
sections.text: We could add varying levels of historical accuracy so that user could take on a challenge or have an easier time. For example there could be a mode that includes far more of the problems and manual parts actually needed in real life to use the machine.

title: Rapid Triage
tagline: Real-time patient monitoring for smarter, faster emergency triage.

sections.text: Rapid Triage Real-time wearable triage for mass-casualty incidents — continuously monitoring patients, prioritizing care, and helping responders find who needs them most.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: In a mass-casualty incident, one of the biggest challenges is simple: there may be far more patients than available medical responders. Traditional triage gives responders a snapshot of a patient's condition at one moment in time. But a patient who initially appears stable can deteriorate while responders are helping someone else. With dozens of patients spread across an incident site, continuously reassessing everyone becomes extremely difficult. We wanted to ask: What if every patient could continue being monitored after their initial assessment, even when no medic was standing beside them? That inspired Rapid Triage — a wearable monitoring and response system designed for situations where medical resources are limited. A responder can place a Rapid Triage device on a patient and move on. The wearable continuously collects vital signs and sends them through a local network to our backend. Rapid Triage analyzes those measurements over time, detects concerning trends, calculates patient priority scores, and gives responders a live view of which patients may require attention first. Instead of triage being a one-time decision, Rapid Triage turns it into a continuous process .

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Rapid Triage connects patients, incident commanders, and responders through one coordinated system. Each patient receives an ESP32-based wearable containing multiple sensors for collecting physiological measurements such as heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, and ECG data . The device transmits measurements over a local Wi-Fi network to our backend, where they are timestamped and stored in Tiger Data as time-series data. But individual measurements alone do not tell the whole story. Our Python processing pipeline continuously transforms incoming measurements into clinically relevant monitoring features such as recent averages, changes over time, persistence of abnormal readings, and physiological trends.
